New Quick Print, Agartala, Tripura-1 M: 9436129362/ 9862208628 Tribal Research & Cultural Institute, Government of Tripura January 2015 Rs. 253/- Dedicated to the memory of Maharaj RadhaKisor Manikya Foreword Formerly an ancient kingdom, and now a north-east- erly province of the Indian Union, Tripura has an im- mense treasure of folktales of varying types. Some tales are myths; some tales are, packed with episodes; some tales have a voice of truth and warning. The tales presented here have been selected not to trace any trait of national character, but to examine the quality of life and thoughts of the people of Tripura dur- ing the medieval period, and to point out the persistent preoccupations of the people of Tripura. It is a pleasure to contribute a foreword to Dr. Jagadis Gan-Chaudhuri's book, Folktales of Tripura. In prepar- ing this book, he has made extensive field survey and dexterously utilized most of the published books on folktales of Tripura. He has looked at the tales, not through the coloured glasses of romance, but as a stu- dent of social anthropology. His writing is marked by clear- ness and grasp. ; By putting together a large number of folktales, by translating the tales into English, by annexing a bibliog- raphy, by adding a list of motif index, by furnishing a

rational interpretation to some myths, the author of Folktales of Tripura has added a standard dimension to sociological research in Tripura. He deserves our appre- ciation. (SAILOHNUNA) Director Tribal Research & Cultural Institute Government of Tripura. The folk-tales of the days of animistic belief and subsistence agriculture with its concomitant tears & smiles, fill the pages of this book. These folk-tales, varied in contents & theme, have a rural flavour. These stories tell us much of what Tripura was like in the medieval period. These stories indicate that our literary edifice might have its beginning in the myths & folk-tales; it has grown up from the old animistic simplicity & fantasy to modern humanistic complexity & realism. These stories show that our medieval ancestors were like ourselves, loving as we love, hating as we hate, cheating as we cheat, and that society is a scene of interplay of good & evil forces. These stories reflect the spirit of the age : supernatural view of the world. These stories are beautiful in expression, & lasting in ideas. To the readers living outside Bharat, Tripura is an obscure land, terra incognita; to the readers living outside Tripura, Tripura is merely a name; to the readers living inside Tripura, all the stories are hardly known. Now, they may be interested to see most of the tales collected, compiled, edited & translated in one volume. Some readers may find in these tales a deep sympathy with the flora & fauna of Tripura; with the hills & rivers of lripura; with the rites & rituals of Tripura. They may be wise to find in these tales an element of heritage of

lripura. These stories provide a vocabulary which may be at the disposal of some research scholars. Xl Every care has been taken to render the original version into clear & simple English. Every caution has been taken not to misinterpret any legend, and not to dramatize or romanticize them to a ridiculous degree. However, certain chaotic notions which are likely to confuse the readers have been avoided. Translations, however faithful, cannot give a just impression of the original versions heard from the mouths of the bards, story-tellers, village elders, grand-parents and priests. This attempt does not pretend to be a complete account of the study of Tripura folk-tales. In undertaking this work, my main concern was with the conditions of life and the quality of thinking of the people of Tripura during the medieval period. Behind every story there is a social environment. The factors influencing the medieval thought-patterns have been briefly explained. Several years of research and writing went into the preparation of this book. It is perhaps the first attempt to make the folk-tales of Tripura the subject of anthropological analysis. By attempting to maintain a balance between romantic narration and rigorous analysis, Folk-tales of Tripura may be a contribution to the study of the history and culture of the people of Tripura. It may be a literary pabulum, and a field of research. An appreciation of cultural diversity, a belief in psychic similarity of mankind, a cross-cultural comparison, a devotion to understanding archaic popular thought in its traditional setting, a loyalty to the norms of anthropological research may be discerned here. Larima Fog is generally seen everywhere in Tripura and in other parts of the north-eastern region of Bharat during the autumn, the dewy and the winter season. The density of fog in this region becomes maximum during December & January only. Over the bushy dingles in the eastern

hilly part of Tripura thick fog looks like huge smoke. What is this fog? Is it fog or something else? The hill people of Tripura, watching the vast cloud of smoke, have got an answer to this question. According to, the traditional interpretation, it is not fog: it is smoke, rising from the fire-place of Larima. Larima is a benevolent, kindhearted, pious woman. She lives in an invisible hut in the deep hills. Only a dead person can see the hut. For her benevolence she is blessed with a boon to have an immortal life. From time immemorial she has been cooking rice & vegetables, and providing the last food to the dead persons. There is a jungle track leading to her hermitage. The dead persons are to walk through the track. There is a bulky log of wood placed across the track. This is called Bufang Kebeng. The dead person must cross the log; once the dead person crosses the log, he forgets all the memories of life. Next, the dead person comes to take rest in the hermitage of Larima. The mother welcomes the dead person, offers seat & water and the last food, and gently bids farewell for ever. 2. Pilgrimage of Soul There is a taboo on killing certain insects like butterfly, grass-hopper, wasp, etc. particularly at night. The Tripuri, the Riang, the Jamatia, the Noatia, the Uchai, the Halam, the Lushai, the Garo, the Bachal people observe this taboo with a religious devotion. why? Here is an explanation: Folk Tales of Tripura 15 a The soul is called Fala. The soul of a sleeper is believed to wander away from his body to visit the places,

to meet the persons and to perform the acts of which he dreams. The soul takes the form of an insect like butterfly, bee, black-bee, fly, grass-hopper or wasp. Now, the absence of the soul in sleep has its dangers. If the soul is disturbed, detained away, or destroyed, the concerning person will die. So to disturb, detain, harm, hurt or kill the insect would be fatal to the sleeper. It would be equally fatal to waken a sleeper, because the person’s soul was away and might not have time to come back. The sleeper must not be disturbed in any way & at any time. 3. The Sky Long, long ago the sky was far below, very near the earth, over the human head. It was, as if, a large, wide canopy. It was like a very big bread, soft, sweet and edible. The Tripuri people used to cut pieces of the sky for food. They would relish it. Mortar and pestle have been quite ancient artifacts for husking paddy and pulses, etc. In the hills of north- eastern corner of Bharat almost every family possesses a pair of mortar and pestle. These instruments are made of a particular type of wood, preferably shawl, or segun, or sundi, or gamair. The pestle is a long stick, about six feet. The mortar approximately looks like a barrel-shaped drum, with a slim middle, and a hollow at the top. The mortar looks like a cylinder. One day one Tripuri woman was husking paddy. She was pounding dry paddy at the open courtyard. She was deeply engrossed in the work. Standing beside the mortar and putting a quantity of dry paddy in the cavity of the

mortar, she had to repeatedly strike the paddy with the pestle held vertically. Suddenly and unintentionally, the pestle struck against the sky. ominiaaiaiaad the sky went high above. Folk Tales of Tripura 16 cn ——— A Galaxy of myths The two Indian epics, the Ramayana, and the Mahabharata, have proved themselves to be perennial sources of inspiration and an ocean of wisdom from which a galaxy of folk-tales, myths, poems, songs, dances, dialogues and visual arts have been composed by the people. While explaining certain characteristic features of animal and plant life, the local folk culture of Tripura refers to the corresponding episodes of the two epics. Here are a few examples: 4, Rim-Kala In the hills & forest of Tripura, a kind of wild banana plant is abundantly available. It is called Ram-Kala. Why? During the period of exile, Rama, Lakshmana and Sita evitivated this plant: they used to eat the banana, and used its leaves as plates. 5, Sita-begun in the river valleys of Tripura, a kind of wild brinjal in available. It is called Sita-begun. Why? During the period of exile, Rama, Lakshmana & Sita cultivated this plant; they used to eat the brinjal. 6, Sitd-Kachu in the river valleys of Tripura, a kind of wild arum is available, Its leaf is tinted red. It is called Sita-kachu. Why? While Ravan had been abducting Sita from the forest, Sita’s vermillion fell on the leaf of the arum. So ihe leaf has red spots. 7, Pituli Pata Immediately after the abduction of Sita by Ravana, ihe helpless wife cited a number of animals, birds, plants ae witness. Rama & Lakshmana anxiously went out in aearch of the lady:

A leafy plant was one such witness. It is known as Pituli Pata. The Tripuri people call it Lairuk. Its scientific fame is Phrynium imbricatum. Its leaf trembles even at ihe slight blast of wind. Why? Rama & Lakshaman asked ihe plant: Have you seen Sita? The plant was afraid of Folk Tales of Tripura 17 OO the wrath of Ravana; so, the plant suppressed the news by shaking its head negatively. So, it was cursed. This is why the plant goes on shaking its leaf (or head) almost. continuously. 8. Kingfisher ; The Kingfisher birds are called Machranga. These birds constantly flutter & flicker for few minutes about twenty feet above water, espy the prey and suddenly dive into water and catch with mandibles those small fishes which roam just below the surface of water. This is a remarkable technique and a successful adventure. Why? Rama asked: Have you seen Sita? The bird was brave enough to give correct evidence to Rama & Lakshamana. So, Rama blessed the bird. This is why the bird can catch fish in such an adventurous way. 9. Swans In a lake there was a pair of swan; they were husband & wife. They saw Sita during her impediment. The wife sought permission of her husband to report the incident to Rama. Being afraid of Ravana, the husband discouraged & advised his wife in a low voice to refrain from telling the truth. Thus, the male swan incurred the displeasure of Rama. This is why a male swan’s voice is hursh & rough; while a female swan has a melodious voice. 10. The Black-faced Hanuman Hanuman desperately crossed the sea in search of Sita. There he met Sita in the Asok Kanan and ate dainty

fruits of the garden. The gardeners took great trouble to take him to the court of Ravana. At Ravana’s order, rags were tied to his tail and fire was set to it. Hanuman jumped up to commit arson and disaster. Thus burning down a major portion of Lanka, Hanuman dipped into the ocean and returned. At that time, the scorching heat of the fire blackened his face. To get rid of the shame, Hanuman sought the boon of Sita. By the boon, faces of the entire species became black. Folk Tales of Tripura 18 11. Rhesus Monkey The pelvic region of Rhesus monkey is remarkably reddish. Why? While constructing a long bridge or causeway from Ramesvaram to Lanka, the monkeys were joyously carrying boulders, stone, etc. Rama was chewing betel-leaf. Then suddenly a few drops of red spittle of betel leaf fell on a monkey’s body, particularly on his rectum. This is why pelvic region & rectum of monkey look reddish. 12. Palm squirrel The Indian palm squirrels have their fur remarkably striped. Why the squirrel is stripy? At the time of construction of a causeway between Ramesvaram and Lanka, even the tiny squirrels participated: They were lot strong enough to carry heavy stones; so they used to wallow on the sea-shore to collect sand on their body and roll their body on the causeway to make it smooth with sand & clay. Rama was glad to take one of them in his hand with affection and patted & caressed gently with fingers from head to tail. This is why the Indian squirrels have stripes on their fur. The Aztecs of Mexico have a similar story : a tiny bird tried to extinguish a big

lire, 13, Chhengthum-pha and Naithakbi Chhengthum-pha had been the prince of Tripura. Long ago, one day Chhengthuma-pha was out on a hunting expedition. The young prince had sportsmanship. lle was accompanied by his retinue. He enjoyed the excitement of the adventure. In those days most of the kings of Tripura used to hunt much in their youth. During those days, the greater part of Tripura was acantily peopled, and many persons were crippled and -tiumerous domestic animals & birds were killed by the wild beasts. The traditional weapons of the inhabitants were bows & arrows, traps, snares, knives, sticks, etc. The assistants of the prince erected a mdchdan ina Folk Tales of Tripura 19 tree, out of the reach of the animals. There the prince . and the assistants ambushed silently and comfortably. They were whispering and expecting the passage of a beast. Meanwhile, a boar came out dashingly and gruntingly. The prince shot at the boar; the beast was not mortally wounded. The wounded beast charged immediately and then hurried away rashly. The prince and his companions climbed down to go after the boar. It took some time. Now, a group of Tripuri girls were collecting wild vegetables and leaves at a distance in the same forest. They were used to do many domestic chores, besides helping in the fields. Among the group of girls, a girl named Naithakbi had some qualities of head & heart. Suddenly, she saw a wild boar rushing towards them gruntingly. Naithakbi had bow & arrow in her basket; she at once shot at the animal. The beast was struck down. The beast fell squalling & yelling. The prince along with the attendants & beaters & sepoys reached the

spot, and became astonished to see the animal struck down. The prince appreciated the skill of the unknown hunter and looked around. A flock of black, jungle-crows soared about overhead; the noisy birds were cawing & screaming, clinging to the swaying ends of the branches of the tall trees. The prince saw a group of cheerful girls at a distance, and sent the senior Hadjdarito ask if any one of them had hunted the beast. The prince took rest in the shade of a big tree. The arrival of the prince’s men in the lonely forest had its impact; it produced mixed reaction in the minds of the lasses. The lasses were whispering to each other. Punangti became apprehensive; Malakti became afraid; Karamti too became perplexed. But, Naithakbi stood confidently, observing the squad’s behaviour and assuring her own companions. The self-contained girl had about her an air of positive personality that made her in every Folk Tales of Tripura 20 way a contrast to her companions. Meanwhile the senior Hdjdri came near to the lasses and narrated: My dear girls! you look at the bright young man taking rest in the shade of the big tree; he is our dear prince; he had shot at this boar; the boar was not struck down. The boar escaped. Do you know who later struck down the beast? The senior Hdajdari’s words were hardly out of his mouth, when Naithakbi said: Yes Sir! I did it. Is he displeased with me? Have I committed a crime? The senior Hajari replied: No, No! The prince has appreciated the skill and wanted to know your whereabouts. Naithakbi said: My name is Naithakbi. My father’s name is Chadrai Senapati; my father was a soldier, rather

the commander in the military service of the kings of Tripura. After his retirement, the king granted him lands. Now, he is an old man. The village he lives in is known after his name. The senior Hajari again said: I am certainly glad to - know your identity: you are the daughter of one of our most distinguished soldiers! His courage and the prowess of his company contributed to the strength of the kingdom. Naithakbi said: Thank you for your kind words. The senior Hajari conveyed the information to the prince, The prince too became cheerful and eloquent and spoke a lot in appreciation. Like father, like daughter! Matured & deepened by her father’s wartime experience, she spent many of her playtime hours in drilling & shooting. She is second to none. She was a great pet, for her parents had no other son or daughter. The senior //ajari humorously added: She is fit to be a queen. All the attendants leered, and looked at each other. The atmosphere became light and jolly. The two groups stood apart. The lively, high-spirited prinee had a magnetic personality; while the lovely and iitelligent lass had something unique in her character. Folk Tales of Tripura 21 So nothing hindered the swift budding of one of the great romantic affairs of Tripura. In each group there had been associates who were watching the manners of the two. Meanwhile, an idea flashed out in the mind of Naithakbi: the prince might have taken objection for killing the wounded beast: so she asked her associates not to be afraid but to carry the beast in order to offer it to the prince. They at once lifted it and placed before the prince

and bowed humbly as a mark of respect & offering. The prince was captivated by this proof of Naithakbi’s bold wit. It occurred to him that he did not know the pretty girl before. He chuckled and asked: have you killed the boar? Naithakbi : Yes, Maharaj, | have! The Prince: Since you have killed, you could have taken it! Naithakbi : Maharaj! but you wanted to kill it. I have committed a mistake. Kindly excuse me; and accept it as an humble offer. The prince gladly agreed to accept the offer. Naithakbi said a few words in an easy, cordial way and left the place along with her associates for collecting vegetables. The prince & his associates watched them as they sauntered off. It refreshed them all. The greater the adventure, the cheerful was the prince. So he hit on a romantic plan. He directed a few associates to go ahead toward the village of Chadrai Senapati and if necessary to do a little of chopping & lopping. Next, a few sepoys were to follow & carry the boar, and to start the preparation of a small feast in the house of the Sendpati. The prince wanted to relish the meat jointly. On receiving the information, the Senapati became very glad & grateful and supplied all necessary materials for the feast. While the cooking was going on, the prince along with the senior Hdajari and a few others, reached the village. The Sendpati & his wife went together to a distance to welcome the prince. The honourable Folk Tales of Tripura 22 guests were offered water for washing. The prince’s hands & feet were washed by the hosts. Giving a seat to the

prince, the host duly showed homage to the very important person. The Senapati felt a warm surge of nostalgia, and a sudden uplift of the spirit. By now, the Senapati became an old man with grey hair. Here was a man who fought many battles. He recollected the memories of many events :- several battles, the journey to distant hills, the odds faced, the calamities encountered, the victories own, the paternal love & affection of the old Maharaja, the team-spirit of his colleagues, etc. The Sendpati talked endless of his happy days with the Maharaja. Tears of joy were streaming down his face. The old Sendpati remembered everything and everyone very well. The prince came with a heart overflowing with love. He longed for an opportunity to praise Naithakbi. A scope came along with a reference to the boar. The prince spoke a lot with delight and wonder. The prince appreciated the Sendpati for imparting training to Naithakbi in martial arts. The prince was smitten by the charms of Naithakbi, then a girl of about sixteen. The senior Hajari was supervising the work of cooking, while the Binandids laboured with the utmost ardour to complete the cooking in time. Meanwhile, Naithakbi came back home with fresh vegetables. She carried the wild vegetables & leaves in a bamboo-basket (= Langa) suspended from the forehead over the back with a piece of bark of the Udal tree (Sterculia vilosa). Naithakbi was intoxicated with the delight, but her expression for the moment was little elusive. She went to the kitchen room (o look after the preparation of food. On seeing the cooking process satisfactory, she said a few words in gratitude. ‘She herself prepared Godak, a kind of salad famous in

Tripura, The Sendpati invited the village elders, while Naithakbi invited the young boys & girls. The village was Folk Tales of Tripura 23 fluttering with excitement. The villagers joyously assembed, and bowed to the prince in obeisance. For about an hour the house was full. The elders and the prince were entertained with a sweet drink (= butuk). Come immediately. Tuinangti was cooking in the kitchen

room; she rushed to the door. The Sardar handed the boy over to his wife. In wonder & delight, she took the boy tenderly and pressed the boy lovingly & protectingly to her bosom.
