The first queen is now dead The second queen is enthroned in her stead. The new ‘queen had no affection but pretension Only cunning deception was her contention. The sons suffered a sea-change Into something sad & strange. The jealous queen pretended to be sick A stranger in the guise of a diviner big Prescibed son’s blood-bath as the remedy King ordered the executioner to get ready. In presence of many sympathisers all around The two sons were taken to the cremation ground. They sought time and invoked the mother’s boon Surprisingly hailstorm, lightning came soon. There occurred heavy shower, terrible sound. Black, hot smoke engulfed the ground Folk Tales of Tripura 93 The wetnurse, the executioner left them in forest deep They spent the night in a tree without sleep.

The band interrupted with a instrumental music. Most of the audience were weeping. Recollecting his mistakes, even the king became repentant. Everybody was speech- less. What a grave mistake! Next, Ninangti took up the chord and sang: Oh! my dear countrymen! Attentively hear the story of the Tripuri dynasty which has a history nice as well as nasty. It was a night dark and terrible It was a nymph to protect them from death horrible. Next morning they ran towards forests & hills Full of wild animals and a few rills To quench the junior’s thirst, the senior went for water In the labyrinth the senior lost his path somewhere. The separated brothers moved oppositely helter-skelter. Some unkown hillmen offered them shelter. Wrapt in cloud of sorrow & in unceasing pain They are eager to meet their father again. The mighty crescendo of words of pathos matched with the climax of hysteria in the king’s mind. The climax came when the king wallowed on the floor and wept like a child. He wept on account of his mistake, on account of his cruelty. With a deep groan, he flung himself on the floor. Beating his own forehead, he hissed a word: My son! A spasm racked him. He was in a fit. The king was immediately carried to his bed-chamber for rest and sleep. The faithful wet-nurse was now old enough; she could not walk more than thirty or forty feet from her doorstep. She was left all alone with her memories. Her eyesight became weak. However, she, like others, came Folk Tales of Tripura 94 to enjoy the function. She squatted in a corner of the conference-hall. She attentively and tearfully listened

to the song. After a while, a doubt arose in her mind about the identity of the two bright artists. She stared at -them repeatedly. She correctly identified them. Pleasant moments again occurred. She did not disclose it. She was observing the situation. After sometime, the king grew quiet; he ceased weeping. He was recovering from the quagmire of moha, delusion, illusion, obfuscation, self-forgetfulness, henpeck & lustfulness, into the conciousness of self- assertion, statesmanship, dynamism and fatherly duty. The chief minister and the army chief were moving quickly up & down. The servants were bobbing. At the direction of the king, the chief of the army invited the two main artists. The two artists stood before the king with folded hands and bowed their heads before the king. The king greated & appreciated them and then asked: Are my son, Kutung & Kucung, alive? After listening to your songs, it seems to me that they are still alive. Tell me, where are they? whatever you demand, I shall give & honour you. What a fool am I ? Without thinking the pros & cons, I gave them capital punishment. Their mother miraculously saved them. I shall bring them back at any cost. I shall atone. As I listened, I realized my folly; and I am ready to amend. _ Observing the king’s distressful state of mind, his appreciative, sympathetic and repentable approach, the two artists made the submission: MahGraj! your two sons are alive. If you solemnly undertake an oath and do accordingly, then and then only they may come here to meet you. The king replied: I shall certainly undertake the oath and act accordingly. Tell me the condition, tell me the

terms of the oath. Kucung said: Maharaj! there is a big wooden box in the chamber of the Mah@rdni. Will you kindly take steps Folk Tales of Tripura 95 to open the box in presence of the security staff? This is the oath. This is the condition. Nothing else! The king said: Only this much! only to open a box? Is it a difficult task? The trouble of it is not at all great. Yes, I shall do it now & immediately. The king swore an ardent oath of faithfulness and summoned the ministers and the chief of the army and the security staff. The army chief deployed his staff all around the house of the queen. Then the king, accompanied by the ministers, the nobles and the army chief, proceeded towards the inner apartments of the palace. The two artists were sitting quietly. Meanwhile, an old woman (Dhai-mda) made her way through an anxious crowd and trudged limpingly towards the artists. Tears were rolling down her wrinkled face. Like a loving mother, she hugged the two artists and caressed them. The two artists correctly identified the woman. They too hugged her out of an emotional outburst. The spectors were making guess and conjecture about the two artists. But neither the old woman nor the two artists openly disclosed the identity of the artists. The old woman soon left the room and retired to her apartment. The two artists were waiting in the same room. The queen did not come to the conference-hall to enjoy the function of song & music. She was sadder than ever when her waitress reported about the programme. She surmised something evil. She kept herself inside

her room with doors and windows closed. She, at the tragic crisis of her life, attempted to protect herself by falsehood and deception, as she had done earlier. She _ Stashed Phatikray inside the big box and kept it under lock & key. She carefully kept the key with herself; the key was tied to a corner of her clothe and stashed inside the waist-clothe. Now, she pretended to be deeply engaged in weaving. The king, while marching struttingly towards the room of the queen, thought that the box must be Folk Tales of Tripura 96 interesting and illuminating. For the first time, the king became curious about the mystery of the box. The suggestion of the two artists must be meaningful & significant. The king, forcing his way into the bed-chamber ‘of the queen, asked : Where is the key of this wooden box? That was a hard question to answer. Her evil genius and instinct prompted her not to surrender readily. She said : Maharaj! I will not hand over the key. It contains my personal and valuable things. My father gave it. I shall not allow anybody to touch it. So long as I am alive, | will not allow anybody to open it. As her resistance became stubborn, the king’s doubt inflamed. The king directed the minister and the army chief to engage the servants & soldiers to twitch, to drag the box and to pull it outside. Immediately, the queen ~ rushed, held out her arm and gripped the box. The queen thus shielded herself under the’ custom of etiquette. Not only the servants, the soldiers, even the minister and the army-chief were to maintain a safe

distance from the body of the queen. To overcome the mean stratagem, the king boldly said: I am not interested in what you thing sacred. Let me tell you once & for all, | am interested in what I desire. Having said those words, soon the king angrily caught her with his own arms and twitched her away. She was sobbing, panting and w: ying and beating her forehead. She tried her best too ger out of the grip. Nobody dared to rescue her, to comfort her. The Mahdardj was now extremely excited and angry. Who would stand before his fury! Neither a minister nor a waitress dared approach. They backed out of the chamber. Phatikray was inside the big box; he was almost paralysed with horror; he was straining his ear to hear the angry words of the king, and hurry-skurry of the queen, He became alarmed and his hair rose. He was trembling. Amid a scene of horrible confusion & suspense, the he avy box was lifted & shifted to the conference- Folk Tales of Tripura 97 hall. The two artists instantaneously recognised the box. Herein lay many mysteries. The mystery was to be dispelled soon. And soon the whole assemblage thronged around the box. They were whispering and staring. Suddenly, the king rashly came and stood among them. For a few seconds, those who crowded round him became - respectfully speechless. The king at once orderd to break the lock in presence of all. The security officers broke the lock and opened the lid. There they found a healthy young man: a horror-stricken youth still clad in his night- dress. An awful discovery! The tired king was taking rest at a little distance.

The king asked the minister: What have you seen inside? The minister replied: Dharmavatdr! kindly pardon my audacity; Be kind enough to see the awful discovery. Soon the king came forward and saw the criminal and immediately shouted out: Who are you? Who did stash you here? How did you enter inside the box? At the order of the king, the security officers caught him tightly and pulled him out of the box. The minister and the army- chief asked question after question. But the criminal made no reply; he stood like statue. At the order of the angry king, Kalakray started whipping. After a good deal of thrashing, he made the confession: My name is Phatikray. I am a resident of the village of Nikra Sardar. I have come here along with the dowry of the queen. At the time I was stashed inside the box. The king’s servants carried the box and placed inside the bed-chamber of the queen. Hearing the confessions, the king orderd to beat him more forcefully. Kalakray whipped with all force. The criminal lay unconscious. After sometime he regained his consciousness. The king again asked: Who did come in the guise of a diviner? The criminal admitted: I came. I prescribed the sacrifice of the two princes as a remedy of the mock disease. The queen had no disease. It was a devilish plot for profligacy. Folk Tales of Tripura 98 Thr criminal thus confessed the crime. The queen and the criminal helped each other and encouraged each other in the sinister design. The plot was cunningly executed. So, the criminal was dragged violently into ‘ the middle of the conference-hall. At the order of the

king, salt was applied to his wounds; and then he was kicked, heckled & jostled to death by the assemblage. The king quickly went out of the hall. In an agony of grief and repentance, the king immediately left the hall and threw himself on the empty bed, moaning : motherless sons! what tormented the king most was the deception, the lie that the queen was not simply ill, but she was dying. The ministers and the army officers accepted the lie! It was all through the queen that the king got into serious troubles. She betrayed the king. How great a shame she put on the face of the king! The king summoned the minister. The king said: | was rather reluctant to marry for the second time. You made all sorts of arrangements for this marriage. You did not make thorough investigation about the bride & her family. As a result, all these disasters and defamation happened. Now, I cannot show my face. I have been wrossly misguided. The voluptuous queen blackmailed us and made a mockery of fatal disase only to kill the two boys. By such a wicked device, she attempted to kill the sons. I have also committed a major mistake; I ordered io execute the sons. The lustful game, carried on for a considerable period, was not fated to continue smoothly, for the two sons survived the heinous attempt on their life. By the blessings of their mother, they are alive and the plot has come to be known; otherwise the duo would continue. So, suggest me the nature & type of punishment she deserves for the gravest infidelity! Meanwhile, the waitress of the notorious queen

rushed to the king and said: Maharaj! please come sharp! it is likely that the queen-mother has swallowed poison. (he queen-mother is dying: The queen-mother is dying! Folk Tales of Tripura 99 The disgusted king at once wrathfully & disparagingly said: She should have deid earlier. Let her die. I do not like to see her face. Such was her dramatic fall from a prestigious position. A nemesis! A rogue bites the hand that feeds him or her, and spoils the plate after eating. Those were the hectic moments of tumultuous incidents. The king became utterly depressed & disheartened. The minister and the army-chief were there to comfort the king. Meanwhile, the faithful Dhai- ma trudged limpingly towards the door of the king’s bed- chamber. They became silent and stared at her. In the midst of all din & bustle, the wet-nurse seemed to have a smile implicitly signifying something known to her only. She said: Maharaj! the bad impact of Rahu & Ketu on your fate is gone today. Fate willed it. Henceforth, your good days are coming. The criminals got due punishment. They perished on account of their sins. They deserved it. By the grace of god, the princes are alive. This is a matter of great consolation. The disillusioned king was waiting with bated breathe the home-coming of the sons. The king emotionally said: Mailuma! I shall never be able to repay your debt. Only © your wit & wisdom saved the sons. You go and get the whereabouts of the sons from the artists. My mind is anxious, I am eager to see them; without them my life is a burden. | Mailuma left the king’s chamber and returned

immediately along with the two main artists. The king cut short the conversation with the minister. She was now ready to give the surprise. Resting her hands on the shoulders of the two young artists, the old wet-nurse confidently said: Mahdrdj! these two artists are your sons: Kumar Kutung & Kumar Kucung: hold out your arms to take them into your bosom. The king, in great thrill, stood up and hugged the sons. The sons bowed down. The father Folk Tales of Tripura 100 und the sons were weeping out of joy. The tears were pleasing, life-giving like the old memory. The other members of the team were waiting outside. At the wink of the wet-nurse, Matam & Ninangti came in & bowed down. The wet-nurse gave the introduction. After that, the two headmen and other members came in and bowed down. Matam & Ninangti gave the introduction. With the permission of the king, the army-chief made necessary arrangement for the cremation of the two dead bodies. Kalakray supervised the funeral rite. The situation in the capital was suddenly and positively changed from the next day. There emerged a rosy atmosphere. There was a general air of happiness, which was only natural after the removal of the evil forces, and the reunion. In the presence of the sons and the daughters-in-law, the king felt an inward peace. Shaking off the despondency, the king again set his mind to administration. The wet-nurse had in her heart a very tender love for the two orphan boys. She won the affection of all for her devotion & duty, for her common sense & courage. But she would, on no account, accept money for her

motherly service. For that act of kindness, the king was ready to give’any amount of gift. She felt amply rewarded when the king had expressed his deep sense of solemn gratitude. Kutung, Kucung, Matam & Ninangti used to respect her and take advice from her in domestic matters. Henceforth she was given the supervisory duty over all the domestic servants. The king and the Sardars sat for a long while talking of their experiences. The Sarddrs talked of how the two princes were found in the deep forest, how they were nursed and consoled, how the villagers responded to their songs & music. The king appreciated their service and amply rewarded them with adequate provisions in the capital. Time was passing & rushing onward like a stream. . Folk Tales of Tripura 101 Ce ee The king was growing steadily weaker.-Circumstances _ were altering. Matam and Ninangti were making efforts to make the home delightful and domestic garden beautiful. The two sons were assisting the father in administering the kingdom. A few years passed under the changed circumstances. The old king found himself utterly unable any longer to bear the burden of administration. He lost attachment to life. So, he was now thinking of getting rid of the responsibility. Usually, the throne was to descend from the father to the eldest prince; under certain cricumstances & considerations like character & wisdom, the eldest son could be passed over in favour of a younger. However, here the king had a mind to install the elder son. In consultation with the minister & the army-chief and the members of the royal family, the king had his decision confirmed. On an auspicious day, the elder son was duly and ceremonially

coronated. The new king appointed his younger brother minister. The new king and the new minister had many friends in the hills. They knew the condition of the countryside. They took steps for the safety & security of the subjects. After a few years, the old king happily breathed his last. _ The sons and relatives performed the funeral rites with all devotion and grandeur. 15. The White Elephant In a certain village lived a peasant with his wife and a son. The peasant fell ill and died leaving the wife and the son helpless. The widow thought: it was honourable to earn by hard labour than to beg. She had to go out daily to do household chores in the houses of the neighbours for a nominal salary in kind and food. Thus, she nursed and brought up the only child. The boy came of hardy peasant stock from the uplands of Tripura. The boy had capacious intelligence, courage and earnestness. By the sheer force of intelligence and Folk Tales of Tripura 102 Se industriousness, the brisk boy won the affection and admiration of the people. His name and fame came to the notice of the king. The king appointed him in the household service of the palace. Here he had to do a - variety of work : cooking, sweeping, cleaning, fetching water, cutting firewood, weeding, making road, repairing houses, etc. In every work, he was efficient and ahead of others. He excelled at all indoor and outdoor duties. The qualities of the boy attracted the attention of the king further. The king had a daughter. The royal family observed him from close quarters and decided to choose him as son-in-law. But the king was Rakshash.

The mystery was unknown to many people. He would behave like a goodman during day time, but at dead of night he would get up very quietly and devour animals and birds. It was a strange paradox. It was a common practice in those days to set traps in the hills & jungles for catching wild animals and birds. Some of the royal servants were experts in setting traps. The traps were usually set in the evening and taken back in the following morning. One day the boy was sent lor inspection. Having visited the trap, the boy reported that a young man had been caught in the trap. The king denied it as an illusion; he gave the boy a special shirt to wear. He wore it and revisited the trap and found a big black deer in the trap. Soon, the king’s servants enthusiastically rushed there and brought the deer. A feast was arranged. Friends & relatives were invited. They all sat to relish the meat. But the boy became suspicious; he did not eat the meat. He concealed the meat and dropped the meat below through the crevice of the platform. The domestic dogs and swines ate the meat. From the sound of scratching & screaming by the animals below, the cunning king guessed that something wrong had occurred. On inquiry he ascertained that the boy, instead of eating, dropped the meat. The king said: Folk Tales of Tripura 103 My dear boy, you are hungry; I like to offer you fish. Please come with me. The king led him to a dark room. The boy found there many prisoners herded together in filth & foul air. They

appealed to him to get out of the jail. The king kicked them; they turned into big fishes. This incident confirmed the magic and mischief of the king. The boy’s mind became restless: how could he arrange to get out of the clutch of the mysterious king? With worry and anxiety and the mother far away, the boy prayed for leave of absence. The king magically inserted an amulet inside the boy’s forehead and said: This amulet will guard you against disease & death, go home, see your mother, come back here and get ready for marriage with my princess. The horror of the boy was beyond words; to get out of the palace was a dream, a passion. To-day the boy is free. It was a significant moment. He had to quit the palace precipitately. He turned his steps homewards. He made long strides. The mother used to sit down daily for a few minutes watching the path along which her son would come. The boy reached home and narrated the incidents. The boy refused to be reconciled to the king. The mother consented. After a few days of rest and discussion, they decided to emigrate to the kingdom of another king for safety and security. Accordingly, on the pretext of pilgrimage for the last rite of the deceased father, the boy with his mother left the native place; they travelled, travelled for days together. The journey was very tedious for the fugitives. They found a vast expanse of jungles and a lake. They made a hut there. They made their living by collecting wild vegetables and selling firewood. The promising boy was sure to shine in life. Soon he

became prosperous and his mother arranged his marriage with a poor but obedient girl. The mother was Folk Tales of Tripura 104 lappy to see grandchildren, domestic animals and birds und relatives. Within a few decades the vast expanse of ihe forest was developed into a prosperous village. Now the family was in high spirits. The news of the death of that magician king reached here. The octogenarian mother of the boy also died in due course. The boy is now an aged man; he has children and grandchildren. His life is now a burden to himself. He sincerely likes to die; but because of the amulet life was prolonging unusually. One day he arranged a big feast and entertained the villagers. After the feast, in the afternoon he narrated the story of his life. The moment the narration had been complete, the amulet came out and he along with his kinsmen died suddenly. Not a single member of his clan survived. At the outskirt of that village lived a family of a different clan. That family did not participate in the feast. The family survived. The family consisted of a young couple. The husband used to go out in the morning for shifting cultivation. The wife was pregnant; she used to spend her time in spinning and weaving. The traditional hut of the family was on a raised platform supported by several poles & sticks. Below the platform there were apartments for cow and swine. In one such apartment lived a pregnant cow. The housewife usually used to sit on her loom in the afternoon. Spinning & weaving kept her busy. She was indeed struggling along with the weaving of clothes for

the coming baby. Because of her physical conditions, she could not move freely. The spindle in her hand would slip and fall below the platform. The cow was kind enough to collect the spindle. But it fell daily. The cow became disgusted and set a condition: We are going to be mothers. If you assure to arrange a marriage between the two children, I can take the trouble of collecting & restoring the spindle. She had to agree. Folk Tales of Tripura 105 In course of time, she gave birth to a daughter; while a bull calf was born to the cow. The girl and the bull became friends; they would play, dance and move together. The housewife kept her words and made a simple ceremony of marriage. It was a child marriage. After about a decade, the girl became very self-conscious. All sorts of strange rumours and remarks were now flying about the village regarding the unusual marriage. Now, she was in dilemma; she could not reconcile to a union that had been forced upon her. Being terribly shocked, she committed suicide by hanging in a myrobalan tree. With a heavy heart, the bull too dashed his head against the tree again and again and died there. The souls of the couple were turned into two beautiful myrobalan fruits. One day the king made a pleasure trip into the forest for hunting deer. The king and his attendants took rest in the shade of the myrobalan tree. They saw the two big fruits. The king directed to pick up the fruits. While collecting the fruits from the lofty branches, one fruit slipped, and the king’s elephant ate it. The other fruit

was cautiously gathered and handed over to the king. The queen had no son or daughter. The queen ate the fruit. In course of time, the queen gave birth to a daughter, and the elephant gave birth to a white male calf. They became friends. Again, all sorts of strange rumours and remarks were flying in the capital regarding the unusual friendship. Unable to tolerate the comments, one night the two friends eloped. They were too clever to enter any village or hamlet where their presence would be reported immediately. They had to quit the capital and human settlement quickly. They made long strides and took refuge in the deep forest of the eastern hills of Tripura. Though the police of the whole kingdom was warned; though in every market and village drum-beating was made to inform the people, days and even months passed Folk Tales of Tripura 106 without any hope & trace. The entire kingdom worried of the princess. On the royal family lay the sad stain. At last from the countryside came two young brothers: Bhutua and Rangia; they displayed their .masculinity and assured to rescue the princess. They were slovenly, unclean and without any dignity. The guards brought the two brothers to the capital. What a heaven-sent opportunity! The king became happy and ordered to make arrangement for their rest and food in the royal guest-house. After two days, they were brought to the royal court. The two brothers were very glad to play homage to the king. The king asked their names and address. The two brothers expressed their confidence to take the venture and sought food & shelter for six months. After the preliminary introduction, the

two brothers were directed to retire to the guest-house again. The king and the ministers discussed the problem and the proposal. They agreed to give the two brothers a chance. It was decided that a team of guards and attendants would accompany them with food and other provisions. On an auspicious day they set out amid much hope and excitement. The elder brother, Bhutua, was robust but dull. The younger brother, Rangia, was slim but intelligent; moreover, he was foot-print expert. Identifying the foot-prints of the white elephant, right from the capital, Rangia concentrated his attention on the path; he moved eastward. They travelled, travelled for months with daily haltage. At last, they reached a place named Nana-gomati Doapathar (am Wt esa). The royal guard & attendants made a hut and stored food and turned their steps capitalward. It was Bhutua’s duty to cook, to fetch water, to collect leaves and vegetables and to keep the house in order. It was Rangia’s duty to watch and observe, to search and face any difficult situation. Rangia had no definite Folk Tales of Tripura 107 routine; he used to go out at any time. Rangia told Bhutua: ‘If any body asks: who are there inside? you should reply: Rangia and Bhutua are inside.’ One night during the absence of Rangia, one female demon came and asked: Who are inside? Bhutua replied: Rangia & Bhutua are inside. Hearing the reply, the female demon fled. The female demon visited every night, asked the same question, got the same reply and fled. It continued for about a week. One night Bhutua, out of ego & foolishness, replied: Bhutua and Rangia are inside. At once, the female demon forced her entry, strangulated

Bhutua and cut his tongue and decamped, and descended down to her dwelling in the inferno. Meanwhile, Rangia was out of the cottage for about a week. In the relentless search, he saw a great lake full of lotuses. There he came to see the white elephant bathing and sporting. The moment they exchanged their eyes, a spasm of pain shook them and silenced them for a space, but later they went on fighting and fighting for seven days and seven nights. The scene was terrible. Gifted with the boon of the god, Siva, Rangia killed the elephant. With exultation at his heart, and careless of the devastation all around the lake, Rangia hurried from the battlefield with a tusk of the white elephant. He called out his brother from below the hut, but no response came. He climbed up the stair, found none inside, placed the tusk, took rest and set out in search of Bhutua. At a long distance in a bush Bhutua lay unconscious and his tongue too was found at a little distance. Rangia solemnly uttered the name of Mahadeva Siva for three times and cured Bhutua and restored his tongue also. The two brothers returned home and took food and rest for a few days. Bhutua now became cautious not to utter his name first. Rangia resumed his search. Being a footmark expert, Rangia walked down slowly and followed the footmark of the Rakshashi (= female demon). Folk Tales of Tripura 108 kangia pursued, pursued for a few days and reached a queer place of bushes. There he found a big stone. He removed the stone and found a hole in the ground. A rope-like creeper was stretched and slid down to the

-bottom of the hole. The creeper was ghild lata (=Enteda scandens). The demon, grasping the creeper, climbs up and climbs down. Rangia, consumed with courage & determination, climbed down into the inferno. It was a thrilling experience. He looked around and saw a small palace. He turned his steps towards the palace and there was none to obstruct him. He entered and found the princess weeping. She became astonished. He expressed his adventure and mission. She fervently appealed to rescue her. Rangia assured. After sometime the grotesque demon came back home and became very furious to see Rangia, and instantaneously attacked Rangia. The demon was defeated and killed ultimately. The scene was awe- inspiring. The princess observed it. The moment the demon was killed, she burst out afresh and ran with Rangia. Rangia guarded her and directed her to climb up first. Bhutua was eagerly waiting near the mouth of the tunnel. The moment the princess climbed up and stood before Bhutua, Bhutua was bewildered to see the paragon of beauty. He immediately dashed the stone and closed the mouth of the tunnel leaving Rangia inside! In a few days Bhutua and the princess reached the capital. As they walked along the paths, Bhutua was hailed with amazement; the people clustered round him and praised him. They made long strides to reach the destination. But the scene inside the inferno was horrible. The news of the murder of the female demon came as a terrible shock to other demons. They hurried and assembled inside the palace, saw the mangled deadbody! who dared to kill her? who rescued the princess? They Folk Tales of Tripura 109 rushed and climbed up and found Rangia struggling to

remove the heavy stone. They caught him; he was thrown to the bottom. The demons climbed down and fastened him to a tree. The demons had the intention to punish Rangia very, very severely and devour him. But they had to dispose and cremate the deadbody first. It took time to collect fuel, dry timber, etc. for cremation. While all the demons were engaged in the funeral rites, Rangia was left alone. Rangia solemnly remembered the name of Mahadev Siva and requested the tree to raise its head upward tll the mouth of the tunnel. The tree responded silently and started outstretching. The branch of the tree removed the stone and Rangia came out of the inferno. The tree became small again. Rangia closed the opening of the tunnel. Rangia turned his steps towards the hut. Rangia called, but no response came from the hut. He was extremely tired. He took rest for a few days. There was no food, no provision. He grew hungrier and hungrier. He guessed the mischief of Bhutua. He lost her strength; he lost his mission and vision! He became confused and puzzled! His faculties almost failed! what strange tricks! what a treachery! What a meanness! Bhutua was living in the royal guest-house in princely style. The princess was living in the palace. She informed her father and mother alone of the most vital secret of betrayal by Bhutua. It was kept top secret. As the days passed, many friends and relatives of the royal family came to the palace to express their pleasure at the safe return of the princess. They thanked Bhutua. They insisted on celebrating the marriage ceremony as early as possible. Bhutua gave an air of impression that the

two brothers jointly fought against all evil forces, but unfortunately Rangia had been killed in the duel. Bhutua chuckled evilly. He was in idyllic happiness. The king could not believe the statement of Bhutua. Folk Tales of Tripura 110 But the king was in doubt. He was in a dilemma. He sent a trusted spy eastward to Nana-gomati Doapathar. The spy in disguise, moved and reached the destination. There he found Rangia in forlorn condition. The king’s man made friendship with Rangia, offered him food, nursed him and restored him to normal condition. Now, the two friends turned their steps towards the capital. It took time. Rangia hobbled. Bushes & thorns bruised his feet. The moment the two friends reached the palace, the situation was abruptly changed. The princess identified the real rescuer. All doubt was vanished. The palace became rosy. The impostor fled and fled for ever. The king was glad enough to arrange the ceremony of marriage with Rangia and gave half of the kingdom. Their marriage became a life-long honeymoon. 16. The Khumpai flower In the old days in the eastern hilly region of Tripura, villages were apart from one another. The distance between two villages was about two miles, as the crow flies. There was a big village of 126 families of the Tripuri community living there. Each family had its clearing of shifting cultivation a little away from the homestead. Each village had its council of elders, and Acdi ( = Akcdi = ojha = priest = shaman). The Acdi of that village was an experienced man. He had to visit many houses to officiate worship, to divine the cause of disease and to offer sacrifice, and to prepare

amulets. The priest had two daughters. The daughters would go to the jum field to weed and watch. There were wild animals & birds to pick cucumber, melon, maize, bean, etc. So the two unmarried sisters used to have their first meal at home cooked by their mother and their second meal packed up in leaf packet (= macha bhat) to be eaten at noon in the field-hut. The time was about May-June. The two sisters were working in the field. Suddenly a great gust came, and Folk Tales of Tripura 111 Se ee ee the sky became overcast with thick & black clouds. Thundering voice was heard; threatening hail-storm was about to destroy the surroundings. The two young sisters became very afraid. They stood helpless. The elder sister in soliloquy solicited help and promised to accept the helper as husband. To their astonishment, a snake was soon found preparing a hut quickly and skilfully. The snake built the field-hut rapidly and left the spot silently. The two sisters took shelter inside the hut. A heavy rain followed immediately. In the afternoon, they returned home; they did not tell the queer incident. The next day the sisters went to the field, and took rest & food inside the hut. The elder sister was bold enough to stick to her word. After a mutual discussion, the younger sister looked in all directions and casually loudly invited the elder sister’s husband to take food: Mai canani fdaidi. Surprisingly, the snake appeared, took food and left silently. This was the first day of sharing food by the snake. The two sisters used to feed the snake every day. The quantity of food provided by their mother used

to remain the same. But it was shared by the snake. So the two sisters became a little slim. The mother wanted to know the cause of their weakness. The elder daughter avoided the question. The younger daughter disclosed the fact secretly. The mother passed it to the father. The parents put their heads together to rescue the daughter from the invisible clutch of the snake, and to save the prestige of the family from the odd incident. One day the father said to the elder daughter: To- day do not go outside and assist your mother; and I shall go to the field along with the younger daughter. They took food to the field and worked together and at noon invited the snake from the hut. The snake started eating. Then & there, the father cut the snake with his sharp knife. The father climbed down with the snake’s carcass Folk Tales of Tripura 112 lield on the knife and buried the snake’s carcass near a waterfall. The next day, the two sisters went together to the field and worked till the time of the mid-day meal. The ‘younger sister made a mockery of invitation. But no response came. The elder sister insisted on knowing the liappening of the previous day. The younger sister had to fiarrate. The elder sister sat down weeping & watching the path along which the snake would come. She climbed down and went along the path and found a patch of lreshly-dug earth and a cloud of black flies hovering above it, The two sisters stood at the bottom of a gorge, a narrow, deep place between hills. The place was lonely, soundless, “sylvan and cool. They stood near a waterfall. In those

days wild animals & birds used to drink water from ‘the waterfall. A steep, narrow & mountainous precipice was the outlet of the stream. The flow was neither copious nor strong. The elder sister had a stick which she broke off from “ tree; she stirred the place and found the head of the snake, A very beautiful flower plant Khumpai, flourished overnight near the spot. The elder sister stood helpess and remorseful; while she had been watching pensively, the Khumpai flower blossomed more and more, and a “ush of water from the precipice made the waterfall overflooded. A rare moment of suspense: the flower was blossoming and the stream was increasing and she was being drowned. She was swept away by the exuberant current before the eyes of the younger sister. The famous ‘iver Gomati was mysteriously formed from that day. The younger sister stood perplexed and looked (uestioningly. The drowning sister told: ‘Do not weep and lament for me; this is my fate; the snake around whom your terror had crystallised was a god. Do not go back home, You leave this place, move away, travel & travel; ‘after a long distance you will find the crossing of seven paths; a very big banyan tree stands on the crossing of Folk Tales of Tripura 113 _-_-———————————— eee the paths. You climb the tree; you will find a loom made of gold. You weave clothes with extraordinary designs. You will be queen. This is my most sincere blessing!’ A passion or a fate or a destiny drove her headlong over all obstacles. The destiny of the elder sister completely altered the position of the younger sister. While the elder sister had been led by destiny to a small castle

inside the holy river, Gomati, the younger sister found a place in a trunk of the banyan tree. A dramatic change! The lady of the tree went on spinning & weaving, perfecting designs after designs through trial. & error. Now her memories, dreams and imaginations became part of her existence. When she shut her eyes she saw her parents, sister, friends & fields as though they were there in the flesh. One ancient king of Tripura, Raja Subrai, had a high Station to maintain. He possessed imagination and wisdom. He was a popular king. He gave great inspiration to cottage industry. As an incentive, he assured to marry the lady whose clothe would be found excellent. A wave of enterprise swept over the kingdom. The young girls became very enthusiastic; they sat on loom day and night; the members of each family put their heads together to imagine new design. For a time, it became their be-all and end-all of life. After a specific time, the king’s men collected a very large variety of home-spun clothes. The clothes were displayed in the palace. The judges found the clothe of the lady of the tree excellent. The lady of the tree was duly informed. She became very jubilant. Tears of joy rolled down and gave rise toa new river Haora; fortune smiled on her. The king, true to his words, married her. She now blossomed into the queen of Tripura. The king had a few other queens. But the king had no son or daughter. The king was worried. When the new queen had conceived, the king became very cheerful and hopeful. A long rope was stretched between the royal Folk Tales of Tripura 114

eourt and the new queen’s room for speedy eommunication of the good news. Obviously, the king loved iis new wife more than the others. The other queens became jealous, suspicious, and ‘cliquish. They engineered a plot to make the king hate the new queen. They used to secretly pull the rope frequently; and the king had to rush only to find nothing. When, however, the first son had been born and the rope was pulled, the king did not rush immediately. The, mother was lying unconscious, and the father was absent; in the meantime the clique threw the baby into the Gomati River and reported to the father that the mother had given birth to. a toad. The father became frustrated. Next lime, the clique committed the same tricks. It continued for several times on seven occasions. All sorts of low whisperings and wild rumours were afloat. The king could not show his face. The new queen became the victim of jealousy & hatred. The king ordered to drive her out of the palace. The exiled queen had to live a wretched life. There was an expression of despair on her face. A sudden rush of memories would often leave her melancholic. The elder sister, carried off earlier by the river-god, had a shelter inside the river. She recognised the seven children to be her sister’s babies, and brought them up and nursed them. Years passed on. The babies grew to childhood. The elder sister narrated the history time and again. The tale of their sufferings was heard. She used to sing a song so pathetic that it would bring tears to their eyes. The seven brothers, stung to madness by a sense of

wrongs, sat down together and drew up a scheme of vengeance. For seizing an opportunity of revenge, the seven brothers started frequenting the river ghdat from which the king’s maid servants used to fetch water. At sunrise on the appointed day, they flocked together to Folk Tales of Tripura 115 eee the special ghdt. The seven brothers broke the seven earthen jars of the seven royal maid servants. The maid servants angrily brought new jars from the royal store- house. The seven brothers again broke the jars. They cheerfully blinked at each other. The royal servants threatened to punish them and attempted to catch them, but failed. The children escaped all attempts of the servants. An altercation took place between the two sides. The servants became astonished to know the history, to know the conspiracy of their step- mothers. The servants reported it in various tones & intonation. The reports generated mixed reactions. The cliquish queen started shivering; their halcyon days were not fated to last long. The king and his well-wishers, fresh with hope, sat down to a discussion. On the king’s direction, the exiled queen was honourably brought back home; her dress was torn and ruffled; her hair dishevelled, her body weak and ugly. Suddenly she became restless & remembered many things. Within an hour hundreds of people thronged; the crowd and the royal parents went to the river ghdt and made an earnest appeal to the children to come out of the water. With permission and blessing from the foster-mother, the seven sons emerged from the water one by one and came running at them. The crowd shouted with joy. The parents took them in their lap. The riverine castle and the lady

were like their father & mother for years, far more important in their lives than their actual parents! Now, the riverine castle is almost empty, save for the lady, waiting and looking at the children! Amidst hue & cry, the wicked queens were immediately dragged to a temple and sacrificed, lest they might hatch new plot like poisoning food. They sulked & intrigued, plotted & perished. Folk Tales of Tripura 116 17. The Chhatim tree In the interior hills of Tripura there was a village where only the Tripuris lived. There were several households of them. Their main occupation was shifting _ cultivation on hill-slopes. The jum fields were scattered all around the hamlet. One day two young persons of a family went to work in their jum field. They were brother and sister. They had taken their morning meal at home, and took the mid-day meal in leaf-packet. The parents were ill; the grandmother was very old. So, the brother and the sister went together to weed, nurse, reap and guard the crops. They worked together, gossiped, became tired and hungry. They had earlier built a small hut (= Gairing) for watching and resting. Now, they took rest there and ate the mid- day meal. They resumed their work. While going back home in the afternoon with vegetables, leaves, roots, etc. they used to bathe in a stream. Such was their daily routine for about a week, while their sick parents lay in bed. One day, the sister was bathing in the stream, and the brother had a momentary peep. The sylvan and solitary atmosphere further kindled the passion of the young brother. They worked together, watched the sky,

warded off the birds, smelled the mud and bathed for about a week during the absence of their parents. So far, the brother and the sister were on kindly and respectful terms. The peeping perplexed him. Something unusual & unsocial crept in his mind. However, the evil had not its wild outburst at the moment. He became serious and silent and a little abnormal. He did not eat that night. It was embarrassing to the elders of the family. The elders did their best to make the boy speak. He adamantly refused to speak a single word. The elders continued their efforts for hours and made all sorts of kind proposals to him. He was asked whether he would Folk Tales of Tripura 117 _ ——eeeeeesSSSSSSSSSSsSSsS—sSs like to eat this or that type of food, vegetables, rice, fruit, fish or meat? whether he would like to have any dress or ornament? whether he would like to have a visit outside? whether he would like to have the company of his friends? He obstinately refused to speak a word in reply. The elders made their last proposal. He was asked whether he would like to marry? At this proposal, he stared at them and showed a slight emotion. So, they proposed the names of many girls. But he repeatedly said: No, No. Ultimately, the name of the sister was uttered. Now, he nodded. It was to his liking. It was his only condition. He even seemed gay. But the elders were horrified. How can they agree? It was unsocial, uncommon and unthinkable. The elders became puzzled, confused and troubled by the boy’s strange attitude. Does not that condition alone go far to

prove the boy’s abnormality? Will it get the approval of the village council? What would be her reaction, if she were once made aware of it? As a stopgap arrangement, the elders of the family secretly gave consent and assured to make necessary arrangement during the next winter season. Days passed, months passed. The family apparently continued its normal life. The matter was kept confined to four members: parents, grandmother and the boy. The girl had gone to her bed and fell asleep at the last moment of compromise. Initially she became annoyed, but she could not anticipate such an extremely unsocial desire. Disgusted with the brother’s silence, she retired for rest. After a few months, the grandmother was engaged in drying the rice and other crops in the courtyard. The grand-daughter was engaged inside in cooking. The parents and the boy went to the fields. In the meantime one cock was frequently coming and eating rice unless closely watched. The hungry cock taxed the patience of the old lady. In soliloquy the old woman murmured: Cock, Folk Tales of Tripura 118 how long will you disturb me? We shall sacrifice you on the occasion of the marriage between my grandson and grand-daughter. The grand-daughter overheard it. She came forward and fervently saught an explanation. Now, the girl became extremely socked. She started weeping. The neighbours came to console her. By that time, the parents and the boy came back home. All sorts of strange rumours were now flying about the family and comments were being made on the extraordinary behaviour of the boy. There was a tall Chhatim tree (Alstonia scholaris) in front of the village. In the shade of it, a group of the

village boys used to play games. The girl ran away and climbed the tree, and mounted branch by branch to the top. The villagers followed, but could not catch her. They made all sorts of appeal and proposal to convince her. Birds and animals were sacrificed. The youths clenched their fists, and gnashed their teeth against the boy. On the direction of the village elder, the boy was sacrificed. Suddenly, the soul of the boy turned into a chameleon. The chameleon climbed the tree. The girl climbed the top of the tree and prayed to god fora heavenly abode. The prayer was granted. To help her in ascending, the tree temporarily became very tall. She broke the top branches of the tree, so that none could climb after her, and accompanied the god. | The boy often shoots his arrows to hurt the girl. The rain is her tears and the lightning is her cry. The boy loved and lost his life. This is why the chameleon becomes red whenever it encounters a human being. And this is why the top of the Chhatim tree is flat : twigs springing from several stems form a flat surface, an unvel. 18. The queen’s self-sacrifice A benevolent king lived in Tripura. His face had the expression of determination. He was indeed a statesman. Folk Tales of Tripura 119 The queen was pious and kind-hearted. A fine row of strong white teeth would be seen at the moment of her smile. In a certain part of the kingdom, there was no big tank of water. The subjects brought it to the notice of the king. The king gladly arranged to dig a large tank

there. But there was no water in it, though it was big and deep enough. Not only the villagers, but also the king and the queen were in great disappointment. One night, the king had a very sad dream. One deity foretold : If the queen is sacrificed, water will come up; if the queen slowly and solemnly walks towards the centre of the tank, water will emerge. But the queen will have to submerge herself. No attempt should be made to rescue her. At dawn when the king awoke, he wondered: How can I make such a sacrifice? How can I disclose it? How can I come out of the trouble, out of the dilemma? The king was in great despair. He summoned his friends, advisers and ministers to his council. The councillors were divided in their opinion. The issue was so delicate that no body dared to give clear opinion. Anyway, the queen guessed it and came to know the problem. She gladly volunteered to sacrifice herself. For the welfare of the subjects, she was ready to die. At last, on the direction of the king, the royal astrologers ascertained an auspicious date. On the appointed date, thousands of villagers got assembled on the bank of the tank. The worship of the Ganga-devi was arranged. No animal was sacrificed. The priests and ministers reached there earlier. The air was rent with shouts of praise in honour of the king and the queen. Amidst agony and applause, surprise and suspense the elephants carrying the royal family reached the bank of the tank. The members of the royal family discended confidently and cautiously amid the bustle of preparations for the tragedy.

Folk Tales of Tripura 120 The local residents became extremely sorry for the demand of digging the tank. Their repentance knew no bound. They lay down and wept. The agony hayinted them. Many faces were bedewed with tears. They felt their nerves straining. But the king and the queen remained absolutely calm and quiet. The king did not punish the subjects. The queen did not curse the villagers. Instead, the king and the queen blessed and pacified the people. Now the moment came for the queen to walk alone, to go ahead alone. The king stood like a stone! what a heavy weight on the head that wears a crown! The supreme moment was one of silence of a graveyard! The chief priest led the queen. The final parting! Knowing fully well that death is inevitable, the queen remained steadfast. She gave a look around solemnly! She did not jump; she simply waded placing her feet carefully, so that she would not slip. The moment she had stepped in, water started oozing out from the four sides of the tank. Gradually and gradually, her feet, ankles, legs, knees, waist, head went under water. She was no longer seen! Thousands of spectators thronged, stood in groups, whispered, sat with their hands clasped round the knees or with their legs stretched before them and shouted: Maharani! long live, long live! The sanctity of the tank, hallowed by the sacrifice of the queen and the magnificence of the temple on the eastern bank of the tank and the temporary residence of some kings and officers of Tripura there, made it an object of veneration throughout Tripura. Pilgrims and tourists come here to offer their devotions. The tragic tank

henceforth came to be known after her name! 19. A Monkey & a Girl In the interior hills of Tripura there was a village where only the Tripuris lived. There were 126 households of them. The village was located on a hill. It was Folk Tales of Tripura 121 surrounded by the fields of shifting cultivation. One day seven girls of the village went together to the fields and found a number of monkeys relishing the crops and damaging the fields. The girls became very angry. The youngest girl went ahead and hounded the accompanying dogs to drive away the monkeys. The dogs, barking loudly, drove the monkeys away. The monkeys decamped. There was a tall tree in front of the field; chief of the monkeys was sitting there and observing the situation. The chief decided to take revenge against the youngest girl. ; The girls spent hours in the fields, singing, weeding, nursing the plants and reaping some vegetables. The real touch of Tripura is to be found in the hills and rural villages. There the hum of insects and chirp of birds constitute a part of life.. There is an abundance of greenary and granary. In the afternoon the girls with their crops put inside their baskets turned their steps homeward. On their way back home, about a hundred feet below a stream rolled along. The shadows of trees on all sides of the spring and the stream made the place cool, gentle, hospitable and solitary. Putting the clothes on a branch of a tree, the girls were. bathing and sporting. In the meantime, the monkeys were watching the movements of the girls. While the girls were frolicking,

the monkey-chief silently swooped down, took the clothes and ran away. After bathing, the girls came ashore and did not find their clothes. They became confused, frightened and nervous. A shame indeed! They walked a little and stood in the shade of a swaying and dripping tree and looked all around. At last they found the monkeys sitting high above on the branch of a tall tree, and the clothes were blowing a little in the wind. The girls cried, wept and made earnest appeal. Ultimately, the eldest girl placed a portion of her crops on a cavity of the tree. One monkey climbed down with Folk Tales of Tripura 122 her clothe, took the crops and dropped the clothe. The second girl surrendered some crops and got back the clothe. Thus, the first six girls got back their clothes one after another. But when the seventh girl went to give up the vegetables, the chief of the monkeys suddenly twitched and kidnapped her. The girls tried their best to pacify the monkeys, but failed. They hurried back home and reported the matter. The villagers came to the spot with sling and bow & arrow. By that time, the monkeys fled and retired in deep and distant forest. The villagers returned with a heavy heart. With the distance of time & space, wild imagination went on increasing in volume and volubility. The chief of the monkeys married the girl. In course of time, she gave birth to a baby. The baby was named Tate. The monkeys used to collect edible fruits and vegetables for their new queen. But she detested them from the core of her heart. She was longing to escape.

She had to wear a mechanical smile. Now, she pretended to be pregnant again and wished to eat hog-plum, a rare fruit at that time. All attempts to search out the fruit failed. One day the chief himself went out. She took that opportunity to escape. The chief returned empty-handed and found the cottage too empty. He sat down watching the path along which she would come. But she did not return. The chief and other monkeys became very anxious. They wandered in the forest and asked all. At last one person admitted to have seen a mother and a child moving along a certain path. The chief followed the path, grew weary, sat down to rest and ultimately reached the distination. He became happy to see his wife and son. He held his dear son on his lap and the son’s slim legs were Swinging. He exchanged a look with the parents- in-law. The young boys and girls of the village were about to Folk Tales of Tripura 123 kill the monkey-chief. But the girl’s father pacified them and advised them to wait. In honour of the son-in-law, the father of the girl arranged a small ceremony. The elders of the village were invited. They sat down to that unusual rite of drinking rice-beer. But they cast a mistrustful glance at the exceptional guest. The son-in- law sipped cheerfully; his face was flushed. She poured him one after another jar of rice-beer. Heavily drunk, the monkey-chief lay unconscious and fell asleep. When the family was safely asleep, she got up very quietly and widened the crevice of platform of the hut. Below the platform, pigs & swines were sheltered as the usual

practice. The monkey-chief slipped and fell below and the swines rushed to tear the monkey-chief into pieces. 20. Punish the original criminal In a hilly hamlet lived a few families of shifting cultivators. One day one shifting cultivator went to the clearing and cut down bushes & shrubs. While returning home in the afternoon, he bathed in a stream and sharpened his knife seating on a stone in the stream. His knees were below the water-level; a prawn slowly advanced to whimsically bite the cultivator. Being upset by the pain, the cultivator instantly cut the top end of a bamboo which stood curved because of the weight of the leafy twigs. Unburdened, the bamboo quickly stood straight and hit a squirrel. Being restless by the pain, the squirrel jumped from branch to branch and found a big fruit. The squirrel rushed to eat the fruit. The fruit slipped and fell on a deer: Being afraid, the deer fled recklessly. In the wilderness, many leaves lay thick upon the ground. Decomposed leaves in a humid soil provided ideal shelter to many types of insects and ants. The deer, while running swiftly, had to tread the nest of the ants. Being very annoyed, the ants moved up and down Folk Tales of Tripura 124 Oe a ee ihe adjacent places, plants & trees. The ants found a bat resting on a shadowy branch of a tree. Being terrorized, the bat fled and took refuge inside (he big ear of an elephant. The elephant lay asleep on a high hill full of stones. Being confused, the elephant hastily stood awake and jerked the ears and kicked out a stone. Being dislodged, the stone rolled and rolled and fell

on a hut several feet below. The inmate of the hut was an aged widow. . Chaudhuri : Bat! why did you enter into the ear of the elephant? Bat : Beacuse the ants bit me. Chaudhuri : Ants? why did you bite the bat? Ants : Because the deer trod us. Chaudhuri : Deer! why did you tread the ants?

The Frog’s rumour about Kolkata & trials In a certain rural village lived a rich farmer. It was a traditional joint family of at least three generations. The magnificent buildings, straight and broad streets, cars, crowd, the dazzling pomp of the visit of the dignitaries appealed to the sensibilities of the children of countryside. When they used to go back home on Folk Tales of Tripura 126 liolidays, the aged people and neighbours were eager to know the stories of Calcutta. The old frog too was very

attentive in listening the conversation. In those days, the representative guides from the lirtha-Kshetras like Gaya, Kasi, Vrindaban, used to visit ihe villages of the country for the pilgrimage of the villagers. The family of the farmer decided for a pilgrimage of the elderly persons of the family. An auspicious day in the month of Aswin (September-October) was fixed by (he astrologer. On the appointed date a number of elderly persons under the guidance of the Panda started their journey. The anecdotes of Calcutta drew forth excitement in the mind of the frog. This unexpected and sudden incident was very troublesome to the adjutant stork. The adjutant stork started groaning. The adjutant bird was perching on an adjacent tree. A monkey was eating a Cindra (= a kind of fruit grown in the jum field). The monkey suddenly heard the cry of the

adjutant bird. The monkey became nervous. The fruit slipped out of the hand of the monkey. Folk Tales of Tripura 127 In the shade of the tree in which the monkey had been roosting, a female deer was taking rest. The deer was pregnant. The fruit fell suddenly on the back of the deer. It caused severe pain; the deer ran in pain and fear. A long and large python was lying in sleep in the forest. The innocent deer had no intention to trample any living being. She was simply running. The fowl, out of grief, started scratching recklessly. In the wilderness, many leaves lay thick upon the ground; no body cared to take them up. The ants rushed and started to bite a swine. The wild swine was sleeping at that time. The attacks by hundreds of ants made the swine restless. The swine ran and ravaged the crops of a shifting cultivation. The shifting cultivator lodged a complain against the swine. The Chaudhuri of the village summoned the swine and asked questions. Chaudhuri : Swine ! why did you ravage the crops? Swine : Because the ants bit me. Chaudhuri : Ants ! why did you bite the swine? Ants : Because the fowl ravaged our shelter. Chaudhuri : Fowl ! why did you ravage the shelter of the ants?

Deer : Because the monkey dropped a heavy fruit on my back. Folk Tales of Tripura 128 Chaudhuri : Monkey ! why did you drop the fruit? Monkey : Because the adjutant bird cried out so loudly! Chaudhuri : Adjutant bird ! why did you cry out? Adjutant bird : Because the tailor bird entered into my mouth. Chaudhuri : Tailor bird ! why did you enter into the mouth of the adjutant bird? To punish the guilty, salt and chilli were besmeared on the body of the frog; and then the frog was held fast with a jackfruit tree. The frog, out of pain, rubbed his body against the tree. This is why the body of the frog is prickly; and the Indian toad’s skin is rough and warty. Some city-made news & views puzzled the frog ! 22. The bird had the advantage of moving through the air swiftly & freely. lsut the frog was confined to a small, dirty & muddy place. bird had an air of condescension. To outwit the friend, the frog planned to undertake long & tedious journey to the medieval capital city of Tripura. One fine morning in an early winter, the frog went out from the marshy place. It took many days to complete the journey. The farther the the frog walked, the stranger was the scenery. In the course of the journey, the frog gained a lot of experience and information, At last, the frog returned safely. Meanwhile, the journey became a topic of common Folk Tales of Tripura 129 discussion. A little later many neighbours visited the traveller, and the traveller elaborately described the memories of the journey. They spent many evenings thus & discussed the news. Being pressed by the bird to convey any serious information, the frog expressed a great anxiety and after a pause, a moment later, disclosed the forecast of sad news of a terrible cyclone in near future. A horrible cyclone accompanied by hailstorm, heavy shower, earthquake, deluge & darkness, will leave everything disordered & shattered. The frog became buoyant & cheerful with the opportunity of displaying his experience. The frog next said: Iam convinced about the inevitability of the calamity and so I am thinking of taking refuge inside a bomboo pipc. But I am worried about your safety. Where will you go & reside? The Tailor-bird said: Friend! kindly give me an advice. The frog said: Friend! do one thing; at the very beginning of the ensuing cyclone, you are to move eastward, and up in the mountains you will find the Rabdng bird perching on a branch of a big tree. The Rabdang bird will keep its mouth wide open; you are to enter into the mouth

of the Rabdng bird. After a few months, the cyclone started blowing from the Bay of Bengal in south-west. A howling gust of wind rode menacingly across the countryside of Tripura. It struck cruelly. According to the advice of the frog, the bird quickly moved eastward and found the Rabang bird. Without any delay, the Tailor-bird entered into the wide mouth of the Rabdng bird. Being surprised, the Rabang bird screamed with a shrill cry. Something very serious had happened. At that very moment a monkey was climbing up the tree with a gourd in his paws. The sudden screeching cry of the Rabdang bird struck terror in the mind of the monkey. The gourd abruptly fell on the back of a deer. The deer was frightened and stood perturbed and ran away frantically. Folk Tales of Tripura 130 Tripura abounds in ants, leeches, mosquitoes, gnats, insects, snakes, etc. While scampering off in panic, the deer trod a snake. The snake was seriously injured. The mobile snake now became immobile. Near the hole of the snake, there were bushes & layers of fallen leaves. It was an ideal resort for ants. It was the dwelling place of the Arali ant (= Orali piprda). They belong to a specific group; they are reddish, aggressive, active, & poisonous; their stinging causes acute pain. Unable to move & hunt, the snake devoured the eggs of those ants. The ants became very angry and revengeful. They swarmed and stung a wild boar. The thrust of numerous stings into the flesh of the boar caused acute pain and disease. The testicles of the boar were badly affected. With the swollen testicles, the boar became unable to

move freely. An old widow had her paddy field near that mountain. (he poor boar struggled to collect food, walked limpingly and found ‘the widow’s paddy field. It was the nearest and the only source of food. So, the boar consumed a lot of paddy. The old widow was living in her hut alone. The wild beast would ruin her. She beat her forehead. But she must drive away the beast by frightening. To scare the depredator, she set up a scare-crow, and also a scare- flutter; but in vain. She had no time to continue the loss. Now she ventured to sit in the shade of a tree near the field and to beat the trunk of the tree, and to howl alternately. The innocent tree became annoyed and hurt. Unable (io bear.the pain, the tree made a representation of its pains to the royal court. The complaint was against the widow. The royal court admitted the complaint with the - calmness of a benevolent patriarch. There must be some way of finding out, of proving the fact. The court soon Folk Tales of Tripura 131 -_-_-eee———————— sent the royal pdik & peyaddad to summon the widow. Walking tedious tracks & dingy paths, sometimes with ascension & descension, the pdik & peyadd reached the residence of the widow, and brought her to the royal court. The king seated, and the paik & peyada standing with weapons and the widow standing with folded hands. She looked sad & helpless. The king asked: Did you beat the treer The widow answered: Maharaj! I have beaten the tree, only to scare away the boar. The boar consumed my paddy. I should have a remedy for this. So, the boar should be

held responsible. The king’s pdaik & peyada summoned the boar. The king asked: Did you consume the widow’s paddy? The boar replied: Maharaj! I have consumed the widow’s paddy. Being stung by numerous ants, I have been seriously affected & diseased; for mere survival I ate her paddy. So, the ants should be punished. The king’s pdik & peyadad summoned the ants. The king asked: Did you sting the boar? The ants repiled: Mahdrdj! we stung the boar, because the snake devoured our eggs. We could not control our paternal affection. So, the snake should be punished. The king’s pdik & peyada@ summoned the snake. The king asked: Did you devour the eggs of the ants? The snake replied: Maharaj! I have devoured the eggs. An accident by stampede rendered me handicapped. One deer trod me. Henceforth, I am unable to move freely for my food. Therefore, the deer should be accused. The king’s pdik & peyadad summoned the deer. The king asked: Did you tread the snake? The deer replied: Maharaj! I have trodden the snake unknowingly. One big gourd suddenly fell on my back. Being afraid of a hunter, I frantically fled. So, the monkey, from whose paws the gourd was slipped, should be given a lesson. Folk Tales of Tripura 132 The king’s padik & peyadad summoned the monkey. The king asked: What had happened to you? The monkey responded: Maharaj! the Rabdng bird’s squall terrified & unnerved me; at that moment of confusion the gourd felt out of my hand, striking the deer as it fell. The king’s padik & peyadad summoned the Rabang bird. The king asked the Rabdng bird: What was the matter? The Rabang bird pleaded: Maharaj! one Tailor-bird

ghastfully entered into my mouth; it caused terrible suffocation. I was about to die. So, I had to squall. . The king’s padik & peyada summoned the Tailor bird. The king asked: What made you to infiltrate into the mouth of the Rabang bird? The Tailor-bird pleaded: MahGrGj! the frog warned me about a devastating cyclone and advised me to take refuge into the mouth of the Rabdng bird. He related to us the details of journey. He informed us that he was astonished at the grandeur of the capital & that he met with several people. The king’s padik & peyada summoned the frog. The king asked: What made you to warn the Tailor-bird so sternly and wrongly? The frog said: Maharaj! in course of my journey to the capital, I heard so many news & rumours. I explained those news to my neighbours & friends. The king said: But, cyclone, hailstorm, floods are annual affairs in Tripura. There is nothing uncommon. You have committed a crime by magnifying those news and by misguiding the Tailor-bird. The king ordered the pdik & peyada to beat the frog thoroughly. The others were acquitted & declared innocent. The exemplary punishment left a mark on the back of the frog: the frog became warty. 23. Sarma & Raima Siva, the primeval patriarch, had two sons, namely Sivrai and Hangrdai respectively. The patriarch duly Folk Tales of Tripura 133 bequeathed his very vast kingdom to his eldest son. He expected the prince to think and behave exactly like himself. Sivrai was a wise statesman. He was a benevolent king. His capability, justice and generosity became well- known. The kingdom became peaceful, and the subjects

became prosperous and grateful. The subjects used to exalt him highly. Security, justice, patronage and fraternity were the principal concern of the king. Sivrai was an ideal monarch. After a long period of successful administration, the monarch desired to select his successor. The monarch had two sons, namely. Ompreng and Dongukhrui. Ompreng was least interested in public administration; he was easy-going, otherworldly and gourmand. Dongukhrui was a practical man of affairs. So Sivrai duly bequeathed his kingdom to Dongukhrui. The new king was handsome & healthly, intelligent and active. Under his able leadership, the subjects were happy and loyal. The ruling principle of the king was to maintain law & order, and to leave the subjects least disturbed. Ompreng: was the priest of the village. He had two daughters & one son, namely Oaing Jangrima, Gring Jangrima, & Likai. The priest had to officiate the rites & rituals of this or that house of the big village. He had neither time nor inclination to look after his own family & farm. Likai was a mere child. So, the two daughters had to do all sorts of domestic jobs. All those families, during those days, had to derive much of their subsistence from the forest. They subsisted partly by collecting & gathering, and partly by food production & animal husbandry and crafts. Their technique of food production was the slash-and-burn method. Each family had to select a hillslope for clearing & planting. The jungles & bushes had to be cut down during the dewy season and left to dry for weeks & then burned in early winter. Folk Tales of Tripura 134 The two sisters had to undertake all the energetic

labour. For days after days they had to set out in the morning, to work in the field, to take the mid-day meal in the field and to return home in the afternoon. It was a daily trudge, as many neighbours had to do the same. Time passes very quickly & silently. The two sisters had now blossomed into youths. They were active, young & experienced; they had the fancies of girlhood. They did not take care to build a temporary hut of bamboos & timber & thatching grass on an elevated platform in the centre of the field from which to watch the crops. The hut (= Gdireng) was indsipensable to farming. But their father was indifferent to those requirements. They did hardly get anything at home. His temperance, his indifference to family affairs, his religious ferver, his devotion to the village affairs, endeared him to all, but caused troubles to the children. Here happened something never contemlpated by the father & the daughters. Dongukhrui posed himself as an able king. But his overlordship was a mere pose. He used to indulge in boastful talk. He was a braggart and shallow pretender to virtues. He looked at the elder daughter suspiciously; he could not resist the temptation to impress her with his splendour. He wanted to have her. But two considerations stood on the way: horror of incest, and noblesse oblige. The glamour was a wild & savage impulse. One day while the two sisters had been working in the field, a mighty thunder broke the stillness of the midday. The hopes of their comfort were damped by violent gusts of wind. They felt helpless. They were in dire peril.

here was no hut to take shelter in. A heavy rainfall was impending. And there came the anxious moment when the two girls had to seek assistance. The elder sister implored the forest-deity earnestly for making a hut; and for that act of benevolence she promised to marry the - benign benefactor. The feeling of security & the ownership which a hut would offer, were lacking. Folk Tales of Tripura 135 Dongukhrui lay hidden in the nearby forest; he heard the prayer. In the disguise of a snake, he rapidly built a hut. The two sisters were astonishingly watching the operation; and they took shelter in the hut. They hesitated for a moment. Thé elder sister held herself back from saying a word. She had the qualm of conscience to marry the snake; and that too so hastily! Her conscience prompted her to stick to the promise. The simplest ceremony of marriage took place then & there. The snake retired to the forest alone and stayed down there for a few days, unless there was something quite urgent to be attened to up there. Time went on; the two sisters continued their routine work as usual. In the dewy season, when the sun begins to lose its heat, and when the days get colder & shorter, the shifting cultivators of eastern India begin to select the the site and to cut down the bushes. The two sisters had to undertake all those oprerations. They used to carry packets of meal to the field and to eat the meal at noon. At the time of lunch, the younger sister had to invite the snake thus: Brother-in-law! lunch is ready, water is ready, come,come! In response to the

invitation the snake used to come, eat & drink and depart. For days after days, the lunch of two persons was being shared by three. So, the two sisters were being ‘reduced in bulk & weight. The young sister, in particular, was left smarting under a sense of fear & humiliation. She found it difficult to bear with it; how could a human love tolerate it! so, she decided to confide to her father. One day she got an opportunity; she confessed to her father all that had occurred. The father was imperfectly informed; he became very worried about the sad episode. His brother, in the disguise of a snake, took advantage of the crisis. It shocked him terribly. He became impatient & revengeful. He listened. He was dazed. A feeling of nausea, a dizziness clamped upon his chest & stomach; he was so utterly taken by Folk Tales of Tripura 136 i i surprise that for a moment he seemed to have reached the stage of collapsing by a sudden heart attack. One day the elder daughter fell indisposed. Disordered in health, she declined to go to the field. The father and the younger daughter went to the field, worked till noon and then climbed up the hut to take rest and to eat the lunch. As usual, the younger daughter invited the snake. The father was in ambuscade, hiding behind the door with a sharp knife to attack by surprise. The snake was about to cross the threshold, before the father had sprung upon the snake and cut the snake with one sweep of the knife. The father & the daughter dug a deep pit in the jungle and thrust the dead body into the

pit, and filled the pit with mud & leaves to effect a natural look. They thoroughly washed the hut. They came back home, bathed, changed dress and took the evening meal. They behaved quite normally, as if nothing had happened. The next day the two sisters resumed their job. At noon they stopped working for a while, climbed the ladder and settled themselves on the platform of the hut. Being directed by the elder sister, the younger sister invited the brother-in-law, & shouted to him! But no response! The elder sister became sad & suspicious, and wanted to know the mystery. The younger sister kept silent. The elder sister became restless; she climbed down the ladder (= Ydaklai) and walked up and down the field. She had a pet dog. The dog knew where the dead body of the snake had been stashed & buried. The dog drew her to that dark spot. She hurried across to the edge of the field. A few drops of blood fell there. The father had planted on the grave a small, bulbous shrub of the lily flower (= Khumpui,. The elder sister stamped up & down the spot and found her husband’s grave. The smell was there still. Now the mystery became clear fast. In a dreadful fear, she returned with all haste and gave the younger sister « sad look and then again went back to the spot. She spoke, as if, to him and answered. She stood cross-legged Folk Tales of Tripura 137 and waited and bewailed. Her tragic words reverberated thus: Khumpui has begun to bloom, Stream is rising in gloom! He is buried only here, Murder made him eternally dear!
