She had no fear for herself, for she was sincere at heart, full of love. The drops of blood profusely increased; the overflow was owing to the tears of Oaing Jangrima weeping for her husband. A strong current was flowing below her feet; soon the current was roaring below the waist and them below the chest, until at last she was carried away by the deluge. He desired & died. She loved & lost. The younger sister went down the steep track with a hurried step and followed the elder sister, and entreated her to return, but failed to convince her; she cried & shouted to. her! On returning from the tragic spot, the younger sister’s remorse was such that she felt herself unforgivable. She narrated it and fell unconscious. It was dreadful to think of the tragedy; the younger sister’s life at this period became distressful. She argued with herself continually and came to the conclusion that she herself had been partly resposible for the tragedy and that she should commit suicide. The more she thought of it the more she was convinced that suicide on her part was her only way to peace. Death and death only would be balm to the soul of the younger sister. Thus convinced, one day she comuaited suicide near that spot. A stream had already appeared on the spot out of the blood of the snake and out of the tears of the elder sister. The stream had been known as Sarma. Another stream now appeared nearby out of the tears of the younger sister. This stream came to be known as Rdimd. The two streams flowed nearer one another, formed a valley.

Folk Tales of Tripura 138 The two streams met and got united and the confluence came to be known as Gomati. And quiet flows the Gomatt. 24. Kanchanmala The alien hordes once threateningly moved towards the frontiers of Tripura, as they often had done, for plundering, ravaging, kidnapping and killing. In response, the forces of Tripura were being similarly concentrated. The feudal forces of Tripura had to leave family & field, and to move on foot and to wage hand-to- hand fight with some traditional weapons. The two opposite forces used to advance and to clash, sword against sword, stick against stick. On the occasion of crisis, when a massenger with a royal signal in hand, reached a village, a young man escaped and absconded. The absconder had his residence in the hills, and his wife’s name was Kanchanmala. They were married only a few months ago. They were very fond of each other. Kanchanmala was healthy, handsome, careful & confident. Their wedded life was happy. Every eye was fixed upon the couple. The neighbours used to visit them; they would receive them courteously. Kanchanmala’s husband’s elder brother was an employee in the royal administration. The elder brother was fascinated by the beauty of Kanchanmala. He was apparently on good terms with the couple. But he was secretly contriving to eliminate the younger brother. Meanwhile the news of the battle of Hachi Khung came. And the younger brother fled into the deep hills temporarily. The elder brother took it as an opportunity; he procéeded to turn the episode to his own advantage and to fish out of troubled water. He indirectly and remotely had informed the royal army officers, who sent

sepoys to arrest the absconder. He did it from the capital. Pulling the string from the distant capital, he posed to be a well-wisher of the younger brother & his wife. * Folk Tales of Tripura 139 Within a few days, one day in the early morning as soon as Kanchanmala had finished some domestic jobs, she saw the royal police standing around her house. A few constables were grouped in the village path, talking together and watching and their faces expressing a terror. She was surprised and shocked to see the besiegers. She cried out and said weepingly: We have been married the other day We have had a short time to stay. The holy pandal stands even to-day The sacred symbol is yet to decay. The bambooes used for pandal decoration Even now give our gardens protection. The king’s sepoys look like a flock of red hens The king’s spies look like a flock of white herons. Your elder brother is in royal administration From him seek a wise instruction It will be a strategy good To sacrifice a he-goat from the wood. Bow down to god, lie prostrate on sand With donation in both the hands. Meanwhile, encircling the house the sepoys advanced down to the staircase of the hut; the inmates were in a very critical tension. They called each to the other. The husband said: The sepoys have advanced upon the staircase for arrest How can I now flee into the deep forest? They will soon make a shout There is no way out. Oh dear! wipe out your tears Check your anxiety, your fear Give me a rice-packet for food Remain at home in a careful mood.

While several sepoys & spies stood encircling the house, a few of them climbed up and entered the hut, Folk Tales of Tripura 140 en and demanded soft mattress for sitting there on. The poor husband unfurled a nice mattress. Afflicted and harassed, Kanchanmala again uttered a few words thus: The nuptial perfume served like a magic spell. And still gives us pleasant smell. The remnants of the marriage feast are all seen The used banana leaves still remain green. The remanants of the sacrificial fire are all around Ashes, flowers, & fruits are to be found. A home-spun bed-cover did I keep On which we are yet to sleep How can I remain alone in the dale Take me with you along the vale. In the battle-field if your blood pour out past I will rest there for ever at last. Tears surged in the heart of the husband also. He tried to divert her attention with the words: We are gallantly marching westward For defending our motherland forward. We hold it our duty whatever befall It misfits that tears from your eyes fall. Holding a pole, you may be lost in thought Dry the wet clothes, the battle will be bravely fought. Holding a bamboo of the fire-place, you may be lost in thought Preserve the pots, to the aggressors a lesson will be taught. Ifyou need a brinjal, seek from the elder brother’s house If you need salt, seek from the elder brother’s house Ifyou need a pestle, seek from the elder brother’s house. These were the last words they spoke to each other. Then he departed along with the sepoys. At the army officer’s order he was sent to the battle-field in the

western frontier. There he fought and poured out his last drop .of blood. Mortally wounded, he breathed his last in the. battle-field of Hachi khung. All this the elder brother knew; he knew what had Folk Tales of Tripura 141 happened to his brother. He had one thing in his mind, and another in his speech and a third in deed. About two months had flown. Kanchanmala was very anxiously waiting for news. She did not go to the elder brother’s house for vegetables, spices and tools. Every day at dawn noises awoke her. Night after night she passed without sleep. When she awoke, she would find herself alone. She would walk up & down sadly and perform her jobs. She prepared a kind of country-liquor for her husband. After about two months of stay in the capital, the elder brother turned his steps homeward. As soon as he had reached the village, Kanchanmala rushed out and leered at him and entreated him to come to her hut first. She served him water and seat, and offered him as much ligour as he could drink. To each of her question, he evasively gave brief reply. He said: The brother has been stashed in a splendid building having elephant’s trunk-like towers. The elder brother did go back to his own home that day. What she would like to hear was avoided. Kanchanmala sat there in her house a long while motionless, thinking and thinking and expecting the return of her husband to-day or tomorrow! But why does the elder brother come to her house so frequently? It would be a shame; she retorted with disgust. She remained faithful to her husband. She gave the cunning

wooer a sour look. She was seething with a mental anguish. Bereft of will-power, but faithful to her husband, she passed her days looking to the path. Her eyes became . dull, skin wrinkled & clothes dirty. 25. Tragedy of a Noai bird Long ago in the hills of Tripura every after few miles stood a village of shifting cultivators. In a certain hamlet lived a family. The peasant and his wife used to clear a jungle and sow seeds. They had a son. When the son Folk Tales of Tripura 142 had become adult, the parents arranged his marriage. Now, leaving the responsibility of the household to the son and the daughter-in-law, the old parents started spending their time in devotional songs. But after a few years, the young wife fell ill and died leaving behind her only daughter named Khumti. The peasant married for the second time. The second wife gave birth to a daughter, named Karmti. Khumti was envious. Karmti was tolerant. The heavy work of cutting the jungles, burning, clearing, digging and sowing and bulding a small hut in the clearing would be done by the peasant and his wife. The villagers also helped one another in turn. Such was their collective consciousness in weal & woe. The two teen-aged sisters had the pleasure of going to the field along with other boys and girls of the village. While going and coming back, they used to sing, gossip, narrate tales and joke. The mothers used to cook at dawn, offer the first meal to the young band at home in the morning and patch the second meal in a bundle of banana leaf. One day in the morning Khumti and Karmti went

together to the field. Their duty was to weed the unwanted grass, scare the wild birds & animals, and pluck some ripe vegetables. Karmti did all these jobs faithfully, but Khumti was lolling, loitering and devouring the fresh fruits & vegetables like cucumber, melon, lady’s finger, etc. Khumti was least interested to fill the basket for the consumption of all. However, she was conscious to earn credit from the parents; so she demanded from Karmti some vegetables to be put in her basket and shown to the parents. Karmti first midly denied and afterwards flatly refused to give a portion of the collection. Because Karmti had not yeilded to pressure, Khumti became angry. “In the afternoon the two sisters were coming back home. Karmti was peddling with a basket almost full of ‘vegetables. Khumti was walking and thinking, plotting Folk Tales of Tripura 143 erecting Saas eae ee and devising. A big banyan tree stood by the side of a river; a swing was hanging from the tree. It was made by the boys. Khumti proposed to play in the swing to & fro. Karmti agreed and sat on the swing. Khumti was pulling & pushing at first gently and then violently. Losing the balance Karmti was tottering & trembling. She fell below to the river and sank. A big sheat-fish swallowed her. Khumti came back home alone with the basket of Karmti. The parents asked about Karmti. Khumti replied that Karmti was bathing in the river and would be coming soon. But the veteran grandparents became suspicious; they knew the character of Khumti. With a pretext of washing a dirty clothe, the grandmother went to the river; she sat on a stone and began to wash the clothe and to

observe the situation. Soon she heard a shrill; she became alert; again the shrill came. Karmti made repeated appeal from the belly of the sheat-fish. Being sure, the grandmother shouted to the grandfather & others. They pulled the fish to the bank, cut it open and brought out the girl just alive. Karmti narrowly escaped. It was like a rebirth. It was a serious shock. She narrated the whole episode. The character of Khumti was now completely exposed; she lost all credibility. All the villagers distrusted & disliked her. Words had failed. Her arogance, her rudeness made many enemies. In her despair, Khumti retired & sat in a corner and wept. Khumti’s father made a big basket, kept her inside the basket and closed it tightly. No body was allowed to rescue her. She was crying, weeping, painting and sobbing. The villagers came and saw her with squint eyes from a distance. She went on beating her forehead. But nobody dared to prevail upon the strong instruction of the father. It was only Karmti who would stealthily offer a little of food & water & that too rarely. Imprisonment continued for a few days. All hopes of pardon were vanished. The heart-broken prisoner, Folk Tales of Tripura 144 crushed by disillusionment, shut herself up and became almost a recluse. She had lost her mother; she had no sympathetic nursing; now she was alone, forlorn. Her eccentricity, her abnormal behaviour became very marked. She became a hater of human beings. Henceforth, she stopped to solicit any sympathy from the people; she looked up following the flight of the Nodoi birds. They were wild birds; they would never come close to man; they would not trust any man.

Khumti approached the Nodoi bird for support and sympathy. The birds took pity on her. They came in a flock and roosted on the branches of nearby trees and started offering feathers, bill, nail, etc. Now, Khumti turned into a bird, the Nodoi bird. She broke basket, came out and flew above. She became one of the flock of birds. The birds received and welcomed her. She angrily left lor ever with a vow of never again seeing the face of the relatives! The villagers came out of their respective huts & houses & looked up. Karmti earnestly requested; and tears rolled down her face. But Khumti remained adamant and blessed Karmti for her amiableness. The birds soared higher & higher and took a long flight to some distant, unknown forest. Their honking was no longer heard. 26. Princess Phulkumari There was once upon a time a king who had been ruling Tripura with Rangamati as his capital. The king had a beautiful & lovable daughter named Phulkumari. The king used to remain busy with administrative problems. When Phulkumari was grown up, the king looked at her one day, and ordered to arrange her marriage soon. His councillors became busy to find out a suitable bridegroom. Through the police & other agencies, the whole kingdom was informed. At last, one handsome and brave youth was found. He rejoiced that he would get Folk Tales of Tripura 145 such a beautiful princess. The youth was brave, but obstinate. The wedding was celebrated with great pomp & pleasure. The royal palace was located on a hill on the north bank of the meandering river Gomati. About five miles to the south of the palace was thetseat of the famous

Tripureswari Mata mandir on a hill. In between the palace and the temple, a site was selected and a beautiful residential house & garden etc. were made for the princess & the son-in-law. Things were going on happily with the new couple. And the king was facing problems & problems and waging battles. The soldiers of Tripura were pouring out their blood like water in the battlefields in the Meghna Valley. Here in the Meghna Valley, the fate of Tripura was decided many times. To commemorate a victory in such a fierce battle, the king decided to dig a large tank near the residence of the new couple. A large number of labourers from Chittagong., Noakhali and other areas of the Meghna Valley were summoned and engaged during the winter season. The work had to be completed within the next January. Hundreds of labourers with their hoes were working, cutting & digging day & night. The king made magnificent preparations & costly arrangements for the food & lodging of the labourers. The tiny huts in temporary sheds huddled almost together in rows, thronged with diggers, wood- cutters, earth-cutters, cooks, suppliers of rice & vegetables. Their joyous jokes & conversations produced reverberations. It was a spectale of chivalry. But those happy & chivalrous days were destined to a dramatic interruption. The straight boundary-lines of the large tank were to touch or rather to encroach a portion of the residence of Phulkumari. The son-in-law raised objection. The work was temporarily stopped. The supervisor informed the minister; the minister informed the king. The king had a mind to make a suitable Folk Tales of Tripura 146 I alternative house for the daughter; but the king was firm

in his decision to dig the tank there. The son-in-law was informed accordingly. The labourers obeyed the king’s order and resumed the work in full speed. The labourers & diggers saw the son-in-law standing and went on cutting & dumping earth. When, therefore, the son-in-law had seen that there was no longer any hope of diverting the royal decision, he resolved to sit down on the spot and said: Bury me here, bury me here! Without much ado, he went down to the spot & sat down headlong. The labourers dumped earth over his body. He died then & there. The son-in-law is dead -- was the voice of the diggers & labourers gathered round there. Phulkumari at once rushed to the palace. Overcome with grief and impatience, Phulkumari after acccusing her father, jumped into the water of the river Gomati and died there. The mournful king ordered to complete the work and to name the village after the name of the princess. 27. The tragic fate of Nakha In Tripura’s eastern mountainous region where the density of population was thin, where hamlets were few and far between, where the wild beasts would growl and the birds would chirp and fly about the sky, the stature of the hills people was dwarfed by mountains, rivers, forests and wild animals. In that region on a hill stood a hamlet inhabited by a few families of the famous Tripuri community. It was the only human settlement for miles around. In such a place very few people would remain out of doors after evening. The village foot-paths were narrow & zigzagged with ups and downs. There was a long stream adjacent to the

hamlet and about one hundred feet below the hilltop. The stream had its origin to a very distant mountain.Those ‘peasant families had their jum fields on hill-slopes all around the hamlet. The hamlet would be looked after by Folk Tales of Tripura 147 eer eee a council of elders headed by a Sardar. The name of the Sardar was Chhamprai Sardar. His wife’s name was Khulumti. The couple had a son named Naguray. Chhamprai Sardar was a capable & wise leader. Khulumti was a kind-hearted & steady woman. Naguray was bold & chivalric. - Like any other Tripuri village, this hamlet too had an ojhai (priest as well as physician). In case of any rite and ceremony, disease & death, his service was essential. The ojhai had his wife and a son and a daughter in his family. During the rainy season, one day in the early morning Naguray went to the jum-field for weeding and nursing the plants & crops. After a few hours, Naguray’s mother Khulumti went down to the river- ghat for fetching water. The river was flowing along a long gorge; on both sides cliffs rose like high walls. Suddenly, Khulumti saw something queer, odd and strange floating in the river. Immediately, she exclaimed and cried out and invoked Naguray. The son rushed to the spot and plunged into the water and came out with the body of a young girl. Quickening their pace, the mother and the son rescued the unconscious girl and placed her in the open verandah of their house and summoned the ojhai. The ojhai surveyed the body carefully and examined the pulse and opined that the girl was not yet dead; he administered certain

herbal medicines and expressed a faint hope of her survival. The neighbourhood was ringing with hue and cry. Khulumti watched the girl patiently. The morning wore on to noon, and noon to evening; but the girl did not open her eyes. Khulumti lay awake long hours that very night. The next day in the forenoon the girl opened her eyes and beheld before her an unknown assemblage of anxious villagers. Khulumti offered a quantity of liquid food. Slowly and steadily she was restored to her natural condition. Making some discreet inquiries, Khulumti came to know Folk Tales of Tripura 148 a a a the name of the girl : her name was Nakhapili. She was an orphan. She lost her parents while she had been a baby. Her uncle and aunt nurtured her. Nakhapili (alias Bijali) was found to be quite smart, efficient and amiable girl. She was quite reserved in her conduct and obstruse in her mind. She became an asset to the new family. The ojhai’s daughter Papti and Nakhapili were of the same age; they became friends. Papti assured that here Nakhapili would get food and shelter, compassion and friendliness. Khulumti had no daughter; so, she loved the girl like her own daughter. But the Sardar was anxious about the identity and any possible complexity; on his behalf a search was made, but no trace was forthcoming about the whereabouts of the girl. Khulumti was deadly against the idea of handing over the girl to the hand of her relatives. The Sardar submitted to the strong determination of Khulumti. She said : I do not want such a charming & capable girl leave us. All these made the new home as delightful as the

fullmoon night. Gentility of the Sardar, affection of Khulumti, magnanimity of Naguray, friendliness of Papti, apparently convinced Nakhapili about her safety and security here. Still she would sometime sit silent in solitude with heart heavy with sob & sigh. Now and then joy and sorrow would overcast her countenance. Khulumti’s cooling words would have a soothing effect upon the mind of Nakhapili. One day Khulumti lay on the bed, propped up by a pillow behind her; Nakhapili lay with her head on the lap of Khulumti. Nakhapili went on narrating her tragic experiences : the death of her parents made her dejected. Her uncle and aunt looked after.her. She had to perform most of the domestic chores. But the cruel aunt used to offer her a rotten & stale food; and to rebuke her at the slightest mistake. Nakhapili was, as if, encircled by thorny bushes and poisonous plants. Her inward torments were pitiable. So one day Nakhapili attempted to commit suicide. Khulumti tried Folk Tales of Tripura 149 to make light of the sad experiences and to soothe her nightmarish sufferings. Still, there was need for Nakha to be careful & dutiful; others little knew the strain the situation put upon an orphan, destitute girl! One day Nakha saw a half-dead unfledged nestling helplessly twitching in a puddle; she brought the tiny bird & nursed. But its death alterted Nakha! A foreshadow! After the lapse of some months, Nakhapili got herself almost thoroughly adjusted with the new family. Nagu and Nakha never separated from the company of one another. They passed time as the two loving friends. The Sardar and his wife were happy to see the friendship. One day Khulumti bespoke to her husband : Hear me,

what I tell you in good earnest; I like to arrange the marriage between Nagu and Nakha. I hope you will not raise any objection. The Sardar answered : I see neither any evil nor any good, of accepting your proposal; so you are at liberty to do as you like. But do not make any haste. The Sardar, who had been smoking tobacco & listening with a pleasant smile, was hesitant. After this discussion, a few months rolled away. One day during the rainy season, the young boys & girls decided to go deep into the forest to collect wild vegetables and bamboo saplings (= Muiya). While proceeding in the early morning with packets of food, baskets and knife, they were frolicing, frisking, singing, gossiping, whispering, whistling, flirting and flipping. They were blooming with youthful vigour. Meanwhile, Papti passed a comment : See, see! Nakha seems to be very beautiful, as graceful as the goddess of grace. Nakha at once replied by singing out one couplet from Yadu Kalija with delicate melody. Those were moments of ecstasy for all of them. By a skillful distortion & manipulation words, Chatungray entertained the team. After a few hours of journey, they entered deep into the forest and started collecting vegetables. Nagu and Nakha too started gathering; they, however, maintained a little distance from each other. Folk Tales of Tripura 150 Nakha went down to a spring and washed her hands. There, hearing a hissing sound, Nakha became alert & observant. She saw a python advancing towards her only to devour her. Instantly she retreated, cried out and rushed towards Nagu and sobblingly took refuge in the bosom of Nagu. Setting her aside, Nagu too advanced

and with one sweep of his sharp, long curved, one-edged knife fatally crushed the snake. In response to Nakha’s outcry all the members of the team rushed to the spot and cut the snake to pieces. After the incident, the team started on the return journey. While coming back, the young boys and girls highly praised Nagu for his courage. Papti and Anjakti went a step further & commented : Such a fit of courage was the precondition of marriage; Naguda twice gave prove of his courage; Nakha should consider it seriously. Nakha pinched Anjakti. The incident became the common topic of discussion for a few days. Khulumti henceforth did not allow Nakha to go into the wild forest for gathering. But that poignant moment epitomized a cooperative emotion in the minds of Nagu and Nakha. Her refuge in his bosom, her breath in his body filled his mind with a carnal sensation. Initially, Khulumti was essential to Nakha; and Nakha was essential to Khulumti. Now, Nakha was essential to Nagu; and Nagu was essential to Nakha. The two minds exquisitely coordinated. It was not utterable by speech. Prior to the incident, Nagu’s emotional mind and rational mind worked in harmony. After the incident, the balance between emotional mind and rational mind was a little disturbed. So, Nagu one day made a verbal outburst of his emotion. Nakha graced it with a meaningful smile. Now, Nagu’s eyes were shining with joy. ~Khulumti was adamant to keep Nakha here as daughter-in-law. The hesitant Sardar made the last ‘attempt of search; but no information was forthcoming. So, he yielded to the desire of his wife. Folk Tales of Tripura 151 Meanwhile, seasons changed. The spring season was

about to come. The Sardar and his wife, having decided to arrange the marraige, started discussion with the elderly persons. Having obtained their informal consent, the Sardar selected an auspicious date for formal discussion. It was the second half of Magh (=January- February). In the afternoon the villagers assembled and sat in four groups : the elderly males sat with the Sardar: the elderly females sat with Khulumti; the boys sat with Nagu; while the girls sat down around Nakha. It was the occassion of formal and final settlement of marriage proposal (= Kak chungmani). It was an occasion of drinking, joking, betel-leaf chewing, duet, gossiping, friendly exchange of words about life & love between the boys and the girls. The resonance was pleasing to the ears of the elders. It would resemble the famous war of words between the two birds (=Suk & Sari) about the qualities of Krishna & Radha. Hours passed thus. It was quitting time. The villagers returned to their houses. All the boys including Nagu went to the bachelors’ dormitory. The Sardar & his wife went to the bed. But Nakha in solitude sat silent and thoughtful: there was foul work afoot somewhere! The months of Magh (Janaury-February) and Falgun (February-March) were supposed to be very favourable for celebrating the marriage ceremony. Accordingly, arrangements were made in full swing to celebrate the ceremony. On a day of full moon, preferably in the Godholi Lagna, the young boys and girls were in eager expectation of seeing Nagu and Nakha in their bridal costume. So, they gladly did many things : collected vegetables, & banana leaves, bamboo and flowers, fetched water, decorated the bridal chamber, cooked food & curry, and swept the courtyard, etc..The

Achai (=priest) and the elders supervised the work. The Bhandari (=store-keeper) was supplying all essential things. | Folk Tales of Tripura 152 eee On the auspicious day, streams of relatives and guests were coming in the hamlet. The hamlet was humming with activities, laughing, gossiping and betel leaf chewing and smoking. In the absence of the parents of Nakha, the ojhai & his wife assumed the role of the parents of Nakha. Decoration of the bride and the bridegroom was going on separately. The priest and his assistants were busy with the worship of Lampra deity. A team of middle-aged persons became busy in cooking. The whole atmosphere was surcharged with joy and enthusiasm. Every thing was in good condition. Meanwhile, from a very distant hamlet a Jumia family came to attend the ceremony. The Jumia, his wife and their daughter Khumpoi travelled a long distance to attend the ceremony in the house of their distant relative. The Sardar’s cousin sister was long ago married to the elder brother of this Jumia. The cousin sister died giving birth to a baby. The cousin sister’s husband too died within a year. For nearly two decades social relations between the two families ceased to exist. Both sides remained away & aloof. But now getting an invitation from the Sardar, the Jumia decided to respond and renew the relations. The Jumia and his wife were given a hearty welcome with sweet words, drinking, betel leaf and fruits. The Jumia’s daughter went inside the house of the Ojhai to see the bride; she became a little surprised on seeing Nakha; but she told nothing there. She came back to her mother and whispered. The Jumia’s wife was a

villain-looking woman; she purposely strolled and walked into the ojhai’s house to verify the secret news. Apparently innocently she surveyed the bride quite minutely and became sure about the identity of Nakha; she returned silently and whispered the news to the Jumia; walking casually like a spy, the truculent Jumia pushed through a crowd for confirmation. The three members (=Jumia, his wife, their daughter) had been so cunning that others could not even guess the motive of their movement. They Folk Tales of Tripura 153 sat together and a wicked thought flashed through their minds. In their eyes, Nakha was no better than a Chikaljuk, a witch, a Daini, a Rakshashi! They decided to fish out of troubled water! Now the Jumia wanted to know from the Sardar the whereabouts of Nakha; he asked many questions; he was a pert. The Sardar frankly and freely narrated the incidents: how his wife & son rescued the girl, how his: wife’s and the ojhai’s treatment restored her to normal life, how a search was made to know her identity & ancestry, how Nakha’a amiable behaviour endeared her. After listening to the statement, the Jumia seriously commented : This marriage cannot be solemnised; Nakha is your cousin sister’s daughter; Nakha’s father was my elder brother; Nakha is your sister’s daughter; Nagu and Nakha are brother and sister. It was a bolt from the blue. The untimely disclosure stupfied the Sardar. After a while, he immediately summoned the ojhai and the village elders. It was a crisis; it demanded a solution. The elders sat to lay their heads together. Being summoned by the elders, the Jumia and his wife made an alternative suggestion : arrange

marriage between Chadaray’s son and the Jumia’s daughter. The village elders submitted to the cunning proposal. The new proposal of marriage was accepted & followed half heartedly. But the other side of the scene very pathetic. The shocking news electrified all. All the hopes were utterly damped. Khulumti sat to beat her forehead! Nagu threw away his bridal costume and lost the balance of his mind for sometime; he threw himself on his bed and tossed. Nakha, overwhelmed with grief, sat aghast and hid her face with her hands and set aside her bridal costume. The vilification and verbosity by the Jumia’s wife against Nakha disconcerted most of the guardians and guests. Some of them leered & some of them taunted. The boys and girls were about to run amuck and to punch Nakha. Folk Tales of Tripura 154 The Jumia family alone chuckled for being successful in cheating under the pretence of fair dealing. Afternoon wore on to evening, and evening to night. It was again quitting time. The villagers retired to their homes. The guests were accommodated in different houses. They all slept heavily. Nakha had to leave the house of the ojhai; she sat alone in a corner of the courtyard. In remorse she realised the agony of the tragic mess the Jumia family made of her life. Tears rolled down her cheek. She again fell upon the thorns of life and vortex of domestic politics. At dead of night Nagu silently came out of his room with his knife and a few pieces of clothe and woke Nakha, and convinced Nakha to elope with him immediately. They disappeared and vanished among the high hills and thick

jungles. All that night they travelled. At dawn they took shelter near a spring of water. Nakha cleaned up her muddy legs. Their legs were aching. They encountered dangers. Nagu went to an adjacent Jum and returned with a pile of fruits within half an hour. They attempted to get far away from the villagers. Walking was hazardous. They hid themselves there for the whole day. In the evening they resumed their journey. Thus, they alternately took rest and walked three nights and three days. On the morning of the fourth day they reached a far off place; they expected to live here an anonymous life. The place of their choice was a very high hill covered with thick forest. For about a week they had to live in an abandoned hut (=gairing) in an abandoned jum left fallow. They set to work clearing hillslope for cultivation. They started clearing a patch of the hilltop for building a hut. They perspired and suffered mosquito bites. For a few months Nagu had to walk a distance daily to work in others’ field for food. However, free from social ostracism, they happily passed here a considerable period of time as the two Folk Tales of Tripura 155 loving friends. They dwelt away and apart from other men. They would avoid visiting anybody’s house. So, nobody would know their whereabouts. Days and months rolled on. More than two years passed in that secluled, sylvan enviroment. The cool & calm atmosphere of the hilltop used to brace them up. They banked on the assumption that the long distance & hardship would be formidable obstacles to any search. But in Nagu’s parental home the atmosphere was gloomy. The morbid mother

could not, for a few days, take food for want of seeing the son. A search was made; the boys set forth to search all around; they moved up & down, here & there; but in vain. Slowly the tension was coming down. In Chadaray’s family a young boy of a distant hamlet was doing his ‘bride service.’ After two years of service (=jamai khata) in the bride’s' house, the marriage was solemnised. Now, Papti with her husband was scheduled to go to her father- in-law’s house. Papti’s brother and his friends accompanied Papti. It was more than two days’ journey on foot, they had to halt & take shelter in anybody’s house on the way. On reaching the destination, Papti’s brother took rest for a few days. In course of casual conversation with the new relatives, Papti’s brother came to know that a new, young Jumia had been living on a distant hilltop for the last two years. His whereabouts were unknown. There were woods and steep hills in the midst. However, he was of reserved nature. There was no dog barking, no baby crying, no buzzing, no noise.Nagu’s new place was very mountainous; here high peaks broke off abruptly into narrow, deep gorge; Nagu made a notched track along the slope of an adjacent cliff; Nakha had to haul in water from a spring far below; but the damp track would often render the footing slippery. On getting even an inadequate information, Chatungray & his friends, out of a spirit of adventure, the next day set out for the wearisome journey and on nearing the hill saw a hut on the summit. They scanned Folk Tales of Tripura 156

the area and saw a Jum field and a narrow path. While climbing up the hill, he loudly called out : Naguda! Naguda! look! whom have I brought to you! It was an uncanny surprise to Nagu & Nakha. Nagu & Nakha offered them cordial reception, and reminisced about the early days with the covillagers and talked about many familiar incidents. Nagu asked about the health of his parents. Chatungray passionately enticed Nagu to rejoin the people he had left. Nagu refused. The visitors left in the afternoon. Nakha sat alone and surmised an impending danger. Only Nagu was there to understand what Nakha had appraised, and to listen to her fears. On returning back home, Papti’s brother exploded the astonishing news. It was a great relief to Nagu’s parents and covillagers. They excitedly demanded to know where Nagu was. Within a week, Nagu’s parents and uncle, led by Chatungray, appeared there in the solitary, sylvan residence of Nagu & Nakha. From a little distance below Chatungray whispered : Naguda’s hut is on the top of this hill. It was a pathetic and touching experience to see the meeting of those people who had not seen each other for the last two years under tragic circumstances. An emotional current passed among them. Quickening her pace, Khulumti greeted the son with a hug and exclaimed with tears and cries : My dear Nagu! My dear Nagu! The Sardar, without losing patience with his son’s escape, without raising any voice in disgust, said : Nagu! Why did you stay away so long? Your mother could not, for a few days, eat food, and sleep. You and Nakha should go back with us. Separate arrangements

would be made for your marriage with a beautiful girl, and Nakha’s marriage with another boy. The pressure was personal & persistent. All suspected that Nakha was inauspicious, unlucky, a witch! They gave Nakha a very hard time, blaming, insulting and intimidating. Nakha grew silent; she offered fruits and water to all. Folk Tales of Tripura 157 The pressure continued for hours. Both social and psychological pressure were put upon Nagu. Nagu remained reserved for hours. At last, he spoke out. He refused to wimp out. He stood defiantly and said : I shall stay with Nakha here. Now all the anxiety and anger fell upon Nakha. All the elders grew very impatient and weary. Even though Khulumti was capable, she had a cruel and harsh side as well. With an aggressive grin, she devilishly fabricated the service rendered to Nakha. She swaggered and hurled insult after insult at Nakha. She attempted to bully Nakha into submitting to their proposal and said : You have seriously damaged our family. Is it good on your part? Nakha sat bewildered, confused and shocked. She had to put up with bitter teasing and severe scorn from the elders. Nakha silently tolerated all the blames and kept on thinking about her fate. — Looking down sadly, Nakha said : Mother! for your service and sacrifice, I am grateful to you. For all.the disaster I am responsible. Pardon me. You take back your son. "a The sun went down the horizon. Suddenly a gust of wind accompanied by heavy rain, thunder & lightning stormed the hill. Nakha perceived the arrival of the fateful moment. Quickening her pace, Nakha climbed down the hut and weepingly moved toward a shadowy

forest. Seeing that Nakha had left quickly for an unknown destiny, Nagu also followed her and cried out : Nakha! Nakha! Nakha, while running, lamented : I have no mother, no father, no brother, no sister, no kinsmen. A dreadful disaster will soon happen to me. If you come with me, it will cost ‘your life. You go back, go back! Nagu assured : No harm will befall on you. I shall see to it. Nakha! I can even lay my life for you. Nakha howled : I am unlucky. I am ill-fated. Nagu replied : I will go with you, I will die with you. Folk Tales of Tripura 158 Both of them broke into tears and jumped into a very deep & dark gorge. The cliffs & jungles echoed back their traumatic yell. The tragic fate followed her wherever she went. The heavy knife of fate schreeched down. There was scarcely any autumn or spring in Nakha’s life. Wherever she looked, she saw only despair & depression. Jamatia Folk-Tale 28. Parameswar Baba Garia’s ritual-tale Long, long ago in the interior hills of the eastern part of Tripura there was a big village of the shifting cultivators. There was a shifting cultivator named Laktaya in that village; his wife’s name was Hachukti. The couple had certain virtues like purity of heart, kindness, industriousness, sincerity, honesty & fellow-feeling. On that account, the villagers used to seek his aid & advice. The pious couple were held in high esteem by the neighbours. Though married about a decade ago, the couple had no child. It tormented their minds. It appeared to be an anathema. The man who did not distress any living being,

the man who did not plunder other’s wealth, the man who was god-fearing, had not been blessed with a child! The neighbours had sympathy for the couple; the elderly villagers, particularly the women, while gossiping, made a few suggestions. The husband asked: Then what is fit to be done? The elders replied: Adopt a son. Accordingly, on an auspicious day, with the consent of the village chief and the priest, a poor neighbour’s son was duly adopted. The couple though having no son during the earlier years of married life, were now happy to have a son, the couple started nursing, caring, loving and feeding the son with genuine affection. They would often hug the son lovingly & protectingly. Thus a good fortune came to the family in the form of the son. It was indeed a happy fate that an orphan child was brought to the warm hearts Folk Tales of Tripura 159 & loving arms of the couple who soon loved the boy as dearly as their own little one. But those happy days were destined to a dramatic interruption. Their hope crushed. The son fell ill and died after three years. The couple mourned at the death of their dear son. They tried their best to cure the boy: the ojhai sacrificed a hen, uttered spells and prayed to the deities. They grew weary of the son; they became quite indifferent to their health, food, rest & homework. They used to sigh deeply. Despair took possession of their hearts. With troubled minds, they spent about seven years, seeking a son from Brahma by the pure penances of an ascetic practised as an old tradition throughout the length and breadth of Bharat. After seven years of

penance (= Tapashyda), Brahma became pleased and revealed himself in a dream and blessed the couple and said: | myself shall soon come as your son, and after another three years two daughters will be born to your family. Now, they were overjoyed. The dream revealation became true. A divine son was born within a year, and after three years, the twin daughters were also born. The divine son was nick-named Gariya and the twins were named Mailungti and Khulungti. Right from his childhood, the boy was cheerful & mirthful, helpful & honest. He was never found to quarrel with others or to cheat others. Endowed with certain divine qualities, he was the leader of the children, and dear to all the villagers. His personal character was an ideal one. Admiration for his noble character continued © to grow. There was, however, one problem. The backbone of the boy was unusually stiff and inflexible. For that reason, some people used to call him Siyong Kaurak; and his parents addressed him as Nrisingha. In course of time, Narsingha was abbreviated to Nrisingha. Nrisingha was the protector Folk Tales of Tripura 160 of Bhakta Prahlad and the punisher of Hiranya Kasipo; Hiranya Kasipo was a devil and a hater of Hari. Year after year rolled on. The boy gradually grew into a handsome youngman. The elderly people were there to discuss casually about the marriage of Nrisingha. There were also several romantic adventures, hunting down this young man to their own passions & purpose. His parents also tried to make him indulge in worldly pleasures. Without knowing the real identity of the young man, the parents went on insisting repeatedly. Day in and

day out, the pressure came from various corners. The two young sisters too implored him to be married. But the young man set aside all requests and pressures. The parents and all other neighbours were planning tricks after tricks to convince the young man. At last, he submitted to the pressure and persuasion. It was a great relief to the parents. It soon became a common topic of general discussion. One after another, all the elders of the village thronged usually in the evening in the house of the parents, and the elders were found very active & jubilant in arranging the marriage. Usually, traditionally, the groom’s parents had to proceed through a go-between and duly approach the bride’s parents with some presents. But here, the custom was reversed. The bride’s parents started proposing and approaching. It did not, however, take long time to select a bride. And amid much jubilation, the nuptials were duly celebrated. The new bride was healthy & handsome, brimful of love & affection. Such a bride usually & naturally had a desire to enjoy her youth. But the groom did not do all that ‘man could do to be good husband. So, after a few months, the bride’s side complained. The delicate issue was amicably settled by the village council; divorce was granted. The parents again arranged a marriage with a Folk Tales of Tripura 161 beautiful damsel. After a few months, the second bride too became disgusted, and divorce followed. Thus, the parents arranged marriage for another five times. And divorce too followed for those times. The names of the brides were: Afuti, Nafuti, Kufuti, Kuchangti & Karmati. The stories of marraige, maladjustment, unhappiness and

divorce soon became the topic of discussion & whispering. In derision, the villagers called him Garaya. The literal meaning of Garaya was maladjustment. The parents, in their earnestness for the welfare of their son, made the seventh attempt. They invited the village elders before the marriage; and after a discussion they hit upon a new plan & took a resolution on celebrating a great festivity. The seventh marriage was not at all solemnised. The festival was preliminary to the nuptials. The underlying motive was to excite passion, an ardent desire, to make him prolific and this-worldly. The bold decision precipitated a week-long festival right from the Visuva Sankranti, also known as Chaitra Sankranti It was a time of merry-making, dancing, singing, joking, frolicking, feasting, gift-giving, drinking, visiting & fellow-feeling. The particular emphasis was on dance, drinks, song and lavish hospitality which were the symbols of youth, conjugal life and prolificity. The festival continued upto the 6th day of Vaisakha. | The introduction of the festival to other villages and parts of Tripura passed over steadily. Once again, the parents were hopeful of the success of the design. The son was expected to practise the duties of a householder. But in a dramatic fashion came a startling announcement made by the son on the seventh day of Vaisakha. Waking at early dawn, his mind fully made up, he announced his burning desire to take the vow of an ascetic, of leaving the hearth & home, of becoming a wandering hermit. The boy’s decision of resigning all his responsibility and giving away all his personal possessions shocked the parents and the villagers. But it was a Folk Tales of Tripura 162 genuine desire of world-renunciation, an indication of

his integrity & devotion. Reluctant to become entangled in the worldly affairs again, he, however, gave, blessings and responsibilities to his wife and sisters. His wife Kucangti was made the guardian deity of water, and as such she would be known as Tui Bukma. His first sister Mailungti was made the guardian deity of paddy & rice, and as such she would be known as Mailuma. His second sister Khulungti was made the guardian deity of cotton, and as such she would be known as Khuluma. The young man had an intimate friend, named Takchak-fa. With dogged tenacity, Takchak-fa persuaded the young man to disclose his true identity. Unable to resist the ardent appeal, the young man disclosed his true identity and preached a serious sermon in brief. The preaching had three significant but major headings: Ker The inner meaning of the term Ker was self-control, non-injury, forgiveness & purity; purity in body, purity in mind & purity in speech. An integrity of character should be the motto. To remain incorruptible, one should ward off evil forces. Creative energy should be pure. Kauthaya The inner meaning of the term Kauthaya was self- surrender and self-realisation; a rational control of impulses, feelings, demands & desires. It involves self- examination. It involves penance to rise above the lower self to the level of the social self. Kaubaya The inner meaning of the term Kaubaya was steadfastness to truth. Truthfulness is the essential trait of the ideal self. Truth triumps ultimately. An attempt at extinction of demands & desires, impoverishes a life. So, not’extinction, but rational control of demands & desires, should be the ideal of life. As the young man’s parents, friends & villagers were

alive, it weighed heavily upon them to bid him farewell. But he resolved to quit all his parents, wife, sisters & friends and to tear himself away from home. Folk Tales of Tripura 163 Riang Folk-Tales 29. Adventures of Solong Jabriha Once upon a time lived a young man named Solong Jabriha, who was matchless in courage and strength. While he was child he lost his father. The chief of his village was notorious and envious of this family, because Solong’s father would protest against any injustice of the chief. So, his mother along with his son shifted elsewhere. After a few years she too died leaving her only son alone. His parents were devout saivites. The Lord Siva took pity on the orphan and offered him a knife. Overwhelmed with grief, Solong set out from home and sauntered here and there aimlessly. On the way he - met an unusually tall young man named Jati Klaha. They became friends. They strolled together and met another young man named Khandu Balingha whose ears were very big like those of an elephant. They became friends. They walked together and met another young man called Jati Hakcungha, who could ignite fire simply by rubbing his legs. They became friends. They all set out together and met yet another young man named a Japa Klaha, whose hands were abnormally long. He too became friend. They all rollicked along. They tend to emphasize and display their masculinity in speech, manner and gesture. They have all their adventures in common. Aimless and homeless, these five friends went deep into forest and climbed up high where there was no human settlement. To their astonishment a shanty on

that hill was found. It was the abode of an old wicked witch. She had no food, fuel and fire. They distributed work among themselves. Jati Klaha started begging for rice; Japa Klaha with his long hands collected wild vegetables and fuel. Jati Hakcungha ignited fire. Khandu Balingha cooled them all with his big ears. Solong Jabriha cut and collected green bamboo pipes to be used as cooking Folk Tales of Tripura 164 pots. Thus, the five friends collected the essential materials for the preparation of food. The witch cooked and served the meal. At dead of night while they were asleep, she killed four of them and sucked their blood. Solong was spared. Early in the morning he found his friends dead. With his knife, Solong brought them back to life. Out of anger the young men urinated so much that the hut and the witch were inundated. The friends left the place and again wandered. On their way they found a big banyan tree which had five trunks. They took shelter there for the night. Next morning as usual the four friends went out in search of food and fuel. Solong did not go; he climbed down and was waiting for his fellows. He was, as if, keeping the house. Meanwhile an old man with his daughter was passing by that path. He was going to the house of his relatives. The girl was a paragon of beauty. They met Solong and talked to him. They came to know each other’s _. whereabouts. Solong and the girl became attracted to each other. There in the sylvan environment marriage was performed in an unceremonious way in presence of the friends. A small feast was also arranged. After that,

Solong’s father-in-law returned home.. Then the newly married couple and their friends happily lived there for some time. They built a hut and lived on hunting and gathering. Solong’s wife became the mistress of the house. All passersby and woodcutters would take rest there and get water and fruits from the beautiful lady. Thus, her name and fame spread and reached the palace of the kingdom. It aroused the passion of the king, who wanted her hand by any means; the aberrant king conspired with his henchman. He had contacted some abductors, who suggested the name of (he witch. The old wicked witch came to abet and assured to kidnap the beautiful lady. _ Hard times came for Solong. The witch played tricks. She assumed the form of an innocent girl, visited the Folk Tales of Tripura 165 hut of Solong, talked to the inmates and thus became friendly. One day she took some poisonous cakes for — them. Solong touched the cakes with his magic knife and then ate. So they did not die. As the poison had become ineffective, the witch grew more curious. She went on visiting them, offering fruits and showing sympathy for their wretched condition. Thus, she won the confidence of Solong’s wife. One day Solong’s wife confided. The witch came to know the magic power hidden in the god-gifted knife. The witch was waiting for the opportune moment and kept the family on observation. She used to visit them while the friends were absent. One day in the morning during winter Solong, his wife and the witch were sitting near a fire, warming themselves and gossiping. While Solong was inattentive, all of a sudden,

the witch grabbed the knife and at once put it into the fire. Immediately Solong became senseless and fell flat. Solong’s wife was at once kidnapped and taken to the palace to the great sensuous pleasure of the king, who amply rewarded the witch. The unbearable incident occurred during the absence of the four friends. While retuning and approaching home, they first saw the main trunk of the banyan tree dry. It was an omen. They entered into the house and found their best friend dead. The corpse was left on the floor. The magic power of the knife was known to them. So they searched every nook and corner and scrabbed about for the knife, and at last found it inside the ashes. At the very touch of the knife, Solong revived and narrated what had happened, much to everybody’s astonishment and anger. Determined to take revenge and also to rescue the lady, they left the place lest the king’s agents might endanger their lives further. The condition of the poor lady was like Sita. The lascivious king was like Ravana. The five friends worshipped Mahadeva for blessings and Folk Tales of Tripura 166 made friendship with the subjects who too were disgusted with the king for being utterly destitute of morality and conscience. In a terrible war between the two forces, the notorious king was defeated and killed. The lady was rescued. The subjects captured the palace and released all such ladies, girls and captives. After a great rejoicing, Solong was made king and his friends ministers of the kingdom. Subsequently the absconding witch was detected and killed. In course of time, some corrupt village leaders were also taken to task. The king and the queen

made arrangement for the marriage of the ministers. The distressed subjects too henceforth lived happily. Motifs This is a Riang folk-tale collected from Kathal Chhari in Tripura (south). It reflects the influence of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. It has anumber of motifs, such as: 1. Successful orphan, Solong Jabriha. 2. reward for service of God Siva who offered a knife. . jealous village headman. . unusual heroism of the friends. . blood-thirsty and greedy witch. . magical power of the god-gifted knife. . falling in love and marriage. . physical transformation of the witch into a lass. . banyan tree in service of man. 10. resuscitation of four friends and Solong Jabriha. 11. revengeful friends. 12. punishment of the king & the witch for misdeeds. OANA NAIA W 30. The hen & the wild cat .-There was a hen. Only the other day, the hen laid egg: The hen had to sit on egg to hatch. But the hen could not afford to spend a long time for incubation. The hen had to glean foodgrains by moving here and there, - and by scratching. Folk Tales of Tripura 167 a One day the hen went away in search of food. It was noon, about twelve o’clock. The hungry hen found it difficult to get foodgrains. Meanwhile, one wild cat was conspiring to devour the hen. The wild cat made several unsuccessful attempts of ambuscade. The cat lay hidden in jungles to attack the hen in surprise. To- day the cat got the scope. The cat had to lie in wait, and sneaked and then impetuously rushed & pounced upon the hen and devoured the meat. Eating the meat delightedly, the

cat thought: I must take rest & lie down for a happy sleep. There was a worn-out hut in the midst of a fallow farmland. There the cat lay, curled and fell sound asleep. The egg was in a very depressed state of mind. The egg was bewailing. But the egg did not break down. The egg determined to punish the killer. The hen’s faecal matter was at no great distance; it was in the neighbourhood. The egg and the faecal matter became fumed with anger, and after a serious discussion, implored their friends. A bamboo split was their friend. They said to the bamboo split: Our mother has been killed by a wild cat. We do not want to afflict you with our troubles. We seek your advice. The bamboo split said: I must help you. I have a snake as my friend. I like to take the snake along with us; how will it be? Do you agree? They said: Oh! yes, yes! The snake came and proposed to invite its friend, hornet, to take part in the expedition. The hornet flew into a rage on hearing the sad news and readily joined the team and proposed to invite its friend, a basket (= Brda= ord = tukrij. The basket came forward and proposed to invite its friend, a tall tree (= Mung-Khung). Thus, the team consisted of seven friends. The team was best suited to the occasion and the mood. The expedition led by the egg at last reached the destination where the cat had been asleep. They had to lie in wait so as to command a view of the cat. The faecal matter seated itself near the claws of the cat. The sharp bamboo

split stood close to the back-side of the cat. The egg Folk Tales of Tripura 168 entered into the hearth. The hornet took shelter into a gourd calabash which had been in use for holding drinking water. The snake was waiting behind the door. The tree took its position near the staired trunk of tree ( = Yaklai) used for ascending & discending. Within a short time, they had the satisfaction of seeing the cat awaked. The faecal matter was near to the claws. The cat bent its claws backward & forward. The claws became wet & dirty by dragging along the faecal matter. The faecal matter stank & diffused very bad smell. With a sense of uneasiness, the cat rubbed its claws. Blood was oozing out. The confused cat went to ignite the hearth, From the ignited hearth the egg burst forth its morbid matter. The morbid matter spoiled the face & eyes of the cat. The cat’s embarrassment now increased extremely. The cat struggled to wash the face & eyes with water from the calabash. The hornet was there to sting. It caused acute pain. In a confused hurry, the cat stepped out of the hut (= tang-ghar) with diminished vision. The snake was there near the threshold. The snake was there to bite. The cat cried out: I am doomed. I am doomed. A snake has bitten me! The cat was stepping down. The basket now took the opportunity to cuff on the head of the cat. Unable to bear the acute pain, the cat trembled in fear and tumbled down and fell near the tree. The tree was ready for the ultimate assault: with one sweep

killed the cat. 31. Tit for tat Long ago, a Riang family of Tripura cleared a patch of forest during the early winter season in November- December, and burnt the bushes and sowed seeds and built a hut in the clearing. The hut swarmed with domestic animals & birds. In that hut a hen and a cat lived in great friendship. The hen had a number of chicken. The cat too had several children. There was considerable fellow-feeling even among the two sets of children. Folk Tales of Tripura 169 Time rolled on. Then came the winter season; it was the time of consuming sweet cakes. One day the chickens wanted to eat cakes; they repeatedly requested the hen to prepare cakes. The hen sat silent, wrapped in thought. It was difficult to collect the costly materials: rice powder, banana, cocoanut, sugar, oil, and utensils. Only the rich people can afford it! At last out of motherly affection, the hen humbly approached the housewife of the Riang family. The housewife was kind enough to donate all the necessary materials. The hen came back glibly & happily with the materials, and then started cooking cakes. The chickens were in a jubilant mood. They too rose early and sat and enjoyed the pleasure of the family hearth. In the meantime,the cat got the smell and glibly walked inside the kitchen of the hen. After the preliminary discussion, the hen, out of courtesy, allowed the cat to share the dish of cakes. The cat said: My children also importuned and asked me to prepare cakes. But I am idle. I did not prepare. If you kindly permit me, I shall send my children to you. The hen mildly consented.

The cat went back home and spoke a lot about the sweetness of the cakes. The cat was cunning to obtain permission for her children also and directed them to hurry. Meanwhile, the chickens had devoured all the tasteful and fresh cakes. When the children of the cat came, there had been not a single cake left. But the calves became crazy; they begged. It was not a matter of joke to collect those materials again and make cakes immediately. The hen, however, welcomed the little guests and offered them seat and prepared cakes with dung of swine. The calves felt the pinch of hunger, but could not relish the new cakes. The new cakes were bitter in taste. The calves sullenly returned home and vomitted and narrated the news of step-motherly behaviour of the hen; Folk Tales of Tripura 170 on hearing this, the cat became revengeful and determined to kill the chickens. After a few days, when the excitement subsided, the crafty cat pretending to forget & forgive the past, strolled and visited the residence of the hen and purposely started gossiping in a casual manner with the intention of knowing the place of their sleep. The hen behaved normally and showed the places. The cat came not for a soiree, but for a survey. But from that very night the hen became cautious, and suspected the cat. The hen saw a change in the cat. A danger was dogging her footsteps. She used to close the door carefully and change the place of their sleep lest a criminal should enter the room. The visits of the two friends became infrequent, their conversation had no spontaneity, no emotion.

Midnight came; and now within an hour the deed would be accomplished. The cat moved surreptitiously and infiltrated into the room of the hen. The hen & the chickens had taken refuge inside a vertical drum. It was beyond the reach of the cat. So the cat found the bed empty and started searching here & there. The cat halted for a moment near the drum and heard a low voice. The hen was whispering. The furious cat, stung to madness by a sense of anger, was ready for action. The cat’s eyes were glittering. The cat challenged the hen. The, hen found herself confronted by an adversary more powerful than herself. The hen, roused and summoned by the challenge, did not come out hastily. The hen had taken a few calculated steps. The hen hid a stale egg under a heap of ashes in the hearth. The hen said: Friend! I shall hand over the chickens one after another. You roast each chicken and then relish. You ignite the hearth first of all. The bad-tempered cat had no time to pause and ponder. The cat tried to drive air into the hearth with Folk Tales of Tripura 171 hasty and speedy blows. The fire got ignited and the egg blasted. The blast tarnished the face & eyes of the cat. The cat thwartingly sought the advice of the hen. The hen directed the cat to wash the face with water preserved in a large earthen vat (= Gdmlda). There were several catfishes (= Singhmdch) in the vat. The moment the cat had dipped the soiled face, the catfishes got disturbed and inflicted poisonous wounds into the soiled face and eyes.

The frustrated cat again sought the advice of the hen. The hen directed the cat to rub the face against the fence. The fence was made of sharp splits of bamboo. The rubbing became fatal. The cat was bleeding from many wounds. The cat fled and died on the way. The hen & the chickens slept for sometime. Dawn came. The hen emerged with her chickens out of the drum and found the cat lying dead by the roadside. Noatia Folk-Tales 32. The drought & the Swine Tripura, a small & mountainous kingdom, was long ago afflicted with a severe drought. In those days, Tripura had herds of elephants & deers & troops of monkeys; and there were numerous birds & insects. There were dark places where the sunrays could not penetrate. One day one thirsty swine was digging & grubbing some arum roots with the muzzle. The swine was named Odakjar-pha. It was a hill- slope, dark & cool. Unexpectedly, water oozed out. The swine struggled to make the pit deep and big. The swine drank gladly. The swine prudently engaged one wild bird, named Takkruma ‘(=Mathurad), to protect the pool of water. The weather was hot & bad. The sun was bright in the sky and the warmth of it was scorching; the hours around noon were very hot. The wild beasts were Folk Tales of Tripura 172 searching and moving here & there for water; they came here and sought the permission of Takkruma; Takkruma said: My duty is to protect & preserve the water. I cannot allow you to drink. It is not in my power to grant your request. The owner is Oadkjar-pha. Without his permission,

you can not drink. If you trespass, you will have to face serious consequences; it may ensue quarrel, scuffle and even battle. One day one thirsty deer, being prohibited from drinking the water, stood & leered with the lovely eyes and then asked: How much big & powerful is your lord? The guard was eloquent in praise of the swine. The guard said: My lord has a corpulent body with broad shoulders, a powerful chest, strong hands and legs, long furs, big eyes, incisive teeth & bold head. The deer gave another look and retreated in the face of danger. The next day, there came a monkey. Being forbidden, the monkey asked a few questions about the owner of the water. Getting the reply, the monkey screamed and jumped away. For days together, the guard encountered many thirsty animals and birds, and successfully convinced them not to touch the water. He told how strong & brave his lord was! At last, there appeared the king of that forest: the tiger. The thirsty tiger was obstinate. The guard warned and gave a description of the strength of the swine. The tiger had prowess to be conceited about. To confute the claim of the guard, the tiger gave a description of his own strength, and then asked: Do your lord possess beard? The guard asked: What purpose will the beard serve? The tiger then stroked his beard with a composed and dignified gesture and proceeded to drink water. The tiger’ satisfactorily drank and emptied the pool completely. . The poor guard rushed and informed the swine. I must punish the trespasser, said the swine. The swine -gruntingly hurried to the pool; the guard followed. Being

challenged, the swine became very aggressive. It was Folk Tales of Tripura 173 hard to keep silent when the owner was bubbling over with anger. The owner pounced upon the trespasser. They rushed on each other and hewed each other down; they struck each other, leaping, growling, shrieking, grunting, charging, racing through the jungles & bushes. A terrific eerie had taken hold the locality, and the birds and animals ran swiftly to their nests & caves. Even the guard paid no heed to the battle-cry of the lord, and rushed away in safe distance. The battle raged till the next day. Sometimes, the swine was driven back in disorder, and then again the tiger was driven back in disorder. At last, the tiger fell dead. But the swine was also seriously wounded; the wound bled much; the swine was not healed of his wound. The swine too died. Now, it so was that the guard had not heard the din & the cry of the battle, for both the combatants had already breathed their last. The guard’s heart was pierced with pity & sorrow! The guard slowly & cautiously came forward. The pool was converted into a slush of mud. The mangled dead bodies lay there. Disorder spoke of a terrible struggle. The guard got angry with the peccant tiger. The guard did never eat the meat of tiger. A scope now came unexpectedly. For about three days, the guard went on eating the carrion. Soon the symptoms of indigestion were manifested. Because of overeating, the body could not cope with the surplus. A clogging of the whole system took place. About a week after, it put out the flame of life of the

guard. At that time, a sudden blast of wind blew; with the gust came a sharp bamboo-split; like a dagger, the split pierced into the belly of the gourmand guard: It accelerated the process of death. The guard fell down shrieking & died. There was a clump of bomboos at that place. A-big rat suddenly heard the peculiar sound of shrieking by the guard. Out of curiosity, the rat came out to enquire, and saw three dead bodies. Folk Tales of Tripura 174 The veteran rat had the knowledge of making a flute out of tarsus. The selfish rat was in the look out for tarsus. Now, the rat cut off one tarsus and took pains to prepare a musical pipe. A flute is usually a cylindrical tube made of bamboo or wood; it is a wind instrument with holes & keys to be sounded by breathe stream across the mouth hole. The rat was an expert flute player. The rat, while playing with the flute, would sink into a state of leisurely rhythm. High in the branches of a big tree there was the residence of a monkey. The sweet note of the flute attracted the attention of the monkey. The monkey used to pay attention to the melodious sound. One day the monkey descended down the hill and reached the place of the rat. The concordance gave pleasure to both; the rat was happy to see in the monkey a connoisseur. The monkey would visit daily & sit at ease and appreciate the art of the rat and prattle. Meanwhile, the monkey hit upon a way to plunder the flute. The monkey collected a quantity of gum from

certain trees & plants, and sat by the side of the rat. While the rat had been in a mood of ecstasy with diminished consciousness, the cunning monkey smeared the sticky gum over the eyes of the rat. Leaving the rat almost blind, the monkey hurriedly decamped with the flute. The rat, being cheated, was shocked. The disappointment shocked the rat terribly. The rat lay in the frenzy of sorrow for sometime. The rat, sitting down alone for a while, attempted to grope; broken scream came every now & then. One woodpecker bird was perching and searching termite hidden under bark of trees. The rat heard the voice of the bird and sought the bird’s help. The bird swooped down and removed the gum. (he animal soon recovered from the temporary problem. - Then the rat said: One monkey used to come here being ultracted by the sweet note of my flute. Contrary to my Folk Tales of Tripura 175 expectation, the monkey smeared gum on my eyes and plundered my flute. The rat sought the woodpecker’s help to get back the flute. The careful woodpecker assured to help the rat, but did not dare to cope with the naughty monkey directly, and so devised an alternative plan; the woodpecker made an- appeal to the king of birds. The king of birds became kind enough to pay a visit to the rat. The rat’s hospitality, humility & earnestness impressed the king of birds (= _Takshr-ra). The king of birds wanted to know the whereabouts of the thief. The rat failed to furnish any definite information, but guessed that it would be towards the eastern hills. The king of birds flew eastward till the

king reached the residence of the shrewd & selfish monkey. The cheat was then playing with the flute. Upon finding the flute in the custody of the cheat, the king became calm & quiet, concealing the disgust at the meanness of the cheat. The king said: I sit quietly at a long distance and I am patiently listening to the sweet sound. Your tune is melodious. It is irresistible. So I have come to meet the expert player and to enjoy the tune. How good you are, dear monkey! It was a delicate flattery deliberately committed by the king. Nevertheless, the compliment was very pleasing to the monkey. The monkey offered the king hospitality and invited the other monkeys. They all praised the masterly style of the monkey. The buoyant artist went on playing the flute before a cheerful audience. The king now said: My dear friend! I could not play a flute; will you be kind enough to give me a chance? The monkey nodded assent and handed over the flute to the king. The king played the flute. All the monkeys were wonder- struck at the skill of the king. Enjoying the melody, the monkey requested the king to continue. The king said: As a bird, I am accustomed to perch on a tree or on something like that; if you allow me to sit alone on the Folk Tales of Tripura 176 open back balcony (= verandah) for playing the flute, my performance will produce hypnotic sleep in you. The monkey replied: If I allow you to sit there, you may fly off with the flute! So, I cannot allow you. The king wondering at the refusal, leered and said: If

you do not believe me, you may grease my tail with oil and hold on the tail. All the monkeys nodded assent; so the monkey agreed and arranged to grease the tail. The monkey and the retinue grasped the tail. Being an artist of some honour & reputation, the monkey did not question further, and assumed that the king of birds must have magnanimity. Now, the king clearly perceived that he got a scope to deceive the monkey. Quite content with the arrangement, the king so successfully displayed the skill that all the monkeys fell deep asleep. The grasp became loose. The king flew off with the flute and reached the residence of the rat and handed over the flute to the rat. Lushai Folk-Tales 33. Origin of the Tui-chong stream In a Lushai family there were two sisters, named Tui-chong and Nuengi. They were orphans. They had to eke out their living by fishing, gathering, shifting cultivation and weaving. Like their neighbours, the two sisters would carry their food to the field & eat it at mid- day. They had to walk to the far end of the forest and come back daily, struggling along with forehead- suspended heavy loads in bamboo basket up the precipitous slope to their hill-top hut. One year there was no rain. The streams and springs became dry. It was the summer season. The two sisters went to the forest. It was mid-day. They took their meal. But there was no water. The younger sister fell very, very thirsty; she insisted on getting wafer. The elder sister assured her to bring water from a distant village. Folk Tales of Tripura 177 But Nuengi became impatient to have water here & now.

Tui-chong came to stand beside her and caress her with rather motherly affection. Nuengi became impulsive to Tui-chong’s plea. Nuengi said: If I do not get water, I shall die; then you will be useless to me. I prefer water to your life. _ Tui-chong shook her head slowly & painfully. She said: In all the years you have roamed this forest; have you seen any pool of water in the vicinity? Tui-chong neither expected nor wanted an answer to the question. Her eyes observed Nuengi’s face for a moment. With her will-force, Tui-chong transformed herself into a river to quench the thirst of her sister. Nuengi drank water, but lost her sister. Realising her folly, Nuengi sat aghast near the river. An uneasy murmur ran around the forest. Her agony was plainly visible. The night was approaching. That night, she lay hidden inside the hollow cavity of a big tree, & she plunged into sleep the moment she lay down, deaf to the screaming. In the next morning coming out of the cavity, & looking around, & feeling safe, & lying on a bed of leaves & grass, she was suffering from hunger. It was a lonely place, full of jungles. The only sounds she was hearing were those of birds and insects. The new, weary river was meandering south-west- ward, through hills & gorges to meet the famous Karnaphuli River. Landslides, soil, clay & rotten leaves were whirling down-stream in its swift waters. Far down, where it met the famous Karnaphuli River, there was a prosperous settlement of the Bengali people. The Bengalees had a local king there. The subjects and the king were surprised to see a new river. The king made

discussion with his ministers and sent a team of adventurous, young men. They walked, tripped, stumbled to go deeper & deeper into forest along the river. A few days of tedious walk through leech-infested jungle of the hill tract of Chittagong brought them to the source of Folk Tales of Tripura 178 the new river. A sound was heard. They kept going on, closer & closer, and finally saw a young girl weeping. Nuengi had never seen those men before. She sprang up there wild-eyed. A smile of welcome evoked a similar response simultaneously & spontaneously. They rescued her and took to the court of their king. The king was enjoying the pleasures of the kingdom along with his queen. The queen was his wedded & beloved wife. But the* queen was barren. Now, in course of time, Nuengi gave birth to a son. The wedded queen became jealous, and apprehensive of the promotion of Nuengi. Nobody dared to give the good news to the king. The baby was immediately thrown into the new river. Nuengi was given a false information about the baby. Nuengi wondered vaguely. But in spite of her transformation, the elder sister did not forget the younger sister. Tui-chong rescued and saved the baby. Nuengi subsequently gave birth to six more children one after another. The jealous queen contrived skilfully to throw all the children into the new river. Fortunately, Tui-chong was there in the water to protect the children in her abode in the water. Tui-chong used to nurse the chidren, feed them, teach them and tell them the stories of the previous life, the stories of their mother, the stories of the king & the

queen of Chittagong. Time rushed onward like the new river. The children were now grown up youths. They became curious to see their mother and the king. Tui- chong encouraged and blessed them and showed the way. One day the seven young brothers emerged out of water and confidently strolled towards the palace. The seven brothers soon reached the destination and started dancing and singing. It soon attracted a large audience. The spectators, being astonished, were talking among themselves. The dramatic narration created a sensation. -The hubbub went on increasing. The king came out of his palace and saw the Folk Tales of Tripura 179 handsome children and asked about their whereabouts. The children said: Maharaj! we are your children. The king said: You are liars. Liars are given severe punishment. The children said: Nuengi is our mother. Your queen contrived to throw us into the new river. Tui-chong saved us there. The king ordered to bring Nuengi there for identification.
