The children showed respect; Nuengi caressed them with motherly affection and desperately disclosed the incident. The king wrathfully ordered the executioner to behead the wicked and jealous queen. Henceforth, Nuengi and her chidren were given due recognition and love. History occassionally links some famous men with some rivers. Here, a Lushai girl’s name is associated with a river. Hence, the stream is known as Tui-chong. The stream keeps alive the tragedy of the past. The Tripuri community also have a similar story. 34. The terrible Python In the north-eastern corner of hilly Tripura, there was a village which had only the Lushai families living there. The villagers were then preliterates, and shifting cultivation was their main occupation. The village

swarmed with domestic animals and birds. There was a famous cave near that village. A large & long snake, python, lived in the cave. The snake was very fierce, selfish, voracious. The villagers were afraid of the snake. The snake was a demon. The snake had devoured many animals and birds. The villagers were in great distress and fear. Because of the snake’s depredations, the village council sat together and made a decision: each family, in turn, would send food, demestic bird or animal or even a man daily to the snake in the cave. Folk Tales of Tripura 180 Oo — Days went by and the villagers became forlorn and weary. It was a drainage of their resources. One day the turn came to the village chief's family. The members of the family were in great anxiety. . Suddenly & surprisingly a young traveller reached there. He was very strong, healthy and courageous. Evening came. The tired traveller sought shelter. According to the local custom, for such a helf, the village chief must be approached. The villagers indicated the house of the chief. The chief was pleased with the charming personality of the traveller and offered him shelter. The chief had his wife and children. They made arrangement for the traveller’s food. They offered uncooked rice, vegetables, pots, firewood. The traveller was to cook for himself. While cooking, he started narrating the experience of his journey. But his observant eyes perceived a note of melancholy in the minds of all the members of the chief’s family. He stopped his own story and asked about their condition. He persistently enquired and learned the tragic story. The chief was scheduled to send his young, beautiful daughter to the

snake. The young man laughed and assured them to sleep in peace. He immediately volunteered to go to the snake next morning. It was a great, great relief to the chief and indeed to all the villagers. The chief at once informed the villagers. All the elders rushed to the house of the chief. They blessed him and narrated their tragedy. Tears came to their eyes. The next morning all the villagers flock to see the strong man whose strength & courage became the talk of the village. Every family offered him fresh fruit, but nobody dared to accompany him. Like Bhima, the young guest started on his journey to the snake. He was not in a hurry. He was walking & strolling leisurely and confidently. The traveller took an Folk Tales of Tripura 181 as. «. ihe omy weapon. The snake became angry to see the strange late-comer. The snake was about to coil him with th. long tail. The traveller charged at the snake w.tit the sharp axe. A battle ensued. The day which had begun in the morning passed very painfully, for anxiety accumulated with’ each moment. All the villagers were eagerly waiting for the traveller. At last, in the afternoon, the traveller killed the snake and happily came back with the axe stained with blood. Returning to the chief’s house, the lonely traveller was amazed to find himself standing amid a crowd of admirers. He became the guest of every house. He was overwhelmed by their hospitality. He was taken to the forest 8 field, in hunting & fishing. Slowly and slowly, the chief’s daughter and the guest started loving each other passionately. The chief was glad enough to arrange

the marriage, and the villagers were very happy to have him among them. 35. Changsili & a Python On Lushai Hill lived a peasant family. The peasant made his clearing during the early winter for jum cultivation. The peasant had his wife and two daughters. The name of the elder daughter was Changsili. The daughters were young enough to help their parents at home and in the jum field. The heavy works of cutting & burning the bushes, and sowing the seeds were jointly performed by the parents & the daughters. After that, the parents were taking rest at home, while the daughters were going for weeding, and nursing the young plants. Their mother, who had walked up & down the hut-ladder & the steep track of hills, became sick. Every day at dawn the peasant’s wife used to cook rice & vegetables, and wrap up in banana leaf some rice & vegetables for the daughters. The two sisters would carry their food to the field and eat it at mid-day. They Folk Tales of Tripura 182 had to walk to the far end of the forest & back daily. Things were going on as usual. After a few days, things turned a different turn. A snake cast its lustful eyes upon Changsili. The snake had its nest in a hollow tree, at the bottom of the jum field. When the two girls had been away from the village, the snake tried to take advantage of the situation, and became successful. At the direction of the elder sister, the younger sister had to call the snake. In response to the call, the snake would come & coil itself up in Changsilt’s lap.

Being afraid, the younger sister would turn away from the offered food. But she had not been idle. She would weed out the unwanted grass, dug up some root, collect some vegetables & banana leaves. Working in this way and eating no meal at noon, she became weak. When sun was about to finish the day’s trip over the sky, the two sisters, like many of their neighbours, would come back home with basket full of vegetables, fuel and green leaves. In the evening, the parents and the daughters used to sit around the fire-place, and gossip. But hunger kept the younger daughter on the edge of sleep; she would speak little. In front of all, the mother wanted to know the cause of the younger daughter’s weakness. The daughter avoided. One day in the morning, while Changsili had been away in a neighbour’s house, the mother again asked. Now, being entreated, she disclosed what had been going on in the jum field. Allowing the daughters to leave for the field, the mother sat aghast. She was shocked & surprised; and discussed the problem with the peasant. They planned to kill the snake; the peasant would go to the field along with the younger daughter; Changsili would be asked to nurse her mother. The next day, the father and the younger daughter went to the field. The father took in a packet the clothes of his wife. The younger daughter followed after the father and. chattered on in a soft voice. Reaching the field, they Folk Tales of Tripura 183 worked for a while and took rest for meal. Dressed in the clothes of a woman and with a sharp dah, the father

cut the snake. The following day, the two sisters went to the field, and the younger sister had to invite the snake. But no snake came. The elder sister was disappointed. The younger sister had to resile from the question. Changsili leered, and tears rolled down her face. In the afternoon, the two sisters returned home, and found the father lying on the floor just near the _door-sill obstructing the passage. Changsili said: Father, get up; I like to scrape off the mud off my draggled feet, on the door-sill. The father remained there with a machination. Not bothering about the father, Changsili started to scrape the mud. Suddenly, the father sprang up and cut the daughter. To their astonishment, many small snakes swarmed from the stomach of Changsili. They then & © there killed almost all the little snakes, except one. Only one snake quickly escaped and hid itself in the forest. In course of time, the snake became very strong, ferocious, greedy and epicurean. The hissing sound of the snake was terrible. In the still fall nights, the villagers could listen to the awful sound. The snake rendered the people’s life not worth living. There were many children who had been frightened by the snake. The snake would spring at them with wonderful quickness. The deadly snake would sway its hood. It devoured many wild & domestic animals & birds. The deadly snake’s next demand was human flesh. It demanded little children. The villagers in turn had to send one child. One day a wandering Chin came to that village; he found the villagers very gloomy; his host was weeping. He asked the cause. They were weeping & panting. That

day, it was the turn of that family to send their child. The visitor was a strong man like Bhima. He assured them and said: I will kill the snake; please give me a goat. Folk Tales of Tripura 184 He proceeded to the cave in the jungle and pushed forward the goat. The snake swallowed the meat & the forearms of the young man. Within a moment, by a quick turn of his wrist and sharp knife, he killed the snake. The young man came back confidently and laughingly. The villagers ever remained grateful to him. They rejoiced. 36. A fair face hiding a foul heart There were many monkeys in the hills of Tripura. But one monkey was very lovely. The monkey was fashionable and an agreeable speaker. He had a swing. The monkey laid a trap to prey some other animals or birds. The trap was his swing. The monkey was careful to see that the branch of the tree from which the swing was to hang was strong. The rope was strong & properly fastened. The monkey liked the feeling of going up in the air and coming down again with a rush. One day one bear came and saw the monkey enjoying a good swing without any risk. It was alluring. Being tempted, the bear too wanted to enjoy and sought permission. The tempter smiled and readily gave permission and quickly climbed up the tree-branch apparently to fasten the rope for the safety & security of the heavy animal, but actually to weaken it, to slacken it, to make the swing accident-prone. The tempter climbed down and said: I have verified and checked, and you may sit firmly in the seat and

enjoy. The bear got on the swing. The monkey left the spot with the secret intention of collecting spices, & rice to relish the fresh flesh of the bear. The evil device of the tempter worked; the swing could not bear the load. It fell down on a deep ditch. But the bear jumped & fell to the adjacent ground. There occurred no physical injury. The cunning monkey rushed to the spot with spices, etc., but found the prey unhurt; the monkey at once changed his tone and started showing Folk Tales of Tripura 185 sympathy for the accident. He sought apology. The bear wrathfully & seriously reviled: You notorious monkey! you made a plot to kill me and to relish my flesh! Now, I shall teach you a lesson. My sharp eyes had followed all your doings. The bear immediately gruntingly marched forward to chase the cunning monkey. The monkey ran away and climbed up a tall tree. The bear failed to hunt the monkey, and ate the spices & rice of the monkey. Since then the bear and the monkey were not in good terms. 37. Raid begot revolt The Lushai people had their settlements in the hills bordering Assam and Tripura. As shifting cultivators, they had their villages scattered here & there. And each village had its headman. For a considerable period of time, they were accustomed to adventurous, unsettled life. Dari Pa was the name of one such headman. Dari Pa was adventurous and ambitious. He felt homely in risks & raids. He had a band of youths. To him they looked for guidance. They used to obey every order of their master. It should not seem strange that every

village had its headman, and every headman had his band of youths. It should also not seem strange that those bands used to descend from the hills to the plains of the Meghna Valley particularly during the winter season for raid, for loot & scoot, for headhunting & kidnapping. In one such occasion of raid, Dari Pa’s band of youths captured a little boy named Sibuta, and took him to the house of Dari Pa. Sibuta became the slave of Dari Pa. Sibuta was active and energetic, intelligent & obedient. Dari Pa had only one daughter named Darlalpui. The father had great affection for the daugther. The daughter had great influence over the father; and she seldom failed in persuading the servant to do as she wished. Thus for year after year, the kidnapped boy was reduced to slavery, drudgery, & ill treatment. Dari Pa, his wife & daughter Folk Tales of Tripura 186 did not pause for a moment to consider where such ill treatment might lead them! Dari Pa went ahead with his adventurous way of life. His band kidnapped a few boys for their master. Dari Pa was happy to have a team of servants and errand boys. Sibuta too gave them necessary guidance. Sibuta “was now a young man. Dari Pa, being pleased with his long service, set him free. Sibuta left his master’s village and moved to a distant hill, cleared jungles, built hut and started hunting, fishing, gathering & shifting cultivation. Sibuta married a young, energetic girl. Sibuta had his friends & sympathisers; within a few years, they migrated to settle in the hill of Sibuta. Thus a village grew up. Sibuta became the headman of the new village. Sibuta had to suffer

from the practice of raid. He did not encourage raid. Time rolled on. In one raid, Dari Pa was seriously wounded. No magic, no sorcery, no animal sacrifice could cure him. At last he died. He had no son. His band took the scope to raid the master’s house; Dari Pa’s wife and daughter were vexed and angry at the outrageous behaviour of the known band. They were equally shocked at the cowardly behaviour of some neighbours who had not dared to protect the two women. Shrinking from fear and hoping to have sympathetic treatment from the old slave, Sibuta, the forlorn mother & the daughter migrated to the village of Sibuta. Sibuta did not forget the memories of bitterness & cruelties. His neighbours were also aware of those unhappy incidents. At his order, the mother, the daughter and their nine cattle were twitched, fastened and beaten to death. Not even a drop of water was given to them. 38. A battle for water One day a bear was wandering in the deep forest of Tripura in search of food. The bear found a small lake, and was pleased to find the water of the lake clean, cool Folk Tales of Tripura 187 and pure. The bear wished to enjoy the water exclusively by himself. With this selfish motive, the bear engaged a monkey to guard the lake against any encroachment and trespass. Days went on. Day & night the monkey was sincerely protecting the lake. One day a deer came there. The deer said: Brother! I am very thirsty; kindly permit me to drink a little water. The monkey replied: Brother! this lake belongs to my master, who is a very powerful bear. I

can not allow you. Sorry. On hearing the name of the bear, the deer immediately fled. After sometime a pig came there. The pig said: Sir! | am very thirsty; please allow me to drink a little water. The monkey answered: This lake belongs to a ferocious bear; I can’not allow you to drink its water. Being frightened, the pig left the spot at once. After a few days, a young tiger came there majestically and started drinking the clean water without caring for any permission. The monkey rushed to the spot and tried to dissuade; the tiger made a growl; the poor monkey fled and perched on a tree. But the dutiful monkey went on chattering and squeaking loudly. The monkey had two intentions: to annoy the tiger, and to bring the episode to the notice of the bear. In the meantime the bear started coming back & heard from afar a noise. Indeed, the unusual chattering of the monkey was heard by the bear from a distance. The bear thus apprehended something bad. On reaching the spot, the bear saw the tiger drinking the water leisurely. The angry bear challenged the tiger, but the tiger went on drinking & bathing defiantly. Now, the bear charged at the tiger with fury. The tiger defended and a battle ensued. Their eyes sparkled. The water of the lake was violently agitated. The two belligerent animals were panting and sobbing. The monkey was beating his own forehead. The scuffle continued for hours. The two animals came to the shore and after a period of sobbing Folk Tales of Tripura 188 resumed the quarrel with spirit and courage. There was a jungle all around the lake. The adjacent bushes, and

jungles were stifled and dashed violently. They, while screaming, rushing & chasing each other, reached the top of a hill and fell to a deep gorge, several hundred feet below and died. The wise monkey realised the difficulty of using the water all alone. He invited his own fellows to settle there and narrated the whole episode. The monkeys decided to allow others to use the pure water cautiously. For protecting & preserving the pure water and for providing drinking water, the thirsty users used to present some gifts. 39. The Lushai chief Lirshi Long, long ago there was a rich man, named Lirshi. Lirshi was the chief of the Lushai community. The Lushai people were shifting cultivators. They were widely distributed in Tripura, Assam, Mizoram, Chittagong, etc. The residence of Lirshi was at a hill of Assam, but it was adjacent to Tripura. As an administrator, Lirshi was remarkable for neutrality, objectivity & strictness. He vowed to punish the evil-doers, & to protect the honest people. He instilled a respect for law & order in his area. He used to receive & care for the guests, strangers and the local king’s employees on tour. He looked after the poor & needy. He used to keep a close & critical-watch on the members of the village council in particular & on all the villagers in general. In those days any journey outside the limits of a man’s own village was risky and rare. But Lirshi, accompanied by his trustworthy persons, undertook a journey to a distant village. The purpose of the journey was to judge human character. It was not an adventure. He kept the intention within himself. They travelled and

travelled and crossed many hills and valleys and streams Folk Tales of Tripura 189 and at last reached a village in the evening. With a previous understanding, Lirshi got separated from his fellows and went quietly away. He sat in the shade of a tree near the village. He posed like a very poor beggar and made a mock-attempt of loitering, crawling from house to house for food & shelter. The householders drove him away. The children attempted to throw dirt. But he remained quiet and silent.. Meanwhile, the companions strictly concealed the identity of Lirshi, but introduced themselves as the friends of Lirshi. Knowing their identity, the village headman received them gladly and made arrangement for their comfort. Almost all the villagers offered them hospitality. The strange beggar became an object of neglect and derision. He remained outside till late in the evening. In that village there were two brothers. They were very poor. They had to work hard for livelihood. They were sympathetic enough to offer him shelter and food. On the following morning, the companions dramatically disclosed the identity of Lirshi. The news surprised all the villagers. They had heard the name & fame of Lirshi, but did not see him. The surprise visit of Lirshi seemed to be a dream. They rushed to offer him a grand reception and warm hospitality. Lirshi accepted their hospitality, but he never idealised them. However, he never forgot the genuine sympathy of the two poor brothers. He halted there for two nights only. Then they turned their steps homeward. Being invited by Lirshi, the two brothers too went to Lirshi’s village with him. While going back home, Lirshi and his companions

had lively discussion with the two brothers. The stories of their sufferings were recounted. Lirshi offered the two brothers very hearty hospitality and loaded them with gifts. Folk Tales of Tripura 190 Kuki Folk-Tales 40. Eclipse Once upon a time at a Kuki hamlet lived a rich headman. He had seven sons. Like their neighbours, this family too had to depend on gathering, hunting, fishing and shifting cultivation. One day the seven sons went to hunt and killed a deer. The six elder brothers asked the youngest brother to guard the dead deer. The youngest brother sat in a shade of a tree. The carcass was pulled from the jungle & placed in an open place. The carcass was to be protected from tigers, jackals, crows & vultures. The deer was squalling & yelling in the shade of the tree. The six elder brothers, leaving the youngest brother alone, went away to collect firewood, leaves, roots & vegetables. They took time to return. Meanwhile, a gust of wind blew and a few worn out leaves from the tree fel? down on the carcass. The magical power of the leaves reanimated the deer. The deer instantly fled away. In the mid afternoon the six elder brothers found the youngest brother beating his forehead and crying} They enquired about the deer. The youngest brother narrated what had happened. The elder brothers did not believe the statement, and supposed that the carcass had been stashed or sold out. So, they thoroughly thrashed him; the youngest brother fell unconscious in the shade of the tree. The six elder brothers returned home in the late afternoon. Their father enquired about the youngest son. The evasive reply of the six sons seemed unsatifactory to

the parents. The parents became very anxious & annoyed. The father was thinking of going there for a search. He was preparing a bundle of bamboo-splits to be used asa ‘burning torch, and a dado. Folk Tales of Tripura 191 Meanwhile, another gust of wind swayed the tree and a few leaves fell down on the body of the youngest brother; the boy immediately came back to consciousness; he stood up and turned his steps homeward with the leaves and a piece of bark of the benevolent tree. The parents were very happy to see their dear son again. Upon being asked by the parents, the son narrated what had happened. The leaves & the bark were kept securely. The next morning the father advised the son to get the leaves & the bark dried in the rays of the sun for preservation. The sun was shining brightly. -The sun got the hint of the medicinal value of the leaves and the bark. The sun swooped down to snatch the bark & the leaves. The veteran father was on guard with his black dog. Instantly the dog sprang forward and caught the sun and devoured the sun. Very quickly darkness followed. The sudden loss of light bewildered the people. Being directed by the aged father, the black dog let the sun pass out by the rectum. The cause of the lunar eclipse and the solar eclipse lay in that very accident. The moon is the husband, while the sun is the wife. 41. Earthquake Over the surface of this earth numerous animals, birds, human beings, flora & fauna are visible. In the underworld also similar human beings live. A beetle

maintains relations between the two worlds. The people of the underworld require animal-dung; and the beetle carries animal-dung. The beetle is frequently sent to collect animal-dung. The beetle gets tired in travelling a long distance and in carrying an ever increasing quantity of animal-dung. The tired beetle sometimes tells a lie and reports that there is no man or animal on the other world. All of them have died. The people of the underworld doubt about the correctness of the report and to verify the statement, Folk Tales of Tripura 192 they shake the earth. The earth trembles, and the animals flee, the birds fly and the human beings shout & blow conchshells and run helter-skelter. Thus, knowing the existence of the living being on earth, the dwellers of the underworld accuse the lazy beetle for telling a lie. The people of the underworld threaten the beetle and compel it to collect animal-dung. The animal-dung turns into gold in the underworld. The occasional shaking causes earthquake. 42. Origin of a poisonous creeper There was once upon a time one Khucong Kuki chief, named Raja Subharay. The raja had a beautiful daughter. The royal family was in search of a bridegroom. The raja had several right-hand men. They gave the whereabouts of another Kuki family living at a distant hemlet. In that family there were seven brothers; they were hardworking and able-bodied young men. The raja gave consent for the negotiation. The seven brothers rejoiced that they would get such a beautiful princess. The marriage was celebrated with great pomp at the village of the raja. After two days, the new couple left for their own residence. The new couple were given

a hearty reception by the villagers. A feast was arranged. As the new couple had been sitting for a long time during the ceremony for about two days, their eyes shut with fatigue and they felt fast asleep. When at last the bride awoke, it was found that the groom lay dead. The bride began to weep at dawn. The other brothers rushed to console her. The village elders too came to show sympathy and to arrange the cremation. After a few days, the village elders directed the second brother to marry the bride. But alas! they fell fast asleep, when at last the bride awoke, it was again found that the.second brother lay dead. In this way, the first six brothers were married one after another, and the six brothers died mysteriosly. Folk Tales of Tripura 193 Now, came the turn of the seventh brother. Obeying the advice of the elders, he too married the bride in a very simple ceremony. There upon, they both went to bed. At night the bride fell into a deep sleep. Horror let him have no sleep. He was thinking & thinking. The seventh brother pretended to be asleep. A serious thought came to him; he stayed there in the same bed a while, & looked around. A terrible fear fell on him. Slowly & silently he left the bed and stashed himself in a dark corner. At about mid-night, the seventh brother saw a strange thing: he saw a poisonous small snake springing out of the nose of the bride. The deadly snake swayed; searched around, found no male and retreated back into the nose of the bride. The seventh brother was terribly frightened; but he

did not get perturbed. All was not well as it should be with the lady; she was a witch. He thought of nothing, but how to punish and kill the bride. When day dawned, he poked her in the side with his elbow and said: Get up my dear fair lady; let us go into the forest to fetch leaves, vegetables & firewood, etc. They walked a long distance across the precipitous jungle country. She peeped back at the house again & again. When they reached the middle of the deep forest, he said: You collect some leaves & vegetables; I am digging out some roots & tubers. He dug a deep pit near the shade of a big banyan tree. Overcome with anger & impatience, he beat her savagely with a chump. He seized the bride by her head and threw her out into the deep pit and covered the pit. Thus she died a pitiful death. The seventh brother returned home and made a mockery of mourning for the accident. The sad loss was reported to the bride’s parents. The raja suspected some evil. With his retinue he came there and made a thorough search on the jungle, but failed to locate the spot. Disappointed and distressed, the raja, along with his retinue, returned home. For days & nights he could not eat, sleep and rest. Folk Tales of Tripura 194 Then, one night the daughter’s soul appeared in dream, and narrated the episode. The soul made startling revealations thus: I am Ndg-Kany4. I came to kill the six brothers for their crime of head-hunting. My dead body has been buried near a banyan tree. From my navel a

creeper has already begun to grow. The creeper has medicinal value. Its juice is poisonous. The juice is powerful enougl to hurt any animal, any enemy and to stupefy fishes. Accordingly, the raja again visited the spot and saw a creeper growing out of the dead body. He left it undisturbed. Chakma Folk-Tales 43. Dhobi and Kobi Long ago in the hills of Tripura in a certain village lived a small family. Three members, the father, the mother and one daughter, composed this little family. The daughter’s name was Dhobi. Dhobi, about five years of age, was equally skilful in physical and in mental -@X€rcises. The family subsisted on shifting cultivation, gathering, fishing, animal husbandry and basketry, etc. Any family of the village could reclaim & cultivate from the unused hills as much ground as it could handle; but the family had to inform & obtain the consent of the headman and to make a ritual worship. After one year, the land would be left fallow; it would revert to the headman for redistribution. Legally all lands belonged to the king. Like the Tripuri, the Riang, the Noatia, the Jamatia, the Halam, the Kuki, the Lushai, the Garo, & the Uchai communities, the Chakma community too had to practise shifting cultivation. Each family had to select a hill-slope for clearing & planting. The bambooes, bushes, trees & creepers had to be cut down & left to dry during the Folk Tales of Tripura 195 dewy season and burned after several weeks. Some heavy works would be done by the villagers jointly & joyously. Planting would be done by poking holes in the ground. Planting before the rainfall and weeding after the rainfall

were their routine affairs. The parents of Dhobi used to go to the field for planting & weeding. The weeding operation had to be repeated three times. While working in the field, the mother would often get tired and insisted on drinking water. The father had to insist on the continuation of the work. She said: I am very thirsty; give me water. He said: Wait a little, wait a little. After sometime, she would give reminders, while he would persuade with humour to weed a portion of the field. The weather was very unkindly at that time. The sun was scorching the fields & forests; the streams became dry. One day it was about noon; the atmosphere was uncanny and severe. She cawed to her husband: My dear! I shall die soon. You bring water immediately. She retired, and sat in the shade of a tree. He rushed to the stream below and found a little of water inside a pit, the pressure of wild deer’s hoof made the pit. In another very shallow pit made by some crab, there was still less water. He offered the deer’s hoof’s water to her, and kept the crab’s pit’s water for himself. She eagerly swilled it and said: Pray, give me your share of water. He said: There is no water for you, not even a drop! The shrew woman became impatient; she started reviling her husband. She squabbled. He sat staring at her and trying to hide his thirst and annoyance; at last, he broke into an anguish: Your thirst is insatiable; you turn into a tortoise. Surprisingly then & there the woman was turned . into a tortoise. He sat down in disappointment and

muttered: How foolish I have been! Oh dear! oh dear! Folk Tales of Tripura 196 To sighed the tortoise. Let me depart! Let me depart! The tortoise slowly & slowly walked down the hill-slope and immersed into the stream-water far below the course. Going back home in the afternoon, the moanful father now beheld a pathetic scene. Dhobi was anxiously waiting; she asked: Where is my mother? The father could have cleared up the mystery with a few words; but instead, he replied: Your mother has gone to her sister’s house. She will come back tomorrow. The next day, he went alone to the field and spent the day in weeding, nursing,®& guarding. While returning, he went to see the tortoise down the stream. He did not forget her; he muttered and beat his forehead. The tortoise waggled the head up & down and stared pathetically. Thus seven days were passed. Meanwhile, Dhobi’s restlessness & anxiety went on increasing. The father tried to resile from the main topic & digress other topic. Dhobi became suspicious and adamant and said: I will go to my mother’s sister’s house. The daughter’s earnest appeal put the father to trouble and compelled him to clear the mystery. On waking the next morning, the father & the daughter cooked & ate and took packet (mocha bhat) of mid-day meal and set out for the field and the stream. Dhobi cried, called upon & invoked her mother. The tortoise walked out of the water. They sobbed. Dhobi became draggled & emotionally surcharged. Market, town, city & motor vehicle to-day mean little to lakhs of citizens of Tripura; but during the medieval period all those meant something astonishing. The growth

of town & city in the the rural society of Tripura was slow unless the kings encouraged the promotion for the purposes of administration & defence. Most of the markets of Tripura in those days were located along the western fringe near the Bengali settlements. The hills people had to walk several miles to reach a weekly market. The hills people would carry their goods like bamboo, baskets, cotton, jute, vegetables to sell, and they would Folk Tales of Tripura 197 -_- eee ee buy such things as kerosine, dry fish, utensils, tools, ornaments, medicines, blankets, etc. In those days, they would carry a long knife, without which travelling was risky. One day Dhobi’s father went to a distant weekly market. The day’s weather was dull; the clouds hung heavily. The path was slippery. There were numerous fire-flies glowing intermittently. The father of Dhobi had a bomboo-torch (chunga-batti) in his hand. He turned his steps homeward. It was a weary walk. He trudged almost half the way. Suddendly a gust of wind extinguished the bamboo-torch. He found himself alone and confused. So he sought refuge in an adjacent hut. By a strange decree of fate, it was the hut of a widow. The little family consisted of two members : the widow and her daughter named Kobi. At his arrival, they were smiling cunningly. He wanted to rekindle the torch for going back home. But they said : Wait a little, wait a little; take rest and smoke. He wanted to avoid them and leave the hut. He sat on his haunches limpingly only to lift the basket (=Langa) on his back. The widow made a pretension of helping the

man, but she pressed him closer to herself. He earnestly assured her that he had no intention to cajole her, no desire to marry her. The passionate widow had a certain wild attractiveness. She wanted to persuade him for marriage. To this end she used all her arts. For the moment she persuaded him to halt for the night. He agreed. The woman had a flock of cocks & hens. One cock had the rare capacity of understanding the meaning of human language. The cock jollily cast jokes at her, and humourously threatened to disclose her game. The woman too threatened to kill the cock. Thus they bantered at each other. The next morning she struck into a bargain. She made the proposal of marriage a public affair. His halt Folk Tales of Tripura 198 and presence in her house set the scandalous tongues wagging. Inexpressibly shocked, the man condemned the garne as a wicked malice. But the woman’s neighbours forced him to marry her then & there. The next day he returned home with the new wife and her daughter, Kobi. Dhobi was of about the same age as Kobi. Their arrival surprised and shocked Dhobi. She asked: Who are they? The father did not tell his daughter the true story, and the actual reason. Instead he said: You are alone; so a companion has been brought for you. And the elderly woman will serve you as the substitute of your mother. She will cook for us all. The villagers assembled there. A hubbub of voices were heard. The talk between the father and the daughter was sentimental & touchy! The daughter asked: How shall I address her? The father replied: You address her as your

aunt. Dhobi reconciled. But the aunt did not hug her in affection. Dhobi felt neglected & rejected. Months & years rolled & turned like a wheel. The new members spent a great deal of their time & thought over their own interests. The untoward event of remarriage complicated the relations. Kobi & her mother were on bad terms with Dhobi & her father. It became a broken family, a divided house, though both the sides used to maintain a veil of courtesy. Soon the home life became filled with bitterness, cunningness, diplomacy & quarrelling. Kobi & her mother contrived to discover some of the secrets which Dhobi & her father guarded so tactfully. Their inquiry apparently failed to expose the history of the tortoise. So, Kobi stealthily set out to watch the activities of Dhobi & her father. After traversing a distance of jungles, Kobi sat in a hidden place and saw Dhobi & the tortoise in a gloomy state of mind. Kobi quickly returned home and reported to her mother. Now | when the circumstance came to her knowledge, Kobi’s ‘mother determined to turn it to her own advantage. But before she could derive any advantage from that episode, Folk Tales of Tripura 199 she must, by any means, manage to upset Dhobi’s father’s mind and to upbraid him, to charge him with something disgraceful. Now, she plotted to put a psychological pressure on the mind of Dhobi’s father. She pretended to be remorseful the moment the father & the daughter used to set their feet in. She alleged: You have your former wife; you have suppressed that fact; you still maintain connection with her; you have enticed and kidnapped

me; tell me what made your first wife to be transformed into a tortoise?
