At the princely order, the minister arranged to dig a pit at a remote place and put the fruit in the pit and made a strong fencing and placed a signboard prohibiting the use of the tree and the fruit. Year after year went by. The entire episode became a matter of the past. Memory faded. Now, in Tripura there was a peasant family. It was a

family of three generations with old parents, married sons and grandchildren. The old parents had no control over their emotion; the old woman became a byword for shrewishness; the old man was equally quarrelsome. One day it reached the climax and provoked the old woman to leave the home alone. Sad & lonely, she walked and walked and entered into the forest where the fruit had been planted. The seed germinated, grew into a tree and bore fruit. She read the signboard, and purposely ate a fruit for suicide. But surprisingly she became jubilant, young and beautiful. Happily she turned her steps homeward. The old man, out of repentance, left home in search of his wife. Whomsoever he had met, he would ask: ‘Have you seen my wife?’ The common reply Folk Tales of Tripura 217 was: No. The old man too walked & walked and at last saw a young lady. She identified him and disclosed the mystery, and led him and offered him one fruit and got the result. They returned home with great joy. The news created a great sensation, and reached the ears of the king. ; - The king soon directed the minister to verify the news. The minister summoned the jubilant couple, and sent a few guards to the forest for bringing some fruits. An octogenarian person ate a fruit in front of the king and immediately became a young man. Now, there occurred an wild rush of the old people. They became young, happy, uttering songs and shouting. But the king was overcome with grief, holding his handkerchief to his eyes to hide his face and repenting for killing the Hill Mayna. Garo Folk-Tales

47. The tragedy of possessing the magic silk clothe In the old days in a Garo hamlet lived a rich man; he had his wife & one daughter. The daughter was very beautiful. According to the prevailing matrilineal system, the family had been in possession of a mysteriously woven and wonderfully decorated magic silk clothe. The great great grandmother of the family got it as a gift from some unknown source. Since then, she had been guarding it with utmost caution. The grand old lady fell sick and as she felt that her end was drawing near, she called her daughter to her bedside and said: Dear child! take this silk clothe; preserve & protect it; touch it. The daughter touched it; soon the form of her body was instantly changed into a bird; the grand old lady uttered a mantra; instantly the bird’s body was changed into that of a girl. The daughter was astonished to see the magical Folk Tales of Tripura 218 transformation. The grand old woman taught her the special spell. After a few days, the grand old woman closed her“éyes: In course of time, the daughter was married. She had her children. She too fell ill and called her daughter to her bedside and said: Dear child! take this silk clothe; preserve & protect it. She taught the special spell connected with it. Thus, a few generations passed. And the unique heritage passed on from generation to generation. It was unfortunately the last generation. The rich man’s wife suddenly died of an accident; she could not teach the special mantra connected with the clothe. The rich man did not live long after his wife’s death. He

arranged his daughter’s marriage, and within a year he died. Now, the very beautiful daughter and her husband were the only members of the family. The young couple became the custodians of the family’s property. They were looking after the affairs of the family with care. The beautiful daughter was now the young wife of a young husband. The young wife had a very hazy idea about the magical silk clothe; the young husband had no idea about ‘is One day, the young wife took out the richly decorated magic clothe from the store room only to dry it in the sun rays. She spread it in the courtyard, with a strict instruction to her young husband that under no circumstance he should touch the clothe. She then went down the hill to a nearby stream for bathing and fishing. - Suddenly the sky became overcast with cloud; bank of cloud was moving rapidly. The rain was falling heavily. A mighty thunder broke the stillness of the day. The husband very loudly called for the wife. Because of the squall of rain, she did not hear properly. The special silk clothe was getting spoiled. So, the anxious husband rushed to the courtyard to take the clothe inside. The Folk Tales of Tripura 219 ee ee ee moment he had touched the clothe, he was changed into a peacock bird. The young wife rushed to the spot to protect the husband; she too touched the husband; then & there she was transformed into a peahen. This is the reason why peacock & peahen become impatient at the sight of impending rainfall and hailstorm. 48. Raja Abong Noga -Formerly there flourished a Garo king named Raja

Abong Noga in the hills of north-eastern part of Bharat. The Raja’s kingdom suffered a severe famine. The main cause was drought for a few years. An extreme & protracted shortage of food resulted in starvation, disease and death. Despite the misery & tragedy occasioned by the famine, the king did practically nothing for the welfare of the people. The Garo community conadeiedi of a number of clans. Each clan had its own village on hill-tops. The villages were scattered here & there. The villages stood apart from one another; between two villages there were hills & jungles. The Garo people subsisted on fishing, hunting, gathering, basketry, weaving, jum cultivation, etc. The raja forced his subjects to build a beautiful house for the royal family; to build a garden, to dig a pond, to cultivate an orchard. Not only that, he assigned the work of gathering, fishing, hunting, etc. to the clans for the consumption of the royal family. The royal family had its essential commodities supplied on account of the forced labour. The members of the royal family whiled away the time in the garden, in the orchard, in the palace, in pleasures. They were living in clover. Stricken with sorrows & sufferings, the subjects were enduring pain in collecting, in gathering, in fishing, in cultivating for the royal family. It produced anguish in the minds of the subjects. Their faces hinted that they disapproved the royal order. Protesting against the exploitation, the subjects carefully contrived a plot to take revenge, to kill the Folk Tales of Tripura 220 members of the royal family one after another. When a certain period of time had passed, the subjects became restless. They killed his daughters, named Mene, Meje,

Chini one after another. They attacked the royal guard. Next, they attemped to kidnap the king and the queen, but failed. The king and the queen escaped and fled to a remote hill. Only a few servants accompanied the royal couple. Now, the king and the queen fell in great trouble. The servants were displeased with the king & the queen. The queen was unskilled and inexperienced in domestic duties & chores. One day, she sought the instruction of the servants about the process of sowing seeds. The servants misguided her. According to their instruction, she boiled the seeds & then went to sow the seeds. The seeds did not germinate. The king had one grand daughter named Keme. The wet-nurse protected Keme from the hands of the killers. The maid servant was the wet-nurse; her name was Nogang. Nogang said: No, no, the baby is my daughter. Thus, she saved & nursed the baby, Keme. Keme was married to a prince named Ushung Raja. Ushung Raja was the founder of a principality, at Durgapur in the district of Mymensingh. 49. Raja Gangbo Nokma In the very old days there was in a Garo village a man named Gangbo Nokma; he was a quick-witted, cunning fellow, a thug. By means fair & fowl, he earned a lot. Fired with anger & jealousy, the village elders made a secret plot to kill the thug. The plot was to set fire to the thug’s house at night when he would lay sound asleep. The house was made of bamboo, timber, thatching grass and cane. All combustible materials! And accident of fire was a common experience in those days. The fire would be taken as an_ accident.

The cunning fellow suspected something fishy. He Folk Tales of Tripura 221 told his wife : We should not make the neighbours suspect that we know their plot. We should remove & stash our valuable things away in the deep forest before hand, and we should get away at the right moment through a narrow passage, an egress. Let us continue to live with an apparent carelessness. One day at midnight, the village elders fastened the doors and set fire to it. The cunning fellow & his wife hurried out through the secret passage, groping their way out in the darkness, & spent the night in the forest. The village elders were at once warm with joy. The next morning Gangbo came out of the forest and posed like a ruined peasant. With a gloomy face, he sat aghast near the homestead and tended to beat his forehead. The villagers were surprised to see him alive. They gathered around him. In their presence, he filled up a few bags with ashes. Gangbo carried the sacks of ashes all alone and went a long distance and reached a lonely place. A stream was flowing there. He dropped the ashes in the water and uttered a magic spell imploring the river goddess to punish the elders who had committed arson. ~ Just after a few days, Gangbo appeared again confidently and smilingly and opened a purse of coins in presence of the villagers. The curious neighbours asked about the coins. He replied: The valuable ashes of my hut have been purchased by some foreign merchants. So, the accident has been a blessing in disguise. It was a market day. The greedy villagers, without

losing time, burned down their own huts, and rushed to the market with sacks full of ashes. But alas! none purchased the ashes. The sellers of ashes became the laughing-stock of the people. They came back home empty-handed. Fired with anger & hatred, the villagers decided to kill all the cattle of Gangbo. They were about to assault him physically. Gangbo said: I did not advise you to burn your own huts. You did it at your own risk. Folk Tales of Tripura 222 The angry villagers forcibly took away all the cattle and slaughtered them. Being- implored by Gangbo, the villagers spared the skins. Gangbo washed & dried up the skins, punctured some skins and made some bags and moved southward. Gangbo travelled & travelled towards south-west. He went up the hillocks & down the hillocks. The rugged features of the mountains were getting softened towards south-west. He went up to a rising ground to look farther. He saw a peasant cultivating his land with plough & a pair of bullocks. He went there and said: Brother, lama leather merchant. I am at present very thirsty. Kindly give me drinking water. The farmer directed him to go farther and to seek water from his children. Gangbo went to the farmer’s house and said : Children! your father has sent me for money. You show me the treasure. The children refused to give & refused to show. Gangbo yelled out: Dear friend! your children are not giving. The busy farmer, without enquiry, said loudly: Give him what he wants. The children hinted at an earthen pitcher full of coins and jewellery. Gangbo put inside his bag many coins and smilingly left the farmer’s house and moved towards

the farmer and thanked him. Following a different track, he decamped and came back home. On reaching near his village, Gangbo strolled leisurely with a leather bag suspended from the forehead behind the head. In presence of the villagers, he opened the bag and started counting the coins. The villagers rushed there and asked about the coins. He replied: Thank you for slaughtering my cattle and giving me the skin. By selling the skin, I got such a huge amount of money. There is a great demand for such skin. Folk Tales of Tripura 223 The foolish villagers slaughtered their own cattle, dried the skins, and carried the skins to the weekly market for sale. They displayed the skins. But nobody purchased. Eager for making money, that day the villagers had gone to the market earlier. Gangbo left home late in hopes to improve his fortune by any means. While travelling towards the market, he came across a clothe- merchant near a prosperous village. The elderly people of the village went to the market; the children were left behind. Gangbo made friendship with the children and the merchant and wanted to purchase clothes on credit. To befool the merchant, Gangbo showed a house as his own; his name was Onjawa; his father’s name was Manjawa. In his dialect Onjawa means ‘will-not-give’; Manjawa means ‘could not get’. Ignorant of the thug’s dialect, the merchant noted down the names & handed over the clothes and reminded the thug to get the money ready after sometime. After a few months the merchant came and stood before the house and called on the buyer; the house- owner came out and denied and gave him a good

thrashing. Nevertheless, Gangbo came back home and dressed himself fashionably. Afterwards, the angry villagers returned from the market and tied the swindler up and thrust him into a basket and carried him to a distantly located pond. There, taking the burden off, the unburdened carriers walked away to take rest & food in the shade of a banyan tree. Meanwhile, a young cowherd came to see the strange basket and asked the captive: Who are you? where are you going? The captive replied: I am being taken against my will under the orders of our king to be the bridegroom of the lovely princess’. She loves me. I do not love her. Folk Tales of Tripura 224 EG The cowherd said: You are a fool. You are denying the hand of a princess! I am interested. The captive said: If you are interested, immediately release me, and you take and get into the basket & remain silent. This was quickly done. Gangbo very rapidly drove away the cattle towards his village, leaving the cowherd inside. Now after taking rest & food, the carriers returned to the spot and thrust off the basket into the deep water of the pond. Returning home, the carriers were astonished to find Gangbo alive and in possession of many cattle. They asked about the cattle. Gangbo said: Thank you for thrusting me off. Inside the pond, there are many cattle. The villagers made many baskets and got into those baskets. Gangbo thrust off the baskets into the pond. There they died. Gangbo got rid off his enemies. He became chief. 50. The Polyglot Chieftain Dampo’s Darling Once upon a time, there was, among the Garo people,

a rich chieftain; Dampo was his name; he had one wife and a daughter & a son. They got on very well together. The chieftain used to call her in private: My dear Darling. He was a landlord; he had fields & farms, domestic animals & birds, servants & relatives. Dampo was a polyglot; he had the mysterious gift of understanding the dialects of animals & birds. But the gift was a blessing as well as a curse. Divulgation of the esoteric knowledge would be fatal. ~ One night Dampo & his wife lay awake in bed; their cow-shed was not far away; Dampo heard a conversation between an ass and a bullock. The ass said: It is a pity to see you always toiling for our master. You pretend to be sick; do not eat fodder. The bullock said: I am grateful to you. Thank you. I shall follow your advice. Dampo, on hearing the conversation, chuckled. His wife wanted to know the cause of his laugh. Dampo gave an evasive reply, & said: It is nothing. | am a madman, please sleep. The wife was not satisfied with the reply. Folk Tales of Tripura 225 She did not insist, because it was the first occasion. With a friendly smile, she simply said: I am your only pretty dear! will you not tell me the cause of your laugh? The next morning the servant found that one of the bullocks had been seriously ill. Dampo directed the servant to harness the cunning ass in lieu of the sick bullock. Not at all accustomed to the drudgery of dragging the heavy plough and yoke, the ass became utterly exhausted. The ploughman also gave the ass a good

thrashing. In the afternoon the ass saw the sick bullock taking rest in a serene atmosphere in the shade of a tree; it added insult to the injury of the ass. 3 At night the chieftain remained alert and awake to overhear the conversation between the ass and the bullock. The shrewd ass said: My dear friend! I have a secret news for you. Our master has been seriously thinking to sell you to some beef-eaters, who will cut you to pieces. So, if you like to live, do not pretend to be sick. The bullock thanked the ass for the timely warning. Dampo overheard the dialogue and smiled again and murmured. The murmuring sound awakened the drowsy wife. It was the second occasion. She became suspicious. She leered and asked: What makes you to smile all by yourself? Are you mentally all right? What are you thinking about? Do you see anything funny about me? Please tell me. I am your only wife? I am the half of yourself! They could not sleep till late at night; from time to time she went on asking this or that question. She sat & remained awake for hours. Knowning fully well that the confession might turn out to be something fatal, Dampo consoled her and seized her hand and said: My dear darling, please sleep, please sleep! There is nothing in my smile or laugh. I was simply relaxing. For about three months the nagging continued off & on. Slowly & slowly she was becoming intolerant, aggressive and adamant. She was complaining publicly Folk Tales of Tripura 226 a ca ee & persistently, and asking awkward questions. At last she beat her forehead & cried out: Your love for me is a

pretence. Your confidence in me is a farce. Thus the nagging went to the verge of insanity. Now the chieftain said: My darling! You did not refrain from asking me silly questions on a very negligible issue. And | tried my best to dissuade you. But in vain! So, one day | shall reveal and then die immediately. If you agree, I shall disclose tomorrow. Prepare delicious food for me as the last meal. The wife agreed. She was found to smile after a long period. She started the preparation. But the chieftain’s pet dog, overhearing the conversation, became very sad. The dog stopped eating & drinking; tears were rolling down the muzzle of the dog. The dog lay motionless in front of the house. Meanwhile one hen, being chased by the majestic cock, seriously disturbed the mournful dog. The dog scorned the hen and the cock and forbade the birds to refrain from enjoyment in view of the impending danger & death. The cock paid no attention to the dog’s advice. Then the dog said: Yesterday, | overheard the conversation between our master & his wife. The master failed to dissuade her. She repeatedly insisted. The master submitted to her pressure and agreed to explain the cause of his soliloquy. After the disclosure, he will die. The master warned, but she stuck to her insistence. So, a tragic incident is impending. The sprightful cock gremaced & impromptu remarked: What type of chieftain is he? How can such an average man manage the difficult problems of the people? See how I have kept more than thirty hens under perfect control. He fails to control even only wife! He fails to

control trifling problems! The lady has bewitched him. He is little better than a henpecked husband. Such a spineless, worthless fellow should have an ignominious Folk Tales of Tripura 227 end. It is a matter of shame that we honour him as our master. After overhearing the conversation between the dog . and the cock, the husband came to his senses. He became animated & assertive, daring & dynamic. It was mid-morning; the sun was shining brightly; the wife & her assistants were busy in the kitchen room; the chieftain was busy in allotting duties to the servants. About two to three hours later, the wife invited the husband for dining. She served the delicious dishes. Dampo relished the food and appreciated the preparation. After that he sat in his verandah for chewing betel leaf & smoking. The hubble-bubble was ready. His wife, after taking the breakfast, sat beside him. Chewing the betel leaf, she eagerly leered to know the secret. Dampo, as a sort of ultimatum, confidently warned about the dire consequence. But she became furious with anger. Dishevelling the hair, she beat her forehead. Dampo suddenly stood up, and catching her hair kicked her and thrashed her thoroughly. She was panting, sobbing and crying. The dog & the cock silently observed the scene. The curious neighbours rushed, but nobody dared to restrain the husband. Being deluded & debunked, she truckled and did never attempt to annoy the husband. In course of time, they got reconciled and lived happily. 51. Chela Asanpa & Brar Once upon a time in a Garo village dwelt a hero; Chela Asanpa was his name, a man of gigantic body, immense strength and superb courage. He was young,

gay and volatile. He was a voracious eater & matchless wrestler. Chela Asanpa’s special hobby was wrestling. He defeated all the youths of his village one after another. He had his traditional weapens; milam (= two-edged sword) and spi ( = a rectangular shield). He would often grapple Folk Tales of Tripura 228 his opponent bare handed and easily knock him down. He was a man of a number of adventures. One day while travelling along through a dense forest, Chela Asanpa encountered a big wild buffalo. The buffalo attacked him and inflicted a gash. Chela Asanpa lifted the beast off the ground & dashed it against a huge rock; the beast died. Chela took the carcass to a stream, washed it, & then roasted it and consumed it. Chela girded himself for the next adventure and followed a track across the hills. He travelled & reached a village where another strong man had been splitting bamboos with his mere hands. The strong man offered him hospitality with food, drink and lodging; the host slaughtered a domestic animal for the food of Chela. After the lunch, Chela made a formal proposal of wrestling . The host agreed. The next day in the morning, they cleared a site, bathed,.took breakfast and rested for a while. Then they started the game. They roared, struggled, jerked & wrestled. Two goats while fighting agrily draw apart and dash together. Similarly the two wretlers were to threaten each other, approach, draw apart & dash. The villagers stood around with bated breath. The game continued for hours. At last Chela made the last attempt & hurled down the opponent. The villagers congregrated there, applauded; & the wrestlers too

appreciated each other. The host again entertained Chela & slaughtered a pig & on the host’s request, the village priest sacrificed a hen and cock, examined the intestines and found auspicious sign about the luck of Chela. Chela turned his steps homeward; while travelling through hills & forest, Chela saw a large & long python. The python coiled & entangled a male deer. The deer struggled to come out of the clutch of the snake, but failed. The deer cried out and died. The snake was relaxing only to relish the deer. Chela twiched & lifted up the dead deer. In the twinkling of an eye, the angry snake entangled and coiled Chela. Chela very promptly caught Folk Tales of Tripura 229 hold of the python’s head with one hand, and uncoiled himself with another hand and then killed the snake. Returning home, Chela relished the meat of the deer. Chela again girded himself for another adventure. After travelling a long distance, he saw a strong man; this strong man was husking paddy; he held a big, flat rock.on his palm; a big basket of paddy was placed on the rock; he blew the chaff far away with his breath. Chela introduced himself. This strong man offered him hospitality with food, drink & lodging. After the lunch, they sat together for friendly conversation. Chela expressed his desire for a duel. The host agreed. The host slaughtered 25 cocks & hens to entertain Chela with a very rich, delicious dish. The wrestlers dined together. Then they started the game. They roared, chapped, danced, laughed, struggled and wrestled in presence of the villagers. The children, youths and elders stood around and enjoyed the game.

Chela came out victorious. The defeated host took the defeat sportingly. The host’s 15 wives, 26 sons and 32 daughters prepared meal and meat-curry with the fried flesh of 25 ducks & 9 cocks. Chela thanked the host for the hospitality. Chela resumed his journey. As he travelled in the hills, he came to a Garo village; he introduced himself; the villagers offered him moderate food, and lodging in the bachelors’ dormitory (= Nok phanto). He observed the gloomy face of the villagers. The villagers told him of the depradation of a wild tiger, and advised him not to sleep in the open portico of the Nok phanto at night. Chela smiled confidently and slept in the portico. He had his weapon near his bed. At about midnight, the tiger silently came with blood thirsty ferocity; and tiger’s eyes were like two torchlights. Chela instantly lay awake, watched & crouched down with the weapon in his hand. The tiger jumped up. Instantly, Chela inflicted fatal injury with one sweep of the sword. The wounded beast jumped Folk Tales of Tripura 230 backward & died on the spot. The next morning the villagers rushed to the spot; they were very happy to see the monster dead; the grateful villagers arranged a feast for Chela. Chela, next, travelled westward and then turned towards north. There in the hills a big elephant rushed at him with evil intention. Chela, catching the elephant’s trunk, hurled & whirled the elephant. The elephant was flung to the deep gorge with tremendous violence. Chela was now travelling homeward. But still it was at a long distance. On the way, he had to halt ata village; There he saw another strong man. Brar was his

name. Brar was uprooting stiff clumps of bamboo with his bare hands. Suspecting the stranger to be an enemy, Brar stood up with his weapons (= milam & spi). Chela smiled & introduced himself. Brar welcomed him and offered him befitting hospitality. After the supper, Chela expressed his desire for a game of wrestling. Brar agreed. The next morning the two players bathed, ate together and came to the ground near a river. The two strong men struggled, roared, dashed, wrestled for hours. The curious villagers stood all around with bated breath; they talked among themselves, encouraged and watched with great suspense. At last, Brar defeated Chela. For the first time Chela’s bragging was wounded unexpectedly. However, Brar received again gently and again offered him customary hospitality without expecting anything in return. While leaving the home of Brar, the defeated wrestler made a formal invitation to Brar. After a few days of rest, Brar decided to comply with the request. However, on his request the village priest sacrificed a few cocks & hens and examined the entrails and found some omens. The divination seemed inauspicious. Now what to do? He was in a dilemma. His aged mother blessed the son. Brar sharpened his weapons. Meanwhile, Chela too had sacrificed hens & found good signs. He too kept his weapons ready. Brar was Folk Tales of Tripura 231 approaching towards the village of Chela. Chela was anxiously waiting for the arrival of Brar. There was a very big simul tree (Bomlaz malabaricum). It was a sylvan and shadowy environment. Chela lay in ambush and crouched down with weapons in hand. Walking a long distance, Brar got tired; he casually struck the simul

tree with his weapon; the weapon penetrated the trunk of the tree. Chela instantly and savagely attacked Brar; Brar’s head fell on the ground. Chela treacherously killed Brar. The people mourned the murder of Brar. Chela killed many animals & birds, & defeated a few strong men; but he could not tolerate the shame of only defeat! 52. Delong’s exploration Long ago, far removed from a Garo hamlet, there was a primeval forest. With its high ranges, deep gorges, towering trees, wild beasts, incredible swarms of mosquitoes, ants & blackflies, & flocks of birds & poisonous snakes, and a melancholy of the wilderness, the primeval forest was a geographic nightmare for a solitary gatherer or hunter. Naturally, the people’s fears & rumours grew into a myth, ranging from the claim that the thick forest had been the abode of fairies & elves, to the legend that the wild tract was a queendom. Strange monsters guarded the forest. Numerous fishes used to frolic in the waters of streams inside the hill tract. The melodious songs of the frairies enchanted the air of the area. The mysterious forest was rejected by saints and shunned by men. In that Garo hamlet dwelt a brave boy; Delong was his name. Delong was endowed with certain qualities to make a happy life; he was young, strong, honest, courageous and faithful & benevolent. Delong and all other children of the hamlet had been hearing those hair-raising tales; but Delong alone became curious. Years rolled on. Delong was now a youth. His curiosity Folk Tales of Tripura 232 grew into an obsession with everything sylvan. Born in a family of shifting cultivators and hunters, the boy was

tough, self-reliant and adventurous. He planned to explore the wild & fanciful forest. He took dry food, clothes, weapon & a few personal belongings. He made his plan public and sought the permission of the headman and the blessings of the parents. The elders were disconsolate. To them, it was a dangerous & foolish adventure. They were in tears. He comforted them. He had no difficulty in prevailing upon the elders to let him go. One day by the mid-morning, Delong set out. The villagers came out to encourage, bless and watch the brilliant adventurer. The neighbours stood looking on, while Delong looked back frequently as he moved forward. The scenes gradually faded from their view. There was no youth to equal Delong in discipline & devotion. He was ready to struggle to the death to explore the romantic region. He had no prospect of seeing any person to speak to for days to come. At long last, he entered the forest. There he came across several wild beasts: buffalo, leopard, tiger, wolf, elephant, deer, dog, monkey, bear, boar, etc. Because of his saintly character, the wild beasts did not even attempt to attack him. The python and the dangerous cobras hissed and slipped; one deadly cobra swayed obediently & left. One hog, uttering a grunting bleat, side-tracked. With their sharp eyes, ears & noses, the beasts found in him no danger. He abstained from killing any of them. It was a tropical forest; there were plenty of edible roots, tubers, vegetables & fruits. He gathered some vegetables; cooked them and ate..In the stream & springs there were plenty of fishes some of which popped to the surface water. He cought some of them, cooked & relished

them. Almost everywhere he had to encounter creeping plants & tangled bushes. He had to force his way along with difficulty. Folk Tales of Tripura 233 He moved deeper & deeper into the wild forest, ducking under the dangling branches of trees, side- stepping many trees, plodding & plopped down in the shade of a tree. Thus, he went on roaming in the forest. The sense of sadness & loneliness or the melancholy of the wilderness never came over his mind. Every slight noise used to make his pulses thrill with joy. He was thoroughly enjoying every moment. As the wrestling sun would daily sink out of sight beyond the mountains, he would climb up a big tree for rest during the night; he would ususlly select a trunk from which a few branches simultaneously had shot out. The wild forest was the safe resort of many types of birds, such as kite, vulture, fowl, waterhen, lapwing, dove, parrot, koel, crow pheasant, small green bee eater, woodpecker, crow, hill myna, flower pecker, etc. Flock of small birds would soar overhead and sing melodious songs. One woodpecker perched upright & ran up & down the tree-trunks in search of insects. One day in a deep jungle of tall trees he saw many bats with heads hanging downwards from the branches of trees. Some chirpy birds were flitting from branch to branch. One day he flung himself on a pile of leaves. He was scanning the cloudy sky. He was thoroughly in love with the natural environment. The cloud looked like a huge mass of puffy cotton: slowly & slowly the bank of cloud disappeared, and the air became bracing, fresh and crisp.

As he travelled deeper & deeper into the vast wilderness, he saw a valley, a wild open valley full of. flowers. The vast valley had a lake at the middle point. The water of the lake was clean & clear; the water rippled. At the centre of the lake stood a hillock. A narrow causeway linked the hillock to the bank of the lake; the causeway was dark, murky, obscure, shadowy and very narrow. It was a secret route. He had an uncannny sense of fear. Ahead lay the first hurdle. It seemed to him that the crux of the mystery of the Folk Tales of Tripura 234 El forest lay in the hillock. The isolated hillock was protected by a ring of clear water. Delong did not hastily march towards the hillock. He halted on the bank of the beautiful lake for rest, bath and food. He had to brood over the question: Am I in the right place? and decided to take the last risk. It was worth a try. By the mid-morning of next day, he started crossing the causeway. He trudged cautiously and set every step slowly & carefully. Crossing the causeway and climbing the top of the hillock, he saw a track; walking along the track he found a narrow ravine between boulders of rocks. Delong penetrated further. He was looking around & murmuring. The murmuring was hardly out of his mouth before a stout dog came out with a fierce bark within a short distance of where he was standing. Immediately a young girl came to protect the stranger. The dog obediently stopped barking and stood there observing the stranger. The girl’s black and

sharp eyes scanned the stranger. She gently asked: What makes you to come to this abode of the queen of herbs & plants? Delong replied: My innocent love of adventure brought me here. She said: Welcome, follow me. Delong followed her obediently and passed through a number of gates; they crept down the narrow passage, they crawled; they strolled through a labyrinthine, zigzag track; and entered into a very beautifully decorated hall. Being directed by the girl, Delong sat there. The girl went inside. Situated atop a hill, the magnificent house was encircled by a low stone wall; it wore an aspect of peace & plenty. A thrill of awe ran through his heart. After a while, there appeared a maiden of superb beauty, tall, slim, graceful, magnificently attired in very fine clothes. She was the queen of herbs & plants. Her noble mien bespoke her a lady of no ordinary kind. The queen scanned the visitor and came to know his history. Satisfied with his noble character, the queen smilingly Folk Tales of Tripura 235 offered him a glass of water; the water had excellent capacity of healing. The queen was not a witch; she had genuine sympathy for all beings. Similarly, Delong was honest to the backbone. This bred a trust between them that ignored formality. The first girl stood looking on with an expression on her face that boded him good will. Delong was very glad to accept the queen’s invitation to spend the night in her residence. He had a sound sleep. The next morning the fear turned to relief as he had not experienced anything awkward during the last night. By the mid-morning the queen offered him a little

quantity of food & drink and then took him to a garden on the eastern side of her residence. This herbarium had very useful creepers, herbs & plants of excellent medicinal value. The queen alone knew the qualities of those herbs. The queen taught him about the qualities of certain plants & allowed him to spend the second night there. On the third day, the queen led him to another garden on the western side of her residence and explained to him about the latent power of certain poisonous plants. She walked slowly & talked softly,which marked her dignity. By the mid-morning of the fourth day Delong, with a bag full of useful roots & seeds, turned his steps homeward. When the queen approached to bid him farewell, he could not check his emotion. His parents were eagerly waiting for his safe return. To the numerous questions of his parents & the neighbours, Delong gave evasive replies. But he took care to develop a herbarium and to cure the patients. He became famous and popular. He did not marry. He had a friend named Neurot. Neurot had his wife & children. Delong imparted Neurot a little knowledge of the medicinal plants. One day the two friends set out for the queendom. But Neurot was not allowed to enter into the queendom. Disapponited Neurot returned Folk Tales of Tripura 236 ON —————— home. But Delong never returned home. The queen’s last advice was like this: an unscrupulous person should not be in possession of occult powers. 53. Life in a wily woman’s family Long ago in a Garo hamlet lived a family of seven members: mother-in-law, daughter, son-in-law and four daughters, namely Awil, Singwil, Nose, Dimse. The

mother-in-law was a cruel, ugly,old woman; she disliked the grand-daughters; she was envious of their beauty. The old woman was an incendiary and a shrew with a natural instinct to promote quarrels. She was like a poisonous arum plant. Such a person requires an eye- sore. Awil & Singwil were her eye-sores. To disparage them, she was out to manoeuvre a number of plots. She mixed bran & husk with the rice husked by Awil & Singwil; she put hair into the rice cooked by them; she added a quantity of salt with the curry cooked by them; she dropped sand into the drinking water drawn by them. One day the mother of Awil & Singwil told Awil & Singwil to bring down paddy from the granary, to thrash the paddy with their feet and to dry the rice in the sun and then to draw water from the stream about one hundred feet below the hamlet. The two sisters diligently thrashed the paddy and spread them out in the courtyard to dry. Next, they had to fetch water and to take Nose & Dimse to the stream: for a bath. Their parents had gone -to the jum field. So, Awil & Singwil requested the grandmother to protect the rice from cock, hen, sparrow, dove, pig, etc. The cruel woman got an opportunity to belittle the grand-daughters; she stashed the rice. Upon returning from the stream, the grand-daughters found no trace of the rice and asked the old woman: Grandmother, grandmother! where is the rice? The grandmother answered: A pig ate up the rice. It was mid-afternoon. About two hours later, their parents would come back and see the work left undone.

Folk Tales of Tripura 237 Their mother would rebuke & punish them. So, the two sisters forebodingly brought down another basket of rice from the granary and started pounding them without drying them. They had to feed the grandmother and the two sisters also. Meanwhile, the parents returned and found them pounding the rice with mortar & pestle. The tired mother asked: What! why you have not yet completed the task? They went on pounding the paddy with an expression of grievance & injury in their face. The grandmother limpingly came forward to add a pincher : leaving the rice unguarded, they went to the stream to dabble; meanwhile a pig and a cock ate up the rice. Now they are pounding another basket of rice. The two sisters found no time to open their mouths; the angry mother thoroughly beat them. Will your grand- mother tell a lie? You were callous and negligent at that time! That was not the only occasion. Their father had gone to a weekly market. The old woman implicated the two grand-daughters in something wrong. Their mother did not verify & did not give them a chance to express their opinion and rashly beat them and flung them inside a pig-sty for the rest of the night. The next morning the parents left the house for the jum field. The two daughters remained confined without food & drinking water. At about mid-morning, a few children came there to play games with some seeds. During the game, one seed rolled into the pig-sty. One boy went to collect the seed. Awil made an appeal: If you kindly rescue us by opening the door, we shall give you the seed. The boy opened the

door and got the seed. The two sisters came out. Awil said to Singwil: We shall no longer stay here. You collect some feathers from the fowl-house. I am cooking rice. Singwil collected feathers and Awil cooked rice. They ate and sat together. Awil lamented: Why should we remain here! We are the worst victims of the jealousy of Folk Tales of Tripura 238 i the old woman. Each afternoon our cousin sister comes home tired, but happy to be greeted warmly by the loving grandmother. We find ourselves struggling with the tasks of managing an unkind family. We are writhing with wrenching confrontation. We are not getting any justice even from our mother. Our father is indifferent.Even hell is better than this house. So, let us leave it and take refuge among the flock of doves. Let us stick these feathers to our body and fly away. Miraculously, the two sisters were transformed into birds. They flew out and met a flock of doves. The doves received them heartily. The entire flock of birds perched on the branches of a tall tree. All the old birds gathered together and comforted the two new birds. The new birds narrated their tragic story thus: All the lies the grandmother speaks And tears roll down our cheeks. We were not in a hurry To add extra salt into the curry. We were not of whimsical mood To put hair into our food. We were given the task To take out paddy & to husk. We asked grandmother to guard She stashed rice & blamed us hard. Mother beat us with firewood With her own hand rude. All the duties the elders told

We accomplished, gay & bold. We had been toiling for years We got blames, beatings & blears. Now vanished all hope, all respect We have nothing to expect. The parents of the two sisters were working in the jum field. They heard the tragic song. At first they could Folk Tales of Tripura 239 not believe it. The two birds repeated the song twice or thrice. The parents became astonished & worried; they left the work, and hurried back and found the pig-sty empty. They cried loudly and entreated their daughters. In response the birds pathetically repeated the same tragic song! The false blame and the cruel beating rankled in their mind. The parents were little suited to comprehend the jealousy of the grandmother, and to feel in time the consequences of agony of the daughters. All aged persons are not mature & sensible; all children are not childish! 54. How the alienated dog became avengeful! Long ago animals used to have their own markets; the animals had their own kingdom; the animals used to talk to each other; they lived in amity & enjoyment. One day, the dog went to a weekly market with a quantity of peas (= Matar) for sale. Other animals had their vegetables, roots & tubers for sale; they sold their products. But the dog could not sell the peas. No purchaser came to ask the price even. The customers retreated; because, all the peas were banal, decomposed, fetid, hackneyed and and stale. The dog displayed it to the customers; and tried to touch the hearts of the customers. But in vain! The customers could not tolerate the offensive smell of the rotten, fetid peas.

As time went on, the rotten peas were diffusing the stench. Initially, the neighbouring sellers left that corner of the market. Both customers & sellers were affected. The air of the entire market became redolent with the stench. It evoked reaction. A number of animals protested, abused & reviled the dog and ravaged the shop. The unfortunate dog went to the chamber of commerce; the tiger was in the chair. The dog made a complaint and sought redress. The tiger showed no sympathy and rather wrathfully cried out: You idiot, get out; you have spoiled the goodwill of the market; how did Folk Tales of Tripura 240 you dare to befool the customers? Your fetid peas have spoiled the business of others! The tiger spurned the dog. The poor, forlorn dog was going back in the evening. The dog was brooding about his fate. No beast lent a sympathetic ear to his appeal! On the way, the dog came across a man. Observing the pale muzzle of the dog, the man asked: What happened to you? you seem to be in some distress! The dog narrated the unhappy incident and then said: All beasts hate me; where can I live in safety? The man said: Do not worry; come with me, live with me. I shall feed you and teach you a counter-strategy. Henceforth, the man and the dog became friends. They lived together. Alienated from the animal kingdom, the dog shifted allegiance. The wild animal became a domestic animal. The dog started guarding the house and the cattle of the man. The man had a hobby for fishing and hunting. The man had steady nerves for hunting. And the dog had

sharp eyes, ears and nose. The hunter trained the dog in the strategy of hunting. The hunter’s traditional weapons, bows & arrows, had limitations too. The dog’s efficiency helped the hunter a lot. Reversely, the hunter’s steady nerves and weapons helped the dog a lot to take revenge. Khasia Folk-Tales 55. The Lazy moon . Long, long ago there lived a family of six members: husband & wife and four children. Out of the four children, there were daughters, and youngest of all, a little son. Their names were Ka Sngi (= sun), Ka Um (= water), Ka Ding (= fire), and U Bymai (= moon). In the beginning, the sun and the moon were equally bright. The three sisters had love and affection for the little brother. The sisters did all outdoor and indoor jobs. Folk Tales of Tripura 241 The parents also would not ask him to do any work. There was nothing that they would not have given to the little boy. So, the boy became lazy & licentious, indulging in excessive freedom. Years rolled on. The little boy grew into a handsome youth. The loving sisters gradually became annoyed with the wayward brother. He had a vein of frivolity which disconcerted the serious minded sisters. He was a foppish masher, a fellow dressing showily to attract the attention of the young girls. As the sun had a fair face, the young brother was harbouring an intention to marry the sister (= sun). The sister got a smell of the intention. The sun came to know the evil intention of the brother. The sun became very angry. The horror of incest terribly annoyed the sister. The sister contemplated to

teach him a lesson. She discussed the matter with her sisters; they, too, supported. One day in presence of the sisters, the eldest sister (= sun) charged him thus: How dare you harbour such incestuous intention; I nursed you. I held you in arms, I fed you. I carried you on my back like a mother does! You deserve a severe punishment. We will besmear ashes over your face. Then & there the sisters smeared black ashes over the face of the brother (= moon). The besmutted brother left the parental home with his head downcast. Henceforth, the disparaged moon was having a pale light and black spots. The three daughters remained at home to look after the parents. After the quarrel, the moon went to live separately. 56. Into the valley of death Formerly, the animals, the birds and the human beings had a common language; it was the language of men; when men talked, others could understand. And the animals and the birds held men in high esteem as the dispenser of justice & as their lord. One day on an invitation from the lord, all the creatures got assembled and participated in a festival. It Folk Tales of Tripura 242 was a festival of dancing, singing & feasting. The participants were in a joyous mood. They were laughing, clapping, screaming, fluttering, dancing and joking. The sun & the moon were the children of the same parents. The sun was sister; the moon was brother. The sun & the moon came rather late. They too started dancing; but their steps were a bit unrhythmical. So, some of the spectators, like the frog, the mole, the monkey, the owl, etc., were laughing at the brother and

the sister; they were talking among themselves jeeringly. The moon & the sun felt sad & insulted and went home. Their home was in a cave, the abode of the dead. Immediately after that, there was nothing but darkness. Living in the deep darkness was troublesome. All the creatures became worried. It was a chaotic situation, a pandemonium. The lord asked: ‘Who will go & bring back the sun & the moon from the cave, the abode of the dead?’ Hearing this, all the creatures kept mum like a picture dumb. One elephant was there; the elephant said: My lord! I shall strive to do the best I can. But I am bulky; however, | shall allow myself to be used in any ceremonial parade after the arrival of the sun and the moon. Next, the horse, the goat, the tiger, the leopard came forward to strive to do their best. Soon came forward a beautiful bird, the horn-bill bird. The horn-bill said: My lord! leave this task to me. I am confident enough to convince the sun & the moon. I assure you all. With the good will of all, the horn-bill went alone and flew & flew down the cave and reached the destination. The sun received the horn-bill coordially. The horn-bill, after taking rest for a while, narrated the appeal of all creatures. The sun smiled. The mischievous smile enchanted the bird. Forgetting the mission, the bird slowly started to woo the beautiful sun. The sun disliked the bird’s prattling and gave the bird a good Folk Tales of Tripura 243 thrashing. Being insulted, the horn-bill had to leave the place then & there and related his sad experience.

The lord again asked: Who will volunteer for this task? No: response came. The lord asked: Who is absent? All looked around and found the cock absent. The lord summoned the cock. The cock came and made the submission. The cock said: My lord! I am ready to go; I am even ready to sacrifice myself for such a noble cause. But I am a poor bird; I have no dress, no strong tail, no crest, no regalia. If you provide me all these, I shall go on this mission. I shall feel amply rewarded & honoured if you select me as a sacrifical bird in holy rituals. The lord was glad enough to provide the required articles and to accede to the last will. The cock confidently undertook the long & tedious journey. The cock flew & flew for days & nights to reach the valley of death. The cock was panting & sobbing. The sun was kind enough to receive the cock warmly and offered the messenger seat, water and rich food. The cock said: Thank you for your kind hospitality. I am really grateful to you. But I am an ordinary bird. I do not deserve such rich food. Please give me a handful of rice & husk. The humility of the cock pleased the sun & the moon. The sun now asked: Dear sir! will you kindly let me know the purpose of your visit? The cock explained his mission honestly, and promised to atone for the crime committed by some irresponsible creatures. The cock said: I will sacrifice my life. My lord will arrange to kill me, & offer my blood & flesh to you.

The sun was very pleased with the cock and blessed the bird. The sun & the moon pardoned the criminals; their anger cooled down. They agreed & assured to reappear, and said: Very early in the morning when the red tinge will be visible in the eastern horizon, you alone will be able to forecast my arrival; you loudly announce my arrival. , Folk Tales of Tripura 244 57. The Tiger and the Cat Long ago, tiger and cat were children of the same parents. They were wild animals. They had no hearth and home, no winter-garments. They used to suffer from cough and cold particularly during the winter se:ison. On one dusky winter evening the cat ventured to undertake a long journey for collecting fire from a human settlement. On reaching a house, the cat got the smell of fish-curry. The inmates had been asleep. The cat sneaked through and relished the fish-curry and fell asleep in a dark corner, & cared little to return to its lair. Late at night, the worried tiger came in search of the cat and growled. The inmates awake and chased the tiger with shouting, sticks and stones. The tiger fled. The cat remained inside and never returned. Thus the two animals got separated. Manipuri Folk-tales 58. The Sun & the Moon There was, long ago, a peasant named Piba. Piba had his wife and children. It was a poor family in the eastern region of Bharat. A landlord employed Piba as his servant, and Piba stayed with the landlord for a long time far away from home. _Piba’s wife had to do all domestic chores: she had to clean the hearth and home; she had to fetch water and

bring firewood; she had to make fire and cook food; she had to tend the children and the domestic birds & animals. Piba was honest, dutiful and laborious. He could not tolerate anything causing damage to the interest of his landlord. Though sometimes overtaken by hunger or sleep, cold or heat, he was always loyal and amiable and able. But at first there was no moon & no night. There were two suns. The common people, and particularly the servants found that living and working always in the light Folk Tales of Tripura 245 were very troublesome. The landlords used to take advantage of the continuous flow of light. They would keep their servants almost aways engaged in various occupations. The landlord had his wife & children; they would not let Piba rest. It tormented Piba. He could not go home for a long time. His health deteriorated. He was suffering from a nostalgia. One day Piba fell ill. The landlord came to see the servant. Tears rolled down the face of Piba. The landlord allowed him leave for a few days. Piba spent a considerable period of his life remote from the wife and the children. Now even a short leave animated him. He hurried homeward and at last reached the destination. But alas! the wife was found bed-ridden and the children were hungry. Piba himself was hungry when he reached home. There nothing was ready. Piba was tired and lost his temper. The landlord had given the nominal salary. Piba immediately purchased rice and vegetables and prepared food. After a long time, the members of the family got the pleasures of the hearth & home. There was a beautiful lake in the vicinity. One day

Piba’s wife had seen a big fish in the lake. She now requested her husband to catch the fish. But how to catch such a big fish from such a big & deep lake? It requires a big net. A simple trap will not do. He had no such net. The wife reported that her father had been in possession of a special net; it had been woven by seven maidens within seven saturdays; the father had been guarding the special net sacredly & secretly. With a great hope, Piba went there and reported about the sickness & wish of his wife, and humbly requested the father-in-law to lend the special net. The old man was hesitant; but at last agreed and handed over the net with precautions. Piba came back home with the net in a bag of clothes. Reporting the matter to his wife, Piba went tg the lake and started casting the net. The net had in it the power of magic. So the big fish was Folk Tales of Tripura 246 enmeshed in the net. But Piba failed to bring the big & heavy fish to the shore. The problem lay elsewhere. It was not a fish. Pakhangba was the lord of the underworld. The lord assumed the shape of the fish. The enmeshed lord was feeling very uneasy. Piba, too, was in great trouble. The sad news reached the court of Pakhangba. The ministers convened an urgent meeting and decided to summon Piba. Pakhangba had three sons; they hurried to arrest Piba. When they had gone a little way, the youngest son turned back & retreated; but his two brothers, having reached the destination, arrested Piba

and drove him to the court. The ministers and judges immediately started asking many questions. The god- fearing Piba narrated all the episodes frankly & freely. The ministers & the judges became pleased with Piba and pardoned him. Not only that, they offered him a golden sickle, a powerful horse and divine power and instructed him to free the fish with the help of the sickle. Piba, following the advice, cut the net to free the fish. The fish vanished. Piba restored and refunded the net. Hearing the dramatic adventure, the father-in-law did not rebuke the son-in-law. Piba started practising archery diligently. Within a few days he became expert in archery and riding. He was contemplating to strike the sun. Every day the sun rises in the east. There was a high mountain in the east. Piba, riding the horse, galloped & galloped & at last went up on to the top of the mountain. Piba lay in ambush. The moment the sun had been rising, Piba made a successful attempt of shooting the sun. The blow became fatal. Suddenly there came down deep darkness. Then the wounded sun was turned into the moon. The other sun remained unhurt. Henceforth, the sun and the moon went on rising alternately. Night was thus made for rest and sleep. Day remained for work. Time was thus divided into day and night. It was a great relief particularly for the servants & labourers. Folk Tales of Tripura 247 59. The Lady of Loktak Lake For a long period, Manipur was a princely state in the north-east corner of Bharat. Long ago, Manipur consisted of a number of small principalities. Moirang was one of them. The heart of Moirang was a beautiful &

big natural lake called Loktak. A royal dynasty ruled over Moirang for centuries. Chingkhu Telheiba was one of the kings of that dynasty; he had no son, no daughter. His brother Chingkhu Akhuba was to succeed; so, he was called Jubrdaj; he had a beautiful daughter named Thoibi. One prominent clan had a chief; the chief was surrounded by an aura of brilliance; the chief had friendly relation with the royal family. The chief had a son named Nongban. Nongban was active & energetic. There was another principality in Khumal. In course of time, the dynasty got reduced; it lost its power & prestige. Purenba was a scion of that dynasty. For his qualities, he was included in the ministry by Chingkhu Telheiba of Moirang. Purenba had a daughter named Khamnu, and a son named Khamba. There was another senior minister of Moirang. He was promoted & became the chief minister. His name was Chawba. He had a son named Feiroijomba. The chief minister had the quality of sportsmanship. So, Thoibi, Nongban, Khamnu, Khamba, Pheiroijomba belonged to the same generation. They were all contemporaries & competitors, actors & reactors. One day the chief minister, accompanied by his retinue, set out on an adventure of hunting wild animals in the deep forest. Purenba too accompanied him. In course of the operation, while the retinue started shouting, beating, setting fire, to startle the beasts, one wild animal charged and attacked the beaters. The beaters fled away. The animal rushed towards the chief minister. Purenba stood by the side of the chief minister and struck down the beast, and thus, saved the life of Folk Tales of Tripura 248 the chief minister. The horrified chief minister was

panting & sobbing. Out of gratitude he wanted to do something for Purenba. Purenba expected his daughter (= Khamnu) to be married with the chief minister’s son (= Pheiroijomba). The chief minister agreed. After a few days, Purenba became ill. The local astrologers, priests, quacks and physicians failed to cure him. So, his health was deteriorating sharply & daily. He died shortly, leaving scanty provisions for the children. The good-natured generosity of Purenba dried up his income. His pocket was like a bottomless basket. When his orphan children had fallen on evil days, the neighbours & relatives did not come forward. Purenba had casual friendship with a Naga chief. Hearing the sad news, the Naga chief sent a messenger to enquire and if necessary to take the children to his house. Khamnu & Khamba went along with the messenger. There, in the Naga chief's house, Khamnu & Khamba had to do a lot of domestic jobs like sweeping, collecting firewood & vegetables & leaves, cutting jungles, planting, weeding, scaring wild animals & birds from the field, On attaining adolescence, Thoibi had a cheerful life of freedom & friendship. She had her retinue. They played & wandered about. One day, they loitered along the woods. A love of wilderness & solitude seized the young girls, Thus, they used to wander from hillock to hillock, singing, screaming, laughing and joking. In one such adventure, she met Khamnu. Thoibi took pity on Khamnu and proposed an offer of accommodation in the palace. Khamnu politely refused the offer. Knamnu insisted on staying in the Naga chief’s house in the hills along with her younger brother. Being convinced, Thoibi presented her a costly shawl clothe and a few other things. The

shawl clothe had been a gift to Thoibi from Nongban. Khamnu returned home with a basket full of wild vegetables and the gift. She cheerfully hurled the shawl Folk Tales of Tripura 249 on to the bed of Khamba. Khamba was glad to receive the costly shawl and enquired about the donor. Khamnu spoke a lot about the beauty & magnanimity of Thoibi. So, Khamba could not suppress a desire to see her. The next adventure of Thoibi was water-sports in the lake: bathing, splashing, swimming, diving & boating. Her father arranged a few small boats. A royal order reserved a corner of the lake for the girls and made trespassing a punishable offence. With all preparations and legal protection, Thoibi with her retinue set out to enjoy the adventure. From the Naga village, Khamnu & Khamba descended in the pretext of collecting firewood & vegetables. Khamba sat in the shade of a big tree at a long distance; Khamnu jumped into the water and started enjoying the sports with her friends. Khamba was passionately observing the scene and then prepared a raft and started gliding easily & smoothly. As soon as the raft had reached the middle of the lake, a gale blew; Khamba lost control of it; the gale carried the raft into the restricted area. A cruise of the retinue of Thoibi reacted sharply and arrested the trespasser. Thoibi was to decide his fate. Khamnu was in a great dilemma; she gave no sign that she had ever seen and known him before; she pretended, as if, she knew nothing. When he was about to be carried ashore, Thoibi noticed certain marks of identification & pressed Khamnu; and then Khamnu disclosed his identity. Thoibi

was considerate enough to order his release. Henceforth, Thoibi and Khamba became friendly. Khamba’s personality fascinated Thoibi. But alas! there was another young man who was already fascinated by the charm of Thoibi. He was Nongban. Nongban came from a prominent family. The royal family & his family were friendly to each other. Nongban was surrounded by an aura of raffishness. The probability of marriage between Thoibi & Nongban was in the expectation of all concerned. Nongban too used to give Folk Tales of Tripura 250 her costly gifts. He would stand by the side of the royal family in weal & woe. All these he was doing with an eye to get the hand of Thoibi. But it had no effect now? While alone, the angry youth murmured something which was awkwardish in a polite society. The volatile & unpredictable youth made up his mind to harass & disturb the competitor (= Khamba) by any means, and if possible to suborn him to death. Nongban made several attempts to defame Khamba. He thought of it with such a passionate whim, all through the period, that whenever a crisis came, he was there to embroil Khamba. For a considerable period of time, Nongban alone had been larking about with the girls of the royal family; he was their hero; now he became loathful against Khamba. He hid his disgust. He had at once recognised in Khamba an enemy, a competitor. A rival star was rising in the sky! The first occasion came with a wrestling match organised in the capital of Moirang. The news of the match was given limited publicity. So, a limited number of participants came. Nongban knocked them down one

after another. His victory was repeatedly applauded. He was about to be declared champion of the match. Knowing the news at the eleventh hour and being inspired by the Naga chief, Khamnu & Khamba came to the ground and after some initial talk with the organisers, were anxiously observing the game. After a hard struggle, Khamba knocked down Nongban. Nongabn left the ground hurriedly and gruntingly. Now all the eyes of the spectators fell on Khamba. The organisers enquired about the whereabouts of the winner. But Khamba remained silent with a smiling face. On his behalf, his elder sister replied and timely disclosed their true identity. The discolsure came as a pleasant shock to the organisers. Even the king himself came forward and decked him with a garland. The chief minister now recollected the promise and within a few days Folk Tales of Tripura 251 arranged the marriage between his son & Khamnu. Thus Khamnu & Khamba again came in the full glare of publicity. . The second occasion came when a red bull had gone mad, committing all sorts of depredations in the hills. Being whispered by Nongban, one fortune-teller (= Maiba)... urged the necessity of sacrificing the animal, the failure & negligence of which would be followed by flood, famine & pestilence. The royal police struggled, captured & brought the animal to the capital. The bull remained violent. But how to tame the bull? Nongban and Khamba were called in. Both agreed to try their hands and thus to win the credit. In the toss, Nongban got the chance to start first; but he failed; he could not even dare to approach the bull. Then came the turn of Khamba. The

moment Khamba & Khamnu had approached, the bull became quieter; the bull got the smell of their hands with which they had fed the bull long ago. They gently caressed the bull’s dewlap. The bull was their domestic animal. When they became orphan & unable to feed the domestic animal, they let loose the bull in the jungle. Since then, the bull became savage & vicious. After a long period, the known smell of the kind hands pacified the bull. Khamnu & Khamba humbly requested the king not to sacrifice the innocent bull. The king granted the prayer. The docile bull got a shelter in the capital. Dedicated to Siva, the bull would be seen in the roads of the capital, strolling gracefully & majestically. The third step of Nongban was the adoption of the strategy of divide & rule to be applied to the royal family itself. Through casual & carefull gossip with the retinue of Thoibi, the strategist came to know that Thoibi was secretly taking utmost care to weave a fine shawl for Khamba. Akula Subha Chandi’s ritual-tale (ad 2) In a certain country lived a poor Brahman family. Being stricken with utter poverty, the Brahman had to

go out for begging daily. The meagre alms reduced the family to live from hand to mouth. Disease, poverty and starvation became the world of the family. Once the Brahman fell ill and for a few days he could not go out to beg. The pinch of hunger became very unbearable. The wife was weeping, and the husband was tossing. So, the benevolent goddess Akula Subha-Chandi pitied the family. Disguised as an old woman beggar, the goddess one day came to the house and called out : Jay Radhe, jay Radhe; mother, give alms for Vaishnav. It was noon. The poor wife offered a glass of drinking water and narrated her tragedy. The benign beggar consoled the wife and instructed her: Every Tuesday in the forenoon worship the goddess Akula Subha-Chandi with flowers, durba-grass, basil leaf, water, fruit, betel leaf, betel-nut, banana, lamp. Giving the advice, the old woman directed her to close the eyes; when she had closed her eyes, the old woman disappeared. The poor wife did what the old woman had told her. Soon, she got the result. When the Brahman had gone out before, no one had ever given him a handful of rice. But» henceforth, every householder gladly gave him a handful of rice. Not only that, the kitchen garden had enough of arum, brinjal, bean, cucumber, cotton, pepper, pumpkin, mango, jackfruit, plantain, etc. The wife used to prepare wick and sacred thread with the cotton. The sacred threads were highly prized. The fruits and vegetables were offered to the deity first. Thus, duly worshipping the goddess, the prosperity of the family steadily advanced. Here the Brahman underwent a transformation from an idealist into a

Folk Tales of Tripura 259 materialist, from a shattwik into a tamashik, from a disciplinant into an epicurean. Ego and pride came. He _ detested vegetarian dish and became addicted to the non-vegetarian dish of fish, meat and egg, etc. He denied the blessings of the goddess, and for all his prosperity he gave credit to his efforts & enthusiasm. One day in the late afternoon, the Brahman went to the local village market and purchased vegetables, fish, meat and egg. But he did not purchase betel leaf, betel- nut, banana, sugar, etc. for the worship of the deity. In the evening he was coming back home with all those things; suddenly a violent gust of wind blew away all those things. He returned home empty-handed. How was it that such natural calamity broke out then and there? Nobody else was affected! It was a mystery. On an enquiry, the wife came to know that the Brahman had not purchased things essential for the worship. The Brahman again went to the market for those things. The Brahman came to his senses. On another Tuesday, the wife arranged the worship of the goddess. She invited one milkmaid to pay homage to the goddess. But on some pretext, the milkmaid did not come; she neglected. Next day, all the cattle were found dead. The cattle-man and the cattle-woman, beating their forehead, rushed to the house of the Brahman. The wife diagnosed the cause of the mishap and consoled them and advised them to take a vow of worshipping the goddess. The wife accompanied them and sprinkled the sacred water of the jar of worship. To their astonishment, the cattle came back to life. They

were delighted. They, too, started the worship. One day in the evening the Brahman went to the weekly market. All transactions were damped by downpours and mighty thunder. The rain was falling heavily. The sellers and the purchasers were shrieking. The current of water was flowing forcefully below their feet. Their keen eyes were accustomed to darkness & Folk Tales of Tripura 260 deluge. The Brahman was returning amidst deep darkness. He was silently uttering the holy name of the goddess. A tigress lay in ambush. When the Brahman had been passing along the rural path, the tigress jumped and growled to gobble him. The Brahman warned the beast not to harm the devotee of Akula Subha-Chandi. The tigress said : I-am in crisis. My husband has been caught & caged by a hunter. I can forbear & spare you, if you pray before your goddess for the release of my husband. The Brahman consoled and assured her. True to his word, the Brahman and his wife humbly prayed. Surprisingly, out of gratitude, the two animals came to the courtyard of the Brahman very early in the morning with rich presents and left immediately. | Thus, the name and fame of the Brahman spread far & wide. It reached the ear of the king. The king’s agents went there with palanquin to bring the Brahman to the royal court. The Brahman was feeling honoured at the invitation. The king and the queen welcomed the Brahman in a befitting manner. The king wanted to know the mystery behind the name & fame of the Brahman. The Brahman said: Maharaj! it is a miracle. The ways of the god are indeed wonderful. He recounted his own history and

narrated the greatness of Akula Subha-Chandi reverently. Bright with the light of a great happiness, the Brahman was confident of the solution of any problem of the king also. The king then told : We are in mental crisis. My son is missing. I have engaged all my energies & ‘agencies to find him out; but failed. If your goddess is merciful enough to grant my prayer, I shall worship the goddess with all respect. : The Brahman added : Maharaj! 1 am completely convinced and dependant on the goddess. If you sincerely and seriously pray, the goddess will definitely restore . your dear son. I shall certainly pray. You, too, pray. Curiously enough, however, the following morning the prince was found walking alone homeward about half Folk Tales of Tripura 261 So ce ee a mile from the palace. In wonder and delight, the royal guard rushed to bring the prince. The parents came to _ the gate to hug the son. The Brahman was engaged to perform the worship of Akula Subha-Chandi. 2 Ananta Vrata’s ritual tale Long, long ago there was a Brahman named Sumantu. He married Bhrigu’s daughter Diksha.
