At the eleventh hour, she was taken outdoors & laid upon the floor; the water of Ganga River, the sacred leaf and milk were offered; the Gita was recited. She breathed her last. The funeral rites were performed. Now, Sila became almost orphan. She used to play with the children of the neighbouring houses. She used

to draw pictures of gods and make clay models & idols and worship those idols. But, Sumantu married again. And the newly married wife was a shrew. She could not tolerate Sila. Sila could understand the step-motherly treatment; she would tolerate and digest. Sumantu was henpecked. Taking advantage of the situation, the step-mother would often depreciate and disparage Sila. Sumantu was a husky man. Time rolled on. Sila became adolescent. Sumantu was in search of a bridegroom. One day one young man named Kaudinya, being thirsty, came to the house of Sumantu; he saw Sila and proposed to marry her. Sumantu arranged the ceremony as simply as possible. Sumantu had a desire to give a quantity of rice, a few clothes & ornaments to the daughter as wedding gift. The step-mother violently turned down the proposal of giving the customary gifts and concealed the ornaments; her grimace, her punnage created paranoia in the mind of Kaudinya. With a tearful eyes, Sila left her parental home with her husband, Kaudinya. Folk Tales of Tripura 262 The newly married couple had to cross the river Yamuna in order to reach their destination. Being tired & thirsty, they went to the river to bathe. On the bank of the river they saw an assemblage of women. It was the 14th day of the month of Bhadrapad; the women were performing the Puja of Ananta-vrata. Sila asked : Sisters! what are you doing ? One woman answered : We are performing Ananta-vrata. Sila asked : What is the benefit of this vrata ? Another woman replied : The devotee’s desires are fulfilled. Sila questioned : What is required to perform the vrata ? Sila instantly took part in the worship and offered

her scanty provision of dry-food as oblation to the god. The women sang & danced in honour of the god. And then they relished the prashadam. Sila and her husband resumed their journey. After a long & tedious journey, they reached their village. Reaching the new home, Sila found it full of provisions : rice, paddy, pulses, vegetables, dress & ornaments. Sila found herself in peace & prosperity. Days, months & years rolled on. But, Sila did never forget the blessings of the god Ananta. She continued to perform the vrata solemnly & secretly. As a mark of performance of the annual ceremony, she used to put a sacred thread round her arm. She used to entertain the guests & the neighbours. Thus, she became very popular. Kaudinya had no fixed income. Still, the family was solvent! Prosperity without hard labour has a degenerative effect. Kaudinya became wayward. Perhaps, Sila did not bring her solemn & secret devotion to the notice of Kaudinya. Kaudinya, too, was careless; he did not enquire about the mysterious income! He became lazy through luxury. One day Kaudinya was surprised to see a fourteen-knotted thread round the arm of Sila. He became suspicious. He became adamant to know the mystery of the thread. He asked: Tell me the meaning; Folk Tales of Tripura 263 perhaps it contains magical formula to make me henpecked. Sila earnestly submitted : It contains no magic, no spell; it is a simple mark; it is a memento of the worship of the benevolent god Ananta. Kaudinya angrily ‘replied : Damn your Ananta. I dislike all these feminine rituals. Immediately, he snashed and snatched the sacred thread and threw the thread into fire. .

Sila rushed and rescued the half-burnt thread and preserved it into a pot of milk. She tended to beat her forehead. He frowned, spoofed & left home struttingly & came back in the evening. Time rushes onward like a stream. The woman of the neighbouring homes gathered and sat with Sila comforting her. Roaming here & there aimlessly, Kaudinya returned after dusk. Meanwhile, there was none to bring back the domestic animals from the field. Taking this advantage, some thieves decamped with the cattle. On the following night a few burglars stole all ornaments. Only a_ few relatives came to console; but they quarrelled, abused & left. The elders cuffed him; the youths pommelled him; the villagers refused to give him alms. To complete the cycle of misfortune, one day just at noon a mysterious fire reduced Kaudinya’s house to ashes. The villagers rushed to help, but before the terrible fire nobody dared to proceed forward. The misfortune of Kaudinya became the topic of popular remark & gossip. Kaudinya had no particular notion about the cause of his sudden distress. But, Sila had her belief. Abused, beaten & criticised from all corners, Kaudinya now came to his senses and asked Sila about the cause of the crisis. Sila said : This is an act of god Ananta. You deserve it for your misbehaviour. Kaudinya repented and left home in search of the god, Ananta. Again, he became equally desperate to find out the god. Leaving behind houses Folk Tales of Tripura 264 and fields, he reached a very dense forest. Much of his | decisions were decisions hot from the mind, and much of his talk was glib lacking depth.

Deep in the forest, he came across an old mango tree; the tree was full of ants & insects. Kaudinya stood. there & asked the tree : I am seeking Ananta Dev; have you seen him. The tree replied : I have not seen him. Next, he saw two adjacent lakes full of flowers, plants, water and birds. He asked the lakes : Have you seen the god Ananta? and got a negative relpy. He swilled a quantity of water, and went ahead. He met a donkey and an elephant and asked them the same question and got a negative reply. Kaudinya moved further and saw a cow, and asked about the god Ananta and got no positive hint. Moving ahead, he saw a bull, and asked the same question and received a hopeless reply. Walking had risks, as the trails had luxuriant growth of creeper, grass & thorn-bush. Snakebite was another risk. Distressed & depressed, the young Brahman decided to commit suicide. He climbed up a tree & perched on a branch and made preparation to hang himself. Meanwhile, an old Brahman suddenly appeared there and sat in the shade of the tree. The intelligent & good humoured old man directed Kaudinya to climb down. Kaudinya came down & sat and devoutly knelt & prayed for guidance. The old man asked : What are you doing here in this deep forest? The young man said : I am preparing to hang myself. The old man said : Do not act rashly; please indulge in heart-searching; you are likely to have committed a gross mistake. Kaudinya felt a touch of fatherly affection; he could not check his emotion. He went on narrating his own

history. After that, the old man remarked : You are responsible for your suffering. Your arrogance, your laziness, your atheism are at the root of your suffering. Do not blame others. Do not misbehave with Sila. Allow her to worship the god Ananta. You too worship the god Folk Tales of Tripura 265 for fourteen years. It will wash off your sin; you will get back your peace of mind as well as prosperity. Getting a satisfactory answer, the young Brahman wanted to know about the history of the mango tree and the two lakes. The old man explained : In his previous life, the mango tree was a Brahman; but he was fraud; he did not teach his students sincerely & effectively. The two lakes were, in their previous life, two sisters; They used to love each other; but they were very selfish & cruel; they would not give alms to any beggar. The donkey was a very angry man in his previous life; the elephant was a very arrogant man in his previous. The cow was an epicurean man in his previous life. The old Brahman led the young man to a cave. The interior of the cave was a big, beautiful garden full of ‘plants, flowers and fruits. The god Ananta sat on a majestic throne and his four arms had four emblems : Conch, wheel, mace & lotus. The young man was fortunate to see the god for a moment. The old man disappeared. The young man became puzzled for a few minutes. With a conviction that the old Brahman had been the god Ananta himself, Kaudinya turned his steps homeward. On the way, he replied to the inquiries of the

lakes, elephant, donkey, cow, mango tree, etc. Returning home, he found her virtuous wife worn out, eagerly waiting for the husband. The return of the native consoled her. He admitted his fault and promised to worship the god Ananta. The couple devoutly started to perform the Ananta-vrata. And one after another the friends, the neighbours started visiting his house. Again, the family became peaceful & prosperous. 3 Andheswari’s ritual-tale There was a village on the eastern bank of the mighty river Meghna. A peasant lived in that village. The peasant _had his wife and seven sons and seven daughters-in- Folk Tales of Tripura 266 law. The peasant had agricultural lands, cattle, domestics and ponds. The family was a fine example of peasant life. At first, all went well. The daughters-in-law were doing their work in a spirit of co-operation and good will. There was a team-spirit among them. They used to go to the pond in the afternoon. To- day they had a lot of chores. So, they went there in the evening. The first six wives promptly washed and filled in their jars, and hastily turned their steps homeward, leaving behind the youngest wife. The youngest wife was slow; she was behind the time. She was left behind; she lagged behind. ‘The path was dark and opaque. She sank into the tangle of fear. She sat down and went on weeping.

Meanwhile, a benevolent deity, in the disguise of an old woman, appeared there. The deity was kind enough to come in time. The old woman asked : Why are you crying ? The youngest wife with tearful eyes explained. The old woman consoled and advised her to mutter the name of -Andheswari and to remain hidden inside a bush. The divine protection was full-summed; neither snake nor dacoit could do any harm to her. Her safety & security were assured by Andheswari. Her husband came and searched from a distance, but could not find her out. Next day, in the morning she returned home safely with her jar of water. While the parents-in-law had a sleepless night, the six wives hypocritically chuckled internally, and exhibited anxiety externally. The deceitful, double-tongued wives further confused the matter; they secretly manipulated a plot and whispered Folk Tales of Tripura 267 it to their respective husbands. They cooked a slur on the character of the youngest wife. They meant to imply that she had been kidnapped & raped by some ruffian. The youngest wife was forced to undergo an oath & ordeal. How? At night a bag full of coins would by placed near that pond & on the way to the pond : the presence or. absence of the treasure would serve as a test of character; if it would remain untouched by any dacoit or deity, her chastity would be proved. Accordingly, arrangement was made. The young wife muttered the sacred name of the deity with all devotion. Her chastity was proved. The reputation of Andheswari Devi was established. 4 Ashtalokpal Thakur’s ritual-tale In a certain country lived a king who had one queen
