Amidst the hardship, however, he never relaxed for a day his habitual vigilance, discipline and duty. Days, months and years rolled on. The daughters grew up. Now, they were doing the household jobs. It was a relief to the father. | But the life of the Brahman was following the old traditional routine. He had to go out to beg in the morning and to come back at noon. One day he did not return till late afternoon. It was an unusual delay. The daughters were very worried. They got a handful of unhusked paddy in the jars. They took the grains in a tray and placed the tray in the open courtyard for sun-drying. They had a mind to husk the grains and to prepare a meal. However, Folk Tales of Tripura 268 being very anxious, they went to the palace for reporting. The royal guards consoled them, but could not give any information at that moment. They soon came back home and found that the crows & sparrows had eaten the grains. Anxious, hungry & helpless, they were weeping. Meanwhile, there came a female beggar; she was old, feeble, sickly and weak; she had a wallet and a stick.

She said: Oh! grand-daughter! I am thirsty and hungry, and give me water & alms. The daughters felt very sorry for the poor woman. They went inside and found only two grains. They offered drinking water and those two grains. The old woman wanted to know the cause of wretchedness of the family. The daughters narrated the sad history of the family. The woman took pity and advised the daughters to put one grain inside the cooking pot and to offer one grain as alms. The woman advised them to worship Ashtalokal Thakur daily and duly. Narrating the rules of the ritual, she directed them to clean the eyesore with palm. At that very moment, the woman vanished suddenly. The two daughters had opened their eyes and found the place vacant; the woman disappeared momentarily. She passed away from the courtyard leaving the daughters happy. Their hovel was turned into a beautiful house; the cooking pot was full of rice; their jars were full of grains. | When the Brahman had gone out before, no one had ever given him a handful of grain or rice. But to-day every householder gladly gave him a handful of rice and vegetables, etc. Then he turned his steps homeward in a joyous spirit though he had been overburdened. He was confused, hesitant and astonished to see the beautiful house. The two daughters went together to the gate to welcome the father. Their joy knew no bound. They ate together. The daughters narrated the story of the arrival of the old woman. They came to the conclusion that Ashtalokpal Thakur had come disguised as a beggar. From Folk Tales of Tripura 269 that day onward they started to worship the deity with

all devotion. Thus, the prosperity & fame of the family steadily advanced. Ever since the first domestic tragedy occurred about a decade ago, the Brahman overcame many troubles in order to nurse and protect the two little daughters. Now, the blessing of the deity made him popular and prosperous. He gave up begging. He resorted to the hereditary profession of priesthood. Begging injured his health and fame. Prosperity & peace proved to be recuperative. The two daughters became very active, energetic and considerate. They made friendship with the king’s daughter. The three friends had many occasions to enjoy the pleasure of conversation spiced with play, gossip and sing. Gradually, the two daughters began to think seriously about the life of their father. Upon the death of their mother, the Brahman had to bear hardship. Upon the marriage of the two sisters a few years later, who would look after him? He would be all alone ! The last years would be saddened by loneliness. He had devoted his time & energy to the upbringing of the daughters. Now, it was the turn of the daughters to think about the last days of their father. They indirectly insisted on the remarriage of their father. The father denied at first; but repeated insistence put him in dilemma. Presently, in the royal place, the queen was seriously thinking about the marriage of her daughter. The king, with the ministers and other dignitaries, was very busy. The problems of administering a kingdom kept him preoccupied. War, famine, flood, disease & death became his world. The king had to take an active & leading part in governmental affairs. So, the king had little time for

domestic affairs. But the queen’s pressure & persistence rather forced the king to curve out time. The king wondered to see the pretty princess and promised to arrange the marriage according to the earliest opportunity, preferably tomorrow. Folk Tales of Tripura 270 ——— The royal discretion and declaration put the queen in a great crisis. She did not expect such a quick response. It threw her into confusion. The mother and the daughter put their heads together. They were not ready to leave such a major issue to chance & accident. After much delibration, their choice fell upon the Brahman. They knew the family quite well. The queen sent one trustworthy guard to call in Rumna & Jhumna. The two sisters were surprised and happy to know the considered opinion of the queen. The two sisters, accompanied by the guard at night, came back home. They prostrated before the small shrine of the deity, Ashtalokpal Thakur. Then they, falling on their knees, entreated their father to agree to the proposal. After much solicitation, the father agreed. Next day, very early in the morning the daughters and the father awaked. They bathed and worshipped the deity. It was still dawn, and the crimson tinge was glowing in the east. The song of birds awoke the king and the queen too. The Brahman, dressed in fine attire, confidently made his way into the royal garden within the palace compound. He was the first man to be seen by the king. He was called in. The king chose him. Upon the announcement of the selection, a great preparation was made. In the evening, amidst pomp & pleasure, the marriage was solemnised. 5. Baidyanath Thakur’s ritual-tale

Once upon a time a poor Brahman family lived ina - certain village. The family consisted of three members: the Brahman, his wife and his son Yadu. Yadu was blind right from the date of his birth. The Brahman’s premature death caused by malaria impeded the usual life-pattern of the family. The widow once thought of taking refuge in holy Vrindavan which was crowded with devotees, Brahmans, cows, monkeys and widows. He dropped the idea thinking about the lot of the son. Folk Tales of Tripura 271 Now began a life of tremendous hardship on the part of the widow. There was poverty all around. Drought, cyclone, famine and epidemic would come alternately. The widow had a gruesome life. She had to eke out a livelihood and to nurse the blind son. The mother & the son had to live on leaves, arum, roots, tubers and gruel. She sold out her ornaments & utensils. At last all the meagre resources were exhausted. One day there was not even a single grain in the house. The mother was weeping. The hungry son repeatedly demanded food. Great was the sorrow of the mother. She lost control over her nerves; her rage knew no bounds; taking an old broomstick she had thrashed the son soundly till he hobbled out of the house howling with pain & tears. The poor and blind boy sat in the shade of a big tree which stood by the side of the village path. The boy sat & fell asleep until midnight. Now, it happened that on that very night Siva & Parvati were passing along the path. Siva and Parvati were passing in the disguise of old man

& woman; they saw the boy and took pity on him. Hearing their conversation, the boy roused from sleep. They asked him : What ails you ? Why you are here till midnight ? The boy answered and lay prostrated before them. Siva & Parvati pitied him and advised him : You and your mother should regularly & devoutly worship the god Baidyanath. The god Baidyanath will restore your eye- sight and remove your poverty. Yadu took the dust of their holy feet. In the twinkling of an eye, the gods vanished. Yadu got back his eye-sight. Full of spirit and hope,-¥adu came back home and told his mother : Mother! mother! you turned me out, but Sri Sri Baidyanath Thakur has blessed me with eye-sight and good fortune. The mother out of repentance, hugged her son; very early in the next morning, they rose up, bathed, plucked flowers, leaves and started worshipping the god Baidyanath. Since then, they lived happily. Folk Tales of Tripura 272 6 Bipad-Nasini’s ritual-tale A few stories, illustrative of the greatness of Bipad- Nasini Devi, are as follows : 1. The story of Maharaj Dharmadev In the ancient city of Avanti (modern Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh) lived a king named Dharmadev. The king and queen were benevolent and pious. The god-fearing royal family had the tradition of worshipping Mahamaya Devi daily and devoutly. One day the Devi wished to have a wide publicity of her another form, the form of Bipad-Nasini. This model or mould was least known. So, the deity hit upon a plan. The Devi confounded the thinking-process of the queen. The queen was obviously unaware of the design of the deity. Nobody in the royal family knew it. The queen did

not keep the king informed of the psychic change. The queen who had been a naturally virtuous lady, now turned into a notorious woman indulging in tastes disagreeable to the royal family. Her devotion to the deity went on decreasing. The domestics, the maids, the sweepers, the attendants became the friends of the queen, The degenerous queen became alienated from the courtly manners and etiquette. Upon being requested by the queen, the sweeper’s wife, secretly bought and brought a quantity of beef for the queen. One trustworthy servant of the king chanced to see the forbidden meat. He privately informed the king. The saddened king did not see with his own eyes the outrage perpetrated on his own household. The king was busy with administrative problem's. The king summoned the queen and sought an explanation. The queen denied the charge and replied that the sweeper’s wife had supplied flowers only. The queen assured the king to show the flowers after the worship. The queen thought herself saved for the moment. But an extraordinary tension overtook her. In case of her failure, the king would order to place her on the Folk Tales of Tripura 273 pointed stakes and kill her. The king had his spy all around. It was very difficult to hush up and suppress it. To come out of the danger, out of the life-and-death question, the queen very, very earnestly went on chanting the name of the deity. She prostrated herself before the altar of the deity. That day, she took no food, not even water. With complete devotion & dedication, she prayed and got her heart’s desire. Bipad-Nasini Devi magically & mysteriously transformed the lump of beef

into flowers & fruits. The ways of the deity were wonderful. Being recovered from the danger and tension, the queen opened the door of the temple and came out with the basket of flowers. The king was happy to see the flowers & fruits. But the queen henceforth started to worship the deity in the form of danger-averting goddess. 2. The story of a poor Brahman In the ancient city of Kasi in northern Bharat, there once lived a poor Brahman named Satyaban. The name of his wife was Abhaya. They were honest, pious and gud-fearing. The priestly job and begging were the two means of their livelihood. The Brahman resorted to the two means alternately. They were devoted to each other perfectly. One day the Brahman set out in the morning for begging alms from door to door. The wife, after doing the domestic jobs, sat down watching the path along which her husband would come with the wallet of alms. The “interval between the two times was of a few hours. Meanwhile, an ascetic came to beg alms. The wife had nothing to give as alms. The ascetic had no idea about the extreme poverty of the family. So, he insisted on giving alms. It was against etiquette to refuse & reject such a prayer. The wife, being in a dilemma, stood up to welcome the hermit and offered a glass of water. While she had been inside the kitchen for bringing water, she beat her forehead and murmured. However, at the time Folk Tales of Tripura 274 of offering water, she struggled to maintain a smiling face. But behind the apparent generous hospitality, there was a violent inner commotion! Nevertheless, Abhaya

could not long resist her emotion. She fell down on the courtyard, tossing & weeping. The wallowing woman did not forget the name of Bipad-Nasini Devi. The hermit was not at all prepared for such a tragic situation; he stood perplexed and numbed for a moment. According to his norms of behaviour, he could neither run away nor touch her. In an embarassing situation he went on visibly consoling the woman from a safe distance. Just about that time, the benevolent goddess appeared in the disguise of an old, grey-haired woman with a stick in hand. The old woman asked : Abhaya! why are you weeping? what ails you? do not weep; tell me. Abhaya cleaned tears & laved her face with water and replied. On hearing the reply, the old woman consoled & assured and confidently directed Abhaya to bring a handful of rice for the saint. Abhaya hesitatingly went in and amazedly found the jar full of rice and came out smilingly with enough of rice for the saint. The saint blessed & left. The two women sat together and discussed many problems. Abhaya was no longer crazy with difficulty & despair; she became happy & grateful; she humbly enquired the identity of the old woman. The woman said: | am distantly related to you; your mother was my cousin sister; our parents were different. I travelled a long distance; so, prepare food & curries for all of us. Abhaya was glad to give food to the aunt, but she had no vegetables. From her facial expression, the aunt understood and again directed Abhaya to inspect the kitchen room. This time Abhaya hopefully went in and amazedly found the basket full of vegetables.

Abhaya came out with the good news and requested the aunt to go to the nearby pond for bathing. In the meantime, Abhaya would quickly cook. At the time of Folk Tales of Tripura 275 cooking, the thought of clothe and utensils for the aunt came to the mind of Abhaya. In this case also, the aunt’s blessing worked wonder. Abhaya found a bundle of new clothes stashed in a corner of the house; and a few new plates in the kitchen room. Satyaban was yet to come back. Abhaya was cheerfully & eagerly waiting for Satyaban. She was rather counting every moment. The age-old tradition dictated Abhaya to feed the husband first, and thereafter the two women would eat together. The old aunt knew it, but she had a different design; she insisted on eating together before the arrival of Satyaban. Abhaya had to submit to the insistence of the aunt. The two women ate together and afterwards fell asleep on a mattress laid on the floor of the cottage. Waking in the mid-day, the kind-hearted aunt gazed upon Abhaya sleeping sweetly and crept away silently & quickly. After a while, upon waking, Abhaya found herself left alone, but found the cottage astonishingly turned into a beautiful house, and the mattress transformed into a bed of roses, and her husband watching the new house wonderfully; Abhaya enthusiastically narrated what had happened. Thrilled by the divine blessings, Satyaban, flinging the wallet then & there, hastened and wandered through the villages & forests in search of the aunt. He rummaged. Tired & hungry, Satyaban travelled & travelled, till he came to a lonely place and sat down in the shade of a

spreading banyan tree. And there, after enduring hour upon hour of earnest desire & devotion, Satyaban was blessed. One youthful damsel of superb beauty came there and asked Satyaban certain questions. Satyaban passionately replied. The damsel said : It is difficult to see the deity, but I can suggest you procedures & principles to have the blessings of the deity. Satyaban agreed. The damsel said : Go to the locality and collect flowers, sacred leaves, fruits, sweets, oil, earthen lamp, Folk Tales of Tripura 276 pot, worship the deity. I shall wait till your arrival. Satyaban had a coin of one rupee tugged in the waist clothe. He readily followed the advice. After bathing in stream water, Satyaban sat down to worship the deity, Bipad-Nasini Devi. Sitting at a little distance, the damsel was watching the rite. But every attempt of Satyaban to offer flowers at the altar of the deity would fail; instead the flowers would automatically reach the feet of the damsel. It surprised Satyaban. Satyaban humbly wanted to know the identity of the damsel. The damsel smiled and disclosed her true identity and advised Satyaban to remain truthful and faithful to Bipad-Nasini Devi. Satyaban devoutly knelt and prayed for blessings. The moment Satyaban prostrated & bowed to the Devi touching the ground with the eight parts of his body, the goddess vanished. Satyaban was now basking in the sunshine of the divine favour. Fortune smiled on him. Satyaban delightfully turned his steps homeward. But no sooner had he turned homeward through the deep forest, than he faced a danger. A lion lay in ambush. With a loud & defeaning roar, the lion jumped and stood on the path.

Never had Satyaban seen such a ferocious beast. Satyaban fell down and lay almost dead. However, the lion took pity on Satyaban and sat calmly by his side. Satyaban came back to consciousness. Then the lion said : My wife left me; I am suffering from the pangs of separation. You are fortunate to receive the divine blessing. Kindly arrange our re-union. Satyaban said : How can I be of any service to you? I may try only! With those words, Satyaban chanted the holy name of Bipad- Nasini Devi and put vermilion & oil on the forehead of the lion. Surprisingly, within a very short time, the lioness appeared. The happy couple thanked, stood away and allowed Satyaban to go home. The jubilant devotee returned home. Satyaban and Abhaya now achieved their heart’s desire. They went on Folk Tales of Tripura 277 devoutly worshipping the goddess daily. But the lion did not forget the kindness, and the lion was thinking of repaying the deep debt of gratitude. The chance came : one day the king’s servants were carrying the royal treasures along that mountainous path. The lion took the opportunity; ambushed with his retinue and howled & roared suddenly. The servants, flinging the treasures, fled frantically. The lion decamped with the treasures. Waking at the dead of night, & their minds fully made up, the lion & the lioness descended to the human settlement and found out the house of Satyaban and offered the treasures. Satyaban and Abhaya were now blissfully happy, each absolutely devoted to the other. And both of them were completely devoted to the goddess. To that idyllic condition were added their honesty, fellow-feeling, discipline and

integrity of character. Thus, the family became the focus all eyes. When their news came to the king’s ears, the king sent a messenger to Satyaban. As soon as he had received the king’s message, he started on the journey and presented himself before the king. The king welcomed Satyaban and wanted to know the mystery of his name & fame. Satyaban humbly admitted the role of the blessings of the deity. The king told him that the power of the goddess would be put to the test. The king’s son was missing for a considerable period; all attempts failed to find out the prince. The devi’s power could be of the greatest service to the king in such an urgent case. Satyaban must fulfil the royal demand or lose his life. Satyaban replied that he would try; but sought a few days’ leave for the purpose. Taking the king’s permission, Satyaban came out of the palace and returned to his own place. Abhaya was eagerly waiting. They discussed about the matter and resolved to worship the deity for a solution of the special problem. At the end of the rite, the couple, very solemnly prostrated before the altar of Folk Tales of Tripura 278 Bipad-Nasini Devi touching the ground with the eight parts of body. To their delight, the missing prince appeared then & there. Satyaban welcomed the prince & offered him food & fruits and afterwards led him to the palace. The king favoured Satyaban with valuable gifts. By the grace of the goddess, the couple became the parents of a son. The paean of public praise bestowed upon the family. Days, months and years rolled away, and the child completed first five years of his age. From

Abhaya, the son heard the stories of his maternal uncle’s house. The curious son desired to see the maternal uncles. So, one day Satyaban and the son went there bedecked with costly dress & ornaments. Now, one greedy maternal uncle had a retinue of rogues. Those swindlers & trickgters made a plot to cheat the guests under the pretence of a picnic. Satyaban agreed, little dreaming how fateful the picnic was to be to him & to his son. There in the deep forest, the cheats gripped the mouth of Satyaban & his son to prevent any outcry and then killed them. The criminals decamped with those ornaments & money. On the scheduled date Satyaban did not return with the son. It worried Abhaya. Meanwhile all sorts of wild rumours were in the air about the assassination. It reached the ears of Abhaya : Where he went? What became of him? By whom he was slain? Abhaya immediately rushed to the house of her parents and from there to the picnic spot. By that time the shocking news had spread like a wild fire. Hundreds of people swarmed and followed Abhaya and thronged the picnic spot. In presence of the anxious crowd, Abhaya chanted the name of Bipad-Nasin1 Devi and sprinkled sacred water on the dead bodies. To the wonder and astonishment of all, the unfortunate victims got reanimated and opened their eyes. They got up as it were from a trance. Great was the joy of Abhaya, Folk Tales of Tripura 279 her husband and son and the crowd assembled at the sudden miracle. They all came back shouting in praise of the Devi. 7 Dhanya Purnima’s ritual-tale In a certain country lived a rich Brahman. He was a

landlord. He had his wife & children, agricultural lands, cattle, domestics, ponds, temples. The landlord’s court was the centre of socio-economic and religious activities. All the big festivals would be celebrated here and the villagers would gladly participate. Wealth came to the family instantly. That day five festivals were scheduled to be held: dedication of a large tank, dedication of twin ponds, landgrant to a Brahman, first feeding ceremony of the son, and Dhanya Purnima-vrata. The first four ceremonies were celebrated devoutly and gorgeously. Thousands of villagers were invited in the feast. But the annual worship of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata passed unnoticed & unobserved. No one took any notice of the vrata. The neglected deity decided to teach the landlord a lesson. The benevolent deity now became malevolent. The blessings of the deity were at the root of the Brahman’s prosperity & popularity. After being rich, he became a little ungrateful; he lost the balance & sanity of mind; his ego, his self-assertion now became powerful & prominent. All donations and dedications were indeed ego-centric. Sometime afterwards, the landlord lost all his riches and became very poor. The elephants, the horses, the cows, the ducks, the fishes, the pigeons died. The barn, farm, the store-room became empty. All the domestics & servants ran away. The house lost all its grandeur & splendour. The forlorn fate of the Brahman became the common topic of gossip of the villagers. Those, who had benefited from his lavishness, were the very ones who avoided him in his distress. He bemoaned; but he did not cringe to his friends for help. Folk Tales of Tripura 280 Leaving his wife and son at home, the wretched

Brahman, out of anguish, volunteered for exilement. He travelled & travelled without any fixed point of destination. With a cane-stick in his right hand, and a wallet hanging from the left shoulder, he was wandering alone aimlessly. On the way, the Brahman came across various categories of people. He came to know the sorrows & sufferings of others also. On the first day he came across a vendor of betel leaf. Formerly, his business was running quite easily. Now, he lost all customers; all his efforts to disburden the basket of betel leaves from his head failed; it was unbearable & painful to go with the load on the head. But why? The vendor asked : Thakur! why are you leaving your home? Where are you going? The Brahman recounted his history and told that he was going in search of the god to know the cause of his destitution. The betel leaf vendor requested the Brahman to know the cause of his wretchedness, and farther reminded the Brahman to put a knot in a corner of clothe as an aid to memory. On the second day, the Brahman came across a woodcutter. For a considerable period of time, the woodcutter was unable to unload the burden from his shoulders; nobody came to purchase the bundles of firewood. The Brahman and the woodcutter talked to each other about their sufferings. The woodcutter asked the Brahman : Sir! where are you going now? The Brahman replied : I am going in search of god to know the cause of my trouble. The woodcutter entreated : If you find the god and know the cause, then kindly ask the god about the cause of my dejection. The Brahman

assured. The woodcutter requested the Brahman to twist the corner of his clothe into a knot as a reminder. On the third day, the Brahman was about to cross a river. There near the river ghat (= landing stairs on the sides of a river or lake or pond) a crocodile was found. The poor crocodile had half of its body in the water, and Folk Tales of Tripura 281 half on the shore; the body was stuck there; the crocodile failed to plunge into the water. The villagers got the scope to beat the crocodile. The tired Brahman sat there, washed his legs & hands. The Brahman and the crocodile had a long conversation. The crocodile asked the Brahman: Where are you going? The Brahman answered: I am going in search of god to know the cause of my distress. The crocodile appealed : If you meet the god and know the cause of your distress, kindly on my behalf ask the god about the cause of my mortification. The Brahman consoled and assured. The crocodile requested the Brahman to twist the corner of his clothe into a knot as a mark. On the fourth day, the Brahman came across a milch cow. The milch cow was suffering from the heavy burden of her big udder full of milk. The calf avoided the milk. The milk was not oozing out. No milkman came to squeeze milk from the cow. The cow was lowing in pain and her bell clanking. The Brahman and the milch cow spoke familiarly. Being requested by the cow, the Brahman assured the cow and twisted his clothe into a knot as a reminder. On the fifth day, the Brahman reached a village

market. There were a few well-stocked groceries; certain quarters were marked for certain goods; the fish & meat market had stench. The tiny shops in temporary sheds, huddled almost together in rows along both sides of narrow lanes, thronged with sellers & purchasers, had stocks of various goods & vegetables. Haggling produced reverberations all over the market & the noise was heard from a distance. It was evening. There were myriads of bamboo-torch (= chunga batti). In that market two merchants were in great trouble: one oilman and one vendor of lime. Their business was going very very dull. All people and purchasers avoided them. They approached the Brahman. The three had a discussion about their problems. On the appeal of the businessmen, the Folk Tales of Tripura 282 Brahman assured them to enquire about the cause of their despair, and twisted two knots in his clothe. On the sixth day, the Brahman, leaving behind human habitations, came near hills and forests. The hungry & fatigued Brahman sat in the shade of a big mango tree. The fruitful tree was overburdened with numerous sweet mangoes. Animals, birds, human beings did not even touch its fruits during that season. Not a single mango fell down below. Why? asked the tree! The afflicted Brahman disclosed his own agony. Knowing the purpose of the Brahman’s travelling, the tree exhorted the Brahman to know the cause of its problem. The Brahman assured and twisted his clothe into a knot for the sake of memory. On the seventh day, the Brahman entered into the deep forests. The misfortune shattered his health, but not his spirit. In the forest the Brahman came across a wild elephant. The elephant was in distress. While

devouring the wild banana plant, the two long trunks of the elephant penetrated deep into the plant; being unable to draw out the trunks, the poor elephant stood entangled for days together. The elephant did not know the cause of the distress. The Brahman too opened his mind. Then the elephant requested the Brahman to be kind enough to know the cause of the distress as well as the remedy. The Brahman assured and twisted his clothe into a knot. The Brahman tottered along and groaning, stopping at intervals as he had been fatigued, and then going on again. The forest was lonely. Those, who had expected some redress, did not come part of the way with him. The rough path had ups & downs. He was at a loss : what to do? where to go? He sat in the shade of a big banyan tree and fell asleep. When he had roused from sleep, he found a grey-haired old Brahman standing nearby. The poor Brahman felt sure that the stranger Brahman could give some valuable information, if he were approached Folk Tales of Tripura 283 — in the right way. After listening sympathetically to the history of the wretched Brahman, the stranger smiled and consoled. In answer to the inquiries of others too, the stranger smiled and assured. In great suspense, the distressed Brahman devoutly kneeled and tearfully prayed for guidance. The white-beard old Brahman now replied to all the inquiries thus : 1.The landlord Brahman family had committed a serious mistake : five rites were scheduled to be held; the first four were performed; but the Dhanya Purnima-vrata was not held. 2.The betel leaf vendor cheated & swindled one female

worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. The woman cursed. 3.The woodcutter did not give firewood to a poor female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. 4.The crocodile swallowed an ornament of a female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. 5.The milch cow kicked one female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. The woman did not get milk. 6.The lime vendor, cheating one female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata, took exorbitant price. The woman cursed. 7.The oilman sold adulterated oil to one female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. The woman cursed. 8.The mango tree did not give its fruit to one female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. 9.The elephant threatened one female worshipper of the Dhanya Purnima-vrata while she had been collecting banana leaf. The old Brahman suggested certain remedies : 1.The landlord Brahman should devoutly perform the Dhanya Purnima-vrata. 2.The betel leaf vendor should donate betel leaf to an honest Brahman. Folk Tales of Tripura 284 3.The woodcutter should donate firewood to an honest Brahman. 4.The crocodile should vomit and donate the ornaments to an honest Brahman.- 5.The milch cow should donate milk to an honest Brahman. 6.The lime vendor should donate lime to an honest Brahman. 7.The oilman should donate pure oil to an honest Brahman. 8. The mango tree should donate valuable treasures hidden beneath its main roots to an honest Brahman. 9. The elephant should serve an honest Brahman for twelve years. Giving all necessary instructions, the old Brahman vanished suddenly & surprisingly. The wretched Brahman was feeling well that day, hopeful, cheerful, ambitious and confident. To the wretched Brahman, the white-beard Brahman was Sri Sri Thakur in disguise. Knowing the cause of troubles, the wretched Brahman delightfully turned his steps homeward. On the way back,

he met the sufferers one after another. 1. The elephant was eagerly waiting for an answer. The elephant asked : Oh priest! have you seen Sri Sri Thakur? Have you asked the cause of my suffering? The Brahman replied; Yes. I have seen Sri Sri Thakur. Sri Sri Thakur said that once you threatened a female worshipper of Dhanya Purnima- vrata while she had been collecting banana leaf. The woman cursed; that was the cause of your suffering. You should serve an honest Brahman. The elephant said : You have seen Sri Sri Thakur; what Sri Sri Thakur has said is surely correct. So, you are the honest Brahman. I shall serve you, come, ride on. The moment the Brahman rode, the trunks were released. Riding on the elephant, the Brahman proceeded. Folk Tales of Tripura 285 2.The mango tree asked the question and got the reply and offered the treasure. 3.The oilman asked the question and got the reply and offered pure oil free of cost. 4.The lime vendor asked the question and got the reply and offered lime free of cost. 5.The milch cow asked the question & got the reply and accompanied the Brahman to offer milk. 6.The crocodile asked the question & got the reply and vomitted the ornament for the Brahman. 7.The woodcutter asked the question and got the reply and offered firewood free of cost to the Brahman. 8.The betel leaf vendor asked the question and got the reply and offered betel leaf to the Brahman free of cost. The Brahman returned home with a lot of wealth. The situation again became rosy. He took the greatest delight in devoutly performing the Dhanya Purnima-vrata.

The neighbours again became frequent visitors to the house. They too started the worship. 8. Garai vrata’s ritual-tale There was once a poor Brahman in a certain country. The Brahman had his wife and an only son. The family was dependent on alms. The family was living from hand to mouth. But the family was not long destined to live a simple life. The Brahman’s wife once fell ill and died. Many villagers came to the house to express their sympathy and some elderly neighbours suggested the widower to marry again. Now, began a life of hardship. The widower had to do indoor and outdoor jobs. It was his daily duty to feed his child in the morning, and he himself would eat either stale rice or fried rice, and then to go out for alms, and at last to come back home at noon for food & rest. Year after year went on. The son grew up. The father arranged the marriage of his son. Folk Tales of Tripura 286 a In those days the villages were apart from one another. Between every two villages there were fields and forests and streams. Density of population was thin. Flood, famine, epidemic and attacks & invasions would horribly enfeeble the people. The Brahman often used to sit in the shade of a big banyan tree while going out for begging. And now entered on the scene the sinister figure of a charming damsel. She took a curious interest in the family affairs of the Brahman. She used to meet the Brahman at noon in the shade of the banyan tree. Day after day rolled on. Slowly happened an episode of extraordinary importance: introduction gradually turned

into intimacy & acquaintance into attraction. She continued her efforts for over months and made all sorts of kind proposals to him. He was asked whether he would be treated kindly & intimately during his illness in old age by the son and the daughter-in-law? He was asked to leave the responsibility of earning to the son! Initially; the Brahman obstinately refused to say a word in answer. But slowly and gradually he became infatuated and obsessed. He felt that the son would be disloyal to him and the daughter-in-law would be hyprocrite. The Brahman was no longer frank & free and transparent to the son & the daughter-in-law. The Brahman swallowed the first bait of the damsel. The alienation was almost complete. Having estranged the father from the son and the daughter-in-law, the damsel started the second round of her game. She tried to indicate the futility of observance of rites & rituals; of vows & worships. The observance was a great handicap to happiness & well-being; cleanliness, washing, whisking were symptoms of mania; vegetarian diet was a torture on the body. One should eat fish, meat, egg and enjoy this life. Here also the damsel’s influence had its affect on the Brahman. Folk Tales of Tripura 287 Being deprived of judgment & inspired with sensual passion, the Brahman now started quarrelling with the son and the daughter-in-law over trifling issues. He himself stopped observing the vows, rites & rituals, and prevented the son & the daughter-in-law from cleaning, worshipping, rising at dawn, etc. So, they had to do all these things during his absence. The evil impact was already well under way. The damsel now made the proposal of marriage. The field

had already been made ready. The Brahman became aware of the need. The repressed impulse came to the level of conscious desire. He agreed to the proposal. The long period of amour, and fear of social ostracism led him to a dilemma. But he could not resist the temptation. In the evening, after taking the meal, he disclosed his desire. The son and the daughter-in-law reluctantly and tacitly consented to the proposal. The next morning the Brahman eagerly went out for begging and at noon sat in the shade of the tree and passionately expected the arrival of the damsel. As usual the damsel came, and the Brahman gave the good news. It was the month of Aswin (= September-October). The Brahman talked to an astrologer. The astrologer studied an almanac and found the last day of the month of Aswin auspicious for marriage. The Brahman himself informed and invited his friends and relatives. Meanwhile, the reluctant & hesitant son secretly made consultation with a few wise men and Brahmans of the locality, and he was convinced about the untrustworthiness of the damsel. She was Alakshmi in the disguise of a damsel. Now what should be done to protect the family from the curse of Alakshmi in the disguise of a damsel? How to prevent her entry? How to disillude the father? How to bring about a peaceful solution without resorting to violence? How to maintain the unity of the family? The socially approved method was to resort to magic, Folk Tales of Tripura 288 ES witchcraft and sorcery. The magicians were the primitive physicians & philosophers. Accordingly, the son solicited the service of an ojhai. Being advised by the elderly well-

wishers, the son had to take a few steps: to intensify cleanliness, to stick to the traditional rites & rules; to allow the marriage to be solemnised; to enclose & encircle the homestead with the spells of magic; and to discourage begging by the father. On the appointed date, the marriage was solemnised in the shade of the banyan tree in front of the temple of a village deity. Strangely, nobody knew the whereabouts of the damsel. Even the Brahman did not ask ? On the third day, the Brahman was to come back home with the new wife. They were in two separate palanquins. The moment the bearers were about to cross the boundary of the magically protected homestead, a mighty eerie terribly broke out; to the wonder of the Brahman and to the tacit delight of others the new wife died; the dead body of a black crow was found inside the palanquin. 9 Hari-Parameswar’s ritual-tale Long, long ago Menaka had a beautiful garland of fragrant flowers. She presented the garland to Durvasa. Durvasa presented the garland to Indra. Indra placed the garland on the head of his elephant, Airavata. The elephant threw it on the ground. It enraged Durvasa. Durvasa cursed Indra & his retinue. The Devas were afraid of being afflicted with disease & death. Taking advantage of the adversity, the Ashuras started preparations to torment & torture the Devas, to plunder & devastate the Devaloka. The alarmed Devas made an appeal to Brahma. Brahma suggested the Devas to collect all sorts of medicinal plants for crushing & churning with the help of the Ashuras. The great exercise would result in the production of Amritam. The Amritam would make them

strong & deathless. Folk Tales of Tripura 289 Putting a huge quantity of various medicinal plants in the sea of milk, the Devas & the Ashuras started churning the sea. As the churning went on, a number of objects arose, such as Kamadhenu, Parijatam, Apsaras, Chandra, Garal, Dhanvantari with Amritam. Mahadev Siva swallowed the venom. The Ashuras snatched the pot of Amritam & fled away. The Devas approached Vishnu for the recovery of Amritam. Vishnu assumed the form of Mohini. Mohini approached the Ashuras. The Ashuras were captivated by the beauty, flirtation & amour of Mohini. On Mohini’s ° advice the Ashuras sat down and closed their eyes. Mohini was expected to serve Amritam to every one of them. Meanwhile, Mohini vanished with the Amntam. The Ashuras opened their eyes and found themselves betrayed. They chased but failed to catch Mohini. Rahu went ahead & sneaked into Devaloka. Surya & Chandra detected him. Vishnu cut him. The invigorated Devas defeated the Ashuras. The deadly poison of the Kalakuta snake was to have a horrible affect. On Brahma’s request, Mahadev Siva gulped it down, but stopped it in his throat. So, Siva became Nilakantha. Not only that, when Mohini had been fleeing with Amritam, Mahadev Siva, in a moment of ecstasy, embraced Mohini. The flickering moment of the joint image found its expression in Hari-Parameswar. 10. ITU Puja’s ritual tale There lived a poor Brahman family on the bank of the holy river Ganga. The family consisted of four’ members: husband & wife and two daughters, Jumno & Umno. The family was dependent on alms. Almost daily, the husband used to worship the family god and then set out for begging and come back at noon.

Days, months & years thus passed on. The winter season came. The sun lingered shorter in the sky. During Folk Tales of Tripura 290 the night dew-drops dripped off the leaves & roofs. Preparation used to begin for celebrating Paush- Sankranti. During the winter season, in December & in January, the local people used to prepare various types of cakes & sweets. The poor Brahman used to get the smell of those cakes. So, he, too, became very eager to relish cakes. He asked his wife to prepare sweet cakes. But she had no fine rice powder, banana, molasses, milk, sugar, etc. The Brahman begged & collected the essential materials. His wife was happy to prepare cakes. Long before dawn, she sat frying cakes one after another. The husband had suspicion; he surreptitiously went on counting the number of cakes prepared. After the preparation, they went to sleep again. In the following morning, the daughters craved & longed for cake; out of motherly love, she gave two cakes only and warned not to ask for more. In the morning the husband got up and bathed and sat to eat all the cakes. His wife served the cakes. He found that there were two cakes missing. He became angry and consumed the cakes. He did not offer even one cake to his wife. He was a greedy man. The greedy husband did not stop there. He became vindictive. He pretended to visit the house of a relative, and took the two daughters along with him. They walked a long distance and crossed fields & villages. The relative’s house was supposed to exist beyond a deep forest. It was already evening. They entered the forest. Being

exhausted & thirsty, they sat in the shade of a big banyan tree. The daughters fell asleep. The cruel father deserted the two daughters then and there, and quickly turned his steps homeward. He had no penitence. The mother had no voice. After about two hours, the two wayworn sisters awoke and found themselves helpless in the midst of deep forest. caey heard the howling of the beasts. It was very difficult Folk Tales of Tripura 291 ea ee to move either backward or forward. They became afraid and perturbed. The helpful banyan tree offered them shelter. They climbed up the tree and spent the night. The next day they moved forward and reached a place near a river; they found a few women worshipping a god. They narrated a heart-rending tale of their journey. The women received them kindly and consoled them and listened to their tragedy. They offered them temporary shelter & food. They taught them the procedure of worshipping the goddess Itu. Being convinced about the material benefit of worshipping the goddess Itu, the two sisters returned home and started the vrata and got the benefit. The sober daughters did not take revenge against the wild father. Rather, the insincere & cruel father changed his tone. The family became solvent and happy. One day the king and the minister of that kingdom came to visit that part of the country. They became thirsty and sent for drinking water. The two sisters supplied water in a small pitcher. The small pitcher was deserving of disregard & neglect. But its inexhaustible source was striking. The king and the minister became fanciful and proposed to marry them. The king married Umno. The minister married

Jumno. The poor girl suddenly found herself surrounded by attendants & servants and in the midst of plenty & pleasures. So, Umno was at a loss; she suffered from schizophrenia. She neglected the worship of the goddess ITU. Consequently, the royal family suffered distress one after another. The king ordered to behead Umno. The royal executioner took her to the lonely field of execution, and out of merchy handed her over to her sister Jumno at night. Umno lived there incognito. After the marriage of the two daughters, the wild father, like a dog’s curly tail, reassumed his old character. He felt proud of being the father-in-law of the king and of the minister. He used to ramble & strut. He was Folk Tales of Tripura 292 To surrounded by a few retinue. He utterly neglected the vrata and spurned the sacred pitcher. Soon, the consequences followed. Day by day, he became poorer & poorer. The neighbours neglected him and refused to give alms. He went to the house of Jumno. Jumno gave a good quantity of rice & pulses & spices. On the way, Itu’s emissary mysteriously looted those gifts. Next, the wayward husband sent her wife to the house of Jumno. Jumno was careful & affectionate. The mother and the two daughters met together; they were not, however, allowed to swerve and behave waywardly. Jumno kept them within limits and imposed certain restrictions. They were asked to go to bed early and to rise early and to worship the goddess Itu. They stayed there till the month of Agrahayan (November-December) and performed the annual worship of the goddess Itu. Discipline & devotion bore fruits. The goddess brought to the mind of the king the memory of Umno. The king

became eager to see Umno, and ordered the minister to restore her. The minister found the braggart order extremely difficult to comply with. The dejected minister came back home and went straight to bed. Jumno cautiously wanted to know the cause of depression. The minister explained. Jumno confidently disclosed the fact of Umno’s presence in incognito. The minister became happy to have a sound sleep and to assure the king the next. day. The king arranged to decorate the avenue with banana plants & flowers. And Umno promised to worship the goddess regularly. Their mother and father also promised to worship the goddess Itu. 11. Kalkinarayan Thakur’s ritual-tale There was a village on the eastern bank of the mighty Meghna River. And there dwelt a poor Brahman with his wife. His income from priesthood and begging was meagre & uncertain. So, the couple had to live from hand to mouth. Folk Tales of Tripura 293 The Brahman’s wife was active, energetic & practical. A Kayastha family lived in the neighbourhood. The prosperous Kayastha family had agricultural lands, cattle and domestics. Every day in the morning the wife used to collect a quantity of fresh cowdung from the cow-shed of the Kayastha family. It was her usual duty to sweep the courtyard with a broom in the early morning and then to sprinkle cowdung mixed with water. She used to save a little quantity of cowdung for manuring the kitchen garden. It added to the income of the poor family. In the rural countryside everybody’s business was known to everybody. The villagers used to visit the houses of the neighbours in season and out of season. The wife used to covertly collect a little more quantity of cowdung

than what had been essential for sprinkling. The extra quantity of cowdung was used for commercial purpose. In the countryside there had always been different types of character : honest, foolish, simpleton, sincere, cruel, whisperer, miser, plotter, dunce. One such hypocrite secretly informed the Kayastha family about the covetous acquisitiveness of the Brahman’s wife. The Kayastha family first observed, then dissuaded and at last protested. The wife fell ashamed and dishonoured. The disgraced woman reacted violently at her own home. She proposed to sell her utensils & ornaments for the purchase of a milch cow. The Brahman shared the sentiment of his wife. The Brahman carefully set out for the market with the ornaments and utensils. On the way the Brahman met a peasant. The peasant’s old mother fell seriously ill; she was about to die; her last wish was to donate a milch cow for a safe passage over the Baitarani River. The peasant requested the Brahman to accept the donation. Fortune seemed to be favourable! The Brahman gladly & readily accepted the milch cow and blessed the dying mother. With a splendid spirit, the Brahman came back home with the milch cow and the ornaments & utensils. Folk Tales of Tripura 294 Abruptly and directly, the family’s financial position improved. It soon became the-talk of the village. The Brahman was aided greatly by his wife. She played an important role in the improvement of the family’s financial position. After having gone to a good deal of hardship, trouble and disgrace, the wife enthusiastically took care of the milch cow and the calf. The excess quantity of milk and cowdung was sold honourably and confidently. The Brahman family had a very poor neighbour : the

husband fell ill & died leaving behind his widow and an only son. The Brahman family took pity and employed the widow & her son as domestic. The boy’s duty was to take the cow to the field for grazing. There was a big banyan tree on the bank of the river. The cowherds & village boys used to sit and play in the shade of the tree. One day the boys fell asleep, while their cattle went far away. They awoke and did not find their cattle. They shouted and cried. They were anxious and worried. Seeing the weeping boys, the kind-hearted Kalkinarayan Thakur came there in the form of an old Brahman and addressed them : Grandchildren! why are you weeping? Are you afraid? Do not be afraid. The boys told the cause of their weeping. Then Kalkinarayan Thakur advised them to worship the god Kalkinarayan Thakur. The boys asked : Grandfather! grand-father! what does one gain by worshipping Kalkinarayan Thakur? The grand-father replied: Whatever one loses, he will find; one’s desire will be fulfilled. The timid and simple- hearted boys promised to worship the god. To their wonder and delight, the entire herd of cow were then seen coming homeward. It was a great relief. So, the boys, without any delay, arranged the worship of Kalkinarayan Thakur that very evening. Since then, the worship of the god became a weekly affair. The boys used to visit only five houses to collect Folk Tales of Tripura 295 five betel leaves and five dottles of tobacco only. The place of worship was not fixed. The time of worship was fixed : in the evening. It was a simple ceremony spiced with

singing, dancing, joking, smoking, etc. Soon the worship of Kalkinarayan Thakur became an occasion of gaiety & social festivity. ‘Now it happened that on one’evening the term of the Brahman’s domestic boy came; all his friends assembled at the courtyard of the Brahman. Upon the completion of the ritual, the boys were chewing betel leaves and smoking tobacco. They relished it as prashadam. Meanwhile, the Brahman returned home, and saw the boys chewing & smoking. The Brahman became irritated & furious; he hurriedly kicked & spurned the altar of the god. The sensation was enormous anleniilcstavens the village. The boys fled. Now it happened that on that very night the Brahman’s cow & calf vanished. The Brahman searched for the cattle and asked every body : Have you seen my cow & calf ? The common reply was: No. He went on asking and reviling the boys. The Brahman accused the boys and sought justice from the Gaon Panchayet. The Gaon Panchayet summoned the boys, and gave a hearing to the accuser and the accused. After due deliberation, the Goan Panchayet dismissed the charge. and directed the Brahman to arrange the worship of the god, and to humbly invite the boys in the worship. The troubled & perplexed Brahman then & there invited the boys and the members of the Gaon Panchayet, and arranged the worship in the evening. The jubilant boys ranted the air with the praising sound in honour of their dear god. A lame man and a blind man came, tossed & wriggled in front of the altar. Surprisingly they became cured. To the wonder and delight of all present, the cow and calf appeared, on the completion of the worship. The

deity’s reputation was established. Folk Tales of Tripura 296 12 Kankhaila Thakur’s ritual-tale Once upon a time an old woman was aufedae from earache. For a remedy, she took a vow of devoutly worshipping the presiding deity, namely Kankhaila Thakur on the last day of the month of Bhadra. Kankhaila Thakur was a malevolent deity. The old woman requested one woodcutter to supply firewood, and one milkmaid to supply milk. But on the appointed date the woodcutter forgot to supply firewood, and the milkmaid forgot to supply milk. The poor devotee fell in trouble. However, she had will power and tenacity. She rushed to the houses of the neighbours in search of firewood and milk. The neighbours were kind enough to offer her firewood & milk. She made a simple arrangement for the worship of the deity with all her heart. The deity was pleased with her sincere devotion. With the divine blessing, she became cured. But a strange thing happened. The negligent woodcutter had gone to forest; there he fell ill and became unable to move; he lay unconscious. The milkmaid’s crisis was of a different type : all her cows & calves lay dead in the cattleshed. The village-life was violently agitated. All sorts of wild rumours were afloat in the air. The woodcutter was brought in, and an ojhai was engaged to cure him. Sunilarly, an expert in animal disease known as Goala, was engaged to animate the cows. But all failed. None of them could say how it happened. So, a great chaos & _ confusion followed. Some people suspected the possible curse of the old devotee to be a cause of the crisis. So, the people went to

her house and expressed their anguish in patois. Then the old devotee said : I humbly requested the woodcutter to supply a bundle of firewood; but he neglected and deceived me. Kankhaila Thakur became displeased at this. I humbly requested the milkmaid to supply milk : the milkmaid assured me; but on the appointed date she Folk Tales of Tripura 297 ee took no care to supply milk. Naturally, Kankhaila Thakur became displeased at this. Then the villagers realised that the negligence of duty had been the chief cause of the crisis. An old man suggested the members of the badly affected families to make a vow of worshipping the deity. In presence of all, the members of the two families made a solemn vow of worshipping the deity. Instantaneously, the woodcutter and the cows & the calves got back to life. The villagers were delighted. 13. Karmapurush Thakur’s ritual-tale There was once a Brahman in a certain village. The Brahman had his wife and two daughters named Sonai and Rupai. The family had homestead, agricultural land, pond, cattle and the hereditary profession of priesthood. The family was neither poor nor rich. The Brahman had a happy family and a moderate income. Suddenly a domestic tragedy occurred. The wife fell ill and died. It was a severe blow from which the family never fully recovered. Sonai & Rupai were mere children then. The Brahman had to play the double roles. The struggling life tended to have an evil effect on his mind and character. It led him away from devotion and duty. The debauched Brahman ceased to command the respect of the neighbours and the devotees. It badly affected his

profession. He was reduced to a pauper. He sold his agricultural fields. And at last began begging. Year after year went by. The Brahman had already injured his health by doing home work and farm work. It was too heavy for him. His ill temperament & poor health frequently forced him to give up work for recuperation. Upon the earnest appeal of the daughters, and the suggestion of the neighbours, the Brahman married for the second time. However, for such a widower, it was difficult to have a beautiful bride. The poor Sonai & Rupai would not get time for rest; they had to live in stern severity. They had to perform all Folk Tales of Tripura 298 dcmestic chores. One day the step-mother took a quantity of broken grains in a tray and placed the tray in the open courtyard for sun-drying and directed Sonai & Rupai to guard the grains. The Brahman went out for begging; the wife was sleeping inside. Meanwhile, the sparrows and the crows swooped down and gulped all the grains. The screaming of the birds awaked them. They scared the birds. But the damage had already been done! Being afraid, they went on weeping. A benevolent deity pitied on the poor girls. The god came in the disguise of an old Brahman beggar. The beggar said : Oh grand-daughter! why are you crying? The grand-daughters narrated their tragic history. The beggar consoled them and asked them to search out a few grains. They found only three grains. The beggar counselled them to put the grains in three pots, one in each pot or jar. In addition, the beggar advised them to worship Karmapurush Thakur on the last day of the

month of Jaishthya. Giving the advice & blessing, the beggar vanished. Fortunately, that day was the last day of Jaishthya. The two sisters bathed and collected flowers, leaves, water, twigs, etc. and sincerely worshipped the deity. To their surprise and delight, the three jars became full of grains, and their cottage was turned into a beautiful house. When the Brahman had gone out before, no one had ever given him a handful of rice. But to-day every family gave him rice and vegetables, etc. He was astonished to see the beautiful house. The two daughters narrated what had happened; now the family became the devotee of Karmapurush Thakur. The family’s prestige & position increased steadily. The homestead was developed into a pleasure-grove. There were fruit trees and garden of flowers. The bumming of bees, the fragrance of flowers and the screaming of birds added to the peace & prosperity of the family. The Brahman’s wife desired to enjoy the pleasures Folk Tales of Tripura 299 perenne ea all alone with her husband. The wife, a selfish woman from the beginning, made a plot of inventing a story of crime which would seem to imply that the two daughters had been either culprits or possessed by some evil spirits or seriously ill. With that evil intention, earthen jar shreds were secretly & stealthily strewn on the bed below the quilt. When in drowsiness, the two daughters were to toss, the murmuring sound would be heard. The sound was interpreted by the step-mother as the proof of her suspicion. She used to whisper; often she had irritation causing the teeth to grind together over any mistake committed by the step-daughters in doing anything.

The Brahman’s personality was paradoxical and weak. He was henpecked. There was an impression of acquiescence on his face spiced with meanness. Nevertheless, being abetted by the wife, the Brahman plotted to banish the daughters. The hypocrite father told the daughters : My dear daughters! your step-mother has not been treating you affectionately; so, I shall take you to your mother’s sister’s house, and you stay there for a fortnight, and then come back. The. next morning they started. It was a long journey. They ‘travelled and travelled for hours on foot. They had to pass through a deep forest. The sylvan & shady paths were narrow, nasty & zigzaged, up one slope of the hills and down the other. There was a very big banyan tree by the side of the hilly path. The two sisters were very tired; they fell asleep. The opportune moment arrived. The father tore his umbrella and tainted it with some reddish liquid and left it there; it was a testimony to an attack by a tiger. Leaving the sleeping daughters in the deep forest, the father very speedily turned his steps homeward. The wretched daughters, faint with fear & fatigue, were awakened by the screaming of the home-coming birds. Meanwhile, darkness had set in. To Sonai, it was not at all an accident & attack; it was a betrayal, a crime, a conspiracy, a dodge. There was no human settlement in the vicinity. With all devotion & dedication, they Folk Tales of Tripura 300 repeatedly, uttered the name of Karmapurush Thakur for rescue. The benevolent banyan tree slowly lowered one of its long & tall branches down to the level of the ground. The two sisters carefully sat on the branch and

tied themselves to the branch with clothes. The tree again slowly raised its branch high above beyond the reach of any beast. They spent the night there silently & sleeplessly. Mysteriously, the next day a prince and a police commissioner’s son went out for hunting; being very tired those two hunters sat in the shade of the banyan tree. The two sisters saw the two handsome young hunters. They dropped their long hair. One hair fell in front of the prince’s feet; another hair fell near the feet of the police commissioner’s son. It surprised them; they saw upward and found the two sisters. Being assured, the two sisters climbed down and narrated their tragedy. The hunters disclosed their identity. The poor sisters accompanied the hunters and reached the royal palace. The king consoled them and duly arranged the marriage. The prince married Sonai; the police commissioner’s son married Rupai. Despite her post-marital affluence, Sonai did not abandon the pre-marital practice of worshipping the deity with cheap & ordinary materials like flower, leaf, grass, water, earthen pot, mango-twig, broken rice, etc. Success, but not monetary reward, attended her efforts; she had been rescued and married quite honourably. Now, in the interior courtyard of the palace, Sonai, without any bustle & stir, was silently & solemnly arranging the worship of the deity with those cheap & ordinary materials. The prince unexpectedly went there and saw the poor & unimposing ritual; to the prince it was below the dignity of the royal family. The prince reviled Sonai and spurned & kicked out the altar & the materials. The angry prince ordered the guards to take her into the forest and to kill

her there. Following the order, the guard & the Folk Tales of Tripura 301 executioner took her into the forest; she was weeping. The kind-hearted guards felt very sorry for her; they left, her in the forest and warned her not to come back into the palace. Sonai, under the cover of the night, had wandered & wandered and at last reached the house of Rupai. Rupai and her family accepted & consoled Sonai and kept it strictly secret. To the attendants & domestics, she was the friend & relative of Rupai. The family of Rupai continued to be peaceful & prosperous. But the picture of the royal family soon became pathetic. The royal family was going rack & ruin. The prince suffered from leprosy. The aged king convened a meeting of his councillors & counsellors. After much deliberation, they accused the prince whose arrogance & haughtiness had brought about the tragedy. The decision of the court was communicated to the prince. The repentant prince asked the guard & the executioner: they said : If you promise not to punish us, we shall tell you. The prince ‘promised, and then they told him that they had not executed the capital punishment. The prince directed them to go to the house of Rupai and to beg pardon on behalf of the prince and to enquire about the whereabouts of Sonai. The elders of the family of Rupai maintained a meaningful silence and commented that for such serious problem the prince himself should have come. The royal guards went back and conveyed the comment. On hearing the comment, the king sent the prince. The prince had to regret and to promise before

the elders. Then, Sonai appeared & accompanied the prince. The prince became cured. The royal family regained its peace, prosperity & popularity. The notorious step-mother and the henpecked father, too, had to suffer a lot. They were reduced to beggars. The trees of the garden died. The birds left. The couple were starving. But they did not come to their senses. The news of their wretched condition reached Folk Tales of Tripura 302 the ears of the daughters. There was a great gap. The father did not know the condition of the daughters; they might have been killed by a wild beast long ago. One day, Rupai came to the house of Sonai. The two sisters had now peaceful family life. They discussed among themselves about the condition of their father. They planned to distribute clothes, grains and money among the beggars. With this plan, they approached the prince and the king; the prince and the king approved and arranged it on the auspicious day for the worship of the deity. One day the henpecked father heard that the king of that country wished to distribute clothes, grains, rice and money particularly among the beggars. So, he decided to go to the capital and receive the donation just like common beggars. The two sisters were observing; when their father had come, they identified him. But they didnot disclose their own identity; they fell back & sent a guard to bring him inside. The poor father was trembling. The father was astonished & delighted to see his daughters. The daughters offered him water, good clothe, fruit and food. The royal guards brought the step- mother also. The daughters gave her water, good clothe,

fruit and food. The two daughters did not forget the cruel, merciless treatment of the step-mother and the father. But they did not misbehave with their parents; they treated heartily and equally and lavishly. Banishment & rejection by the parents had left a deep sense of hatred; but they never exposed it for the time being. But whenever the two daughters had recollected the past events, the notorious step-mother resiled from the topic and the effeminate father posed to be deaf & dump. What greatly added to the mental shock of the two daughters was the absence of any expression of repentance from the side of the parents. Then the two sisters, in presence of the parents, talked to one another; Sonai asked : What awaits a Folk Tales of Tripura 303 eee traitor? What is the fate of a deceiver? Rupai replied : Divine punishment comes unexpectedly & certainly. Surprisingly & suddenly the step-mother collapsed then & there. The father left the palace to lead a forlorn life in the lonely crowd of his village. 14. Kojagari Lakshmi Puja’s ritual-tale , There was an adventurous, considerate & enterprising king? The subjects were happy in his kingdom. He used to protect the innocent citizens and punish the criminals. The spacious royal palace had guards & servants, queen and prince; it had temple, guest house, rest house, etc. The capital was the hub of communication; trade & transport flourished in the capital. There were a few well-stocked shops; purchasers & salesmen used to throng to the weekly market. Bargaining, haggling, conversation would create a reverberation. The distinctive sound from a blacksmith’s forge would recall the vanishing days. One day the king’s guard through drum-beating made

an important announcement : If any merchant’s rare merchandise is left unsold, the king would be kind enough to purchase it. The royal proclamation became a topic of discussion among the merchants. One day one Karmakar (= black- smith) prepared a statuette of iron; it looked liked a girl. The blacksmith called it Alakshmi. Nobody was- ready to waste money by purchasing an ugly statuette. It reached the ear of the king. The king purchased it and kept it in his temple. Preservation of the statuette of Alakshami (= goddess of poverty) in the temple generated reaction in the minds of the benevolent deities. Shortly after that, one intelligent ant made a passing remark : See the consequences of our king’s wrong decision: by purchasing a statuette of Alakshmi, our dear king’s condition is deteriorating. He can not even afford to eat clarified butter. The ants were swarming & talking to each other. The king gave one pensive look and smiled. The queen Sat down next to the king; she observed it and asked the king to explain the cause of his smile. The king was Folk Tales of Tripura 306 afflicted; and kept back his remorse by pretending to be mentally disturbed. Getting an evasive reply, the queen insisted on knowing the significance of the mysterious

smile. The king tried to divert her attention and lighten the matter as a trifling issue, a silly outburst of his distress. But the queen became petulant and showed childish impatience to know the mystery. Then the king said : I am forbidden to disclose the cause of my smile. The consequence of disclosure will be very fatal. Still her eagerness did not subside. The king silently led her to bed and tried to desist her : Listen, my dear lady, if I disclose it, I shall die; will it be good for you? The queen said : I do not believe it. I am not afraid! You are to disclose it. It is something mysterious. I must know it. The king said : If you are ready to take the risk, be patient; wait and sleep to-night. Tomorrow in the morning we shall have a bath in the holy river Ganga and then disclose it in time. They got almost no sleep. The next day in the morning they went to the river and the king bathed and then asked her : Now, I am ready to disclose. You are to choose either of the two options : My life or the secret mystery. You cannot have both. The queen preferred the mystery. The king sighed and gave a pensive look again & a faint smile. Meanwhile, the king’s attention was drawn to a conversation between two animals; a sheaf of green & fresh grass was floating down the mid-stream of the river. The she-goat asked the male-goat to collect it for her. The male-goat threateningly replied : Do you think that I am as fool as the king to risk my life to please a wife? The

she-goat silently submitted to the logic & the stick. As the king listened to the conversation, he realised that he had scarcely been aware of his kingly position during the last few months. His soft'& sweet words failed to dissuade her. The king in him stood up. A stern thought suddenly flashed through his mind. His fury turned against her. Folk Tales of Tripura 307 eee The king snatched his own hand out of the queen’s -with a sharp movement. For the first time, the queen felt herself being thrust aside by her husband. In a commanding voice the king said : You should know that I do not want to disclose it for public interest. Go away, go away! You have crossed your limit. The queen was choking with tears! Her knees trembled. She fell flat and sat watching the bold king Ssweepingly going back alone. She was quite unprepared for the sudden change of mood of the king. A lack of sense of limit abruptly reduced her to a forlorn woman without hearth & home. Nobody would offer her shelter. Where to go, when there was a tiger on the land, & a crocodile in the water? Forest was the only resort. She stumblingly distanced herself from the capital and reached a deep forest. Exhausted, distressed & tired, she sat in the shade of a big banyan tree. The journey was hazardous, because of an absence of road, and presence of leeches, snakes, shrubs and thorns. She followed the Ganga. She tramped through the forest of lower Bengal. She wandered on tothe coastline of the Bay of Bengal. There she saw animals, birds, fishermen; nature was closed at hand; but life was hard. Hunger

dogged her steps. At night she would climb a tree for rest, safety & security; she lived there incognito. In farming & fishing hamlets, she earned her food by working with the people. The homeless waif was forced to earn her own living working in the peasant families in Sundarban and thus attained a little of maturity. She was in turn a cook, a water-fetcher, a dishwasher, a wood-cutter, a nurse, etc.; she carried water &- wood; she washed utensils; she swept courtyard; she scrubbed floors. Some shrew women used to pun & spoof her. She happened to see an asram (= hermitage). One aged saint established it; the saint used to teach the local people ‘through the tales of the Ramayana and the Mahabharata. The villagers used to serve him food & clothe, etc. The Folk Tales of Tripura 308 saint offered her shelter. One day she found an assemblage of the local women & girls in the hermitage. Making all arrangements, they started worshipping the Lakshmi Devi. It was the full-moon night of Aswin (September-October). The frail, fugitive woman asked): What are you doing? They replied : We are worshipping Lakshmi Devi. She again asked : What will you get by worshipping Lakshmi Devi? They replied : Lakshmi Devi will fulfil our desires. You may worship the Devi and get her boon. She said : I have nothing to offer, no new dress ! How can I worship? I have no money for dakshina! The ladies assured her. was gloomy. He was helpless. Now miracle happened. By the grace of Lakshmi Devi, the iron image of Alakshmi in the king’s temple at the distant capital slowly & slowly melted away. The change attracted the attention of the king. But he found no explanation, and he asked Dharma- raj to explain the cause. Dharma-raj explained : The sooner the idol of Alaxshmi is vanished, the better. The forlorn queen has recently earned the boon of Lakshmi Devi some where in her wandering. The king grew grey with age & tension. Now he started feeling better and he was regaining his spirit. The king sent his police and spies in search of the queen. After a search, they found her in the hermitage in a cheerful mood. Then the king personally went there and brought her back. The reunion made them happy again and they started worshipping Kojagari Lakshmi Devi. The king revoked the proclamation and the queen refrained from the inquiry. Folk Tales of Tripura 309 lS acai at ate 15. Kshetra Devi’s ritual-tale There was once a poor Brahman in a certain village. The Brahman had his wife and an only son named Bishnupada. The Brahman fell ill and died. The premature death of the husband, led the wife to the ocean of sorrows & sufferings. One day the widow had felt her poverty so much that she was about to commit suicide. But considering the future of the child, she made an alternative settlement. The widow had a poor brother living in another village. The brother had his wife. The widow with her son went to her brother’s house for food & shelter. For a handful of rice, the widow had to do all

domestic chores. There was an expression of distemper on the face of all. The poor brother was in a great dilemma; his wife was poisoning his ears secretly. One day, the cold war reached its climax. After the wigging, the brother showed the sister the door. This melancholy rebuff drove the widow & her son to the open road. With a heavy heart and tearful eyes, the widow travelled and travelled. Fatigued and hungry, the mother & the son drank water from ponds & streams and hobbled and sat in the shade of a banyan tree. Soon the son fell asleep at his mother’s lap. After a while, one benevolent goddess named Kshetra Devi, took the form of an old woman; the old woman with a walking-stick in her right hand, walked limpingly and came near the widow and asked : What ails you ? Where are you going? The widow fell at the feet of the old woman and narrated her tragic history. The old woman consoled her, blessed her and offered her a handful of fried rice from her knapsack. The old woman offered some useful seeds of paddy also and directed her to clear a patch of free khash land and to sow those seeds. The old woman stayed there for hours and requested the woodcutters to donate bamboo, cane, thatching grass, etc. and build a small cottage then and Folk Tales of Tripura 310 To there. Affectionate, calm, placid, motherly, the old woman exercised a fascinating influence upon all the donors and the builders of the hut. Some of them cleared the adjacent bushes and sowed the seeds. The old woman was the last to depart. Making the minimum essential

arrangements, she advised the widow to worship Kshetra Devi with such cheap ordinary things as leaf, grass, flower, water and wild roots & fruits. The widow started worshipping the deity right from the next day morning. A stream was purling by the side of the hut. She used to fetch water from it and offer cool water to the villagers & travellers; through this service she gained the sympathy of the people; the villagers voluntarily offered her roots, fruits, vegetables. The seeds sowed that day rapidly sprouted and grew into plants. Every eye in the locality was eagerly directed to catch a glimpse of the hut and the inmates. The hut seemed to be an abode of peace, a new hermitage. The widow’s history became the common topic of discussion. The villagers stood by her side. She was no longer left alone. Year after year went by. By the time, Bishnupada grew into an adult boy. He was active, energetic, hardworking and honest. Every day he used to get job. While his mother had been worshipping the deity with dedication, Bishnupada was working in the field as daily labourer with devotion. Their financial condition improved rapidly, and their name & fame spread widely. In that district there lived a rich landlord family. The landlord had his wife and a daughter. The landlord was a practical man of affairs; he was in search of a bridegroom; he preferred an honest & laborious poor boy; he rejected the proposals from lordly families. He had no fascination for the spoilt child of rich parents. His choice fell on Bishnupada. He sent his proposal to the widow through a middleman. It was beyond her imagination.

The middleman described the prosperity of the landlord, Folk Tales of Tripura 311 and the beauty of the daughter. The widow sought the blessings of the goddess and the advice of the villagers. On an auspicious day, the marriage was duly solemnised. The landlord was prudent enough to build a separate & independent house for the new couple. The landlord employed several workers to build a beautiful house, to dig a big pond, to decorate the homestead with garden. On the other hand, the widow’s brother became poorer and poorer. The brother & his cunning wife were starving. One day they heard that the landlord of the district was constructing houses, digging pond; and for the huge work the landlord was calling for labourers. So, the poor brother decided to go there and work there just like common workers & labourers. All the works were being done under the able supervision of Bishnupada. Now, Bishnupada’s maternal uncle was working as a labourer. After a few days, Bishnupada had a doubt about the identity of the new labourer. He discussed the matter with his mother.
