Next day, the mother and the son came together to the spot-& observed and talked to him. Being sure of the identity of the new labourer, the mother & the son called him & asked his whereabouts, treated him very kindly and gave him sufficient money for an honourable living. 16. Manasha Devi’s ritual-tale Long ago in Bengal lived a rich merchant named Chand Sadagar. The merchant had enough of wit. He was a devout devotee of Siva. The fervid warmth of devotion made him rather intolerant of any other cult. The merchant used to go abroad in connection with export

and import of merchandise. The merchant’s wife was named Sanaka. The couple had seven sons. Chand Sadagar had money & man-power to venture on voyages in the distant seas adjacent to the countries of south-east Asia. The voyage brought him fortune & fame. Once again the merchant resumed his voyage particularly during the winter season. On leaving home, Chand Sadagar had given Folk Tales of Tripura 312 instructions to Sanaka. One such instruction was to worship Siva regularly. Sanaka followed the instruction; but being persuaded by another woman, she added the worship of Manasha Devi, the presiding deity of the snakes. | After a few months, Chand Sadagar returned from the voyage in peace and with profit, unhampered by any disease or accident. The members of his family and the relatives & neighbours received him joyously. He brought many items of gifts. It was the time for a rest and for the management of the household affairs. One day the merchant in a leisurely mood was strolling here & there in the courtyard; the children were playing: The ladies and domestic assistants were engaged in various odd jobs. The atmosphere was quite homely and peaceful. The merchant casually saw in one corner of the big courtyard a small & simple altar. He asked Sanaka about the altar. It was the altar of Manasha Devi. Soon there broke out an altercation between the two devotees over matter concerning which they held opposite views. When the altercation waxed warm, the husband spurned out the altar. No one dared to protest openly; but everyone in secret spoke ill of him. . After a few months, the rainy season came. The rainy season continued for a few months. It was a period of

heavy rainfall, thunder, lightning, cyclone & flood. It was a period favourable to the insects, snakes, lizards, frogs, leeches. Manasha Devi was waiting for this season in order to teach the merchant a lesson. Chand Sadagar’s anger and abuse tended to the destruction of his family. His life during this time became far from comfortable. He fell ill & remained bed-ridden for a few days. His first six sons had to go out for various errands; and one day in the evening some poisonous snakes bit them. They died. The local ojhas were called; they failed to exorcise the venom. Many endeavours were made to induce Chand Sadagar to worship Manasha Devi, but with no avail. He Folk Tales of Tripura 313 es was asked to give his consent only, and to leave all details to be arranged by Sanaka. He adamantly stuck to the worship of Mahadev Siva only. He incurred the sin of spoiling the worship of Manasha Devi. During the next winter season, Chand Sadagar again set out in his voyage for business. He set out with seven boats (= sapta dinga) full of merchandise, and several assistants. The sad memory of the tragedy was vivid, and so the merchant made his way in grim silence. But alas! Suddenly and untimely the sea became violent. A mighty cyclone broke the stillness of the sea. The waves were rolling in and the foam was splashing over the rocks & the beach. The turmoil.of the waves wrecked the seven vessels. The veteran crew’s keen eyes, though accustomed to darkness & cyclone, strained in vain to catch a glimpse of the doomed vessels. No earthly power could save the vessels which were in such dire peril.

The merchant & the crew struggled to save their lives. They were flung ashore. At long last, at dawn a _ crimson tinge was glowing in the east. They returned home empty-handed. But Chand Sadagar was not the man to abandon hope so long as the least possibility of cherishing it remained. Now his only hope lay in the life of his seventh son, Lakshmindhar. The father arranged the marriage of Lakshmindhar with a charming bride named Behula. The merchant, his crew, his artisans, his carpenters took every precautionary measure to ward off any danger, to check any possible infiltration of any insect. The bridal chamber was made with utmost care. There, however, remained a very narrow escape, thin nest hole, hair- breadth passage. Through that hole, a snake made its way in and bit the groom; Lakshminadhar died of snake bite. It was inconceivable to the family. At his marriage, the villagers had been present. The family, the villagers & the neighbours plunged in grief. It brought tears to their eyes. It shocked them. Folk Tales of Tripura 314 The shamans, the magicians, the snake-charmers were called in immediately. All of them failed. Rushing to the courtyard, the village elders suggested to set on sail the deadbody with a faint hope that an able .ojha might see and cure the victim. The elders acted with good will, courage and promptitude. Without losing any time, a raft of banana plants was prepared. It was then that Behula bethought herself that she should accompany the dead husband. It was a very, very hard and risky task. But Behula was ardent, earnest, tenacious, chaste, courageous, adventurous. A great tenderness soon filled the hearts of the elders. With a

heavy heart & tearful eyes, with a feeling of horror & faint hope, thousands of people rushed to the river bank to see, to bid farewell, to bless and to encourage Behula. Deeply moved, they all said good-bye to Behula. Utterly cast down as she was by the tragedy, she argued to herself that she was not responsible. She was absolutely alone in the world, & she spent a long time on the river & on the sea. The green valleys, the luxuriant paddy fields, the human settlements made no appeal to her mind, Life became intolerable. The raft was moving along with the stream of the river. The mournful young bride was weeping in melancholy. And by a strange decree of fate, Behula came across a woman. The woman was washing clothes in the river. The washerwoman took pity on Behula and wanted to know the cause of her melancholy. The washerwoman stopped the raft for a while and consoled Behula and instructed her to venture for a sojourn in the heaven. Taking instruction from the washerwoman, Behula made a desperate attempt to approach the gods in heaven. She reached heaven and stood before the gods and began to dance & sing. She proved herself an expert actress. For hours together, she continued to dance & sing. It pleased the gods. The gods told her that she might ask for any boon. Folk Tales of Tripura 315 Here, at that moment, Manasha Devi intervened. The Devi laid down one condition: Behula’s father-in-law should be compelled to worship Manasha Devi. Behula must take care of it. Behula agreed. Then, all the gods blessed Behula and gave the boon of becoming the mother

of son. Manasha Devi specified the boons : Lakshmindar would get back to life; Lakshmindar’s elder brothers too would be alive again; Chand Sadagars seven doomed vessels would be buoyed up from the bottom of the sea; all the merchandise would be restored along with the vessels. Behula bowed to the gods in general and to Manasha Devi in particular touching the ground with the eight parts pf body. Behula hopefully turned homeward and reached the earth. On her way back home, she found her husband alive and the vessels floating with machandise and the elder brothers of Lakshmindar guarding the vessels. With a splendid spirit and ranting the air with shouting in honour of Manasha Devi, they all happily returned home. Henceforth, the family became the ardent devotees of the Devi. Chand Sadagar gratefully agreed to worship the Devi. ; 17. Mangal Chandi Devi’s ritual-tale . A few stories illustrative of the greatness of Mangal Chandi Devi are as follows. 1. The story of Kalketu & Phullara Marici had a son named Kasyapa. Kasyapa had his wife Aditi and several sons; the eldest son was named Indra. Indra had his son Nilambar and daughter-in-law Chhaya. For committing some mistake, Nilambar & Chhaya were cursed and turned into human beings, and came to be known as Kalketu & Phullara. By profession, Kalketu was a hunter. He earned great reputation by hunting many wild animals & birds. The profession of Kalketu caused a massacre of the wild life. The wild animals and birds became alarmed and anxious; Folk Tales of Tripura 316 they rushed to Mangal Chandi Devi for help. The Devi took pity on the poor animals & birds. The Devi’s blessings

saved their lives. Kalketu henceforth found no prey. He became unsuccessful in hunting. His eye-sight became hazy. His target failed. For two days, he could not hunt down even a single animal or bird. On the third day, the hungry hunter caught an iguana. Kalketu and Phullara struggled to roast it. They had been suffering from the pinch of hunger; the moment they sat to devour the nasty insect, suddenly & surprisingly the iguana turned into a beautiful woman. The couple became confused & perplexed. The woman disclosed her identity. She was Chandi Devi. The couple bowed to the Devi touching the ground with the eight parts of body. Being pleased with their devotion & dedication, the Devi blessed them and favouréd them with very valuable gifts, and advised them to give up hunting, and instead, to develop a beautiful habitat in Gujarat. The couple travelled & travelled and at last reached Gujarat, In Gujarat they laboured hard to clear a wild tract and developed the place into a pleasant habitat. But the builder found no purchaser. Kalketu again prayed to Chandi Devi. Kalketu needed the divine help. The Devi was highly impressed by the deeds of the couple. The Devi was kind enough to shower a heavy rain on the kingdom of Kalinga-raj. The kingdom was inundated and many subjects migrated to the new habitat of Kalketu. The Kalinga-raj, on inquiry, came to know about the builder of the new settlement and sent his guards to arrest Kalketu. Kalketu in distress again prayed to the Devi for help. The Devi secured the release of Kalketu through a dream-revelation to the Kalinga-raj. Since then Kalketu & Phullara became the devout devotees of Mangal

Chandi Devi. 2. The story of Dhanapati Sadagar Once upon a time a rich merchant lived in Bengal. Folk Tales of Tripura 317 ee ee ee His name was Dhanapati Sadagar. He had two wives, named Lahana & Khullana. The merchant’s family had an aged old maid servant named Durbala Durbalawas a widow; she was serving the family for many years, she had no child. The merchant was content with his hearth & home. He got his devoted & dutiful wives. There was good relation between Lahana & Khullana; they were capable of managing the family-affairs during the absence of the merchant. They were cheerful. Now Durbala was a woman of mean intellect. She was jealous of the atmosphere of amity & good-will obtaining in the merchant’s family. She was like Kaikeyl of the Ramayana. Her cunningness matched that of Kaikeyi. Being jealous and desirous of depraving the fidelity of the family, Durbala, though illiterate, was too clever to put a wedge for splitting the solidarity of the family. Her manoeuvre was very slight, almost negligible. Yet it had an influence on the imagination of the young wives. Domestic jars placed together often sound and make noise. The difficulties & temptation which beset the young ladies were capitalised by Durbala. Alienation between Lahana & Khullana became quite visible. The merchant was, at that time, at distant lands. Lahana engaged Khullana in grazing & pasturing the domestic goats. Khullana lived but little at home; she spent most of her time outside in tending the goats. Her mother died when she was still a child. Her father married again. Lahana took advantage of that situation. Habituated to hardship, Khullana had the mental stamina

to face the troubles. But one day one goat went out of the flock. In the afternoon, while counting the number of the goats, Khullana came to know that one goat was missing. So, her heart was panting with fear. She had her companions there; one of them looked on all sides; another girl climbed a tree; another girl went to the river-bank. But Folk Tales of Tripura 318 the goat was out of sight. So, Khullana sat down weeping and beating her forehead with hands. Meanwhile an old woman came there, consoled Khullana and advised to worship Mangal Chandi Devi. Khullana devoutly knelt and prayed for guidance. The girls then & there collected leaves, flowers & water & devoutly worshipped the goddess. By the blessing of the Devi, Khullana got back the goat. ’ The instantaneous result of the worship impressed the girls so much so that henceforth they made a simple hut in the shade of a banyan tree and started worshipping the deity daily. They used to sing and dance in honour of the Devi. Thus the drudgery turned into a devotional pleasure. It had its far-reaching impact. It brought about - a change in the mind of Lahana. Lahana’s heart was now yearning for affection and attachment. Khullana was relieved of the outdoor duty of grazing the goats. Moreover, the merchant safely returned from voyage with a good margin of profit. Not only that, Khullana was going to be the mother of a child. The sweet laughter of Lahana & Khullana again echoed through the house. Next, having decided to go to SriLanka for business, the merchant called an astrologer to consult an almanac and suggest an auspicious date for setting out. The priest

worshipped Mahadev Siva. The merchant was an ardent devote of Siva. However, Khullana in her own way made a, very simple arrangement of the worship of Mangal Chandi Devi. Placing small earthen jar as the symbol of the Devi, Khullana offered water, twig, flowers, fruits, grass, etc. Being intolerant of any rite, other than that of Siva, the merchant scolded Khullana and spurned out the altar without considering the future result at all. On the scheduled date, the merchant started for SriLanka with boats, merchandise and assistants. They all reached there safely, but on the basis of a false allegation, he was arrested and imprisoned. Meanwhile, Khullana gave birth to a son. The son Folk Tales of Tripura 319 was named Srimanta. Days, months and years passed away. Srimanta grew from babyhood to childhood, and from childhood to adulthood. The mother and the son used to devoutly worship Mangal Chandi Devi daily. The son heard the stories of his father from the mother. The long absence of the merchant was painful to the family; the family was reduced to poverty. The boy, being possessed of manly qualities, made efforts for the purpose of maintaining the family. And he took the risk of going to SriLanka. Reaching the destination, he explored the island and rummaged in search of his father and the crew, and at last got the information. He met them in prison. But even during the voyage he did never forget the name of the Devi. Every day he used to chant the holy name. : Being pleased with the dedication and dependance of the devotee, the Devi got the release of the merchant & his crew through a dream revelation in the mind of

the king of Srilanka. Moveover, Srimanta had certain sterling qualities; he was courageous, generous, industrious, tenacious and eloquent. The king of SriLanka was impressed. The king had found in the boy all he had sought for the princess. The king arranged the marriage of his daughter with Srimanta, and favoured the entire group with valuable presents and gifts. Thus, the greatness of Mangal Chandi Devi was established. The merchant & many others became the sincere devotees of the Devi. 18. Niyat Chandi’s ritual-tale In a certain village lived a poor Brahman. The Brahman had his wife and his only daughter. The daughter’s name was Kamala. The wife fell ill and died. At that time Kamala was a mere baby. The family was dependent on begging: Poverty-stricken, shabbily dressed and apparently doomed to failure, the Brahman with the baby in his armpit had to go out daily in the morning for begging Folk Tales of Tripura 320 alms. The afternoon was for coming back home, bathing, nursing & feeding the baby and taking rest after the lunch. Year after year went by. Under the paternal affection, Kamala was growing up. Her mother had died about a decade before; and as she grew up, she had to be preoccupied with domestic chores. Orphanage and poverty forced her to do many odd jobs and to learn a lot. She had no formal education, no degree; but her remarkable common sense and serious mind made her precocious. She used to think about the future of her father : Who would look after him in old age & in illness & in case of any accident? After her marriage, he would be alone, forlorn, disheartened !

Kamala insisted on the remarriage of her father. Repeated requests, appeals and arguments had left an impact upon the mind of the widower. Slowly he admitted the logic of the request. Being convinced, he agreed and contacted a ghatak (= match maker). On an auspicious day the marriage was solemnised. Kamala now seemed to be confident of the future of her father; she was happy to see her father and the step-mother; she had respect for the step-mother. But alas! The father fell under the influence of the step- mother. Kamala had reputation in the village. The step- mother became jealous; she used to offer Kamala adulterated milk and food, and to direct Kamala to do all sorts of drudgery and to blame Kamala for any omission & commission. Kamala had an unhappy childhood. The Brahman’s remarriage obviously opened up a period of cold feud in the family. The step-motherly behaviour shocked Kamala. One day Kamala burst into tears; avoiding direct conflict, Kamala made an appeal to her father thus : Oh father ! kindly purchase for me a she-goat; I like to remain out of the house as long as possible in tending the she-goat. By begging alms & selling kids, I shall maintain myself. I do not like to be an unnecessary burden. Folk Tales of Tripura 321 The father purchased a she-goat for Kamala. Grazing the goat almost throughout the whole day became the vocation of Kamala. A timely diversion indeed for avoiding the step-mother. She used to take rest in the shade of a big banyan tree along with other children of the village. For feeding the cattle of others, she used to get her mid-

day meal in the field. One day while Kamala fell asleep; the goat went far away. The goat was not tethered. Upon rising from the sleep, she did not find the goat. Worried about the mischievous reaction of the step-mother, Kamala was anxiously running here & there in search of the goat. Not far away from the grazing ground, there were a few houses of peasants. Kamala went there in search of her goat. There she found a few women worshipping a village goddess. It was dusk. She asked : Whom are yoy worshipping? Why are you worshipping ? The women replied: We are worshipping a benevolent goddess named Niyat Chandi. By the blessing of the goddess, the lost property returns home, the mutilated head gets rejoined, one’s desire gets fulfilled. Kamala again asked : Will my missing goat come back? The women confidently replied : Certainly, devoutly pray to the goddess. Being assured, Kamala turned her steps homeward slowly, awfully, devoutly murmuring the name of Niyat Chandi. She sat in the shade of the same banyan tree and continued to utter the holy name of the goddess. Meanwhile an old woman limpingly came near Kamala and asked : Grandchild! in case of any danger or crisis, pray to the goddess Niyat Chandi. The old woman assured, consoled and vanished. To the wonder and delight of Kamala, the goat returned leisurely cudding the food. In the evening, ‘Kamala came back home with the goat. But surprisingly, the cold-hearted parents were found indifferent & least worried about the cause of the late arrival of Kamala. On another tragic occasion, being scolded by the step- mother, Kamala left home with tearful eyes and sat in

Folk Tales of Tripura 322 the shade of a tree. Kamala fell asleep. Meanwhile, that -old woman again limpingly appeared and made a prophecy: Grandchild! day after tomorrow your marriage will be solemnised. To-day your father will unexpectedly get more than sufficient alms for the purpose of your marriage ceremony only. Do not think for the bridegroom. The old woman vanished immediately. Kamala returned and informed the father. To the step-mother the divine message was a great relief. The parents had a mixed reaction; they whispered and made an arrangement for the ceremony. The invited neighbours & guests were in great doubt & uncertainty. Nobody knew the whereabouts of the bridegroom. Naturally all wild rumours were afoot. Hour after hour went by. It was midnight. The invited guests became restless. How to relish the feast in such a situation of anxiety, uncertainty and tension. The invitees were moderately arrayed in costumes of medieval India. Kamala was absolutely devoted to the deity. Astonishingly, after the midnight, a bridegroom with his retinue appeared. The news that an unknown bridegroom had been coming, caused much jubilation among the invitees, young & old. The doubt & derision soon turned to pleasure & praise. It so happened that in another village one bride’s nearest relative died at that time; so the sad death forced the bridegroom to turn to the house of Kamala. Obviously, the bride, Kamala, was in the highest mental tension. All eyes were cast upon her. She got a scope to worship the deity. The kind-hearted deity forgave and appeared in dream to remind Kamala. Kamala got up and silently stepped in the temple and performed worship very simply. Kamala came back and found the

husband in a mood of suspicion. Where did you go ? asked the husband. The narration of Kamala could not satisfy him; he wanted to verify the divine capacity of Niyat Chandi; he said: Tomorrow I shall go to furthest corner of your village on foot, but I like to come back on a boat. Folk Tales of Tripura 323 It was a challenge to Kamala. Kamala accepted the challenge and went on murmuring the name of the deity with earnest devotion. The next day the groom & his retinue set out for a pleasant stroll, walking, gossiping, bantering at each other and talking to the villagers. The sky was clear & clean. The people then could not even dream of rain. But to their astonishment, the rain fell heavily and inundated the fields & paths. The groom & his retinue became wet & draggled; they had to hire a boat for coming back. The deity’s greatness was thus proved again. . On the fourth day, the bride was scheduled to take leave of her parents for the new home. The groom again planned for an ordeal. To conceal his motive, he put forward the pretext of the possibility of dacoity; Kamala’s ornaments might be snatched away by the criminals on the way; so Kamala should be dressed like an ordinary lady and stash the ornaments in packet. Kamala agreed. The new couple started their journey. On the way they had to cross a river. The groom dropped the packet into the river and remarked: I like to see again the capacity of your deity. Kamala was shocked! What a foolishness on the part of the groom! The agony of Kamala was terrible : How to

appear before the new relatives in shabby dress & without any ornament. The first impression would be very poor & pathetic. The fact that the marriage had been quickly & rashly and whimsically solemnised, annoyed the groom’s parents. Paradoxically, they were displeased with Kamala. The shabby dress added insult to the injury. For the scarcity of big fish the blame again came upon the new bride. A big Raghab boal fish Was purchased; but the fish could not be cut to pieces! All wild rumours were in the air. The invitees surmised something evil & ominous; they refused to take food; they left. On humble appeal, they assured to eat after seven days. The jealous step-mother, the callous father, the Folk Tales of Tripura 324 foolish husband, the mobbish new relatives were the lot of Kamala. She had none except the deity. So, she had to pray to god for supererogation, for affording Kamala a store of surplus spiritual merit, for eking out the deficiency of her husband. Kamala had to trust on god, but to keep her powder dry. Kamala went ahead with a sharp knife to cut the Raghab boal fish. She easily cut the fish into pieces, and to her great relief, she found the packet of ornaments & costume inside the belly of «the big fish. While cutting the fish, she was surrounded by the inquisitive mob. On being asked, Kamala narrated the incident. Now Kamala was in a position to array herself in proper dress & ornaments. But the huge quantity of food was bound to be putrefied. It was a great loss and harassment to the family. The unthinking relatives were there to blame

Kamala. At Kamala’s request all the vats full of cooked rice, pulses & curry, were carefully arranged inside the temple; Kamala, locking the door from inside, remained in deep meditation inside the temple for one week. After seven days, the invitees kept their words and came back to take food. In their presence, Kamala confidently opened the door; and all the cooked food & curry were found hot, fresh and pure! The villagers enjoyed the dainty dishes and praised Kamala & Niyat Chandi. Passing through a number of ordeals, Kamala became confident and popular. But she remained a devout worshipper of the deity. She did not forget the holy name of Niyat Chandi. It was her daily routine, under normal circumstances, to worship the deity first, usually in the forenoon, and then to take some food. Gradually the financial position of the family also improved considerably. Year after year rolled on. The family had been prosperous & popular. Kamala’s father-in-law grew old. He had a desire to earn spiritual merit through some social work. All the members of the family and the neighbours favoured the desire. His proposal to dig a big Folk Tales of Tripura 325 Tw pond & donate it was approved. The task of digging the tank was started in the winter; many diggers were engaged. It took more than one month. The tank was large, deep and north-southward long. The tank was scheduled to be duly & ceremonially dedicated to the public; the water-goddess was scheduled to be worshipped. However, the tank remained dry. The donor was worried. At night the donor had a dream - Oh devotee! sacrifice the grandson, that is, the son of

Kamala; and the tank will fill with water. Naturally, the father-in-law was in great dilemma. Sacrifice the grandson, for the merit of the grandfather? The old man could not eat and sleep; his face displayed the expression of anxiety & agony. The auspicious day of dedication was approaching. The old man was weeping alone inside a dark corner of the house. Kamala asked and entreated: at last he told the message of the dream. Kamala’s world was the world of crisis & ordeal. She prayed to the god and consented. Her consent electrified. On the appointed date, thousands of people thronged to see the ghastly scene. An elaborate arrangement was made. The goddess Ganga Devi’s worshiping with sixteen items of worship attracted the mob, neighbours, & relatives. The grandson was bathed, anointed, dressed and fed and then sacrificed with a Ramda (= broad, curved knife with one cutting edge). A great mass of water suddenly rushed into the tank. A great hue & cry followed. The audience shouted in honour of the goddess and in honour of the boy. | The young boys & girls plunged into the water for swimming & bathing, rollicking. Even the elderly people also bathed. Kamala was sitting in the shade of a tree and observing seriously and silently. She was all along praying to the goddess. The situation was grave, serious, solemn. It was almost afternoon. After the completion of the tragic ceremony, after the completion of bathing of all, Kamala stood up, slowly proceeded to the water. The Folk Tales of Tripura 326 audience suspected that Kamala was going to commit suicide. Kamala took unusual time inside the water. The people were in great emotion & suspense; they were

keenly observing every moment. After a while, Kamala emerged with her son. The crowd shouted & shouted and greeted the mother & the son. Kamala gave all credit to Niyat Chandi. Now Kamala lived happily ever afterwards. 19. Sani Thakur’s ritual-tale Once a prestige fight between Lakshmi Devi and Sani Thakur led the quarrellers to Sribatsha Raja for a judgement. Lakshmi Devi is the wife of Vishnu; Vishnu is the preserver of the world; Lakshmi Devi herself is the presiding deity over wealth and fortune; she is a benevolent goddess; she is respected & worshipped by crores of devotees. On the other hand, Sani Thakur is a malevolent deity; he can make people suffer a lot; he is feared & worshipped by lakhs of people. He can turn green fields into a desert; he can reduce a king into a beggar. The squabble continued for days together. Many controversies arose over the claim of supremacy. The gods in heaven refused to pronounce a verdict. The quarrellers came down to earth; they approached an honest king named Sribatsha Raja. The wise king expressed his inability; but the quarrellers forced him for a verdict. The king was in,a great dilemma. He had a passion for clarity and logical thinking. He had received them with due honour and requested them to appear after about one week. Meanwhile, the king in consultation with ministers and scholars, prepared two beautiful and costly thrones - one of gold, and another of silver. On the appointed date, the litigants appeared. The king received them cordially and offered them the new thrones. It so happened that Lakshmi Devi sat on the throne made of gold; while Sani Thakur sat on the throne made of silver.

After the initial exchange of goodwill, the litigants Folk Tales of Tripura 327 aE EEE EEE insisted on the pronouncement of the verdict. The king said : My Lord! You have already done the delicate job; when they sought clarification, the-king explained. Sani Thakur became very angry and cursed the king and strutted away alone. Lakshmi Devi became pleased; the Devi sat for a while and consoled the king. But Sani Thakur recklessly caused drought & disease, flood & - famine, chaos & confusion. Unable to mitigate the troubles, and unable to tolerate the hue & cry of the subjects, the king, in presence of the ministers & friends, handed over the administrative responsibility to the eldest son. Slowly & steadily the kingdom and the public life became peaceful. Abdicating the throne, the king & the queen voluntarily went into exile. The queen’s name was Chintamani. Chintamani took clothes, ornaments & coins in a wallet. They travelled & travelled without any destination. Unaccustomed to walking on foot, the royal couple had to halt frequently. The subjects became astonished to see the pitiable condition of their dear king. Some of them offered them fruit, milk & dry food; but the king did not stay in their houses for fear of divine curse upon the innocent subjects. The royal couple used to take rest & sit in the shade of any big tree or near some temple. One day in the evening they came near a purling river. The hope of easily crossing the river was damped by downpours & violent gusts of wind. A mighty thunder struck terror. Even the wild birds were taking their shelter. But the royal couple had no shelter. They expected some shelter on the other

side of the river. The king called out loudly with a view to get service. A faint reply came from a boatman. The boatman had a small open vessel; he expressed his inability to carry the couple and the bag at a time; he would be able to carry any two at a time. Thinking pros & cons, the king agreed to embark the bag. In the dusky evening the boatman decamped forever. After a while, Folk Tales of Tripura 328 the duskiness, the rain, the thunder & the river vanished. The malevolent god created delusion & hallucination only to rob the valuables. Divestment was followed by disillusionment. It was broad daylight. The sky was cloudless. The gentle wind was blowing. Divested & disgusted, the king & the queen sat in the shade of a big banyan tree and fell asleep. The next morning they walked a distance and then took rest for a while. Here they came across a fisherman. The poor fisherman, out of respect & sympathy, offered one fish; it was a shol fish. The queen had no utensils, no spices; the king gathered dry leaves & twigs for roasting the fish. After the initial roasting, the queen went to a river to wash and to strip off the skin. The king and the fisherman were engaged in talks. Suddenly, the peeled fish slipped & escaped. The queen screamed. The king and the fisherman rushed to the spot. The fisherman was astonished. The king, in grief, sighed & remarked : The curse of Sani Thakur! ; The king & the queen moved on and reached the end of the boundary of his own kingdom. The famous river Godavari was flowing as the natural boundary of

the two kingdoms. The river had its beginning in the l'raimbakeswar Hill; in the hill there was a small village of woodcutters. The woodcutters built a hut for the couple and offered utensils & tools. The king, too, started going to the forest along with the woodcutters for wood, roots & vegetables. With the free gift of nature, they used to add their labour and sell those things in markets. Thus, the king had to eke out a living. The king assuaged his unhappiness by associating himself with the poor and simple hills people. Besides, the king had fidelity at home. So, the king began to forget about the prosperous mode of early living as king; he began to feel easy about the simple life far away from the capital & busy court. They began to feel about approaching death; the inner conflict Folk Tales of Tripura 329 was slowly fading away. They adopted a simple mode of life. They had little need for contact with the court & the capital. But the malevolent deity machinated to put the poor couple to another serious trouble. One day one merchant was sailing through the river Godavari; the merchant had an export & import business. However, because of the machination of Sani Thakur, the vessel was washed ashore & carceened on the shore. All attempts to draw out the vessel failed. Sani Thakur appeared on the spot in the disguise of an old astrologer. The merchant requested the astrologer to count his fate. The astrologer pretended to have seriously studied his fate and then prescribed : Convince a chaste lady to kindly touch, thrust & press forward the boat; the task would be easy. So

saying, the astrologer left the spot. The merchant’s rowers successfully convinced many women of the adjacent villages to press forward the boat. But the boat did not tilt & slant. On the basis of the information of ladies, the rowers and the merchant went to request the poor queen. The poor king was in the forest at that time. So, she refused to go; but being entreated by the neighbours also, the queen went & touched the boat. Momentarily, the boat was drawn out. But alas! Being charmed by the beauty and elegance of the queen, the cunning merchant twitched her and embarked on the boat and kidnapped her. The rowers were ordered to drive speedily. The neighbours returned home with a heavy heart. The tragedy became the topic of common discussion for a long period. On returning home from forest, the poor king found the cottage empty, and came to know the sad news. He was dumbfounded. Somebody offered him dryfood; he munched it and left the cottage for ever and reached the river bank. The vicissitudes, which had begun to assail him, showed signs of affecting his health. The tragedy had almost completely disheartened the poor king. He was sensible of the fact that he owed his downfall Folk Tales of Tripura 330 solely to the curse of Sani Thakur. He was no party to the quarrel ! He gave everything he had in the world to live the life of a poor woodcutter, but here also the curse dogged him! He became distressed, distracted, dishevelled, untidy and untrimmed. For about a decade he remained in that condition expecting the return of the merchant and the queen. The villagers used to offer

him some fruits and food casually. The cowherds knew him as a mad man. All sorts of strange rumours were current among the graziers. The enervated husband engaged himself in making bricks. On each brick he used to engrave the name Chintamani. To conceal the imprint, he used to join two bricks together. Thus he piled up pairs of bricks. He was partly compensated by the blessing of Lakshmi Devi : the bricks would be turned into gold. The merchant, having spent about ten years in business in distant lands, was coming back home along the same river Godavari. During this time, the Satan made all staggering proposals to the queen Chintamani; but Chintamani, like Sita, did not swerve from the line of chastity and fidelity. So, she too became dishevelled, rough, shabby and untidy. On the way back home, the greedy merchant stopped for a while where his boat had been carceened. There he noticed the pile of bricks, and at once directed his oars-men to plunder the valuable bricks. The local cowherds and graziers had already become friendly with their mad grandfather, that is, the forlon husband. The old man called the boys; the boys rushed and resisted; some of them informed the villagers. The villagers informed the local police and came to help the old man. A scuffle and quarrel occurred. The police arrested the merchant and his oars-men, and brought them to the court of the king of that country. The jubilant boys continued to rend the air with shoutings & screamings. Folk Tales of Tripura 331 The king permitted the old man to argue in favour of his claim of ownership of the bricks. The old man briefly

set two conditions : That man would be the owner of the bricks who could foretell the imprint; & who could open the pair of bricks. Then the king asked the merchant to foretell the imprint. The merchant failed in the first test and the second test too. The king afterwards asked the old man to give his proof. The old man said : The imprint was Chintamani and then he easily opened the pairs after pairs of bricks. The king remanded the merchant to prison along with his oars-men. In view of the excitement which the case had aroused, now the wise king became inquisitive about the whereabouts of the old man. The old man was standing and narrating the curse of Sani Thakur. All the courtesans were looking at him and hearing his strange history attentively. His every word was clearing up the mystery. The king was horrified to know the consequences of the terrible curse of Sani Thakur. With the king’s permission, the old man rushed to the vessel in search of Chintamani. So many people accompanied the old man. They searched each & every corner of the vessel. At last a sound of moaning was heard from a dark room. The old man rushed there frantically and called out : Chintamani! Chintamani! She opened the door. The period of curse was over. Ten years of terrible life did havoc. The couple now became the elated guests of the king. The king became delighted at finding them reunited and happy; the king treated them very respectfully; offered them food, dress and other hospitality. Sribatsha Raja and Chintamani happily stayed in the royal guest-house for about a week. Sribatsha Raja

donated all the bricks to the king; while the king gave him elephant, dress, ornament, and food at the time of departure. Folk Tales of Tripura 332 20. Sankat-trani Devi’s ritual-tale In a certain country, there was a rich merchant, whose name was Dhanapati Sadagar. He had acquired enough of wealth through business. He had his devoted & obedient wife. Though possessed of wife & wealth, and a beautiful garden-house, he had no peace of mind. For, he had no son, no daughter to inherit, to carry on the business & to look after in old age ! As usual, this year also the merchant set out with sapta-dinga (= seven boats) full of merchandise and assistants, helpers, oarsmen & rowers. The voyage, started from the local river, leaving behind many villages & fields, continued for day after day. One day in the dusk the merchant’s fleet stopped for rest near a river- ghat; at that moment the merchant & his men heard the sound of drum-beating, cymbal-beating in pairs, clanging of bells and conch-blowing. It heralded some auspicious, ritual worship. It pleased the merchant. He sent one intelligent assistant to enquire about the worship. The assistant reached the house, stood with folded hands and politely asked : Aunts! what does one gain by worshipping this deity? The ladies replied : The holy name of this deity is Sankat-trani Devi, whatever you want, you will get; a sonless will get a son, a poor will become a richman. Upon getting the siietiecapianis information, the merchant himself landed, reached the house, prostrated himself before the altar and asked the details of the worship, and resolved to worship the deity himself. So,

though he had gone a long way, he returned home with his mind highly rejoiced. At home, with a great hope, he devoutly and duly arranged the worship of Sankat-trani Devi. Spending about a fort night at home, he resumed his voyage leaving behind his wife and retinue of maids & guards. By the grace of the deity, in due course the wife gave birth to a pretty baby, girl. With such a nature, adventurous, courageous, Folk Tales of Tripura 333 eloquent, the merchant, after travelling over distant lands & making profitable business there, returned home after twelve years. His joy knew no bound at seeing his pretty and lively daughter of about twelve years of age. With exultation at his heart and careless of the consequences, he had not paused for a moment and he declared that her marriage would be arranged tomorrow. At the sudden & unexpected announcement, the merchant’s wife was rather shocked. She went on praying for a mercy of the deity. Mysteriously, all night busy clouds had been racing over the sky, carrying a deluge of rain with them. The wind was howling and shrieking in fury. The wife exclaimed : A terrible night, by far the worst since we were wed! The merchant’s daughter drew aside a curtain and peeped out. But at a very early dawn a faint shriek from the outhouse of the merchant’s villa was heard. The merchant came out and saw a youngman shivering helplessly with cold. The youngman was brought in and offered clothe & food. The merchant asked his whereabouts. The reply was astonishing and hopeful. The boy was the son of a landlord; he set out from home in search of a suitable

bride. The news electrified the family. Weary with the terrible night of waiting, but bright with the hope, the merchant’s wife appeared with wondering eyes and tenderly treated him with motherly affection. Slowly the boy regained his strength & energy. He became cheerful. Now came the opportune moment. The proposal was made and the daughter was shown. The boy consented gladly and at dusk the nuptials were duly celebrated & solemnised. The villagers were entertained with a feast. The merchant & the young man then achieved their desire. After two days, the new couple were given a befitting farewell with valuable presents & jewels & ornaments. On the way there were fields, forests, rivers and fear of Folk Tales of Tripura 334 dacoity. There were thugs, robbers. The young husband persuaded the young wife to find a way out. They skilfully put the ornaments into a bundle and devoutly praying the goddess, dropped the bundle into the river water. A large Raghal Boal fish swallowed the bundle. The relatives & friends and neighbours rushed in on hearing the news of the arrival of the young couple, and they vied with one another in heaping flatteries and praises on the handsome couple. They were surprised to know that the bride had been the daughter of the famous merchant, Dhanapati Sadagar. But why the great merchant did not bedeck his dear daughter with ornaments? It was a highly disquieting situation which must be cleared up without delay. To add insult to injury, the fishermen tried their best, but failed to catch even a single big fish from the landlord’s large ponds which had been full of fishes, big & small. It succeeded in accumulating a mass of

suspicion about the people’s whispering; the husband communicated it to his new wife personally. She entreated her husband to request the fishermen to go to the river-ghat where the bundle of ornaments had been dropped, Astonishingly, there the fishermen caught a good number of big fishes, including the large Raghal Boal fish. So, the excitement had calmed down. The villagers were jubilant to prepare the feast : fetching water, mincing vegetables, digging a ground for oven, cutting banana leaves, washing rice & pulses, gossiping, laughing & whispering. But alas! even the young men failed to cut the Raghal Boal fish into pieces. The villagers were in a disposition to believe on insufficient evidence. The credulous people again whispered & whispered. The new bride came to know it through her husband. Now a sense of duty brought her for the first time face to face with those villagers. She was a young bride of strong religious convictions. Chanting the holy name of the deity, she cut the big Kaghab Boal fish with one sweep of a Folk Tales of Tripura 335 Ramda (a curved one-edged, heavy knife). Discovery of the bundle of ornaments from the belly of the fish was a great relief to the bride, but a wonder to the audience. Here her husband came to explain the circumstances of dropping the bundle. Nevertheless, the suspicion of the credulous mob reached its climax. The eyes of all were fixed with thrills & whispers, on the display of efficiency by the bride. The mob became feverish with excitement; the chaos & confusion continued. Suspecting the bride to be an evil nymph, all the villagers ran away rather than walked out without eating.

The landlord was utterly ashamed; his wife was beating her forehead. During their short married life, the groom had no cause to complain of the bride’s conduct. The new bride was greatly shocked to hear that she had been accused on suspicion of being a nymph. She went on chanting the deity’s name. The deity determined to subject the villagers to trouble. That very night, they suffered from various diseases : cold & cough, dyspepsia, fever, pain, vomiting, etc. And every patient dreamed a common dream : the only remedy was to relish the feast. The next morning they all assembled spontaneously. The bride touched the cooked & presérved food, & instantly all the curries & rice became hot & fresh. Being convinced of the greatness of the deity, the villagers joyously ate and determined to worship Sankat- trani Devi. 21. Satera Lakshmi Devi’s ritual-tale A certain part of Bengal was once afflicted by a famine and drought. Many animals & human beings died. Being pinched by hunger, a Brahman started for another kingdom in the east. The Brahman had his wife with him. A pious and well-to-do peasant offered them shelter free of rent. The peasant had an outhouse. The Brahman was allowed to stay there. At the request of the peasant, Folk Tales of Tipura 336 his neighbours used to invite the Brahman to officiate their rites & rituals, worships & sacrifices. The Brahman thus became the priest of the village. The Brahman was not, therefore, dependant on begging. The Brahman’s wife was active and energetic; she had self-respect. She was particularly grateful to the peasant for giving the shelter free of cost. There they got the foothold. Implicitly, the couple had no right to develop

a flower-garden and a kitchen garden around the outhouse. So, once she had a foothold & a little of saving, her chief concern was to purchase a small plot of land and to build their own house & garden and temple. The pious lady used to pray to Lakshmi Devi regularly and devoutly. Being pleased with the devotion of the lady, Lakshmi ‘Devi appeared at one night in dream-revealation and advised the lady to worship Lakshmi Devi for the fulfilment of her desire. It was the 16th of Bhadra. The next day was the 17th of Bhadra. She told her husband about the dream. They, without delay, immediately started to worship the Devi. So, the Devi popularly came to be known as Satera Lakshmi Devi. Henceforth, as the days passed on, the priest’s income went on increasing. The devotees (a74™) gave him fruits, lees, donation & food gladly and profusely. The priest used to come back home jubilantly and to hand over the bag to his wife in splendid spirits. Her mind was now vibrating with a new conviction. They soon purchased a plot of land and built a house, a kitchen garden, a flower garden and a temple for the worship of Lakshmi Devi. Not only that, two daughters were born. They were named Raiiuna and Yamuna. The Brahman family reached the height of its prosperity & popularity. It was a time of its self expression. In the few years that remained of her life, the wife faced no problem. At that time, she seemed to be preoccupied with household chores and nursing the daughters. She Folk Tales of Tripura 337 took an active part in household management. She was

active enough to make the family stand on its own feet.. But alas! She once fell ill and died. It was a terrible blow to the family. At the suggestion of the friends, relatives & neighbours, the Brahman married again. The well- wishers expected the step-mother to look after the two daughters with love & affection. But she soon fell far short of the expectation. She devoted time & care to the comfort of herself & husband. Her cool-hearted disposition alienated the two daughters. The step-mother’s main concern was to get rid off the two daughters. She used to poison the ears of her husband. Not only that, she pretended to be suffering from osteo-arthritis because of the heavy pressure of work. Hiding earthen jar shreds below the quilt of bed, she used to toss over the shreds at night and squirmed her body; it was designed to indicate the symptom of her disease. All through she maintained a show of affection. Suppressing her anger & hatred, she had a command of honeyed words. The two daughters had to drudge all mean & heavy works; still they were blamed, and they were offered stale food. So, their blood began to boil within them to see the satanic wickedness played under a cloak of motherly tenderness. Dodge and drudge went side by side. Without ascertaining the fault of the daughters, the Brahman determined to award punishment to the poor girls. He paused a few days in suspense as to in what way he would punish the daughters. One day in the morning, after the first meal of the day, the Brahman directed the daughters to get ready for visit to their

mother’s sister’s house. The daughters had never heard the story of their mother’s sister; they had now no doubt left in their minds about the evil intention of their father. The father took the two daughters with him and started for forest at a long distance. They passed through Folk Tales of Tripura 338 villages, farms and fields. They travelled for hours. The daughters became tired, but the father did not listen to their appeal. He turned a deaf ear to all their supplications. At long last, they entered into a deep forest and sat in the shade of a big banyan tree. The journey was long, tedious & wearisome. The two daughters sat and fell asleep. The father was waiting for that moment. Leaving the two young daughters there, the father immediately & quickly started coming back home. At a‘little distance from the tree, he purposely tore his umbrella and left the umbrella & reddish spit of betel leaves there to indicate his tragic death at the hand of a wild tiger. It was a crime, a hypocrisy, a breach of trust. Till the public knew nothing. The nasty sabotage went on secretly. The unfortunate daughters were awakened by the screaming of the wild birds. Darkness had set in; there was no human settlement in the vicinity. The forest was infested with wild animals. Their life was in great danger. They were weeping, beating their forehead, accusing their parents, and sobbing. Faint with fear & fatigue, they, with all devotion & dedication, repeatedly uttered the holy name of Satera Lakshmi Devi as the only saviour. Seeking shelter, they hugged the banyan tree. The Devi made a mysterious instruction to the tree; the tree

opened a cavity at its huge trunk. The two sisters entered into the cavity. In the following morning, the tree again opened the mouth of the cavity. The two sisters came out and sat in the shade of the benevolent tree. By the grace of the Devi, a prince and a police commissioner’s son that day entered the forest for hunting; they came across the two sisters and asked their whereabouts. They consoled and assured protection and honourably took them to the king. The king also offered fatherly blessings. The prince married Ramuna, and the police commissioner’s son married Yamuna. From rags to royal palace! The two sisters continued to Folk Tales of Tripura 339 ee be the devout devotees of the Devi and convinced their respective mother-in-law to consent to the worship of the deity. The two families enjoyed the blessings of the Devi. Meanwhile, the dramatic vicissitudes of the fate of the Brahman became quite manifest. Every day he became poorer & poorer. The cruel treatment to the daughters enraged the deity. The Brahman and his second wife incurred a sin. The alarmed villagers almost stopped to invite him for officiating a worship. Poverty at home, unpopularity in the locality, profaneness in the temple, disorder in the kitchen, dryness in the garden, ill-health, etc. spoke of a pathetic condition and mental disorder of the Brahman & his wife. The neighbours, looking down at the Brahman with stern eyes of reproach & surprise, tried to avoid him. The royal family of Ramuna had a network for collecting information. The father-in-law of Yamuna had at his command, a network of watch and ward. At the request of the two sisters, the informants were watching

the Brahman closely. From the spies the two sisters got all information about their parents; they now discussed with some anxiety about the wretched condition of their parents, and decided to request the king for favouring the beggars with gifts of cowrie.. At the humble request of the daughter-in-law, the king agreed. The king discussed the matter with his ministers & officers, and fixed an auspicious date, and the police commissioner arranged to announce the news through drum-beating throughout the kingdom. One day the poor Brahman heard that the king — wished to favour the poor beggars with gifts of cowrie. So, he decided to go to the capital to receive the donation. On the scheduled date numerous beggars swarmed even from the distant villages of the kingdom. The royal administration made adequate arrangement for food & rest & comfort of the poor beggars. Folk Tales of Tripura 340 The ceremony of donation was to be held at spacious premises of a Lakshmi-Narayan temple. The beggars were made to stand in long queue. One employee prepared a record & register of the beggars. When the king & the queen arrived there, the beggars ranted the air with shouting in honour of the king. The one-day ceremony continued for hours together. Ramuna & Yamuna went there to see if their father was arrived there; they sat in a corner. After a few hours, the two sisters identified their poor father from a little distance. However, they had to check their emotion; they had to observe protocol and royal etiquette; they were not in a position to directly & openly rush & call their father. They talked to the security officer and gave a hint by

winking & then left the spot. ' Upon coming the turn, the Brahman received the donation and came out of the line. Then the security officers requested the Brahman to wait there for a while. At this, the Brahman became nervous, afraid & suspicious. When the ceremony was over and the beggars left the temple, the shabby Brahman was escorted to the royal palace through the back-door. The two sisters were eagerly waiting in the palace; they went together to the door to welcome the Brahman. The Brahman became astonished to see the daughters there. The Brahman could not expect & imagine it. The two,daughters forgave him and did not directly blame him for his dodgery. With torn clothes, long beards, untrimmed hair, the Brahman had a look of poverty. Soon the royal barber shaved his beards & trimmed his hair. The two daughters gave him washing materials, oil, good clothes, sandal, sweet scent, etc. for a comfortable bathing and then offered dainty dishes. After the eating, the Brahman was in a happy mood. They sat together for a gossip. Only when he enquired what had happened in the forest, then only the two daughters recounted. The guilty father became ashamed Folk Tales of Tripura 341 of his mean treachery and seemed to suffer from an inferiority complex. The next day, the vulgar step-mother was also called in. Though she had not a grain of common sense, though she had a coarse mind without any degree of morality, the two daughters treated her cordially. They all lived together happily for about a week. At the time of their departure, they were favoured with many gifts on behalf of the two families. Two

palanquins were hired & prepaid for their journey. 22. Santoshi Mata Devi’s ritual-tale Long ago there was a village named Bhadreswar. In Bhadreswar lived a merchant. The merchant had his wife and seven sons. It was a happy family, though not a very prosperous one. He seemed to have devoted himself to his own family which had been increased by additions of seven sons one after another. Thus the family went on peacefully, until the merchant contracted an internal disease from which he died prematurely. After the merchant’s untimely death, the business was not successfully carried on by his sons for a few years. During that period the widow had to labour very hard to maintain the family. After a few years of struggle, the senior sons became experienced enough to run the business profitably. The situation was retrieved. The seventh son of the family was named Ramu. While his six brothers had been earning, Ramu remained unemployed. He had a hobby which did not bring in bread & butter. He had no source of income. He was dependant on his brothers. Any way Ramu’s life at tKis period was comfortable. The relations among the members of the family were amicable. Ramu was co-operating with his mother in domestic chores. But a few years later Ramu was destined to live in very different circumstances. Their mother now thought of arranging the marriage of her sons. It was her main Folk Tales of Tripura 342 concern. She used to discuss the matter with her relatives, astrologers and match-makers. So, on a wave of familial happiness, the seven marriages were arranged one after another within a period of seven years. At first

all went well. In those medieval days what was supposed to be a life of fraternal amity, was not altogether true. So long as the mother had been in-charge of the kitchen room, all the boys used to*get equal treatment. The internal situation slowly & subtly deteriorated with the new arrivals. They had not been on good terms. The aged widow could easily guess the whisperings; but she was in a mess of traditions & sentiments. Her newly won happiness was fated to be brief. The condition of Ramu and his newly married wife was pathetic. The name of Ramu’s wife was Savitri. The couple had to do all odd jobs; but they would not get fair treatment. The mean tricks worked smoothly. Ramu was fated to get stale food even before the arrival of Savitri. Now as an insider, Savitri came to know it; she kept Ramu informed. Savitri did never open her mouth. To such domestic insult, there was one remedy on her part : to inform & alert her husband. Time passed. Alienation became apparent. Ramu determined and declared that he would have to go away for a time. There was something about his decision which made his mother thoughtful and his wife anxious. Ramu had no fixed destination. He left home alone. It was a joint family. Some members of the family chuckled evilly. The lot of Savitri became precarious. She had to wash all the utensils, sweep the courtyard, clean the cowshed, fetch water, mince vegetables, etc. Not only that, she was directed to collect firewood from the jungles. At dead of night, Savitri would often awake with a sense of foreboding. Exhausted physically and depressed

mentally, Savitri had her head cast down. It became a routine-bound duty for Savitri to go to Folk Tales of Tripura 343 gan RC a a eT the forest at about mid-day for cutting & collecting firewood. Being worried & tired, Savitri one day sat in the shade of a tree and fell asleep. Savitri was snoring. Meanwhile one benevolent deity appeared in dream. The female deity assured & consoled Savitri and vanished. Being surprised, Savitri stood up. She quickly returned home with a heavy faggot. Her life-pattern continued the old routine. On another day, after finishing almost all the housework, Savitri, with a rope and a chopper in her hand, went to the forest. Because of gradual deforestation, she had to enter deep into the forest in search of firewood. Loneliness, rustling of leaves, chirping of birds, gleamy light & bowery surroundings constituted an awful supernatural atmosphere. She was feeling very uneasy & unsafe. After a while, the sound of a chorus came from a distance and reached her ears. A faint hope! She eagerly proceeded and found a group of women near a stream and in the shade of an old tree. They had a similar lot. They resorted to the worship of Santoshi Mata Devi. Savitri asked : What does one gain by worshipping Santoshi Mata Devi? They replied : Domestic problems and difficulties are solved by the grace of the Devi. Savitri got a hearty welcome. She became one of them. It was Friday. Henceforth, she joined them on every Friday for a few weeks for the worship. By the grace of the Devi Santoshi Mata, the husband of Savitri got a shelter. One kind-hearted sethji pitied on

Ramu; offered him food & shelter. The sethji engaged him in his shop and observed him. Satisfied with his honesty, the sethji offered him an opportunity to stand on his own risk & responsibility. By learning the trade secret by trial & error, by the patronage of the sethji and by the subtle grace of the Devi, Ramu opened his own shop. At one night Devi Santoshi Mata appeared before Ramu in dream and said that the next day he would get a huge profit, as much as that of one month put together. Folk Tales of Tripura 344 ES But he should keep the shop closed for one month and go back home with money. Ramu was surprised to see the dream coming true; so he followed the advice. After a long separation from the hearth & home, Ramu turned his steps homeward with a splendid spirit. It was early in the morning; and almost all the members in the family were still in bed; Savitri, awoke at dawn, was cleaning the courtyard with a broom and sprinkling a liquid of fresh cowdung there. In the meantime, Ramu surprisingly & suddenly reached home and modestly shouted : Savitri! The situation became rosy steadily. During his absence, Savitri was exposed to all sorts of hardships. The situation had gone worse before it went better. The end of her unhappy time was now very near. Now the mystery was clearing fast. Savitri disclosed the story of her devotion to Devi Santoshi Mata to his husband only. Ramu informed his mother & brothers about his own business and sought separation immediately. Ramu engaged some carpenters, thatchers, wood cutters, labourers, etc. to build a separate house within

a week. Savitri was lodged in the well-furnished house set apart for that purpose. One female attendant was appointed to attend to her comfort. Within four weeks making all arrangements for separate hearth & home for Savitri, Ramu left home. Savitri continued to worship Devi Santoshi Mata devoutly and regularly. She resolved to worship the Mata at her own home. Savitri & Ramu lived from that time in perfect happiness. Within a year, Savitri became the mother of a son. On his return to business, Ramu used to send money regularly for Savitri. Now that the hearth & home were separated, Savitri was no longer required to do all odd jobs. The separation brought a great relief. The responsibility of doing those chores fell on the lot of others. A distinct change in their attitude became apparent, from negligence to jealousy. Savitri could sense their characters in an immediate Folk Tales of Tripura 345 way. She could even sense_their words without actually hearing them. Savitri perceived the slow process of deterioration in their socio-economic conditions. 23. Surya-vrata’s ritual-tale There was, in a kingdom of central Bharat, a city, Avanti by name. In it dwelt a poor Brahman family. The family consisted of four members : the Brahman & his wife & his two daughters, Kunti & Parvati by name. The family had to live from hand to mouth. The Brahman had to go out daily for begging alms. Beggary had a very bad impression upon the family. But the premature death of the wife troubled the Brahman deeply. The Brahman, as usual, had to go out in the morning for begging. The two daughters used to cook food. The Brahman used to return at noon. Then they had the

pleasure of taking food together. The afternoon was left for rest & gossip. That was the routine of the family. One day in the sunlit morning the two sisters placed a little quantity of grains of rice in the courtyard; they wanted to get the grains sun-dried by exposure to the sun. Kunti went to a neighbour’s house; Parvati was left to protect the grains from the depredation of birds. With a long bamboo kept nearby, Parvati sat at a corner. She was basking; she lay and fell asleep. Meanwhile, some birds swooped down and devoured the grains. Upon returning home, Kunti found Parvati asleep and the courtyard empty of grains. Kunti roused & rebuked Parvati. The two sisters tended to beat their foreheads and they were weeping & murmuring. Meanwhile one benevolent deity, in the disguise of an old, grey-haired Brahman, appeared there and asked : Grand-daughters, what ails you ? Why are you weeping ? The two sisters replied satisfactorily. The old Brahman consoled and sought a few grains. Kunti & Parvati knew that there was nothing inside the house; they tried their best and got only three grains, and offered the grains. The old Brahman returned the grains and advised the Folk Tales of Tripura 346 sisters to put one grain in a barn, one in ajar, and another in a pot. Putting the grains, the two sisters came back and listened to the advice of the old Brahman. The old Brahman instructed them to worship Surya-deva and asked them to close their eyes. Immediately the old Brahman vanished. To their wonder & delight, this time they found the formerly empty pots now brimming over with grains. That day, they were strolling & pacing up &

down the room & the courtyard to give the good news to their father. Happy with the unexpected fortune, the two sisters became the ardent devotees of Surya-deva. They started performing Surya-puja right from that day. Simultaneously, the financial condition of the family went on improving slowly & steadily. Prosperity of the family added to its prestige. The family was content at last. In the meantime, however, a sensational discovery had been made, quite by accident, of the growth of the princess of Avanti. Because of her monthly sickness, the queen did not enter into the dining room; the young princess was serving; the king was dining. Unaware of the absence of the queen, the king made a light joke with the server, supposing her to be the queen. Being ashamed, the princess reported it to her mother. The queen brought it to the notice of the king. Always busy with the heavy responsibility of administration, the king did not know that the princess had already attained marriageable age. The king promised to arrange the marriage the very next day. The king’s announcement was hasty. The queen became perplexed; the princess became puzzled. Finding a suitable bridegroom all on a sudden within one day was very difficult. How could such a major issue be left to chance & accident? Kunti casually went inside the spacious palace compound. There were several attendants, maids, gardeners, guards. Kunti had an access into the palace. She came to know the royal family’s news. Upon coming Folk Tales of Tripura 347 back home, she discussed the matter with Parvati; and the two sisters, thinking about the future of their father in old age, entreated their father to marry again. At last,

he agreed. The next day rousing the father at dawn, the two daughters adorned & arrayed the Brahman decently and sent him to the royal garden. In the morning, the drum- beating heralded the royal proclamation. The Brahman became the first man to touch the drum. The attendants were there to bid him welcome to the palace. As the court etiquette enjoined, he pronounced ‘Victory to the Maharaja’ & took his seat. In the dusk, the marriage was solemnised splendidly. Nourished in luxury & attended by maids, the princess now became the bride. The middle-aged Brahman now became the bridegroom of the royal family. He forthwith gave up begging and priestly job. The windfall, the unexpected money & other advantages, made the Brahman buoyant & cheerful. His wife was attractive, beautiful and charming. To the middle-aged husband, the youthful wife was dearer than his life. In their conjugal love, the presence of Kunti & Parvati seemed to be offensive, an eyesore. Being ill treated by the parents, they became disgusted with home. Yet, Kunti & Parvati went on performing Surya-Puja and doing domestic duties. Their parents ceased to be god-fearing country-folk; they became epicurean and irrational; they disliked the Surya- Puja. The youthful step-mother deviced a plot against Kunti & Parvati. She placed earthen jar shreds inside the fold of clothes & quilt of her bed. At night she tossed from one side to another over the quilt strewn with dry shreds. The tossing had a pressure upon the shreds; the shreds would break into small pieces. The sound of breaking was interpreted as a bone-disease. And the brittleness of the bones was owing to the evil intention of Kunti & Parvati. In their daily worship, Kunti & Parvati,

Folk Tales of Tripura 348 it was alleged, used to pray for a disease in the body of their step-mother. The effeminate husband easily believed the false allegations. There must be some other reason & machination. But the eccentric & irreligious man did not verify. He proposed to take the two daughters to their mother’s sister’s house for a visit, and told them to remain ready in the next day morning. The two sisters whispered among themselves in derision of their parent’s intention, but could not say anything. They became restless & speechless. The two daughters, particularly Kunti, knew that their father’s design was to throw them in exile, but they had no alternative but to obey. This part of their girlhood was pathetic. Their mother died when they were still children; they did not know & see the mother’s sister. The next morning, the father, in the pretext of visiting his former wife’s sister’s house, left home with the daughters. They were going along the path through rice fields; some cows were grazing and their bells were clanking. The father was purposely maintaining a distance to avoid discussion. After a few hours of journey, they wer: walking through jungle. They were in the midst of the thickest part of the forest, where there had been a very big banyan tree. The two daughters, béing worried & fatigued, sat in the shade of the tree and fell asleep soon. With a show of affection, he massaged their heads to lull them to sleep. The father had been waiting for that moment; he seized the opportunity; leaving the two daughters there, he quickly turned his steps homeward. He tore his umbrella & some clothes to indicate that he

had been devoured by a wild beast. The false & deceptive evidence was left to provide a ground for inferring that their father had been a tragic victim. Such men often make falsehood look like truth. After some time, the two sisters awoke and found themselves left alone in exile. A thrill of fear ran through Folk Tales of Tripura 349 them. The shades of evening were gathering fast around them. By & large it began to grow dark. They thought of hastening back to human settlements; but it had grown so dark already that they dared not make any attempt to find their way back. So they devoutly went on chanting the holy name of Surya-deva. To their wonder & delight, clothed, in the garb of an old, grey-haired begging monk, the benevolent Surya- deva appeared and asked them : Grand-daughters! why are you crying? What ails you? They bowed to him touching the ground with the eight parts of body & answered and said : ‘Save our lives.’ Upon getting the reply, the monk consoled them, and helped them in climbing up to the trunk & cavity of the banyan tree. For the whole night the monk remained sitting below in the Shade of the tree to guard the orphans. In the next morning he set out to seek the assistance of the woodcutters and gatherers. The woodcutters & gatherers materially & physically contributed to build a small hut and to dig a very small pond, and they offered a portion of their dry food. The next day they brought from their homes some old, second-hand utensils, jars, knife, clothes, grains, etc. Slowly and slowly, the hut seemed

to be a hermitage. The woodcutters used to take rest & gossip there daily; they had the virtues of common sense, self-reliance and fellow-feeling. Day after day rolled by. Putting on the rusty brown garment, the monk used to protect the orphans and advise the woodcutters. Thus the hermitage became popular & famous. One day two friends : a prince and a police commissioner’s son, came to that forest for hunting. Being tired and thirsty, they came to the hermitage for rest & drinking water. On seeing the two sisters, they were charmed; they proposed to marry them. In presence of the woodcutters, the monk solemnised the marriage. The prince married Parvati; the police commissioner’s son married Kunti. Now the monk blessed them and disappeared. Folk Tales of Tripura 350 Kunti was pious, sincere & serious. She had listened to the advice of the aged monk; and she had the tenacity to regularly perform the Surya-Puja. So she lived well and happy. But Parvati was frivolous, insincere and undutiful. As time went on, she and the royal family became poorer and poorer. The king’s horses, elephants & cattle died; drought, cyclone, famine, epidemic did havoc. All those calamities occurred after the marriage of Parvati. The worried king seriously discussed the problems with his council of ministers and identified the cause. The king and the prince unanimously decided to abandon and exile Parvati. Parvati was pregnant at that time. The king ordered his guards : Take her into the jungle and leave her in that hut where she had been earlier. Parvati began to weep. The considerate guards consoled her and offered some dryfood and daily needs. The guard, left her there in the forest and returned. In

the hut she had the opportunity of getting all sorts co- operation & sympathy from the woodcutters. After a few months a son was born to her. Year after year rolled by. Parvati’s son was growing. Like the woodcutter, he was acquiring the virtues of self-reliance & laboriousness. From the mother, he heard the story of her sister. The story of Kunti, heard from Parvati, fascinated the boy. Taking permission from Parvati, the son, along with the woodcutters, went to the village of Kunti. He went to the corner. of the village where his aunt lived. There was a very big pond of water in front of the aunt’s house. There was a tall tamarind tree near the ghat (=landing-stairs). The branches of the tree were like canopy over the ghat. The boy climbed up the tree. After a while, the maids came to fetch water with earthen jars for the family of Kunti. The boy asked : Oh maids! whose maids are you ? They answered : We are the maids of Kunti Devi. Being sure, the boy dropped a ring of gold into the jar of a maid. The ring was given by Folk Tales of Tripura 351 Parvati as a mark of identity. The audacity of the boy annoyed the maids. They angrily proceeded to bandy words. The boy said : Go & tell your master’s wife that her sister’s son has done the mischief. The maids strutingly went back and reported the matter to Kunti Devi. The ring convinced her. But the boy had torn & tattered dress. So the maids took him in through the back door. Kunti Devi,had him bathed and anointed, and gave him decent clothes to wear and food

to eat. The boy stayed there for a few days. The village barber was called in to cut & dress his hair. While going back to the hut in the remote jungle, the aunt gave him clothes and food and advised him to take the bundle carefully. But as the boy was passing through the hills, the Sun-god came disguised as a vagabond and stole the bundle. When the boy reached the destination, Parvati asked so many questions and then asked : What did your aunt give for us? The boy said : My aunt gave me a bundle of clothes & food, but on the way a vagabond snatched away the bundle. Deprived of family-life, Parvati became thin, feeble, sickly & mawkish. At last there came a day when Parvati felt that she should go to Kunti’s house for help. Kunti’s house became as good as royal house. In such house, the doors were not flung wide open. There were boundary walls, guards, maids, outhouses. Parvati had to suffer the ordeal. Parvati had weary look & shabby dress. Any way, Parvati along with her son started for the house of Kunti and walked up to the tank. The mother & the son sat in the shade of the tamarind tree. A short while after, the maids came to fetch water. Parvati asked them : Oh maids! who is your mistress? They said : Kunti Devi is our mistress. Parvati said: Then tell your mistress that her sister is waiting here. The maids informed Kunti. Kunti sent back the maids to Parvati. Parvati & her son were taken in by the back door. Kunti received them with warmth of heart and treated them affectionately &

Folk Tales of Tripura 352 cordially and made all good arrangements for bathing, clothing, food & lodging. Kunti knew her younger sister Parvati right from childhood. Parvati became atheist, lacking in devotion & dedication, devoid of decency & decorum. Her thin body and hungry look were disgusting. Right from childhood, Kunti was intelligent, rational, sincere and serious. Kunti observed the behaviour of Parvati closely. Parvati spoiled her son also. Kunti rightly diagnosed the cause of Parvati’s sufferings. Kunti admonished Parvati and tried to rectify her. Kunti arranged Surya-Puja a number of times, and requested Parvati to observe fasting & penance till the completion of the worship. But Parvati secretly ate something right in the morning on every occasion of the worship. Disgusted with such a wayward sister, Kunti at last became tough and tethered and fastened Parvati only to force her to observe fasting & penance prior to the worship. Kunti told Parvati that all her sufferings had come through not observing the Surya-Puja. The frickle-minded Parvati at last observed the worship under compulsion.
