Instantly good fortune started coming. Some positive changes were observed in her manners and etiquette. Her taste for dirty & worn-out clothe and dishevelled hair vanished; she displayed courtly manners ; and falling on her knees, entreated Kunti to explain the cause of her sufferings. Then came references to their paternal home, to the death of her mother, to the poverty of their family, to the blessing of the Sun-god, to the marriage of their father, to the ill treatment by the step-mother, to their exilement, to the reappearance of the Sun-god, to their marriage, to the service rendered by the hills people & woodcutters. After that, the story of Parvati was brought

in : her life in the royal luxury, her negligence to worship Surya-deva, the misfortune in the royal family and her exilement. It took a few days to recapitulate the history. Meanwhile the prince (=Parvati’s husband) travelled Folk Tales of Tripura 353 on for months and months till he came to the dense forest; there he saw a small thatched hut. He entered it and saw one grey-haired hermit. The prince falling on his knees, entreated the hermit to tell him the cause of his sufferings. The hermit narrated that here the prince had met & married Parvati and that Parvati forgot to worship the Sun-god. So all misfortunes fell upon the royal family, and for that mistake, the prince was dispossessed of all wealth. The hermit offered him water, and winked him to go to the house of Kunti. The prince lodged in the hut for the night. The next morning the prince, with the hermit’s blessings, started and hastened on his journey. The tired prince at last reached the house of Kunti. The prince’s friend recognised the prince and gave him a hearty reception. The prince had shabby dress, untrimmed hair & nail, weary and hungry look. The friend first offered the prince drinking water and fruits, and then called in a barber to cut & dress his hair. While the barber had taken the prince for hairdressing, the host sent confidential news to Kunti alone to arrange the preparation of dainty dishes and to stash Parvati & her son in a separate room. After anointment with oil, the two friends had a good swimming. They bathed, dressed in decent dress and relished dainty dishes. Then came references to their adventures, to their marriage, to the

shallowness of Parvati, to the calamities in the kingdom, to the crisis in the royal family and to the exilement of Parvati. The prince suspected that Parvati might have already died. Still the prince had been in search of Parvati. But the friend did not disclose the presence of Parvati in his house; instead, like a real friend, he seriously discussed the cause of the crisis and chaos and extracted promise from the prince to celebrate the Surya-Puja. The next day the prince ‘turned his steps homeward with valuable presents from the friend and an assurance of searching out Parvati by the friend. Folk Tales of Tripura 354 Just after a few days, the friend sent the good news of finding out Parvati. The prince sent palanquin & bearers to bring Parvati. Amidst jubilation, Parvati was received back; the king, the queen, the prince and many others went out of the palace to receive Parvati. Determined to worship the sun-god, Parvati, twitched a few durba grasses for the worship. But the overenthusiastic prince took it otherwise; he thought, owing to the negligence of the gardener the main gate of the palace remained unclean. The prince hastily ordered to behead the five sons of the gardener. The hasty order marred the joy. A great tragedy indeed! Somehow Parvati came to know the sad news. She immediately entreated to stop the cremation till her arrival. She sprinkled the holy water and chanted the name of Surya-deva. To the wonder and astonishment of all, the five sons got back their lives. Thus, the greatness of Surya-deva was established and the Surya-Puja became popular. With replenished fortune, the prince and Parvati started their life anew.

24. Surabhi’s Path The sacred cow of the gods had three different names: Kamdhenu, Nandini, Surabhi. The cow had her abode in the heaven. She is the first mother of the cattle. She had the marvellous capacity of giving milk whenever needed by gods and sages. The sacred cow had a special road running from the sky to the earth; and the cow used to go to and fro all alone. She would only occasionally come down to earth. The Milky-way or the luminuous band of distant stars was the reserved path of the benevolent cow. The furs of her tail were believed to have some magical value. So, one greedy man made a plot to cut a few furs. One day Surabhi came down and was eating green grass. The cunning fellow lay in ambush; he suddenly came out and with one sweep of his sharp knife cut a good number of fur of the sacred cow and then Folk Tales of Tripura 355 swiftly decamped. The angry cow at once went to tread the spot repeatedly and then left for ever. Henceforth, Surabhi stopped coming down to earth, and destroyed the lower portion of the divine path. 25. Features of Snakes Long, long ago the angry sage, Durvasa Muni, in his habitual anger, cursed the gods; the gods were soon to suffer from infirmity and old age. The gods could, however, redeem themselves from the curse by drinking Amritam to be obtained by churning the mythical ocean of milk, Kshira-sagar. The curse badly affected the gods; they started suffering from premature infirmity. The worried gods sat together and decided to churn the ocean with the help of the demons. The gods came to an understanding with

the demons. They jointly churned the ocean. It took a long time and a great effort. After an arduous attempt, at last nectar arose. All were delighted. Many things emerged out of the ocean. The deadly poison also arose. Mahadev was kind enough to swallow the poison and save the earth. The gods and the demons then journeyed onwards to the shore with the Amrita Kumbha. Suddenly the demons snatched the holy pot of nectar, and decamped. The gods tried very hard, but they could not physically and initially recover the holy pot. Then the gods conspired to recover the pot. In the struggle some drops of nectar fell there. Now, many animals, birds, insects and snakes rushed there to drink a little of nectar. Many of them did not get even a drop of nectar. There were lots of Kusa grass. Out of frustration, the snakes started chewing the sharp and pointed blades of the grass. The snakes had to suffer from the indiscriminate act of chewing : their tongues were cut into two halves. Not only that, the famous python snake vomited its entire stock of poison. So, python is poisonless. But the notorious cobra swallowed a large quantity of poison. So, cobra is extremely poisonous. Folk Tales of Tripura 356 26. Sita’s curse Raja Dasaratha was the famous king of the Ikshaku dynasty of Ayodhya. He had three queens, named Kausalya, Kaikeyi and Sumitra. He had four princes, named Rama, Bharata, Lakshman and Satrughna. The names of the daughters-in-law were Sita, Mandavya, Urmila & Srutakirti. Raja Janaka was the father of Sita & Urmila. One day in an adventure made by Raja Dasaratha, the second queen Kaikeyi helped & nursed the king

Dasaratha. The king then promised to give her two boons. lt happened several years ago. A blank cheque! Time rolled on. The king ruled for several years. He became old enough. He thought of getting rid of the burden of administrative responsibility by choosing Rama the next successor. The counsellors agreed and the decision was made public. The king called to his bedside Rama & Sita and gave words of advice. The priests and the ministers fixed the auspicious date and made elaborate arrangements. Kaikeyi had her son Bharata and her maid servant Manthara. Manthara was humpbacked and an evil genius; she machinated & excited Kaikeyi. Kaikeyi requested the old king to grant those two boons. The king was not prepared for the appeal. Kaikeyi said : My prayer is that Bharata be crowned king, and Rama be exiled for fourteen years into the forest. ‘ Dasaratha became terribly shocked. He could not utter a word. But the word of an Aryan king could not be broken. The situation became grave and serious. The alarming news spoiled the atmosphere. Rama came to know it; he volunteered to go in exile. The next day the situation was completely changed. The very next day amid utter grief of a vast crowd, Rama, Lakshmana and Sita left the palace. The members of the royal family and many others stood lamentably. Folk Tales of Tripura 357 Rama, Lakshmana and Sita looked back repeatedly; leaving the chariot, the trio trudged. The village paths were narrow and zigzaged. On both sides of those paths the villagers crowded to see Rama, Lakshmana & Sita. Kaikeyi munched betel leaf and chuckled. Manthara moved and walked limpingly and reported to Kaikeyi. Raja

Dasaratha fell ill. His condition was deteriorating daily. Within a few days he died of heart-attack. Bharata and Satrughna performed the funeral rites. But the king’s departed soul was longing for Pinda- dan from the eldest son. The departed soul went to the deep forest in search of Rama. At that time, Rama & Lakshmana were busy elsewhere in the hills & jungles in collecting wild roots, fruits, leaves and firewood. The soul, on reaching the hut, approached Sita. So Sita instantly and solemnly offered Pinda in presence ofa durba grass, a tulsi plant, a banyan tree, one priest and the river Phalgu. After a few hours, Rama and Lakshmana returned. Sita narrated what had happened meanwhile. The two brothers sat aghast and repeatedly asked about the sad tragedy. Without any doubt about the sincerity of Sita, they innocently sought a proof. Sita had already been in great anxiety. Now she became sentimental. Sita sought deposition and declaration from the grass, the plant, the tree, the priest and the river. But alas! Most of them maintained diplomatic silence. It annoyed Sita. She could not control her anger. The grass, the plant, the priest and the river whined. Only the banyan tree boldly deposed the testimony. So, Sita cursed the whiners thus : Durba grass should be trampled under foot; Tulsi plant should be urinated by dogs; Phalgu-Nadi should be dry & dirty with dung; Priest should be poor. Sita blessed the tree : Banyan tree would be immortal. Folk Tales of Tripura 358 27. Draupadi’s curse It was. one of the tragic episodes of the Mahabharata. Amid a contrasting scene of defeat & victory, of sorrow & joy, of directness & deception, the five brothers and

Draupadi left the ancient capital city, Hastinapur. The remote and main cause was the struggle of succession. The immediate & superficial cause was Yudhishthira’s defeat in the game of dice. In the deceitful game, the Pandavas lost their kingdom; Duhsashan tried to strip of Draupadi’s robes. The five Pandavas and their wife Draupadi, after a series of humiliation, were forced to leave their ancestral home with their heads cast downward. With nothing in their hands but their weapons, they set out for the forests to spend the twelve years of exile and one year in disguise. A ‘great multitude of the citizens of Indraprashtha wept, tore their hair, beat their foreheads and whined at the time of departure of the Pandavas. The village paths in the southern slopes of the mighty Himalayas were narrow and zigzaged, up one slope of the hills and down the other. The Pandavas and Draupadi trudged. Some communities of the Himalayas had the tradition of polyandry. So, Draupadi’s polyandrous marriage evoked no surprise and sensation to the hills people of the Himalyan region. They offered them food & shelter. - But when they turned their steps southward, the social situation was found different. There the people were not accustomed to polyandry. They looked at the fugitives with a sense of surprise and doubt. They chuckled, nudged and winked. One young couple passed a taunting remark. The Pandavas were in utter distress and malady. The taunt infuriated Draupadi. She could not restrain her wounded sentiment. She cursed the giddy couple : In the next life they should be degenerated into cow and ox to experience the striking battle of courtship. Folk Tales of Tripura 359 So, in the rural villages of Bharat it is a common

place to see a fleeting cow followed by a few young oxen. A menstruous young cow becomes restless; the cow tends to run. The cow’s wild low is instantly echoed by ox’s bellow; oxen run wild and run riot, and rush & follow the fleeting cow. 28. A Public curse Once upon a time there was a creditor, and there were several debtors. The creditor used to lend money on interest. Most of the poor debtors used to return the capital along with interest. The rate of interest was, however, high. Nevertheless, one debtor was an exception : he was a cunning rogue, a thug. It was his policy to borrow in small amount a number of times, and to pay back. Thus, gaining credibility, he would borrow a large amount, and delayed and delayed in paying back. The swindler then would approach another creditor of a separate village. Thus, he deceived several persons in this or that way, So, almost all the villagers were disgusted with his behaviour. They used to curse him & criticise him. One day the swindler died of hunger & disease. In the next life he was born as a tree. And the affected villagers used to strike the tree with their knife while passing through their path. And the creditor was reborn as a parasitic Peepal tree. The parasitic Peepal tree had to hug and clasp the notorious tree only to collect and realise the loan lent on interest in the previous life. 29. Marriage of a Mushik-Princess There was a king of the rats. The king and the queen had several sons and only one daughter. The parents had great affection for the only daughter.

When the princess grew to girlhood, the parents cherished an ambition to arrange the marriage of their daughter with the most powerful young man of the world. For days & months, they went on thinking, deciding and selecting. In their judgement, the Suryadev (=sun) was Folk Tales of Tripura 360 the most powerful person. Accordingly, a proposal was duly sent to the sun. The sun was glad to receive the messenger and the message. But the sun declined the offer, and argued that the Megh-raja (= the cloud-king) was superior. The Megh-raja was capable of covering the rays of the sun. So, the sun directed the messenger to go to the Megh-raja. The messenger went to the Megh-raja and spoke eloquently about the beauty of the princess and made a formal proposal. The Megh-raja was glad to receive the messenger and the message. But the Megh-raja declined the offer and argued that the Pavan-raja (= the wind-king) was superior. The Pavan-raja was capable of dissipating the cloud. So, the Megh-raja suggested the messenger to approach the Pavan-raja. The messenger went to the Pavan-raja and tried to convince the Pavan-raja and made formal proposal. The Pavan-raja was glad to receive the messenger and the message. But the Pavan-raja declined the offer and suggested the name of Deoal-raja (=wall-king) as a deserving candidate. The Pavan-raja argued : my capacity to dissipitate the cloud is a fact, but I fail to swing the Deoal-raja. Even when my agents blow violently, the sturdy walls do not shudder. So, it will be wise to approach the Deoal-raja. The messenger now came down and duly approached the Deoal-raja. The Deoal-raja was glad to receive the messenger and the message. The Deoal-raja smilingly

declined the good proposal and argued that the rats living below the surface of wall were very powerful creatures. The rats had the capacity to tear down the strong walls. So, the rats were the deserving candidates. It would be better to select one of the rats. The Mushik-raja (= rat-king or king of the rats) was eagerly waiting for the messenger. The travel-stained messenger had a long journey. His arrival created a sensation in the family. But as the words left his lips, a Folk Tales of Tripura 361 moment’s lull descended. It was a shocking experience. All the children of the Mushik-raja fell back in grim silence. After a few days, the Mushik-raja directed the messenger to select a bridegroom from the king’s own community. 30. A crow & a wood-apple Once upon a time a jungle crow liked to eat a wood- apple. In search of the fruit, the crow moved here & there, and at last found the tree. The crow said : Oh! wood-apple tree! I like to eat your fruit; kindly give one fruit. The tree said : My fruit is sacred; it is used in religious worship as offering to the deities. Your beak is profane; you eat nasty things; you feed on carcass. Do not commit sacrilege. The crow said : Then how can I eat the fruit? The tree replied : If you are so eager, make a pilgrimage to the Ganga, bathe and thoroughly wash your beak. Accordingly, the crow set out on a pilgrimage and reached the bank of the holy river. The crow said : Oh! holy river! allow me to bathe in your water and wash my

beak, for I want to eat sacred wood-apple. The river replied : I cannot allow you to desecrate my holy water; my water is used in all religious purposes. However, if you bring an earthen pot, I may allow you to take water. So, the crow had to fly back and searched out the house of a potter. The crow said : My dear potter! kindly give me a new earthen pot, so that I can take a quantity of the holy water of the Ganga and wash my beak and then eat one sacred wood-apple. The potter said : To dig clayey soil, I require the horn of a buffalo, bring one horn. So, the crow moved further in search of a buffalo and saw a buffalo. The crow said : Dear buffalo! give me your horn, so that the potter can dig soil and make a pot. I shall take out the sacred water of the river Ganga with the pot and wash my beak and eat one wood-apple. The buffalo said : I am alive, how can I offer you my horn myself? Anyway, if a tiger kills me, you can get my horn. Folk Tales of Tripura 362 Next, the crow flew deep into a forest in search of a tiger and found an old tiger there. The crow said : Sir! kindly kill the buffalo. I am in need of horn. I shall hand over the horn to the potter; the potter will dig soil and make a pot. I shall take out water from the Ganga and wash my beak and then eat wood-apple. The tiger said : I am old enough and weak : I cannot hunt, I feed on grass.

Kindly bring a bundle of green grass. Now, the crow went to a meadow and approached the grass and narrated the chain of events. The grass said : Bring a sickle from a blacksmith and cut me. Afterwards, the crow went to the house ofa blacksmith and called out. When the blacksmith had come out, the crow recounted the episodes. The blacksmith said : I shall make a sickle for you, but ‘the fire in my kiln is gone. Bring fire from somebody else. Finally, the crow went to a householder and repeated the whole story. The householder agreed to offer a burning cake of black charcoal. Taking the hot charcoal cake in his jaws, the crow flew back, But when he was flying, the cake became aflame. Unable to carry, the crow shifted the cake and put inside wings. There, the wings caught fire; then the charcoal cake was placed on the back, the back too started burning. When placed on head, head also got burned; when placed inside the mouth, the mouth also got burned. The crow cried : ka ka repeatedly. Thus, the crow collapsed. The crow’s desire to eat a wood-apple remained unfulfilled. 31. A crow, a deer & a jackal In a certain, deep forest there lived a crow and a deer. They were friends. After some years of their friendship, a cunning jackal spied it. The jackal had the evil intention of relishing the flesh of the deer. One night the jackal advanced towards the deer and said : Sir, how are you ? The deer said : Who are you ? The jackal said : I am a jackal. I have no friend or relative

. Folk Tales of Tripura 363 here. I am half-dead. I crave your friendship. The deer agreed and stayed together for the night. The next morning, they went to meet the crow. The deer introduced the new friend. The crow remained strategically silent. Day after day passed in friendly discourse. One day the jackal said : Friend! not far away from this forest there is a field full of crops, corns, sugarcane. I have already tested the sugarcane. If you are willing, I may lead you there. Having convinced the deer, the jackal showed the way. Thus, the two friends used to go there for a few nights to feed upon the sugarcane. The crow came to know the new adventure, and himself remained aloof. The damage thus caused, in course of time, came to the notice of the master of the field; he laid snares and net around the field. That night also the deer and the jackal entered into the field. The jackal identified the net, but did not give warning to the deer; instead, the jackal enticed the deer to feed upon the sugarcane sufficiently. The simple-hearted deer did so and fell asleep inside the field. The notorious jackal passed out and directed his wife to prepare spices in advance. The jackal lay in ambush in the nearby bush. Very early in the next morning the usual hum of insects and the sweet notes of birds were heard. The deer awoke at dawn and found himself enmashed and the jackal outside. The deer frantically sought the aid of the jackal. The jackal said : Friend! this net is made of sinews. To-day I usually take vegetarian diet; so, I cannot

cut it; tomorrow I shall cut it to pieces and release you. With these words, the traitor again lay in ambush. ) In the meantime, the crow became very anxious. The deer did not come home in time. The crow flew here and there and at last found the deer in a wretched condition. The crow said : Friend! feign yourself dead and stay quiet till I make a noise, and without a loss of a moment you get up and run away as fast as you can. The farmer will soon come here with a heavy staff in his hand. Folk Tales of Tripura 364 Following the advice of the crow, the deer tried his best to feign himself, fill the belly with wind and stiffen the legs. The deer lay down, pretending to be dead. Finding the deer dead, the farmer started collecting & folding up the net. The moment the entanglement was removed, the observant crow gave the indication. The deer ran away fast. The farmer became astonished and angry. He flung his staff. The staff struck the jackal seriously. te jackal died. 32. The Crow Pheasant In a certain village lived a fisherman with his wife and son. The family had peace and a little of prosperity. One day the fisherman and his son went to fish. They caught a large number of Magur fish (= a kind of scorpion fish). The father and the son were very pleased; -they filled their basket (= Dula). But the father thought a great deal about how to relish the fish all by himself. An evil design came to his mind. He led his son to another hole. He said to his son

: My dear son, there are several Magur fishes inside this hole also, Your body is slim; you enter into the hole and catch the fishes. The son, on good faith, stepped in. Without giving the son the slightest chance to return, the fisherman blocked the opening of the hole with a large chunk of mud. The son died then and there out of suffocation. The greedy fisherman hurried home with a basket full of fish, leaving the son inside the hole of a distant stream. The fisherman, on reaching home, directed his wife to cook the fish very urgently. The fisherman went to the adjacent pond for cleaning and bathing. While cooking, the mother was thinking about the son; while bathing, the father was thinking of devouring the fish. Soon, the father entered the kitchen room and said to his wife : Let me eat the cooked curry of fish. I am very hungry. The wife offered him seat, water and a dish of rice and fish. Folk Tales of Tripura 365 She sat down watching the path along which her son would return. She asked : Why our son is so late ? Why he is not still coming ? The father said : I have sent him to his mother’s sister’s house with one basket of fish. He is eating fish there! | But the anxious mother could not remain satisfied with the reply. The reply did not touch the right chord in the bosom of the mother. She felt an uncanny pain. She moved to and fro in the courtyard. By that time, the fisherman devoured the fish and burst out into weeping. Suddenly the husband and the

wife rushed stumbling to the spot where the son had been buried. While rushing, they cried and repeatedly uttered : Oh son! oh son! oh son! They unearthed the dead body and brought it home for cremation. The ruffian admitted what had been done. Hence forth, to express the unbearable grief, they used to beat their chest. The parents could not eat & drink anything. So, they died within a few days. In the next life they became crow pheasant (= Kuka Pakhi). Because of that tragedy and repentance, the bird even now weep and often cry out : Oh son! oh son! oh son! Many generations ago, they were Dhritarashtra and Gandhari. 33. A fox & a dove In a certain forest lived a fox and a dove. They knew each other. The bird was lame and old. The animal had a clandestine desire to relish the meat of the bird. The fox intentionally made friendship with the dove. The fox had claptrap. The fox once said to the dove : ‘Friend! you are old enough and ill; if you do not take rich food, you will die soon. The winter season is not far away. During the severe cold of the month of Magha, so many old persons, animals, birds, die; so, be cautious and take nutritious food right from now.’ The dove said : Where shall I get such food? Who will collect it? Who will give me the information? I cannot move! Folk Tales of Tripura 366 The fox said : Do not worry. I am here for your assistance. I shall bring information within a few days. After a few days, the fox came back to report. The

fox said : A paddy field lies beyond this forest. The paddy has been ripe enough. You go and eat as much as you can. I shall hide in the nearby bush and look after your safety. The dove, agreeing to the proposal, flew and swooped down and ate in sufficient quantity. The dove thought of going back happily, but failed because of infirmity and - heavy load of food. The cunning fox was waiting for this moment. The fox came out from the bush and pounced upon the dove only to devour. The dove was not at all ready for the. treachery. What a terrible breach of trust! Suddenly, a strategy came to her mind. The dove said : Friend! you know my old age; at this age bones become unbreakable and flesh becomes tasteless. You are also old; you will not be able to digest my insipid flesh. Out of indigestion you will die soon, Give me a chance to regain my health and fecundity. | promise you; I shall let you eat the soft and sweet meat of my young ones. The dove’s proposal suited the fox. The dove was allowed to fly back to the nest. The bird and the animal thus came to an understanding. They retired. It was a great relief for the bird, a rebirth indeed! The liar taught her a lesson. The simple-hearted bird now thought of becoming equally deceitful. In course of time, the bird regained health and fecundity; now she started to brood. Laying a few eggs, hatching, nursing, feeding, protecting went on one after another. It was another phase of hope and anxiety on the part of the mother.

The fox used to visit frequently and from the bottom of the tree asked about the birth and growth of the young ones. Now, the bird also became tactful and would never disclose the truth. Her reporting was dilatory, behind in Folk Tales of Tripura 367 actual progress. Day after day passed in making reciprocal inquiry. The dove has now become clever to tantalize the treacherous beast. She thought : tantalization was not enough; stern action should be taken against the aggressor. So, she collected all poisonous discharges and put in a packet. Next time, when the fox called out, the dove replied: Yes, my friend, the soft and tasty meat of my young ones is now ready for you. I must keep my promise. I have prepared a lot and put inside a packet. It is ready, you relish. The fox said : I am happy that you are true to your words. I am opening my mouth with joy. You drop the packet. The dove cautioned : Friend! do not let it drop on the ground; do not open it. Swallow it immediately. Agreeing to the caution, the traitor kept his mouth wide open, and swallowed the packet. He could not digest the poisonous discharges. He died. The foxes are well-known as cunning animals. However, this is the tale of a dove who befooled the fox. 34. A fox in a tiger’s cave In a certain village lived a Zamindar family. On the occasion of the marriage of the Zamindar’s daughter a great feast was arranged. The leavings of food, orts, bones, meat, etc. were put in baskets and thrown in a nearby jungle. In search of food, a fox came there and

started devouring the orts. While licking off the dry blood joyfully, one basket got fixed round his neck. It looked like a neck-ring. The fox tried to remove it, but failed. In the mean time a few hungry dogs came there and chased the fox. The fox ran towards hills and jungles. In that deep forest lived a tiger with his wife and two cubs. At that time, the tiger was not inside the cave; the tiger went out for hunting. The cunning fox devised a plan and said to the tigress : Long ago your husband borrowed from me one basketful of meat, now you take out the basket from my neck and return the loan. Folk Tales of Tripura 368 The tigress carefully took out the basket and politely offered the fox a seat for rest. But she could not return the debt. She was not told of such a debt by the tiger. Moreover, during the absence of her husband, she should not take such a decision. Late at night, the tiger came back. The tigress narrated the incident. The tiger became furious, and chased the fox. The deceitful fox was ready for this event. He ran and ran frantically and strategically slipped through a narrow space between two adjacent trees. The angry tiger, while madly pursuing the fox, had to pass through the narrow space, and got himself entangled. The tiger could not extricate himself and lay like a wedge, and expired. The notorious fox came back to the cave and said to the tigress : The poor tiger has become bankrupt, destitute and vagabond; he is ashamed to show his face to you; so he has started for a pilgrimage, and he has

requested me to look after his family. The tigress now had no other alternative, but to surrender temporarily to the fraud. The cheat looks after the cubs, and the tigress goes out for hunting. The fox hardly takes the trouble of collecting meat; he enjoys life, The life in the cave went smoothly for a few years. By that time, the two little cubs have grown up. One night, the two cubs and the fox went together in a hunting operation. They found a swine and hunted it. But the role of the fox in that operation was very negligible. However, they returned with the game. But the cubs took a chance to secretly express their doubt about the fox, and narrated the incident to their mother. Her sons are adult now and capable of self- defence. So, she too exposed the real character of the cheat. They whispered to take revenge. One night, while some other foxes in their noctural roaming, started shouting one after another, this fox could not check the temptation; he, too, went out. The Folk Tales of Tripura 369 cubs stealthily followed and maintained a safe distance and found the fox shouting in chorus. Being sure of his identity, the cubs lay in ambush and at an opportune moment pounced upon the cheat and killed him. 35. A jackal & a crocodile In a certain deep river lived a crocodile with his wife and children. On the bank of the river lived a jackal. One night the jackal went out for hunting some domestic animals or birds. The domestic dogs of the village chased the jackal. The jackal fled and jumped into the river and

fell on the crocodile. The crocodile was surprised and angrily asked : Who are you? The jackal replied : Friend! I am jackal; I live nearby; I teach; people call me Sial Pandit. | have come here for a cruise. The reply softened the crocodile. The crocodile allowed the jackal to enjoy the voyage. The crocodile said : Friend! you are my neighbour, but I do not know your name and fame! The jackal said : It matters little. Our ways of life are different. So, we did not have the chance to talk to each other. The crocodile said : I have seven children. I am thinking of sending them to a teacher. As you are a famous teacher and as you live on the bank of this river itself, I think you will be the most suitable teacher. The jackal said : Do not worry; I shall teach them so that they will be able to count the stars in the heaven, and the sand of the underworld. The jackal’s reply pleased the crocodile. On an auspicious night the crocodile and his wife brought the children and handed over them to the jackal. The teacher started teaching the art of fishing, hunting, and counting. With the help of the students, seven separate caves were dug for each student. The crocodile make weekly inquiry about the health and education of the children. Day after day passed thus. Folk Tales of Tripura 370 Now, the cunning jackal planned to devour the children. Instead of eating them at a time, he thought to kill each child separately and secretly after intervals. In this way, six children were consumed. As usual the

crocodile used to halt in the water for an inquiry and the jackal used to deceive by exhibiting the child seven times. The crocodile used to ask : Where are my children? We want to see them. The jackal used to reply : They are busy, reading & writing. But after sometime the crocodile’s wife became very worried. She became suspicious. She sensed some accident. She insisted on physical verification. Being repeatedly requested, the crocodile agreed. And one night, the husband & the wife surreptitiously came ashore and saw the bones of the children. They became very angry and attacked the jackal and rescued the only child. The jackal escaped unhurt. The jackal, after sometime went out for hunting. This time also the dogs vigorously drove away the cunning jackal. The jackal ran away in fear and plunged into the deep water of the river. The crocodile was waiting for this moment. Immediately the traitor was killed. 36. An elepnant & a jackal & a merchant An elephant lived in a deep forest. The elephant’s body was big, and two trunks long. The forest was full of bushes, vegetables, banana plants and many other trees. One day the elephant consumed those vegetables & banana plants voraciously. The elephant could not go back to its den. The elephant lay asleep on the spot. The elephant lay on a wild spot; many leaves lay thick upon the spot. Decomposed leaves in a humid soil provided ideal shelter to insects and snakes. Below the > layer of the leaves a poisonous snake had its shelter in a hole. The huge body of the elephant had its heavy weight on the leaves. The pressure from above almost closed

the outlet of the hole. At night the snake had to come out for food. Being failed to come out, the angry snake Folk Tales of Tripura 371 came to bite the elephant. The elephant died. The snake too died because of suffocation and want of food for days together. After a few days, a jackal came to see the carcass of the elephant. The jackal became tempted to eat the liver of the elephant. The thick skin of the elephant became very dry. So, the jackal had to break ground through the anus. The jackal started relishing the hindmost meat. It took a few days to reach the heart. By that time the anus became dry & closed. Being suffocated, the jackal, too, died inside the carcass. Days passed. The air became redolent with the fowl smell. One day a woodcutter entered the forest and saw the carcass. The woodcutter used to sell fire-wood in a weekly market. A merchant was a regular customer of the woodcutter. So, there was intimacy between the two. Naturally, the woodcutter talked about the carcass of the elephant. This communication excited the interest of the merchant. He became inquisitive to see the elephant. They decided to go together the next morning. It was the woodcutter’s routine to eat the previous night’s stale rice at about 8 a.m. and then to set out. But the merchant, who must have been of a somewhat restless disposition, grew weary of the costly trunks of the elephant. Set out alone at dawn, the energetic merchant, close on forty, had little trouble to find out the carcass. He smelled the strong odour and searched out. He easily guessed the

price of the trunks. The temptation of earning a good profit, inflamed his energy. To get the trunks, he pulled, shook, pushed, hauled, raised upward & downward, but failed. As a last attempt, he twitched one trunk with all his energy. The trunk came out; but it thrust into the belly of the merchant. Fatally wounded, the merchant too died on the spot. After a few hours, the woodcutter reached the spot and found the greedy merchant dead. Folk Tales of Tripura 372 37. Three donkeys There was a peasant at a certain village. The peasant had his wife and children and domestic animals & birds. Among the domestic animals, there was a donkey. The donkey had been serving the peasant for many years. The donkey carried loads of paddy, rice, firewood, laundry packages, etc. Now, the donkey was old, weak and worn out, unable to carry loads. In the eyes of the peasant, the donkey was useless. Having thus reasoned, the peasant and his son set out from home to sell the donkey in a weekly market. On the way, the father and the son were engaged in conversation. They recollected the memory of the services rendered by the donkey, the memory of riding on the donkey and the like; they became remorseful. They said unto themselves : To-day is the last chance of riding. The son said : Father! you are old enough, you ride first. So, the father rode on the donkey. As they had been going along the path through the paddy fields, they came across a group of boys. The boys passed a comment : The shameless father is as dull as the donkey; he himself is riding and while the little boy

is walking. Hearing the comment, the father got down and directed the son to ride. When they had gone a little way further, they came across a group of old men. They too passed a remark : See, see! the boy is an idiot; he is enjoying riding & while the old man is walking all the way and panting. Hearing the remark, the son got down; now the father and the son and the donkey were heading towards the market. On the way, they met a group of village ladies. They know the peasant. So, they had a frank and free conversation. The ladies suggested : For the whole life you have taken service from the docile and poor donkey. Now when the innocent and helpless animal has been sickly, you are going to sell the old beast! Did you sell Folk Tales of Tripura 373 your parents when they had been feeble? You do one thing : You carry the donkey on your shoulders. Being thus convinced, the father and the son lifted the old animal on their shoulders and proceeded towards the market. On the way they had to cross a river. The villagers had built a narrow bridge of bamboo & wood across the river. Below the bridge a group of fishermen were busy in fishing. They saw the father and the son carrying the donkey and passing through the bridge. They made a damaging remark : See, see! three donkeys! two donkeys are carrying one donkey! Now, hearing the remark of the fishermen, the donkey became angry. The agitated animal tossed and whisked. The burden of the beast had already impeded them; now the sudden jerking made them very shaky;

they lost the balance. They fell down below and died. 38. The monkey equalises the banana A peasant had a garden of fruit-trees. He used to spend all his days in the orchard, sowing & planting, plucking & pruning, nursing a watering, fencing & guarding. His wife or son used to carry the midday meal to the garden. One day he took his meal in the shade of a tree, and leaning back against the trunk of the tree, he took rest for a while. He fell asleep. In the garden a bunch of bananas became ripe. The peasant had a mind to cut down the bunch within a few days. The jungle birds were also watching the fruits. That day while the peasant had been asleep, two crows helped each other to steal one ripe banana; they hurried away and flew out, and perched on the branch of a tree in the hills. The crows had their nest made of leaves & grasses high in a tree-twig. Reaching the safe place, they were about to relish the banana. Having decided to share the banana equally, one cunning crow cut the banana into two pieces. But the two pieces seemed to be a little unequal. The other crow had expected an exactly uniform Folk Tales of Tripura 374 division; and so expressed anguish. Thus, the two birds started quarrelling. Their cawing became louder & louder. A monkey had a residence there in the vicinity. The monkey was friendly with the birds. Hearing the noise, the monkey came round the corner of the nest of the crows. The monkey asked : What is the matter? Why are you quarrelling so loudly?

Both the crows began replying at once and accused each other. One crow said : I took the great risk of stealing the banana; so I deserve a larger share. Another crow said: I kept my vigilant eyes on the peasant from close corner to give signal for stealing; so I had a greater risk of life. So, I deserve a large share. Unable to decide, the crows asked the monkey to decide. The cunning monkey looked at the ripe banana and posed as an honest judge, and made up his mind to tactfully consume the fruit piece by piece. The monkey assured to make uniform division. The monkey said : The two pieces seem to be unequal. If I were to bite outa bit at this piece, the two pieces will be equal. The two crows agreed to the proposal. So the monkey purposely took the larger piece and reduced the larger piece into a smaller one. The two pieces again looked unequal. The two birds resented. So, the monkey took the larger piece into his paws and reduced it into a smaller one. The two pieces again looked unequal. . The contenders contradicted. The contradiction gave another chance. The monkey said : Let us try again. Once more, the monkey set his teeth in the big piece and reduced the big piece into a smaller one. The shrewd monkey paused for a few moments and made a plot of showering some words of compliments. While speaking out those words of compliments in favour of the crows, the monkey took care to hold on the pieces of banana. Next, the monkey swallowed one whole piece, and said: What is the use of the other piece? You will be

Folk Tales of Tripura 375 quarrelling for this tiny remnant! I do not want you to suffer from misunderstanding; so, | may be permitted to eat the remnant. With these words, the monkey swallowed the remnant. The monkey said : I have tried to help you : Thank you. Good afternoon! The monkey jumped away gently. 39. A polyglot landlord’s wife ‘In a certain village lived a landlord. He was judicious and pious. Relatives, friends and saints used to receive hospitality in his house. Once one saint gave him a boon of knowing the dialect of animals and birds. But the saint cautioned : You must not disclose the meaning of the dialect; disclosure will be fatal. The landlord’s wife was very beautiful. The landlord used to submit to her demands & desires. The villagers made gossip about the behaviour of the couple. One day while the couple sat together for idle talk, a few dogs quarrelled among themselves in the courtyard. The landlord understood the cause of the quarrel and laughed a little. The lady became curious to know the cause of the laugh. The landlord set it aside as nothing. But the lady insisted on it again and again. At last, the landlord told the story of the boon and reiterated the condition. Hearing the story, she became more inquisitive and more adamant. Day after day she went on persisting. The landlord said : The result will be tragic. Do you want me to die? Do you like to be widow? The imprudent lady still went on persisting. The landlord said : Well, invite your relatives, my relatives, our friends and advisors. In presence of all, I shall disclose.

It took a few months on the part of the landlord to settle his assets and liabilities, to make arrangements for succession. At last, an astrologer was invited to fix an auspicious date. The manager of the estate was asked to make arrangement for a feast on that date. The news became well-known. The aged people Folk Tales of Tripura 376 — started visiting the house and advising the lady. Their advice, appeal, persuasion and warning became futile. She paid no attention to the moan of her husband. In the courtyard there were a dog and a cock. The dog became every mournful. Indeed, the dog started weeping and took no food. The cock asked : Friend! what happened? The dog narrated the whole story. The cock replied : Your master is henpecked; such persons deserve this. Being a human being, being a learned man, he does not know how to solve this problem! The dog said : Then, what to do? The cock said : I have got seven wives. | beat them daily. So they remain obedient. The landlord was listening to the conversation of the dog and the cock. It brought him to his senses and showed the way out. Having given her a good beating he retired. Fired with anger she fled & sought refuge in her father’s house. After an absence of a few days, her parents brought her back. She became repentant and the parents became ashamed, The matter ended happily. 40. The owl-king’s Judgement In a certain part of-eastern India, there was a kingdom. The kingdom had a peaceful life. The territory consisted of hills, gorges, rivers, valleys and tropical forest. There were numerous wild animals and birds.

The hum of insects and the murmuring of trees were parts of the life. The women had to move up & down the hill to fetch water from the purling brooks about one hundred feet below. In that kingdom lived a king. The king had a very young, beautiful queen. The palace compound was spacious dotted with gardens, large ponds & orchard. One day, very early in the morning, while a crimson linge was glowing in the east, the queen was strolling up and down the garden. One owl, perching on a branch of a bowery tree, was observing the queen. They saw each other. The owl habitually hooted and left sportingly. Folk Tales of Tripura 377 The queen took it to be a contempt, a teasing, a derision. The sad-hearted queen retired in a grieving room of the palace. Absence of the queen during the time of breakfast made the king impatient. The king’s dotage for the young queen was well-known. She was not found in her chamber and bower. The waitresses were anxiously active to find out the queen. At last she was found sad- faced sitting alone inside the grieving room. She did not yield to the appeals of the waitresses. The king was thunderstruck to know the cause of the queen’s sadness. However, the king personally came to pacify the queen with an assurance to punish the naughty owl. The queen came out and ate together. It was a temporary relief to the king. But the king must keep his word. Something must be done. The king and his ministers discussed the issue and decided to summon the owl-king. Accordingly a messenger was duly sent to the owl-king. The messenger

intelligently invited the owl-king. But the experienced owl-king guessed something ominous and politely asked the messenger. The messenger disclosed the matter. The owl-king had a countless retinue of owls. The owl-king summoned the owls and told them about the call to appear in the royal court. The call caused much commotion and anxiety among the owls. They were terrified. The owl-king tried to bring out a frank & free confession from each owl. Every owl knew the sagacity of the owl-king. So without concealing the fact, that particular owl admitted the fact of hooting before the queen out of childish habit. Then the owl-king directed them to assemble in the evening for appearing in the royal court in a flock. The owl-king advised them to pretend to feel uneasy because of drowsiness and dizziness. The owls can see at night. So, the whole flock of owls set out in the evening and reached the capital. They repeatedly uttered : Victory to the Maharaj! victory to the Folk Tales of Tripura 378 Maharaj! Their chorus rented the air of the capital and the palace. The king and the ministers came together to the door to welcome the owl-king gladly, and the royal waiters offered fruits to the guests. An exchange of good wishes followed. Meanwhile the owls started the drama, pretending to feel uneasy because of drowsiness, dizziness. The owl-king diplomatically scolded them. The host king became curious and insisted on knowing the cause of their ill-health. The owl-king replied : My lord! what is the use of knowing the news? kindly tell me the cause of the call! The host king went on insisting to know the news from the guest.

Then the owl-king said : My worthy lord! last night we had a queer topic of discussion. We discussed late into the night. The owls were not unanimous in their “opinion. One group argued that the males were in majority, while another group argued that the females were in majority. They bantered at each and-scuffled. Then they came to me for judgment. After hearing the arguments & the counter-arguments, I came to the couclusion that the females were in majority. I reasoned that those males showing exclusive fondness to females and also those henpecked husbands were females by instinct & temperament. So, to the number of females must be added the number of females by temperament. Taken together, the females would outnumber the males. The owl-king then concluded : My lord! we are poor birds! what is the use of knowing our trifling talks. Be kind enough to give your direction, order or message. The king was intelligent enough to understand the meaning of the punnage hidden inside the concocted judgment. So, the king did not disclose the actual intention of the summon, and rather showed due courtesy to bid them farewell. The king retired and explained the whole episode and tried his best to pacify the rash queen. She could Folk Tales of Tripura 379 not sense his gentle gaze. The fool-hardy queen insisted on punishment of the owl. So demanding, the incautious queen again receded to the grieving room. So the king again sent his messenger to the owl king. The witty owl- king had cordially welcomed the messenger and thus came to know the repercussion of the queen. The owl-king again summoned his entire retinue and narrated the royal reaction. The owls were now afraid of

royal vengeance. But their king remained steadfast and directed them to pretend drowsiness in the royal court. Accordingly, the owl-king, accompained by his retinue, attended the royal court in the following evening and repeatedly shouted the glory of the king. The two kings exchanged their good wishes and enquired about their health. Meanwhile the owls pretended to be very drowsy. The king asked : What happened to you all? Did you not sleep last night also? The owl-king replied : My lord! last night another doubt perplexed the owls. The king became inquisitive to know the puzzle. Then the owl-king explained that the owls were again divided in their opinion as to the number of mouth and the number of anus. Apparently, every normal human being has one mouth and one anus. So, the number of mouth and the number of anus are equal. Naturally according to one group the numbers are equal; however, according to another group the number of mouth is less, while the number of anus is more. How? Those, who are cheat, deceiver, deceptive, liar, untruthful, unreliable, undependable, have all the normal physical organs. But socially their words carry no value; they are changer of words; they lack integrity of character. Therefore, their mouth is equivalent to anus. My Lord! after due consideration, I am convinced that the number of anus is more than the number of mouth. Physically, the numbers of the two organs are exactly equal, but socially anus out numbers the mouth. Folk Tales of Tripura 380 The king understood the implication of the story and bade them farewell. The queen was observing the scene from a distance sitting behind the screen. The moment the king had

entered there, she became furious. She threatened to commit arson, to commit suicide, etc. The king tried to pacify her with love & affection, with wit & wisdom. But in vain. She grumbled and hustled into the grieving room. The domestic tension was mounting higher and higher. The waitresses, servants, females, and even ministers were busy to pacify the queen. But alas! all failed. Endowed with beauty and youth but deficient in wit & wisdom, the queen became adamant. Soon it became a common topic of discussion, fun and laughter. Some rational subjects found that the idiocy of the queen and the dotage of the king had begun to play havoc in the administration. Meanwhile the king overheard a conversation between a cock and a hen. The cock said : Oh hen! have you heard the sad news of our royal family? The henpecked king has been daily suffering & yielding to the undue demand of the foolish queen. Had you been adamant on such a childish issue, I would have you a thorough beating ! Fools understand the language of stick. Hearing the conversation, the king came to his senses. He pardoned her crime again & again. Now, no more toleration. With a stick in hand, the king forced his way inside the grieving room and began to strike her repeatedly. Now she sensed the look of disgust on his face. While she was about to slam and beat her forehead and cry, the servants and the waitresses were eagerly waiting outside and chuckling & squinting. Soon, the wretched creature fell at the feet of the king, and the anger vanished. Folk Tales of Tripura 381 41. A terrible python & a tough woodcutter

In Tripura long ago there was a small village at the foot of a mountain, near a deep forest. All the villagers were peasants. Agriculture, animal husbandry, basketry, fishing, gathering, horticulture, etc. were their means of livelihood. Among the villagers there was a brave & healthy woodcutter. One day he went into the forest with his sharp, curved, long knife (= dao) in his hand to hew wood. As he was wandering about in search of dry bamboo & wood, he suddenly felt a gush of wind. The flurry was pulling him towards a deep & dark place. He flounced. On seeing the woodcutter, a large & long python wanted to make a good meal by swallowing the human body. The python started inhaling wind very forcefully only to swallow the man. The woodcutter was helplessly rushing to the terrible mouth of the snake. A monster indeed! It was a lonely place. The woodcutter was alone. Horribly frightened, he shrieked at the top of his voice. Because of a considerable distance, his tragic voice was not heard. The sound of his voice echoed from the hills. Had it been heard, the villagers would instantly come running one after another along the mountain paths with their knives & sticks to rescue him. At that critical moment the episode of Srikrishna smashing a dangerous snake (= Kaliya daman) came to his mind. Instantly and steadily he defended himself with his dao. He held the sharp blade of the knife towards the mouth of the monster. As he had to rush toward the snake’s mouth, the sharp edge of the knife went on cutting the mouth of the snake. The snake reacted violently, and tried to coil, twist

and entangle the man. Fortunately, there was a tree. The infuriated snake coiled the tree. A terrible struggle followed. In the struggle, the snake fell dead and missed the dinner. The brave woodcutter came out alive and a little hurt. He was throbbing and sobbing. Folk Tales of Tripura 382 42. The king’s judgment In a certain holm lived a heron and his wife who had built their nest on the branches of a bush. These diurnal birds, adapted to a life in the water, remain alone and active throughout most of the daylight hours, and silently stand on long legs in the water and observe the movement of small fishes only to jab its bill into a fish. So long as they remain outside, they wade alone to catch fish and lead a very peaceful life. The moment they come back home for nesting & resting, they start to banter each other. The husband is henpecked; the wife is shrew. Their nocturnal screaming is a great nuisance to the neighbours. Disgusted with their quarrel, one neighbour had come forward and protested openly. But the litigants approached the protester to pronounce a judgment on the matter of their quarrel. The litigants accused each other for cheating, double dealing and deception. The protester failed to pronounce a judgment; he suggested {to make an appeal to the royal court. Next day the herons went to the royal court and approached the king. The king, sitting with his councillors and counsellors, allowed the male heron to vindicate. The male heron said : Maharaj! | have come to a realisation that the women are traitors and deceitful. So | demand divorce. In support of my conviction, let me

narrate an episode, a tragedy : In a certain country dwelt a merchant of immense wealth. His wife was beautiful and youthful. The merchant had to go out on voyage annually with his merchandise. Before leaving, he would make all possible provisions for the aged parents, wife & children. On the eve of his departure, he used to say : If by accident, during my absence, my wife dies, please do not cremate, preserve the deadbody till my return. The merchant had knowledge of navigation. He faced stern realities in the voyage from Bharat to Sumatra & Folk Tales of Tripura 383 Java & Borneo, etc. and back. He travelled through those countries, selling the Indian goods and purchasing their goods. He & his crew had to suffer from disease. Once in such a voyage, at length, after several months, he was returning to Bharat, broken in health. Only one day’s journey was left for reaching home. The merchant and his crew were eager to come back. They became home- sick. Meanwhile, the merchant’s wife fell ill and died. On reaching, the merchant saw the deadbody. He became half-mad, erratic, indifferent, unsettled, uncertain and vagrant. Taking the corpse on his shoulders, the merchant started wandering without rest & food. Thus, he entered deep into a forest and saw atop a hill a flame of a light. He went ahead, climbed the hill, saw from a little distance a cottage; and on reaching there he found a Brahman family. One Brahman & his wife and a son had been living in peace. At the moment of the arrival of the merchant, the Brahman was outside in search of fruits, roots & vegetables, etc. His wife allowed the

merchant to take rest there and offered drinking water. At the time of cooking, the Brahman’s wife dragged the child into the fire. It shocked the merchant; he became astonished & suspicious. After about an hour, the Brahman returned. He was glad to see the guest. The merchant saluted and narrated his whereabouts. Now, the time came for a meal. The merchant was hungry, sad faced and curious. The mother’s treatment to the son was so shocking to the merchant that he could not take food. Being insisted by the Brahman, the merchant expressed the cause of his sadness. Hearing the cause, the Brahman laughed. At this, the merchant became more suspicious. He became afraid and apprehended witchcraft & sorcery. More surprising was the discovery that the father had not been at all perturbed to see the deadbody of his son. The Brahman sensed the look of suspicion on the face of the Folk Tales of Tripura 384 guest. The Brahman brought the son to life with the Sanjtbani mantra. Being astonished, the merchant then & there fell at the feet of the Brahman and made an earnest appeal to animate his dead wife. The kindhearted Brahman brought her to life. It was a miracle! Bright with the light of a great happiness at his wife’s animation, the merchant became extremely grateful to the animator. The animator took nothing in return. They took food together. Next morning the merchant & his wife resumed the travel homeward. It was a long & tedious journey. Though happy, the husband became tired & weary. He took rest in the shade of a big banyan tree; he fell asleep. A river and a path ran in parallel there, and another young

merchant was returning home along the river; he saw the youthful lady sitting in the shade of the banyan tree; she sensed his amorous gaze. The second merchant cajoled her. She made favourable response. They eloped. She left behind the husband who had been struggling against serious difficulties for her life. The first merchant had a faithful dog with him. The faithful dog followed the movements of the paramours and identified the house of the second merchant. The dog returned and led the first merchant to the house of the second merchant. The second merchant had a barren wife; she became jealous at the arrival of another woman. The two women went to the river. Meanwhile, the first merchant reached there; he made a kink to draw the attention of his wife. She came and whispered : She had been kidnapped. He should pretend to be a beggar and seek shelter only to decamp together at night. The other woman was anxious to know the identity of the stranger. The clever & inconstant woman replied : lle is a beggar; he knows me; he is a resident of my father’s village; he has come to see my father-in-law’s house out of affection. Folk Tales of Tripura 385 The second merchant returned from the local market in the evening. After the supper, the new woman whispered: My first husband has come in the guise of a beggar. He is taking rest in the outhouse. He must be killed at night and thrown away. This conversation was overheard by the other woman. She: secretly informed the beggar. The beggar placed a long piece of a banana plant on the bed and covered it

with clothe so as to look like a sleeping man. He stashed himself in a dark corner below the cot with a knife. The alarming communication was of supreme importance. It was a tense moment. In the darkness of midnight, the two ruffians stealthily advanced and assassinated the supposed beggar, and hastily packed him up and proceeded to throw him into the river. Instantly, the beggar silently came out of the stash and stabbed the second merchant to death. Within a moment, the notorious woman changed her utterings and caprice. She remarked : You have done the right thing. The ruffian deserves this. Let us quickly go to our own residence. The faithful dog was with them. The hungry dog was trying to lick the blood stuck on the clothe of the woman. The dog had no other intention. While going back home, the merchant spoke highly about the service of the intelligent & faithful dog. But the notorious lady took it otherwise and determined to assassinate the dog also. She could not satisfy her lasciviousness because of the dog. So, she made a plot against the dog. She said to her henpecked husband : The dog has become mad; the dog can bite us at any moment. It is wise to kill the dog. The ~ tdiot husband killed the faithful dog then & there. The mangled or bloodstained body of the second merchant lay at the outskirts of his house. Right from the dawn, there was a hue & cry, a tension, a cry, a mourning in his house. The members of the family moved Folk Tales of Tripura 386 here & there, found the deadbody, searched the beggar

and the new woman & cursed them. A few young men rushed, and caught them red-handed, and brought in front of a crowd assembled. They chided and kicked the assassinator and handed over him to the police. The verdict of the court was his lifelong imprisonment. The lustful lady was not, however, suffering from any agony; she had no prick of conscience. In pretension, she feigned herself and thus got the sympathy of the crowd. She escaped and went back home. But when she had heard the verdict of the court, she made erratic adventure, hunting down another young man to her passion & purpose. One day the profligate woman eloped with the young man. It did not take long time to reach the ear of the husband who had been struggling in the jail shock after shock. But the foolish husband failed to free himself from the blind love and dotage. He was shocked and died in the prison. The male heron concluded with the remark : Maharaj !the women are untrustworthy & deceitful. The king next permitted the female heron to vindicate her grievances. She had it to say that the males are whimsical and unreliable. In support of her complaint, the complainant recounted a story : In a certain kingdom there was a great friendship between a king’s son and a minister’s son. One day the two friends set out for hunting. In search of wild beast, they moved in the deep wilderness, but found no animal. However, they were astonished to see a beautiful castle in the deep forest. It was a Mayapuri, a dream castle. Seven young beautiful damsels used to live there. The damsels had

capacity to befool even the wild animals & birds. In the previous life, they were human beings. They were seven sisters. They were very beautiful. One day, with their parents, they went to visit a holy place. But on the way, a group of enemy aliens saw them. The profligate enemy Folk Tales of Tripura 387 aliens killed the parents and attempted to rape the daughters. The daughters committed suicide. In the next life, they became Pari (= celestial damsels) Long ago, one day one brother and one sister were going to their maternal uncle’s house. The damsels misled them and brought to the castle. It was not the only instance. In erratic adventures, they were to hunt down young men to their passion & purpose. Here in this case the young man, ignorant of the identity of the damsels, became lascivious; so, he became languished soon. He died. Since then the sister had a lonely life in an abnormal atmosphere. Meanwhile, the king’s son and the minister’s son were captivated. The prince was very much tired; he was allowed to take rest inside the castle. The young damsels took the minister’s son to the forest for amorous sports. The minister’s son had a physique of three young men; so, the damsels were very happy with the strong & stout man. After a long time, the solitary sister got a rare opportunity to talk to a human being, to express her anguish, to disclose the mystery of the castle. The prince was astonished to hear the caprice of the illusive maidens. Out of a chivalrous spirit, he promised to rescue her. But time was very, very short. They must escape. She

warned that the fate of the minister’s son would be like that of her brother. Not only that, the prince would be the next target and victim. So, it would be wise to escape immediately. Being thus convinced, the prince took her and galloped. The celestial maidens were informed of the escape. They rushed and chased. Unable to catch the prince, they played a deceptive game instantaneously. They cried out : Prince! the girl is not a human being; she is a witch. Do not believe her. We warn you. [t that fleeting moment, the perplexed prince thought of self-preservation only. It confused the prince. He was Folk Tales of Tripura 388 in a dilemma. The girl made an earnest appeal : I beg you not to leave me. I swear I am a human being. Their word is not true. Their warning is deceptive. It is no warning at all. | implore you to be merciful and to grant my prayer. Her tears were streaming down her cheeks. But the prince fell into a terrible dilemma. The fraud misguided him. He threw and cast her down. The maidens killed her on the spot. The female heron concluded : Maharaj! thus I have come to the conclusion that the heart of males is as hard as stone; they are fickle-minded. They are power- hungry. They are despotic. Now, the king opened his mouth. The king said : You are generalising and over-simplifying. Indeed, in every caste & community, there are good people & bad people. In the males as well as in the females, there are honest & dishonest persons. It is unwise to blame & curse one entire group and praise another group wholly. Go home

& live peacefully, otherwise my jail is there. 43. A happy Princess There was a princess. She was beautiful and healthy. She grew up. The king desired to arrange her marriage. Many proposals came from different royal dynasties. But the proposals were found unsuitable. At last it was decided that a young man of merits, born of whatsoever parents, might be selected. The young man must stand a test : during the winter season in the month of Pousha (December-January) the boy must remain in deep, cold water of the royal tank; he should remain in water from dusk to dawn; drowning his body upto neck; he should keep standing. In consultation with the council of ministers, and the royal astrologer and the priest, the king fixed the auspicious day of Pousha sankanti for holding the test. It was given due publicity. Festive arrangements were made on the auspicious day. Many distinguished guests, and Folk Tales of Tripura 389 aspirants were seated in the magnificent hall. Thousands of spectators thronged at the four banks of the big royal tank in front of the palace. It was a hilarious moment of laughing, joking, excitement and adventure. Many valiant princes, and sons of ministers and rich merchants, son of police officers and commissioners had gathered there. They were entertained with rich food & drinks. The king formally announced that his daughter would be given in marriage to him, who would tolerate the severe cold in water for the whole night. The atmosphere was diffusing fragrance. The sky was clean. The folkdancers were displaying their arts. The folksingers were singing chivalrous songs. The palace was gleaming brightly. The sun was setting; when the

time was coming for the test to begin, the princess, clad in costly & dazzling robes with a bewitching charm, entered the hall. The arrival of the paragon of beauty excited the aspirants. The moment the brother of the princess gave the signal, the candidates jumped & plunged into the water. The spectators shouted in joy. Adequate arrangements were made for safety, security and health care of the examinees. The ordeal began. What made the occasion so amazing was that instead of being a courtship between the princess and a prince under the affectionate eyes of tolerant parents, it was a public test of ability. Indeed, the sensation was so great that the examinees were the focus of all eyes. The examinees were in sportsman-like- spirit, romantic & imaginative. They were animated by a warm delight. But unaccustomed as they were to such hardship and cold, they strained in vain through the shivering cold of a December night. Many noted princes withdrew one after another. At last at midnight there was none in the water. All failed, and uncomfortable in their wet clothes, they were trembling & pouting. The attendants put out their hands to help them off with their dripping dress. Folk Tales of Tripura 390 The relishable news spread like a rumour. The pomp & show, and the hollow aristocracy and worthlessness of the princes alienated everybody. Inside the palace also a conflict of opinion began; the consensus of opinion was to wait & see. There lived a poor peasant family in a distant and wild corner of the kingdom. The peasant suddenly died leaving behind his wife and a little boy. The widow had to face stress & strain to bring up the baby. No magician

waved his wand over her head to solve her problems. They had to live from hand to mouth. Thus, the poor baby grew through childhood to boyhood. Right from the childhood, he was accustomed to poverty & hardship; as a boy he became keenly interested in assisting his mother. He was never led along the paths of luxury and crime. His physical strength, his diligence, his generosity were an inspiration to the village boys. Here in the countryside, in the summer the peasantry were bathed in perspiration and in the winter they froze. They lived in mud & water, An obscure peasant boy could not hope for a mate more eligible in every way. It was daydream to him. But since it was the question of physical fitness, the boy bent a willing ear to the condition set forth by the king. The news of the failure of the princes inflamed the imagination of the peasant boy. Slowly & reluctantly the mother gave her consent. “The boy journeyed forth and reached the capital. The affectionate mother followed. The gate-keeper did not allow the boy to enter. The boy fell at his feet and the poor mother made a fervent appeal. It created a sensation. On the second day the gate-keeper unwillingly agreed to inform the ministers and the king. The court allowed his entry. The shabby boy became an object of neglect and ridicule. The royal court accepted his appeal after long persuasion. Without any pomp and publicity, the trial began in one evening. From dusk to dawn he Folk Tales of Tripura 391 stood firm in the cool water. His old mother collected some broken pieces of firewood and slowly & measurably

set fire only to warm herself. The next morning in presence of the police guards and-a few other watchers, the boy came out cheerfully and successfully. The royal court became surprised. But there were vested interests. Those, whose sons were found unfit, made difficulties. There again began the conflict of opinion. It was far below the dignity of the royal family. The boy was discouraged and insulted. No body in the court came to his help. Neither the boy nor his illiterate mother dared to approach the king and the princess. Amid a purposely created scene of horrible confusion and furniture-upset, the boy and his mother had to leave the palace quickly in abject despair. The old mother murmured shyly. The boy was seeking an opportunity of avenging the insult. He, with the mother’s permission, set out south eastward and travelled for days and reached the kingdom of the Magh Raja. The court of the Magh Raja was kind enough to offer him temporary refuge and to listen to his tragic history. The king consoled him, and assured him and directed him to go back home. After a few months the king sent his ambassador to the court of the accused king, with the message that the Magh Raja’s brilliant minister, Sukhimi, had the desire to pay a visit. The accused king agreed and sent a formal invitation. With a view to offer a fitting hospitality to the guest-minister, the host-king arranged choicest delicacies. But the guest preferred self-cooking and brought his own attendants. The guest’s attendants made tripod fireplaces at two banks of the royal tank : the two tripods were distantly apart from one another; on one fireplace rice was placed

in a big pot; it was without fire; another hearth was simply ignited, but it was without any pot of curry. The atmosphere was lively and sportive. The matter was soon reported to the host. The host asked the guest : How the Folk Tales of Tripura 392 rice and curry will be boiled in two such distinct and different fire places? How fire would give its effect from such a long distance? Now, the guest brought with him his sharp sense of humour and wit & wisdom. He replied : If cooking is impossible under such arrangement, then how the widow’s meagre fire on the bank had kept the boy warm in deep, cool water? The witty reply produced a laughter, and the host came to his senses. The host frankly and freely narrated the episodes. When the guest assured to arrange the marriage with the peasant boy, the guest winked to stop the mockery of cooking and gave his consent to take food from the host’s kitchen itself. All sorts of delicacies were served. They were to eat & eat. Thus, the embassy ended in a comedy. Within a few months, the king kept his word and splendidly arranged the marriage of the princess with the peasant boy. Thus the boy achieved his heart’s desire. Fortune smiled on the mother and the son. At the order of the king, a beautiful garden house was rapidly built in the native village of the boy. In the village, the princess was the loveliest woman. She would seldom go out; but when she had to go out she would move regally, surrounded by a crowd of satelites. She became the focus

of all eyes. Her tender eyes, mild temperament, good health, rustling of her dress, and a pleasant fragrance would make a romantic atmosphere. 44. An unfortunate Princess There was a princess. She was beautiful and meritorious. The king and the queen were affectionate and proud of her. She grew up from childhood to girlhood. The prosperous life went on peacefully. But now the royal family had the responsibility of arranging the marriage of the princess. It was difficult to find out a suitable match for such a charming and pretty princess. A wide publicity was Folk Tales of Tripura 393 given to the neighbouring kingdoms. The chivalrous instincts of many princes were profoundly aroused. Many kings duly sent proposals of marriage with their sons. A good number of princes personally visited the court, but failed to convince the king. The king then made an alternative arrangement. In every market, drumbeating was made to announce the wish of the king. The scope was kept wide open to all, subject to the condition that an extraodinarily wonderful thing must be furnished by the would-be bridegroom. Birth & station of life were not the considerations. The announcement awakened four friends from their hesitation. They decided to make an adventure. They came from rich families. Not money, but something else must be furnished. However, with a reasonable amount of money for their own expenses, the four friends left home. They travelled & travelled on foot. Being very tired, they sat in the shade of a big banyan tree. There was a temple and a small rest-house near the tree. The atmosphere of the place was serene. They temporarily made it their common place of haltage. Every day in the

morning they used to go out in search of any wonderful thing and in the evening they met together. One day the first friend travelled a long distance and reached a market. There he found an inquisitive assemblage and a merchant. The merchant brought a unique mirror. With the mirror one would see any contemporary incident. The first friend purchased the mirror. The second friend moved to another direction and reached a market. There he found a merchant to sell a magic seat with which one could travel a long distance very quickly. The second friend purchased it. The third friend, in course of his wandering, met a salesman to sell a unique adhesive, with which one could repair and rejoin any broken object or instrument. He purchased it. Folk Tales of Tripura 394 EES The fourth friend was also lucky to get an extra ordinary object with which one could reanimate even a dead person. He purchased it. The four friends, true to their words, came back with great hope. They took rest and talked to each other about their collection. They were very hopeful. The next day in the early morning they tried to test their things. The first friend held out the mirror and concentrated his attention on the palace. To his astonishment, he saw the deadbody of the princess reflected in the mirror. It was a pathetic scene. He at once showed it to his friends. Something must be done before cremation. They rode on the magic seat of the second friend; but because of the heavy weight of the four passengers, the seat broke down. But the third friend was ready with his adhesive to
