immediately repair the seat. Thus, they hurried to reach the palace. The palace was a long way away. It was a bolt from the blue. It came suddenly & unexpectedly. It upset the whole plan. Several physicians were called in, But in vain. The princess died in great agony, The king, the queen, the ministers, the relatives and even the servants were weeping. It was a pathetic scene, There was a great crowd and the police forces were deployed to maintain law & order. The funeral did not take place, but preparations were going on. In the meantime the four friends reached. They, too, were deeply moved. They were eager to make known their noble mission. They wanted to see the princess at least once! An angry police said : Get out. They replied : We can bring her back to life. The police retorted : You are speaking nonsense! They appealed : Please! give us a chance. The police reluctantly said : Wait. Their appeal, through proper channel, quickly reached the proper ear. The bereaved family immediately gave permission. The four friends solemnly sat together beside the deadbody. The fourth friend then applied his Sanjibani Sudha, and slowly and slowly the princess opened her eyes and smiled. Folk Tales of Tripura 395 The situation got changed abruptly. The tragedy turned into a comedy. The palace again became rosy and jubilant. The four friends did the job magnificently and magically. All became very, very pleased with the four friends. They were honourably given hospitality in the royal guest-house for a few days. When thus things came down to normalcy, the royal court enquired about their whereabouts. They, too, frankly admitted the intention of their adventure. Now the king

was caught in a dilemma. The four friends have contributed to save the royal family. But how could one princess be married to four friends? After much deliberations, the court decided that the four friends were lifesavers, and as lifesavers they were to be treated as second fathers. The king profusely rewarded them. The four friends rose from obscure origins to wealth and fame. The royal patrons treated them with utmost magnificence. They became the idols of the moment. In the farewell dinner, they were invited to sit by the side of the king. The queen and the princess served. Their eyes met. The princess gave them a friendly smile. A charming adventure turned into a relation of delicate complexity! 45. Tragedy of a dove bird In a certain village lived a farmer with his wife and daughter. One day the wife fell ill and died. The _daughter’s age was about five years at that time: the friends and relatives arranged for the remarriage of the farmer. During the solemnisation of this marriage, one Kanya-yatri whispered to one Var-Yatri: ‘Having planted on vish-kachu here to-day, we are leaving.’ In course of time, the second wife also became mother of a few children. The farmer was very busy in the outdoor activities. The step-mother looked after the indoor activities. She brought up the daughter by the first wife. The first daughter was diligent and dutiful, compassionate & Folk Tales of Tripura 396 healthy. But the step-mother detested her from the core of her heart. The step-brothers and the step-sisters were jealous. The step-mother had great liking for her own sons and daughters. She used to offer them good meal, and decent clothes, but no work; so they used to get

time for playing and singing. They lived in pleasure & pomp. They felt themselves superior to their step-sister. To the step-daughter, she posed to be sweet-tongued, and equally affectionate. Her talks about the step- daughter had often a subtle edge of taunt. She used even tricks to defame her. Few could catch the irony behind those words! The first daughter would not get good meal, decent clothes and time for games and rest. She had to eat cold, stale rice of the previous night. Her forlorn condition was made still worse by the neglect of her father. So, she had to live in stern severity. The contrivance of the step-mother steeled the heart of the farmer against the first daughter. The daughter had to perform all domestic chores, She would be held responsible for any mistake or misdeed, She had to suffer for the mistake of others. She used to shed a few tears in private. The step-mother was cunning enough not to beat the step-daughter personally. She was a fraud to instigate others against her; she was seizing every chance to poison the mind of others. She looked at her only to find fault with her. Leaving the responsibility of household work to the girl, she drifted into a life of chewing betel leaf and gossiping with the shady womenfolk. So, even the farmer often used to beat the daughter. The step-mother thus created: a very bad impression about the daughter. Thus, a slow quarrel had gone on for years. That was the beginning of a tragic end. In case of any fault by her own children, the step-mother could invent hundred excuses to protect them. She had courtly manners to win the favour of

others; her defects & deficiencies, cunningly disguised, were as great as her gifts. The neighbours used to say : Folk Tales of Tripura 397 ‘She is a good mother; she treats her step-daughter kindly’. But the step-daughter knew it was not so. To suppose an enemy to be a friend is disastrous. One day, the step-mother directed the daughter to husk a good quantity of black sesame. The daughter, after finishing the daily chores, did her best to remove the black shell of the grains. It was her best performance. But the step-mother was there to find fault. While husking and winnowing, a little quantity of useless sesame had to be thrown out. The cruel step-mother said : Why you have thrown away sesame? The daughter said : Mother! all those are useless. I have carefully husked and winnowed. I have not wasted even a single good grain. The step-mother, not satisfied with the reply, became very angry and wild. The daughter apprehended a severe beating in the evening. All angry eyes fell on her. The step-brothers and the step-sisters were about to thrash her. For gloomily looking at them, the step-mother reproached the orphan girl and mollycoddled her own children. For the first time her soul revolted; the pent-up anguish made an outburst. Oft-repeated bitter experience alienated her. The wretched daughter fervently made an earnest appeal to god. Never before did she make such an appeal. This time the response came from some doves. The doves plucked plumage from their own body, & dropped before her. She stuck them into her body and flew into the sky and started living with the doves. A great relief from the horrible pain; it did not affect the

father even! After the real mother’s death, some fathers marry again and behave like uncle. The capricious, domineering and unreflective step-mother and her children looked on! Because of that persecution, the doves even today groan and repeat : Step-mother! bran, bran! (@ae 4M! I W!). The doves wag their heads upward and downward and Folk Tales of Tripura 398 try to convince the step-mother. The doves perch, and repeatedly groan and plead their innocence. Even the father never attempted to relieve her mind. She found herself alone in the family, without the joys of the family hearth. She was mentally & physically tormented. Suddenly a ray of love & affection shone forh, bringing hight & warmth into the innermost recesses. An orphan’s or a dependent’s services or sacrifices are often neglected or ridiculed, and his/her weak points are usually pointed out and laughed at. Some people have a queer mentality; they cannot live without a dose of jealousy. In her next life, the step-mother became a stinging plant. (=Bichhuti). On summing up this story, the step-mother’s attitude of hatred against the step- daughter would diffuse itself in gesture, in posture, in manner, in demeanour; it was too subtle to be usually observed by others, but at the same time, plain & palpable to the step-daughter! With a vanity of being the mother of a few children, the step-mother used to step, as if, as lightly as she hardly trod the earth. The miasma of such vices has been sickening the society. 46. Bhombaldas Long ago there were two physically handicapped persons; they were residents of a village in the Meghna Valley. One person was blind of one eye; and another

person was humpbacked. By the usual corruption of words & names in Bengal, the blind man was called Kana, and humpbacked person was called Kubja or kuja; Kana & Kuja were great friends. Because of their physical deformity, they could not work effectively & efficiently. They became poor. They found no.job in their locality. The rich peasants & landlords were reluctant to engage them in any work. Not only: that, the youths would hoot, the ladies would chuckle, and the elderly persons would avoid them. Life became unbearable to them. One day Kana & Kuja sat in the shade of a big banyan Folk Tales of Tripura 399 tree to brood about their luck & life. After a lot of repentance and emotional outburst, they decided to leave their native village. They had no wife, no son, no daughter and none to support and sympathise. So, on an auspicious day in the morning they left their native village. It was December. Kana & Kuja were rambling without any destination. With a stick in his hand, Kuja was walking limpingly; he had to slouch. Kana was physically thin, but mentally alert. Kuja was physically strong, but mentally blunt. They travelled & travelled for two days and three nights. They were walking along the narrow & low baulk & path through the rice fields. There were tall trees with branches against the sky. There was the hum of insects, and chirping of birds, and clanking of bells in the neck of cattle. Disgusted with hfe & luck, Kana & Kuja were indifferent to the natural beauty. They slept on a haystack, after taking food offered by an unknown peasant family. On the way, on the last day they found a tortoise.

Kuja asked : There is a big tortoise; what shall | do? Kana said : Take it in your hump. After moving a distance, they found a plough, a leveller & a rope. Kuja asked : What shall I do with these instruments? Kana said: Take the instruments in your hump. Hungry & thirsty, they hobbled slowly along the tracks, and in the evening reached a deserted hamlet. There they found a nice but lonely homestead. There was shivering cold. They entered the house and slept inside. The night passed. But about an hour before dawn, Kana heard a queer sound. Being wakeful, Kana awakened Kuja. The outsiders were ghosts. The homestead belonged to the ghosts. They got the smell of human body from the courtyard. They angrily asked : Who are you inside? Kana replied boastfully : I am lion’s maternal uncle. The ghosts asked : What is your name? Kana replied : Bhombaldas. The ghosts asked : What have you done? Folk Tales of Tripura 400 Kana replied : I have killed one hundred & fifty tigers. The ghosts asked : What is the proof? We like to see a louse of your head. Kana thrust the tortoise at them across the courtyard. Being afraid, the ghosts ran away and vanished. In the morning they saw the beautiful garden house, pond, paddy fields and flowers. It was alluring and at the same time mysterious. Who were the outsiders? The two friends collected fruits and ate and bathed in the pond. They decided to stay there and observe the situation. But the next night they had the same suspicious experience. The ghosts came back. The ghosts asked : Who are you inside?

Kana confidently replied : I am lion’s maternal uncle, Bhombaldas. I have killed 150 tigers. The ghosts asked : We like to see your hair. Kana thrust the rope at them across the courtyard. Terribly afraid, the ghosts fled quickly. The two friends had enough of rest, but indirectly encountered the mysterious outsiders again. The ghosts asked : Who are you inside? Kana replied daringly : | am _ lion’s maternal uncle, Bhombaldas, | have hunted as many as 150 tigers. The ghosts asked : We like to see your comb. Kana thrust the leveller at them across the courtyard. Terribly afraid, the ghosts had to pop off the place immediately. » The two friends met the challenge for three nights. Now they had nothing to meet the next challenge. They were worried, Fortunately, that day one Sadhu accompanied by a few pilgrims came there and halted there for rest, wash and food. The two friends felt relieved and narrated the queer experience. The Sadhu sat calmly and meditated for a while. In meditation it revealed to him that it was the house of a rich peasant; the peasant had his wife & children; they, all on a sudden, died of cholera, There was none to perform funeral rites. Being earnestly requested by the two friends, the Folk Tales of Tripura 401 Sadhu stayed there for a few days and started Harinam Samkirtan & performed funeral rites. Surprisingly, the ghosts did not come from that very night. Being directed by the Sadhu, the pilgrims went to Gaya dham and offered Pindadan for the salvation of those souls. Henceforth, Kana & Kuja stayed in the big garden house, and fervently appealed to the Sadhu to stay with

them and to make the house an asram. The saint agreed. The sevasram became the halting pla‘. for the pilgrims. 47. Perils in a deserted village There was an ancient village in the Meghna Valley of the western part of Tripura. It was a deserted village. In 1854 the British administration demarcated the boundary between the Meghna Valley and the kingdom of hill Tripura. The boundary line was demarcated to fix the responsibility of the king of Tripura and the British administration against the récurrent crimes of raids from the side of some hills ‘people. That very ancient village was located near the line of demarcation; it fell within the Meghna Valley region. The village had a queer atmosphere with broken shrines, & tombs and very tall trees & bushes and marshes. Strange tales were told of the remote village. The village was thinly populated. Cultivators were settling on the lands which the British administration had made partly secure. One peasant family settled in that deserted village. The peasant had cleared the jungles, built a hut and cultivated the nearby lands. There was no other family in the immediate neighbourhood. There was a narrow jungle track between the eastern hills and the western valley. The valley had a number of weekly markets scattered here & there. The hills people would travel for many miles across the precipitous jungle country for sale & purchase in the weekly market. With tired body and begrimed feet, they would halt in the hut of the peasant, for a wash, rest and food (= mocha bhat= maidul). The peasant had his wife and only one son. One day Folk Tales of Tripura 402 the peasant fell ill. There was no physician in the vicinity.

The peasant’s sister was married; she was living at a distant village. The sister’s son was a youth. But the peasant’s son was merely a child. The peasant’s wife was keeping watch over the dying husband; she was frightened at the thought of the impending crisis. It was the weekly market-day; the peasant breathed his last. The worried wife requested the hills people to inform the sister’s son. The hills people knew him and he was usually expected to come to the market. But unfortunately that day the sister’s son did not come. The hills people were requested to say like this : Bhagina! you must go to your maternal uncle’s house at once. The hills people sincerely and sympathetically searched but did not find him. They reported it accordingly while going back home. The widow was in serious anxiety. The peasant was dead, and he had died within the hut. The hour of midnight drew near. Crushed by distress & disappointment, the heart-broken widow shut herself up and became almost a recluse temporarily. The hut was in complete darkness. An uneasiness assailed her. Sleep did not come to her eyes. Meanwhile, she heard a voice. Roused by the sound, she sat up. The outsider in a nasal tone said : Mami! Mami! I have got the sad news; so, I have come here. Do not worry; I do not require any light. | require only one packet of salt to protect & preserve the deadbody. The widow supplied a packet of salt and retired to the next room. As a little calm of mind returned, the widow tried to sleep; her little son fell asleep by her side. The outsider sat near the corpse with the packet of

salt. He was glad in his heart, thinking of the feast. The outsider who pretended to be the nephew of the peasant, started a mysterious game, a horrible, a terrible game. He seized the corpse, tore it from limb to limb. The pretender was crunching the deadbody and devouring Folk Tales of Tripura 403 the human flesh. A cannibal! The sound of snapping made the widow extremely anxious. She was in great suspense. She felt that something was going to happen. Anything might happen under the cover of darkness. She stood up silently and peeped at, but darkness blurred the view. She became certain about something mysterious and ominous. Now what to do? She should not wait any moment. Indeed, she could not stand it any longer. She must go away immediately. But how? she pinched the child to give pain. The child shuddered & cried out. The boy’s eyes were blinking against drowsiness. The boy looked up at his mother. The mother closed & pressed the lips of the boy. The pretender stopped snapping and asked from the adjacent room: Mami? why is he crying? There is no fear. | am here to guard you. The widow replied: Bhagina, your brother will go on a nature’s call. This is why he is crying. The pretender again said : Mami! should I come? The widow said : Bhagina! you need not come. I am going with the child. | shall bring him back soon. Taking the child in her bossom, the widow opened the next door and came out at dead of night. Ahead of her was a valley, a dry field, shrouded in a thick mist. Like a wounded animal, she rushed headlong from the

hut. Five minutes passed; the widow did not come back. The pretender came out of the room and called out tauntingly : Mami! Mami! where have you gone? I have finished the Mama. Now, | like to relish your fresh flesh. I am eager to devour the brother! Mami! come soon! come soon! The widow rushed and rushed! She ran in a violent hurry. At a long distance there was a house of another peasant. She cried & sat down aghast. The peasant gave her shelter in an empty, husking pedal hut next to his. Because of uncleanliness caused by death, she was given shelter in the pedal hut. The widow and the child slept Folk Tales of Tripura 404 alongside the pet dogs. When one is extremely exhausted & worried, and the night is cold, one is temporarily satisfied with any kind of protection. The peasant offered some food, but the widow refused because of the uncleanliness. The peasant spread a bundle of dry grass. Her thudding heart eased to a normal rhythm. The widow & the child slept safely till dawn. The night passed. The sun was not long in coming. The sun’s edge was peering over the hills. When the red tinge had been visible in the eastern horizon, the widow rose up. The morning of December was very cold. Now was the time to walk back. The wise peasant along with his wife, sons and servants accompanied the widow. They spoke but little; their minds were busied by thoughts of what had happened during the previous night. On reaching the lonely & gloomy hut, what did they see? A heap.of broken bones, and no corpse! The bed was

stinking strong & offensive smell! Ants, insects and flies swarmed the nasty bed! The bloodstained floor was littered with nasty clothes, hair, nail, skin & intestine, etc. 48. Tragedy at Tal dighi In a certain area of the western part of Tripura there was a very big and deep tank. It was made lovely by a cluster of tall palm trees. So the tank was popularly known as Tal dighi. The adjacent area was marked by the absence of human habitation. The popular belief was that there must be some vicious nymph in the water of the tank. So the people would never use its water. The local people were very afraid of the nymph. According to their belief, the nymph was a young and beautiful goddess of water. One day, a father and his young daughter were passing by the side of the tank. They were residents of a distant village. Their destination was a long way away. They were ignorant about the nymph. They grew weary and sat down to rest in the shade of a tree of the tank. The thirsty daughter went into knee-deep water to drink water. Surprisingly, one iron chain gripped her leg. She Folk Tales of Tripura 405 cried out, and the father hastened for rescue. She was trembling. He pulled with all his energy and brought her ashore. But they failed to undo or untie the grip of the chain. The daughter went on weeping and the father cried out loudly seeking help. A large crowd thronged there and the young boys pulled the chain. Even an elephant was engaged for pulling the chain. The chain was very, very long and endless. The chain was coiled

into a high heap. It continued for seven days & seven nights. At last, the father had a dream. The nymph said : It is futile to try to rescue & relieve your daughter. I am alone, I wish to carry her off. I shall not kill her. The people stopped the rescue operation. In presence of hundreds of people, the chain started winding up. Before the eyes of hundreds of people and before the eyes of the brokenhearted father, the forlorn daughter was carried inside the water. She cried and cried. At the centre of the tank there was a small temple. The tower of the temple was visible above the surface of the water. At the tip of the tower, one golden plate occasionally used to move rapidly. Once a year the daughter would be allowed for a few minutes to come out and sit on the moving plate. The air blew her hair into her face. Her presence flashed like a lighting. She used to weep for her parents & relations. Thousands of people used to throng for a glance of the daughter. In exchange for kidnapping the daughter, the water nymph assured the people to lend the required number of plate, glass, bowl, pan, etc. on such occasions as birth, first rice giving ceremony, initiation, marriage & death. For this, the concerning family would be required to clean & wash a portion of the bank of the tank, put incense & light a lamp. After the ceremony, the utensils must be returned carefully. On several occasions the utensils were made available. The practice continued for many years. One day one such a family took advantage of the

Folk Tales of Tripura 406 duly borrowed utensils. The next day, after thoroughly washing the utensils, returned those articles, except one. Surprisingly, the chain did not come to take back the utensils. It became an issue of common gossip & rumour. In fact, one greedy lady of the family secretly kept one very beautiful bowl hidden inside the heap of cowdung. At night while asleep, she dreamed a very horrible dream. The nymph threatened to destroy the lady’s entire family & clan for the mischief! The next morning the lady unearthed the bowl, cleaned it thoroughly, returned it duly and prayed the water-goddess to forget & forgive. Immediately the mysterious chain came to take back the utensils. Henceforth, the nymph stopped lending. The people angrily blamed that lady. They were deprived of the benefit. The tank was very old, but its water was clean. The length of the tank was in the north-south direction. The people were never seen relieving themselves in the water; they did not spoil and soil the tank. According to popular belief, the tank was a devottar land, dedicated to a deity long, long ago. The tank’s four surrounding banks were equally wide and well-built; the banks had defied centuries of flood, heavy rainfall and storm. After a few years of that incidence of covetousness, one year had an exceptionally heavy rainfall during July- August. All day black clouds had been racing over the sky, carrying a deluge of rain in the evening. It was a terrible night of thunder, lightning, hailstorm and heavy cloudburst. The surrounding area was in inundation. The tank’s west bank ruptured at the middle point, making an easy outlet of water channel for the nymph to retire

to the sea with her big wooden chest full of utensils and the forlorn daughter. The deluge and the departure of the deity were followed by a period of lull. The peoples were leading their usual way of life. After a few years, another Folk Tales of Tripura 407 disturbance came there. A new nymph appeared and resided on trees. The new nymph is called jin. The jin terrible would be found in inauspicious times & dark nights; he would bestride with one leg on the tallest palm tree of the old tank and another leg on another very tall tree in a distant cremation ground. The terrible jin would ask the passersby to pass under his legs. An unsuspecting passerby trying to pass through, would be strangled. The jin killed many passers and peasants. The jin created a havoc, a terror. The people stopped moving in the evening and at night. To get rid of the jin the gaon panchayets of seven villages had met together and requested the priests, shamans & magicians to do the needful. The priests, shamans & magicians, in turn, selected from among themselves the veteran ojhai. In one dark night the ojhai pretended to be an ordinary peasant and started walking along the banks of the tank. Suddenly, the jin appeared and asked him to pass under his very tall legs. The ojhai disagreed and asked the jin to pass under the legs of the ojhai. The bargaining continued. It was a time of suspense. The ojhai threw on the jin a handful of dust charged with some spells. Instantaneously, the jin surrendered and went to pass under the legs of the ojhai. The ojhai threw

on the jin another handful of dust and made him a captive. Now the jin behaved like an obedient servant. The ojhat asked : Who are you ? what is your history ? His recounting was pathetic & thrilling. He narrated thus : ‘| had been a Brahman. I was handsome & healthy. When the foreign hordes started plundering, killing & raping in our house, I| resisted. After a scuffle, they kidnapped me & packed off to a distant land. They directed me to accept their religion. I rejected it. They became furious & went on abusing, beating, kicking me. I was unable to endure; I had to commit suicide. If any kindhearted Brahman duly performs my funeral ceremony at Gaya, 1 shall get salvation from Folk Tales of Tripura 408 hellish sufferings. I shall no longer put the people to troubles. The ojhai narrated the history. The gaon panchayet sent two priests to perform the pindadan ceremony at Gaya. 49. An epicurean thug A young man lived in a certain village of the Meghna Valley. He had no parents, no brother, no sister. He was a handsome masher. He was shirker, epicure and poor. In the same village there was an old widow. She had no husband, no son, no daughter. She had a milch cow. Because of old age, she was unable to supply milk to the shop of a confectioner. The young man one day came and said : Grandmother, grandmother! may I serve you? Every day in the morning | shall carry the pot of milk to the shop of the confectioner. The poor widow said : But I have no money to pay for your service. If you kindly render the service, | shall

remain grateful to you. The youngman said Grandmother! you need not pay anything in cash; you give me tiffin only in the morning. The widow agreed. The young man started serving and supplying milk. The widow used to offer fried rice, beaten rice, etc. to the youngman. While carrying the pot, he used to add a quantity of water to the pure milk. Initially, he did not demand anything for the additional quantity of milk. After a few days he indirectly indicated his desire for a Rasogolla. So the confectioner used to give him a stale sweetmeat almost daily. The young man was satisfied with that. One day at midday, a grocer lay asleep in the house at the backyard, leaving behind his little son in the shop. lt was a small grocery; the villagers used to pass by the front-side of the shop and to purchase necessary things. It was midday; the tired peasants lay asleep. The young man went to the shop and said to the boy : My name is bee; I am hungry; give me a quantity of honey free of Folk Tales of Tripura 409 cost. The boy sought the permission of his father. The drowsy father replied from the bed : How much will a bee drink? Give him what he wants. After a fortnight, one day at midday in a separate village another grocer lay asleep in his living room at the backyard, leaving behind his little son in the shop. Located in a rural village, the shop had few customers; the peasants fell asleep at noon. The young thug reached there at that time and started conversation with the boy in a friendly spirit, and then sought a quantity of sugar

free of cost. He said : My name is ant; I am hungry, please give me a handful of sugar. The boy said loudly : Father! father! one ant wants a little quantity of sugar. What shall I do? The father replied: How much will an ant eat? Give him what he wants. The son gave sugar. The thug relished it and left. After about a month, one day at midday in a distant village another grocer lay asleep in his living room at the backyard, leaving behind his little son in the shop. The shop had an earthen jar full of fresh molasses. The thug saw the jar, and he could not resist his temptation. He entered the shop & sat on a long bench and pretended to be very exhausted. He said: Dear boy! my name is fly. I am very tired & hungry. Kindly give me a quantity of molasses as gift. The boy was hesitant. The trickster said : Dear boy! you may report to your father that a fly is eager to eat molasses. The boy accordingly cried out to his drowsy father. The half asleep father shouted back : How much will a little fly eat? Give him what he wants. The boy gave a handful quantity of molasses to the trickster. The trickster thanked & left the shop. 50. Two cheats In a certain village lived a peasant family. The peasant had his wife and a son. The peasant used to go to the field with plough & a pair of bullox at dawn. It was the normal task of the wife to bring food to the field at about 8 A.M. or 9 A.M.

The son, now aged sixteen, carries food to the field. Folk Tales of Tripura 410 It is almost a daily duty during the summer and the rainy season. One day the wife prepared beaten rice and the son was asked to carry the fresh, warm beaten rice along with a quantity of molasses. On the way the boy could not restrain his greed; he ate one handful after one handful of the tasty beaten rice. He became conscious when the stock had been exhausted. Now what to do? The mother may rebuke, the father may beat! The boy was going on foot along the narrow baulk & path through the fields; he sat down there weeping. In the meantime, a middle-aged cheat was going along the same path. He said to the boy : Why are you weeping? The boy made a correct reply. The cheat said : It is a serious crime; you will be severely beaten. There is a way out. If you act according to my instruction, your skin will be saved. You go back home and tell your mother : My father has purchased a milch cow at a cost of twenty rupees. Give me twenty rupees. The mother, having collected money from the folds of rags & tags, hanging jars & bamboo pipes, handed over twenty coins. The swindler caught the boy in a trap. He was, as if, cast by nature for lying & cheating. He was indeed, adept in these arts. The imprudent boy had been drawn into it by ill company. It was fated to change the course of his life. The villain and the victim made long strides in adventure to escape the hand of the peasant. The peasant

hungrily and angrily came home at noon. They questioningly talked to each other, and came to know the treachery of the son. They were in entire ignorance of the cheating. The villain & the victim passed village after village. On the way they purchased food out of that amount of twenty rupees. So long as the money had been with them, the cheat was with the boy. By that time, he devised to desert the boy and slip. He asked the boy to take rest at a distance, and himself pretended to be the father of the boy and made a proposal to a shopkeeper of selling the Fo"). Tales cf Tripura 411 boy. The merchant agreed and paid. Taking the money the cheat quickly left the place. The boy, after sometime, became restless and hungry. He came to the shop for some food. The merchant offered food and told : I have purchased you and paid money to your father. The boy was shocked, but he had to serve the merchant. He narrated the previous history; & continued to serve the merchant sincerely and thus earned his sympathy. The boy got redemption after several months of hard labour. He set out; he had no fixed destination. The boy became a wanderer. He was actually searching the villain and seeking an opportunity to pounce upon the swindler. He roamed and roamed apparently aimlessly. At last he saw the swindler and fell at his feet without giving the slightest hint of his inner intention. They pretended to be preceptor and disciple. There was hardly a day passed without some minor offence of cheating committed by the two swindlers. A rapacious expression would often flit

across their face. One day the two swindlers reached a village where a very rich peasant lived. The peasant had a big pond in front of his garden-house. There was an old banyan tree on the bank of the big pond. In the shade of the tree the two cheats sat down. The young cheat had a ring. With the elder cheat’s permission, the young cheat alone went inside and proposed to sell not the ring, but the elder cheat. The peasant agreed. The young cheat raised his had and asked the elder cheat : Shall I sell? The elder cheat replied : Sell, sell. The peasant honestly paid sixty rupees for the hard-working labourer! The young cheat decamped with money, while the elder cheat was kept in bondage. The young cheat went to a market & purchased some food and then bought a healthy horse. He rode and drove through a forest path. He was astonished to find a beautiful garden-house inside the forest. The sun was setting; the evening was falling. He sought a shelter. An old woman, seven wives and children came forward to see the strange Folk Tales of Tripura 412 fellow. He told the old woman : Grandmother! I am tired and hungry! I am alone! I am afraid of moving ahead at night! kindly allow me to stay here for this night only. The old woman consulted her daughters-in-law before giving permission. In course of conversation he gleaned that it was a house of dacoits. The old woman’s seven sons were all dacoits. That afternoon they had already set out riding on seven horses. The cheat made a stratagem to rob the robbers. He

put his coins inside a banana leaf-packet and made his horse swallow the packet. In the next morning, while the horse had been excreting, the coins came out along with the discharge. It was purposely displayed to the children and the women. He told : This is a rare type of horse; the horse daily excretes coins. The women became tempted, inquisitive and interested to purchase the horse. A dacoity in the house of the dacoits! An extraordinary incident! A sheer bluffl The cheat left the house of the dacoits and made long strides to go beyond the reach of the dacoits. From a long distance he saw the dacoits riding & speeding through the paths homeward bound. How to escape their inquisitive eyes? At a little distance he saw a washerman washing the clothes of a royal household. By another stratagem he frightened & confused the washerman; he said Washerman! you have stolen some clothes of the royal household; so, the king’s police forces are coming, see, see | The nervous washerman sought his help. He directed him to hide under a heap of hay. The cheat pretended to be a washerman, washing the clothes and hiding the bag of coins. Like a sudden gust of wind, the dacoits speedily passed the washing ghat without asking any question to the washerman. On arrival, the dacoits were astonished and shocked to know the news of the incident. Leaving the bag & baggage, the dacoits turned back speedily and found the pretender; they asked the pretender whether he had seen Folk Tales of Tripura 413 such a man. He replied in the positive and raised his finger towards the rick. The dacoits got down, searched

the rick and twitched the actual washerman and rushed back home. They fastened him with a cord and asked the children to kick him. After taking rest and food, they asked him several questions. The ladies were paraded to identify. The ladies said : He is not the actual cheat. Being released, the actual washerman narrated what had happened in the washing ghat. They again galloped, but the actual cheat fled away very fast with the booty and the clothes. The dacoits retired. The cheat moved forward. On the way there was a big river. There was a ferry under the care of an old woman and her granddaughter. The two women were very poor. It was the grandmother’s headache to arrange the marriage of her granddaughter. The cheat made a mockery of friendship and pretended to be a liberal young man. He showed them the costly clothes, and shook the bag and jingled the coins. He proposed to marry without any dowry. They agreed and assured to arrange the ceremony within a few days. But on the pretext of his mother’s illness, the cheat eloped with the granddaughter suddenly. The grandmother shouted to the people asking them to chase and capture the grandson-in-law. The people replied : Taking the granddaughter by the grandson-in-law is quite natural. Will he take you, grandmother? , Now the young cheat turned his steps towards home with money and wife. The parents became very happy. All their anger vanished. The atmosphere of the home again became afresh with joy. The villagers came to see the son and the wife. But here too he conspired to cheat the neighbours. He said : I have travelled a long distance

to a distant town to learn the technique of minting coins. By that technique I have earned a large amount of money. After a few months, the senior cheat happened to Folk Tales of Tripura 414 nn visit the house of the junior cheat. Now the two cheats are equally adept. They again came to an understanding to undertake any enterprise which would bring profit. The two misfit delinquents became a money-making racket. A wide publicity was given to their new enterprise : money duplicating business. If anybody furnishes one rupee, next day two rupees will be supplied. That was the rate. Many poor people came with their meagre stock and got double the amount. Thus they earned popularity. It was their confidence trick. One day a rich peasant came with a large amount of money. Having shielded themselves from distrust, they were able to attract the attention and temptation of the rich peasant. The customers were in entire ignorance of the evil design of the cheats. By establishing a rapport, they had in mind to decamp with a large chunk of money. The moment that amount had come, they fled and retired into a distant, deep forest. But how to continue there in the hills and jungles without food and comforts of life? So they pretended to be hermits with long beard and hair and a particular dress, Sometimes, they would pretend to be beggars. But the two would never go together. One day the senior cheat went out to purchase some sweetmeat: he ate to his heart’s content sitting in the confectioner’s shop and bought a quantity of sweetmeat in an earthen pot. But he deceitfully poisoned the

sweetmeat. The junior cheat went a step further; he lay in ambush with a sharp knife in hand. The senior cheat was unaware of it. The evening was falling. The place was dark, lonely & sylvan. The moment the senior cheat had crossed the spot, the junior cheat coldly & quickly pounced upon him and stabbed him to death. The hungry junior cheat swallowed the sweetmeat and died on the spot. Thus the two arch-criminals were fated to die together. Folk Tales of Tripura 415 51. A cheat & a fool In a certain village lived a cheat and a fool. The cheat was a well-known thug and shirker. He was never found to plough, to weed, to harvest, to fish and to repair. If there was a feast or a festival, a meeting or a congregation, he would be there. He utterly lost his credibility. So it became ‘extremely difficult for him to maintain the family. He was plunged into great distress. The cheat and his wife, after much delibekation, found an alternative : the cheat will make friendship with the fool, and then the two friends will often pass secretly about midnight for stealing. . The cheat and his wife started visiting the house of the fool. A few days passed in reciprocal inquiries. After a conversation of this nature, they became friends. Now, the cheat said: Fnend! both of us are very poor; we are on the verge of starvation. Let us make nocturnal venture and steal crops & vegetables. The idiot replied : Friend! if you guide, I shall follow you. The cheat assured : Do not think, I am here to manage. It was the month of Agrahayana (=November-

December). The paddy became ripe. The cheat made a survey at day time. About midnight the two friends set out and reaped. The cheat asked the idiot : Friend! will you take the top end or the bottom end? The idiot answered : | shall take the bottom end. So the idiot took the useless stubble, and the cheat had the useful paddy. Quite obviously, the fool’s wife rebuked the fool that night. After a few days, they passed to steal sugarcane. They cut down and piled. At the time of division, the cheat asked : Friend! will you take the top end or the bottom end? The fool instantaneously replied : I shall take the top end. He, therefore, got the twigs, while the cheat got the actual sugarcane. On that night also the fool’s wife chided her husband. Next, they made an adventure to steal pumpkin. Its plant and fruit are edible: At the time of stealing, the Folk Tales of Tripura 416 eee plant was flowering only. They cut down the green and fresh plants. On being asked by the cheat, the fool expressed his option for the hard, bottom end; and the cheat took the soft & delicious top ends. As usual, the fool’s wife criticised her husband. Being rebuked by the wife, the fool became cautious and demanded the top end in advance. This time they attempted to steal radish. They jointly uprooted the edible plants. The cheat asked : Friend! what will you take as your share? The fool took the top ends, that is, the leaves, while the cheat took the edible bottom ends. The idiocy of the fool benumbed his wife. She became very angry. Is

it friendship? Next, they proceeded to steal brinjal. Here too, the idiot committed mistake and the cheat deceived. The idiot claimed the bottom end and received the useless plants, while the fraud bluffed & took the fruits. Once again the fool found himself with nothing, and the cheat & his wife enjoying themselves. Afterwards, the trickster led the idiot to steal potato. The idiot claimed the top end and got the useless plants, while the fraud picked up the edible tubers. The fool’s wife was about to beat her husband. The cheat’s wife Stopped visiting the fool’s house from the very start of cheating. Later, the two thieves went to steal mankachu, (= one kind of arum). The fool changed the strategy and cut down the top ends for himself. He came out with a bundle of useless leaves. The cheat took time to uproot the fleshy plants. The owner of the plants got a hint and pounced upon the cheat. The idiot fled. The cheat got a good beating. He had to take rest for “ month. The idiot visited the house of the cheat. The cheat and his wife severely scolded the idiot for escaping alone, for only one occasion of unfriendly behaviour ! Finally, they went to steal jalkachu (=one kind of arum grown in marshy places). This time, they decided to divide ‘olk Tales of Tripura 417 vertically, and share equally. But in that marshy place lived a very poisonous snake. The snake bit the fraud. The pain was very severe. The fool took the cheat on his shoulder and rushed towards home. Before the arrival of the ojha, the cheat breathed his last. 52. How three cheats befooled a Brahman

In ancient Tripura on the bank of the river Gomati lived a Brahman. He had his wife; but he had no son. The Brahman was poor but pious. He was a priest. The couple had a great desire for a son. So, they devoted themselves to the worship of Siva and Tripurasundari Kalimata, suffering bodily penance. Then the god being pleased, granted the boon. The couple vowed to sacrifice a hegoat to the god. In course of time, the Brahman’s wife gave birth to a son. The couple, being happy with a son, decided to sacrifice a hegoat. The Brahman went to a distant weekly market in the late afternoon for purchasing a hegoat. He purchased fruits, sweetmeats, vegetables and one hegoat. It took time. In the evening he turned his steps homeward. Three cheats saw the Brahman coming back home. The villains put their heads together to befool the Brahman and to relish the hegoat’s meat. They sat down, at an interval of half a mile, watching the path along which the Brahman would come. They were waiting while the Brahman was yet a long way off. They were keeping a distance from each other. Now as the Brahman passed on, the first cheat said : Purohitji! why are you carrying a shegoat on your shoulder? The Brahman replied : This is a hegoat for sacrifice. I have purchased it from the market. The first cheat said : But the salesman put a false symbol. The Brahman said : Everybody knows me. How shall I be cheated? | Paying little attention to the passing remark, the Brahman, overburdened with load, went ahead. After Folk Tales of Tripura 418 some distance, the second rogue met him. The rogue

said : Thakur Mahashay! what happened to you? Why are you carrying a shegoat on your shoulder? On hearing that, the Brahman took off the animal from his shoulder, & placed the animal on the ground and examined the identification mark and resumed his walk with a wavering mind. It was twilight. There was no street-light in those days. For travel at night, the people had to use bamboo- torch light (=chunga batti). When the Brahman had moved further and passed through another turning of the path, the third knave said : Guruji! why have you purchased this shegoat? You are a priest. Do you like to have a goat-herd? Now, the simple-hearted Brahman became confused indeed. He was led into bewilderment. Being puzzled, perplexed & disgusted, the Brahman left the animal on the spot. He went on grumbling and cursing the salesman. The three deceivers met together and decamped with the hegoat for a relish. 53. A thing of barbarity is a joy igi a moment There was a village in the Meghna Valley of western Tripura. A peasant family lived there long ago with his wife and four children : three sons and one daughter. The peasant was a bit cruel, unkind & selfish. He had only a few friends in the village. Some cunning people of the village set their children to entice the peasant’s sons & to lead them astray. The sons became addicted to smoking & chewing. When the children became adolescent, the peasant arranged their marriage one after another. Within a month of the marriage of the first son, the daughter-in- law slowly started to make a mess of things. She tended to delay & procrastinate. The eldest son used to support

her and guard her. So they were separated. The new couple got their own hearth & home and land. Now, they started rising very early in the morning & doing all jobs. Folk Tales of Tripura 419 The next year the peasant arranged the marriage of the second son. Instigating her husband against the members of the family, the second daughter-in-law used to pretend to be sober. The second son started quarrelling with the parents on trifling grounds. Wheedling the people, the second daughter-in-law used to collect some secret news & keep her husband informed. She would outwardly criticise her husband & praise the people; but examined deeply, the criticism was praise, & the praise was criticism. Her etiquettes were deceptive. Their hidden motive was to break up. So the peasant allowed them to live separately, to cook & eat separately. The next year the peasant arranged the marriage of the third son. The third daughter-in-law could not tolerate the peasant’s daughter. The third son used to take the side of his wife and to blame the sister. The sister was made a scapegoat for any misdeed. So the peasant allowed the couple to build their own hearth & home. He was in similar situation for three times. Meanwhile, the peasant’s wife fell ill. She was lucky to get the service of her husband & daughter. After a few months of illness, the aged woman died. The sons performed the funeral rites and shared the necessary expenditure. The peasant became mentally wounded. Moreover, he had the burden of arranging the marriage of his only daughter. He was not a rich man. With all his little savings, he arranged the marriage of his daughter. The

daughter left the parental home. The peasant now really felt lonely. The sons were separated, the wife died, the daughter married elsewhere. The children were to fend for themselves only. The old, pauper, forlorn peasant felt utterly neglected by the children. The afflicted peasant used to plaintively groan & moan. The sons & the daughters-in-law continued to behave wickedly & continued to be negligent. He searched in every direction and called; no one responded. Folk Tales of Tripura 420 — One day, one friend of the peasant came to see him. The two friends had a hearty discussion in whispering voice. The friend gave him a few coins and advised him to count the coins at night. So the peasant intentionally caused to make jingling sound of the coins. It worked wonder. The clinking sound of the metallic coins alerted & allured the sons & the daughters-in-law. One couple heard the sound; they slowly & surreptitiously proceeded & stood under the eaves & near the window to listen the jingling sound of the coins. The next morning, the first daughter-in-law came with a smiling face and with tiffin in her hand. She listened to his demand with seeming respect. Next, the second couple became suspicious; they too committed eavesdropping and heard the jingling sound. The second daughter-in-law equally turned helpful. The third couple became curious to see the sudden change. They, too, committed the same eavesdropping. They, too, started looking after the old father with a friendly feeling. A cheat meeting a cheat! Now he stopped jingling. The purpose was served. He paid back the coins secretly. It was his habit to lard his speech with the word satan &

to talk in snarl. 54. A spoiled child A peasant family lived in a village. The peasant had his wife and son. The couple had to work as servants in the houses of their neighbours. The peasant fell ill and died. After two years the widow also died, leaving behind her teenaged son. The son was very industrious and cheerful. He used to remain always occupied with some kind of work. He, too, had to work as labourer in the fields of others. For his honesty and hardworking habit he enjoyed the affection of the elders. Every day he used to get job. Thus within a few years he improved his lot. Every year Folk Tales of Tripura 421 he started purchasing land. He was a practical man, a specimen of Bengal peasant life. Now he is a young man and owner of lands. His name and fame became well-known. He married a poor and docile girl. He was in delight with land and lady. The couple were laborious, simple and god-fearing folk, free from vulgarity and vices. Their union had been soul to soul. Their marriage was a socio-economic partnership. She used to cook at home and bring food to the field for her husband. Thus she came to know every field, every crop, every cattle. The couple used to discuss : what field was ploughed; what plot was purchased; what was the price; what stock was born or sold; what quantity of seeds was required for each plot; what types of vegetables were to be cultivated and sold; she shared his toil. She used to weed, reap and bring home crops and vegetables. Thus, by mutual love and labour, they became rich with

well-stocked farm of cattle, goat, pigeon, duck, and lands, and ponds teemed with fish. His cottage swarmed with domestic animals & birds. So, they had been feeling happy for years together. The birth of a son added to their happiness. They had great affection for the son. The blind tenderness was too much; they would not allow the son to do any work. He grew very much dependent on the parents. Thus, the boy became idle, idiot and epicurean. He could not eat without fish curry. The couple did not care to think about the injury that a father or a mother can do to a son or daughter by pampering and attaching them too closely : ‘He is too little to do work alone!’ (#4 aq tem) In the midst of his progress & prosperity, his wife suddenly died. It was a terrible shock. He lost his energy and enthusiasm, interest & initiative. The peasant sighed and began to think of getting rid of the family responsibilities. The family did not get time to arrange the marriage of the son. At the eleventh hour of his life, the father gave the Folk Tales of Tripura 422 son three important instructions : 1. I have not made a mess of things. I have to bequeath to you well-stocked farm and fertile land and ponds. So, you may eat fish with every morsel of food. 2. Do not repair house every year. Build a house once. 3. In case of any difficulty or danger, seek advice from a very old man. The peasant did not live long. The thought of his son’s future kept him anxious & worried. The anxiety became acute after his wife’s death.

In his death bed, he often tossed from side to side. He had to he awake the greater part of night and then one day he breathed his last. The neighbours rendered all sorts of cooperation in the performance of cremation and funeral rites. On the day of Sraddha ceremony, all the villagers were invited and entertained with food. After about one year, the boy married a beautiful & smart girl of a middle class family from a suburban village. She was reluctant to go to the field, to look after the cattle, to take care of the crops and vegetables. She was interested in graceful dress and ornaments. She was not a working partner. She was a woman-with-her-own- life. Her mother-in-law was a hub-of-the-family. The boy, to remain very faithful to the advice of his father, used to eat big fish like Ruhu, Katla, Mrigel, every day. If such fish was not available from his pond, he had to purchase from fishermen. According to the second advice, he repaired and rebuilt the paternal house only once with such materials as bamboo, cane, thatching grass, and wooden pillar which need to be replaced after every three or four years. But the boy did not repair the house even after four or five years. The house became very unsteady, uninhabitable and dilapidated because of the ravages of time. During the rainy season, goods & chattels would be damaged. The tinkling sound of the rains on utensils would disturb his sleep; water would seep through the roof. Folk Tales of Tripura 423 But he stuck to the advice of his father! And continued to live there and eat big fish daily. All these incidents indicate the character of the boy.

He had neither intelligence nor industriousness. So, dangers & difficulties dogged him. He started selling lands every year. The father had expanded; the son contracted. Obviously, the paternal estate became smaller and smaller. A naive may be drowned in his father’s pond. When it was at last reduced to the minimum, the son brooded sullenly on the advice of his father. But he was not capable of analysing it himself. Now, the third advice came to his mind. He left home, travelled, travelled for a few days, and reached a distant village and met an octogenarian old man. The old man, with his wit & wisdom, explained : Your father had great affection for you; he gave you advice in figurative speech. The literal meaning of the first advice is that you should live in plenty & pleasure; you need not eat big fish actually; you may eat small fish. Even to eat fish daily is not good for health. About the second advice your father had it to say that you should have built a pucca house of bricks, cement & iron, etc. which has a lifelong duration. The old man’s explanation brought the son to his senses. He returned with a changed outlook. He began to understand. He started to work as a daily labourer in the fields of neighbours. Now he became thrifty & practical. He became set in the peasant life. 55. Two dissimilar brothers There was a poor peasant family in the Meghna Valley of Tripura. The peasant had to work in the fields of his neighbours as a labourer. The peasant was insensible, and his wife was wicked. The family had a small garden house, and a milch cow and a cot with a

quilt and a few utensils. The husband and the wife died, shortly after one another, leaving behind two orphan boys. The two orphan brothers were in great distress. A few generous neighbours came forward with their helping Folk Tales of Tripura 424 hands. They engaged them to tend their cattle. The employer provided food & clothe, but no salary in cash. Thus, petted by all, the two brothers grew through childhood to boyhood leading a peasant life of tending the cattle, cleaning the cowshed, fishing, swimming and cutting green grass for the cows. That way of life continued until the elder brother came to his fifteenth year, and the younger brother came to his thirteenth year. But that way of life was destined to a dramatic interruption. The elder brother was very dull & simple, while the younger brother was very cunning and crafty. One summer morning the younger brother came with a deceptive proposal of arranging the marriage of the elder brother. After two days, the younger brother came with the real proposal of dividing the paternal property. He said: Elder brother! our patrimony is very small; so there is no necessity to invite & request the village council to mediate. The elder brother agreed. So it was almost wordlessly arranged between the two brothers. The division of patrimony of three items took place by a mutual understanding thus : |. The quilt to be used by the elder brother during day time, & to-be used by the younger brother during night. 2. The cow’s frontside to be shared by the elder brother and the hind side to be shared of the younger brother. 3. The caecoanut tree’s bottom side to be shared by the

elder brother, & the top side to be shared by the younger brother. Following the terms & conditions, the elder brother goes on drying the quilt on the fences, watering & manuring the cocoanut tree and tending the cow. The summer and the rainy season passed thus. During the winter season, the cow started giving milk and the tree started giving fruits. The elder brother went on drying and tending and watering, while the younger brother Folk Tales of Tripura 425 went on using the quilt at night, drinking the cow’s milk and enjoying the tasty green cocoanuts all alone. The elder brother, thus deprived days after days, had a grinding sense of being exploited & harassed. The younger brother made use of everything : All is grist that comes to his mill ! The younger brother remains cheerful and buoyant. Drudged at the work, the elder brother one spring morning left home silently. He walked & walked without any destination. He grew tired and hungry. There was a big banyan tree on the bank of a river. In the shade of it, a group of village women were busy to worship a folk- deity. The elder brother sat there; the woman gave him water and fruits. The woman returned home; but the elder brother lay asleep. It was afternoon. One middle-aged person was passing by the side of the tree. He saw the disappointed elder brother in shabby dress. It was an awkward scene to see an unknown young man lying asleep in front of a temple. He watched the scene. A gentle melancholy possessed him. Hearing the murmuring of the person, the elder brother awaked and fell at the feet of the

middle-aged man. The middle-aged man consoled him and asked his whereabouts. While listening, the sad memory of his own past touched the man. Hearing his grievances, the middle-aged man said: 1. Since you have the right over the quilt during the day, you soak it in water before sunset and make it wet; 2. Since you have the right over the frontside of the cow, you reduce the quantity of fodder, and at the time of milching, go on beating the head of the cow; 3. Since you have the right over the lower side of the tree, you stop watering & manuring the tree, cut a little portion of the tree with an axe. Instead of having been cast down and given way to the inevitable consequence of wrong agreement, he became more self-confident than ever and returned home and followed the advice and got good results. With a view to drive him out, the plotter enticed the elder brother with a good job in the house of a zamindar or a king. lot with perseverance. To fill the basket, he had to fish till evening without food & rest; to eat on a plate of three inches he had to be extremely cautious, lest one rice should be wasted. On the ground of health, the elder brother was released, and the younger brother was appointed. Now the new employee fills the basket with fish, crab, mollusc, snail and moss. It created a dormant sensation in the palace and a haunting thought in the king’s mind. | One day the king visited the house of his father-in- law. The new employee accompanied as attendant. Hurriedly the king excreted in an earthen jar. Next day at dawn the attendant was to throw away the spoiled jar. But the attendant pretended to be sick. He did not keep his word. Folk Tales of Tripura 427 As the morning drew on, a different mood seemed to come over the mind of the king. The fear of shame took possession of him. So the king is going to commit suicide by drowning in the water. To save the life of the king, it is essential to silently follow the king and break the jar. Two grave-diggers In a certain village lived a poor peasant family. The peasant had his wife and five daughters and only one son. The son was the youngest of all children. The peasant was poor, but honest and laborious. His wife was cooperative, considerate, frugal and sober. The two young persons made a good match. She looked after the family as well as the field; within a decade the family became prosperous. The couple were happy with their lands, children and cattle. Time passed quickly. The daughters grew to girlhood. The parents arranged their marriage one after another. The daughters had gone to distant villages with their husbands; and presently the son was with the parents. The house, once humming with life, looked

deserted, forlorn and empty. The rural life follows the traditional routines. The sound of birds awakens the peasants at dawn. The peasants, the fishermen, the smiths, the barbers, the woodcutters, the cowherds go out in the morning. They go to weekly markets in the evening. They gossip, smoke, chew betel leaf, and occasionally sing devotional songs, and take care of each other. In such evening gatherings, the neighbours used to tell the peasant to arrange the marriage of the son. The peasant too used to request them to bring information about a prospective daughter- in-law. The local ghatak (=match-maker) had a fair knowledge about the marriageable boys and girls of a few villages. Thus on an auspicious day in the month of Agrahayana (November-December) the boy’s marriage was arranged with a charming, smart daughter of a very rich peasant. Folk Tales c” ura 434 The behaviour of the new daughter-in-law was initially and apparently good. She knew courtly manners; she was sweet-tongued. The neighbours used to comment : The daughter-in-law is very good. She has a smiling face. She has amiable behaviour’. Within a few years she gave birth to a son. It had added to her prestige and position. Now, her real face came to the notice of the old parents-in-law. She was least interested in the economic activities of the family. Her own contribution was very little to the upkeep of the home. She was found extravagant and wasteful. She would treat the hired domestics carelessly, and the parents-in-law artificially. The sign of her zodiac had been such that she could not live without hatred & jealousy. , Crushed by his disillusionment, the heart-broken old peasant became almost a recluse. The neighbours in

whom the old peasant and his wife had confided, began to wonder. Quickly the truth went round the neighbourhood. The peasant was willing either to live elsewhere or to cook separately. The selection of the bride was a terrible mistake! The daughter-in-law detested her parents-in-law from the core of her heart. She seized every chance to poison the mind of her husband against the parents-in- law. Oft-repeated manoeuver, skilful & clever handling of domestic politics created a very bad impression in the mind of her husband against the parents-in-law. There was a certain repellent slyness in his behaviour which, though unobserved by others was noticeable to the old parents. With the birth of a grandson to this family, the breach Folk Tales of Tripura 435 between the old peasant and the son was partially repaired. The grandfather and the grandmother used to teach him good lessons and memorable stories; and occasional presents and nursing during any illness by the old grandparents went a long way in the tender mind of the child. The old peasant’s son did not at first wish to take any fatal step against his parents; but he was over- persuaded by his wife. One night the young wife and her husband decided that, on the pretext of visiting a shrine,

the old couple would be taken to a deep forest for throwing them in a deep pit.
