The Candle burned at both ends Maharaj Dhanya Manikya was a very powerful king of Tripura. He was a king of superb ability & ambition. He ruled strictly & justly. The victories laid the north & south, the east & west of the empire at his feet. The entire Meghna

Valley and the hills of Tripura were brought under one administration. Dhanya Manikya and some of his successors adorned Rangamati (= Udaypur) with tanks & temples. Folk Tales of Tripura 437 The empire was unwieldy in size, and the administration was war-oriented. In the west, along the mighty Meghna River, the Tripuri dynasty had sterner work to do. The Tripuri, the Riang, the Jamatia soldiers and the Bengali Laskar soldiers poured out their blood like water in the battle fields to check the aggressors. Now, one of the servants of Maharaj Dhanya Manikya was very active, energetic and eloquent but corrupt. He had the capacity to accomplish a difficult job. Where others had failed, he became successful. His colleagues sensed that there was something wrong with him, yet could not say precisely why they disliked him. To administer the empire, the king had to maintain | a network of espionage. The spies were his eyes & ears. Through them the minister and the king came to know the dishonesty of that particular servant. So, with the consent of the king, the minister transferred the servant to the big agricultural farm of the royal family. The farm was in the fertile valley of the river Gomati. The farm had to supply fresh vegetables to the royal kitchen. Here also he was successful in maintaining a steady supply of fresh vegetables to the royal kitchen. But the clever servant was in search of a clue for extortion. On paper he maintained the number of labourers unchanged; but really, the number was reduced; the wages of a few dismissed labourers went to his pocket. When the spies had reported the matter to the

minister, the minister, with the royal permission, transferred him to a distant office. Now, it was his duty to collect land tax, house tax, cattle tax, etc. from the villagers. Here also he was found very active in collecting taxes from the householders. Through repeated reminders and requests and mild threats, he collected a substantial amount of taxes. And the deposit to the treasury was quite impressive. But here also he found ample scope for extraction in cash & kind. The resentment of the villagers reached the ears of the king. Folk Tales of Tripura 438 His next transfer was to a forest office. In the forest office, he had to issue daily or monthly permit to the local woodcutters. By paying a fixed rate of fees, the woodcutters could cut down bamboo, wood, timber, thatching grass, etc. from the royal forest. After working a few months, he got the clue to enrich himself. Receiving the fees and issuing the permit, for collecting a prescribed quantity of forest products, he used to wink them to collect additional quantity of forest products for which they had to pay extra fee. Those fees were not shown in the records. After about a year, the matter was again reported to the minister. The minister again transferred him to a distant mountainous tract. The culprit soon found out a scope to enrich himself by unfair means. Disgusted with the dishonest servant, the king disparagingly said : Let him count the number of waves of the river. The minister made order to transfer him to the bank of the mighty river Meghna. He was, as if, ordered to count the number of waves of the water of the

river. Practically, it was no duty at all. But the cunning servant was shrewd enough to find out some means of exploitation. He sat in the shade of tree and found boats passing upstream and downstream. For centuries the mighty Meghna River served as the lifeline of Tripura. Any disturbance in the free passage of the transport system of the river would leave the people in serious troubles. But the notorious servant used to shout loudly and threateningly to every boatman and said to them : Boatman! stop, stop, the king asked me to count the number of waves of the river, but your passage is disturbing the usual waves and the counting process. So, I will not allow you to pass through. The harassed and vexed boatmen had‘no other alternative but to coax the coastalguard and to offer something. He would rave & revile the poor fisherman for something. The live fishes used to flop about in the Folk Tales of Tripura 439 dé boat. He would demand a few live fishes. He became addicted to smoking & drinking. The king’s disparaging comment was caught & capitalised & utilized by the rogue. Thus out of nothing, the coastalguard went on earning something. He was happy. He had no official responsibility. But the news of extraction did not long remain secret. The boatmen stared in surprise at one another and remarked : Our king had _become mad, otherwise why he appointed the coastalguard to count the number of waves of the river? The boatmen were engaged in export & import. One important item of import was dry fish (= sidal sukti. Big earthen jar-loads of dry fish used to herald their odour

in air in advance. It was a popular item of food. The price of fresh fish & dryfish rose. The consumers were dissatisfied with the price rise. News of the people’s discontent was not slow to reach the minister. The minister brought it to the notice of the king. An investigation was made; and an inquiry pointed to the coastalguard as the culprit. He was arrested and remanded to jail. Thus the servant created problem one after another to the administration. The king gave him scope for rectification. But he remained unchanged. At last the king ordered : Place him on the pointed stakes and kill him. One vice was powerful enough to cut his life short. He had other vices also. The candle burned at both ends! 60. Three blind men’s conception of an elephant Having dislodged Raja Lakshman Sen of Bengal in c.1204 A.D., the predatory eyes now turned to Tripura. Tripura was first attacked in 1240 A.D. The Tripuri dynasty was forced to shift from the Barak Valley to the Gomati Valley. Those were the days of pre-street and pre-motor vehicle system. The people had to walk on foot and carry load on head and shoulder. Raja Dangar-pha paid attention to the problem of travel & transport. Tradition has it that Folk Tales of Tripura 440 Raja Dangar-phamade attempts to get a wild elephant, tamed. During those days Tripura had a large variety of wild flora & fauna. The king’s attempt was successful. The king used to travel riding on the elephant. The king had appointed an elephant-driver. The adventurous attempt of the king Atearleth the attention of the people of Rangamati, the medieval capital of Tripura, on both sides of the river Gomati. It soon

became a common topic of discussion. The king would occasionally come out of the royal residence and make a circuit in the capital riding on the elephant. The king would see a crowd of men, women & children on both sides of the road waving hands & saluting with shy smile. The news spread far & wide. It assumed the character of rumour. It caught the imagination of numerous people. They used to visit the capital on certain occasions, such as Durga Puja, Nava Varsa, mainly to see the king riding on an elephant. Three blind men of a village became eager to see the elephant. They requested their village elder. The village elder engaged an escort. The reliable escort took care to lead the blind men to the capital, and contacted the elephant-driver. The elephant-driver agreed to take them one by one near the elephant. Others were directed to wait at a safe distance. The escort sat with the blind men in the shade of tree. The elephant was restrained with a tether. The driver led one blind man; the first blind man went ahead to lay his hand on one leg of the elephant and returned. Then the second blind man was led; he moved his hand with gentle pressure over one ear of the elephant and returned. At last the third blind man was led; he touched gently the tail of the elephant and returned. They all thanked the driver for his kind assistance. The blind men were glad. The visitors turned their steps towards their home. On the way they were engaged in lively conversation & jokes. They had a sense of complacence for the successful adventure.

Folk Tales of Tripura 441 The village elder noticed that there was some excitement among the blind men. They were all in a ferment. The village elder asked : Do you hear? what is thas you all got in your head? what are you thinking about the elephant? The first blind man said : The elephant was like a strong, upright pillar. : The second blind man said : The elephant was like a flat winnowing fan. The third blind man said : The elephant was like a tall & narrow snake. They accused each other. Each of them was astounded at the gross inaccuracy of the other. Each of them was adamant. Each tried to stick to his own experience. Each denied & turned down the experience of the other. The village elder said : Listen to me. Each of you had touched three different parts of the body of the elephant. Those three parts alone do not constitute the elephant. The elephant is a very big animal consisting of many other parts. So your conception is full of mistakes. Still you insist on this mistake! Other’s mistakes are before your mind, but your own mistake is behind your back! : The village elder did not insist further. As a village elder, as a fatherly figure, he had to choose his words with care. That consideration restrained him to comment: You are both physically & mentally blind! 61. Katal & Kakchand The legend was one of drought & distress, famine & fever, migration & movement, starvation & suffering, and disease & death. Each person became a thief to his neighbour. A severe famine broke out in Kashmir in 917-918

A.D. A terrible famine occurred in Kailash-har of northern Tripura about that time. The Kailash-har famine either preceeded or followed the Kashmir famine No rain fell for two years. The drought caused severe Folk Tales of Tripura 442 damage to crops. A large tract of land was left uncultivated. Because of the scarcity of water, cracks appeared in lands. So the famine was caused by failure of the rains and not by high taxes from the side of the kings of Tripura. However, nature’s freaks and official indifference on the part of the nascent princely administration of Tripura aggravated the frightful sufferings of the people. There were two brothers : Katal and Kakchand. Katal was the elder brother, while Kakchand was the younger brother. Right from the childhood the two brothers were active, considerate, & sympathetic. They did never waste time in idle gossiping. There was genuine understanding between the two brothers. In course of time, the two brothers became adult. Through mutual understanding the two brothers took to two separate courses of livelihood. Katal preferred business, while Kakchand chose agriculture. Katal had a substantial amount of money in cash, while Kakchand had barnful of paddy, rice and seeds. The family’s financial position considerably improved. Theirs was a joint family. The parents arranged the marriage of the two adult sons. Things were going well initially. For a few years they led a prosperous, happy life, in Kailash-har, respected by all who knew them. The two young couples became parents with a few children to each of them. The neighbours knew very little as to what kind of domestic life those couples led during the years of their early married life. Nevertheless, Katal’s wife was a little

proud of her husband’s cash money; she was subtly and cunningly making impression from the force of cash money. An ill-feeling was thus generated between the two wives. Kakchand’s wife contrived to find fault with Katal’s wife. At last there came a day when the two brothers had felt that they should live separately. Meanwhile, their Folk Tales of Tripura 443 Se ee ee ee parents had already died. The worldly-wise brothers remained above the disgusting feminine jealousy. They did not allow the malice to spoil the fraternity. Leaving the parental home to the care of the younger brother, the elder brother shifted eastward to a separate plot of land within Kailash-har. The elder brother built his own house and dug a very large tank of similar work: the old tank which had fallen into disrepair, was restored, repaired and enlarged. It took about a year to settle the familial issues, to build huts & houses, to dug dighi (= very large & deep pond) and to perform certain ceremonies. Time passed like the currents of rivers. The next autumn season came. Now, to them appeared the souls of their dead parents in dream and commanded them to journey to Gaya and Prayag for the ceremony of pinda-dan, and ashti- visharjan. So, the two brothers talked to each other and consulted with their respective families, and journeyed to the holy places in the northern part of Bharat. The holy funeral rite of pinda-dan at Gaya and ashti-visharjan at Prayag for mukti was filling the imagination and stirring the innermost heart of numerous faithful Hindus for centuries. The Pandas used to come down to the distant villages to guide the pilgrims. In those days, to complete

the tedious journey, the pilgrims had to face many troubles : lack of proper food, sanitation, medicine & vehicle. The excitement used to subside after a few days. They had to walk limpingly & sobbingly along with bleeding feet. Under such circumstances, a heavy loss of life was quite common. During the absence of the two brothers, a terrible famine broke out. Drought rendered cultivation impossible. Much of land went out of cultivation. Kailash- har and the adjacent countryside became densely covered with dead bodies of men & animals. The parents wanted to sell their children for food, but nobody would buy. Katal could not foresee. and so he did not make Folk Tales of Tripura 444 adequate provision. Kakchand had an adequate stock of foodgrains. Katal’s wife had to feed her hungry children. She approached Kakchand’s wife and offered to pay any price for foodgrains. Katal’s wife went to Kakchand’s house a number of times. Kakchand’s wife was actuated by a indignation to take revenge against the bragging of Katal’s wife. She replied : You have enough money; now eat your money; now eat your money. The next day again Katal’s wife took her hungry children there; Kakchand’s wife cuffed on the head of the child, and dodged and closed the door. Within a few days, Katal’s wife a & his children died together. After several months of painful, tedious journey, the two exhausted pilgrims turned their steps homeward. On reaching home, Kakchand found his wife & children cheerful, and came to know the news of death of Katal’s wife & children. While narrating the news, Kakchand’s wife was chuckling and she concluded : I have taught her a lesson for her swaggering.

Kakehand at once rushed towards Katal’s house. lhe atmosphere of Katal’s house was dreadfully still. At the entrance he saw the carcasses of the cattle. He called out. No body replied. No body came forward. He anxiously opened the ajar door and saw the tragic scene of skeletons huddled together. He stood akimbo and then sat aghast. Meanwhile, Kakchand reached there and reported what had happened. Both were silent; each knew the other’s agony. Katal took a bag full of money and hastened towards the large pond and plunged himself into the deep water. For a few minutes, Kakchand stood on the bank, tears rolled down his face. Like a wounded animal, Kakchand rushed headlong from the scene and reached home and gently asked his wife and children to get ready for a cruise. With bags full of rice, Kakchand along with his wife & children embarked on a boat. The boat reached the centre of the large pond. Kakchand then told his wife : You are a Folk Tales of Trpura 445 woman of an extremely jealous nature. You are extremely cruel. Your jealousy resulted in the breaking up of our home. Your cruelty is largely responsible for the death of the members of my brother’s family. Even a stone would show kindness; but you did not! Kakchand broke the bottom of the boat with an axe. The boat sank. Amidst heart-rending cries, all the members of Kakchand’s family sank down. Thus a prosperous joint family which once held its head high among the citizens of Kailash-har passed into oblivion. 62. Raja Ramgati Meteoric rise & fall of a Bengali peasant suddenly animated and dazzled the people of southern Tripura.

The legend was one of bewilderment and bereavement. In the southern part of Tripura, certain areas like Belonia, Khandal, Dakshinsik & Tishna were the places of occurrence of the episode. It was in Belonia that the tale began. It happened during the late medieval period. The kings of Tripura were in power. By the usual corruption of words & names in Bengal, Suramani came to be known as Sura-kana. One of his eyes was injured; he was blind in one eye. Sura-kana’s son was Ramgati. Suramani was a hardworking, godfearing, illiterate, poor,- Bengali peasant. He was a metayer & a woodcutter. At his middle age, Suramani became physically handicapped. ' Thereupon, Ramgati, then aged about fifteen, had to shoulder the burden of the family. Ramgati had to go to the hills of Tripura for gathering firewood, vegetables, thatching grass, bamboo, etc. The distance between his village and the Tulshi Hill of Belonia was not a long one; the distance was only half a day’s walk for an active young man. He had to force his way along with difficulty, encountering bog, bushes, creepers, grasses & leeches. Ramgati was not alone in that hazardous task. Early in the middle of forenoon they used to set out and return Folk Tales of Tripura 446 in the afternoon. They used to doze and gossip and sit in the shade of a big banyan tree and smoke and wait for the return of all the woodcutters. They used to sell the forest products in the weekly markets‘and thus maintain their families and snudge. The hardships dried their faces & deepened their eyes. One day Ramgati alone halted & dozed peacefully in the shade of the tree. Exhausted, tired & stumbled, he

was brooding over his fate & future and in soliloquy called out loudly : Oh my god! when shall I get relief? And then suddenly came a voice; an oracle was uttered from a mysterious source. The voice was intelligible. The oracle said : Ramgati! your sufferings will come to an end; one day you will be a king. Ramgati woke up, looked at the sky and boggled. He reflected on the slender chance of getting relief from the drudgery. He came back with the bundles of firewood. But from that day, he was dreaming of becoming a king. New confidence, new strength, new vigour came into his mind, blood & sinews. The oracle served like a dynamo to animate him; his life became agog with ambition & activity, Casting aside his swaddling-clothes, Ramgati now started using fine clothes. He had two friends, namely Gour Karmakar and Dhaniram Patari. Gour’s nick-name was Goura Kamar. Gour & Dhaniram became his righthand men; they gave due publicity. People started honouring him and visiting his house at Kalikapur almost every afternoon and giving him gifts from forest & farm. The winter had gone and had left behind it a taste of the coming spring season. After about one year, Gour & Dhaniram talked to a priest & an astrologer to fix the date of coronation. The auspicious day of Maghi Purnima (January-February) was selected. At a solemn ceremony of bhajan, pujan, kirtan & bhojan held at Kalikapur of Belonia, Ramgati was proclaimed Raja. The priest, Radhakanta Thakur of Karaliya Tila of Belonia, officiated the ceremony. Ramgati’s honourable Gurudeva graced the Folk Tales of Tripura 447 occasion. Gour was appointed chief minister, and Dhaniram was appointed finance minister.

Now, the Raja’s preceptor was a tantrika. He required a sakhti in the form of a feminine energy. While leaving Ramgati’s house, the tantrika guru demanded one Sakti from the disciple to be furnished in future. The guru- dakshina was to be paid not now, but after a few years when the guru would reappear in disguise. Ramgati, Gour & Dhaniram assured to arrange it. The preceptor left with the. assurance. Things were going well with the new king. The subjects were paying homage to the new king. Gour provided necessary aid & advice. Dhaniram was in search of.a young lady for the preceptor. The country-bred patan knew. the ins & outs of numerous families. He had his informants. After a strenuous search, one girl, named Ayani was found out. Dhaniram went there and successfully convinced her & her parents. Dhaniram came back alone and informed Ramgati & Gour. A few years after, things took a different turn. The strange thing was that one Khoaj Mullah of Khajuria had a son named Hilal Gazi. Hilal Gazi was physically handicapped. Wearing their traditional dress, he used to visit from door to door for alms. One day Hilal Gazi came to the house of Raja Ramgati for begging. Supposing the beggar to be the preceptor of Ramgati, the illiterate & supersitious supporters of Ramgati started to bid Hilal Gazi a princely welcome. They bowed to him touching the ground with the eight parts of their body. Some of them laid their hands upon his feet and passed the hands over their forehead. Hilal Gazi was not prepared for such a reception. He reminded his true identity. But the credulous villagers would not listen to his identity. They

offered him dress, food & fruits. Meanwhile, at Dhaniram’s suggestion, Ayani was brought from her parental house. In a solemn ceremony, Raja Ramgati handed over Ayani to the guru. Folk Tales of Tripura 448 The week was one of mad recollection, wild & confused. For about one week the ceremony continued. It was a time distraught with anxiety. The guru & the sakti were adorned like Siva & Durga in the week-long ceremony. There was a coming & going of devotees & messengers. The news horribly disquieted Raja Krishnakisor Manikya of Tripura. The royal police rushed to Belonia and arrested Raja Ramgati, Gour, & Dhaniram, & the Guru and the Sakti and few others, and imprisoned them. Many people immediately fled away. Nothing happened till weeks later, when Khoaj Mullah successfully convinced the king about the identity of Hilal Gazi and got him released. The tragedy fell on Raja Ramgati like a thunderclap. The hand of the royal police lay tightly on the hand of Ramgati. The fools became the laughing stock of the police: Who the devil made you Raja? Your offence was one of treason! Ramgati’s legend passed into folk-lore & ballad. 63. Competitive foolishness? A peasant had his wife and three sons. His landed property was neither too small, nor too big. He arranged the marriage of his sons. The first son had one wife. The second son had two wives. The third son too had two wives. There were grandchildren in the family. The family became big and unmanageable. The young wives were quarrelling over the housework, and the children were quarrelling over the meals. Trifling issues tended to become major issues. The cold war put

psychological pressure on the old peasant. In order to get some peace at home, the old parent separated the three sons and divided the property among the three sons equally. He kept about an acre of land for himself & his wife. After their death, that-acre of land would be inherited by that son who had been the greatest fool of them. Folk Tales of Tripura 449 Years rolled on. The old parents died leaving the question undecided. For that piece of patrimony, the three sons began to claim superiority over the other in stupidity. They, however, failed to decide such a knotty question. They brought the issue before the notice of the village panchayet. The gaon panchayet did not decide immediately on their mere assertions, and instead, on a suitable day, sat together to hear their histories. | The first son related his story thus : One day in the late afternoon | went to the weekly market. It took long time to sell vegetables and to purchase groceries. I came back home late in the dark evening. The children were found asleep. My wife was waiting for me. I was very tired. We ate together and went to the bed together. But the door remained open. | asked my wife to close the door. Without considering my hard labour in the field and tension in the market, she asked me to close the door. We altercated for a while and then fell asleep without closing the door. The burglars easily committed burglary; they decamped with all my valuable things, ornaments, utensils, clothes and cash. Over a trifling task, | became sentimental. The price paid for the negligence was very heavy. I am fool indeed!

The second son told his story thus : Sir! you know well that I have two wives. One wife is the daughter of rich parents. Another wife is the daughter of poor parents. They have love & affection for me. They daily wash my hands & legs, and. prepare food. One of them has a son; and another has no son. It gave rise to ill-feeling; one day it outbursted. The rich wife said : With the utensils & vessels presented by my parents | wash my husband. The poor wife said : Since I could not bring such utensils & vessels as dowry, henceforth I like to carry my husband to the pond and wash him there. The rich wife claimed to wash first. The poor wife claimed to wash first. Both of them were uncompromising. A tug- of-war followed. They pulled my hands & legs. I felt Folk Tales of Tripura 450 Oo suddenly on the ground. I tossed, panted and cried out. But they were assiduously dragging me in opposite directions. At the intervention of the neighbours, they fell back. I was the victim of the quarrel of my wives. | am stupid indeed! The third son recounted his sad experience thus : Sir! you know well that I have two wives. For their maintenance I labour day & night. This is love’s labour. | undergo all troubles gladly. But one day I thought of testing their love;_so, | pretended to be seriously ill. I lay bedridden. I stopped talking and working. I was struggling with ill-health. Hearing the news, the first wife came hurrying to my side and expressed her own anxiety during my absence. She was deeply concerned about her

safety & security. She left. Then came the second wife; she said : If you die now, | will be in the sea of troubles. The time was December-January. The atmosphere was unbearably cool. I felt the pangs of the winter deep in my flesh. I was affected with fever, bodily heat and shivering. | consoled them and requested them to cure me as early as possible. I like to lie in the warmth of sunshine; so, I told them to carry me to the courtyard for basking. Placing my arms on their shoulders, I hobbled to the courtyard and lay on a sickbed. I was slowly smoking tobacco. Drowsiness came. Setting by my sides, they were talking loudly & hotly. I dissuaded them. But they paid no attention to my illness and advice. They started slamming, beating their foreheads, scuffling, and abusing each other. They dragged me. Meanwhile, the red-hot dottle from the hubble-bubble fell on my head. As I was shaggy-headed, the dottle started burning my hair. But alas! they continued to scream, shriek, scuffle and squabble. However, the neighbours rushed, and rescued me. Pretence would have been very fatal. I am idiot indeed! The gaon panchayet and the villagers sat for a long time to hear attentively, but did not pronounce their Folk Tales of Tripura 451 verdict then and there. After a period of pause & ponder, the gaon panchayet decided : the property should be equally divided. But dissatisfied with the decision, the fools savagely quarrelled among themselves and perished. 64. The Brahman family In a certain village lived a Brahman with his wife _and a son. The son was endowed with many qualities. The son grew from childhood to boyhood under the loving

care of the mother. The meritorious boy honourably passed all the examinations of Tol and Chatushpati, the ancient Bharatiya academies. The young student became proficient in various branches of traditional knowledge. Right from childhood, his father continued to instruct the boy in the rudiments of learning and at the same time to inculcate certain values. He was brought up strictly by his father. The father disciplined the son with a strict hand. Few students had talents like his; but he should be among the fewer who could remain unspoiled. Entirely different in spirit was the mother; she was an ordinary woman with pride & prejudice, enjoying the moderate material comfort and rejoicing in the son’s growing reputation. The son’s excellence was the main topic of her conversation. She would often admire him openly. She could not check the temptation. The father too was really affectionate; but he had the capacity of keeping the paternal affection balanced & suppressed in order to have something more from the son. His only worry was that the son should not suffer from complacence. The son should not remain satisfied with the present achievement. He should seek more & more knowledge. But the son seemed scarcely prepared to go that length. Admiration here & there made him buoyant. The family got on well till the marriage of the son. There lived an affluent Brahman family in another village; the family had a number of sons & daughters; on the basis of a proposal from such a famous family, the father of the brilliant son agreed to arrange the marriage. The Folk Tales of Tripura 452 newly-married daughter-in-law was smart, sweet- tongued and charming. Now, considering the greater responsibility of the

son, the conservative & sedate father continued to advise, rule & rectify the son. A few years passed, and with the coming of the daughter-in-law, an alienation between the father & the son was taking place slowly and imperceptively. The daughter-in-law seemed to have started slow-poisoning. The new couple did not comprehend the noble intention of the father. The son was now seen to bandy words with the father. The son was only waiting till the parents should find themselves alone. This he had arranged; he sent his wife to her father’s house, and he stealthily kept himself hidden in a very dark corner of the house with a sharp knife in his hand. He had the evil intention of killing his father outright. And while the cold war had been going on, the father remained unaware. At night, the old parents, finding themselves alone, started their dialogue. The mother accused the father for indulging in abusing & reviling the son. The father accused the mother for indulging in eulogy, and expressed his worry lest the son should suffer from complacence. Reciting a Chanakya-sloka, he explained that the indulgent parents and teachers were indirect enemies, while the strict parents & teachers were the real well- wishers. | The son was attentively overhearing the conversation. He had resolved to kill the father, let the cost be what it might. But now he realised his folly. The prick of conscience became acute. What a heinous crime he was going to commit! He sprang up, came out of the dark corner and fell at the feet of the father and confessed to him certain misgivings. He was weeping & weeping. The father pardoned him; but the son insisted on to

pay a heavy price for such an outrage. Nothing but death could wipe out such an attempt at patricide. The next Folk Tales of Tripura 453 alternative was to leave the parental home, and to live with the parents-in-law for twelve years. What a dramatic vicissitude! with a heavy heart & tearful eyes and head cast downward, the boy volunteered to leave the place of his pride to live servile life for twelve years. There he was not allowed to live independently & separately; he was to live with all the members of a big joint family. The mother’s eulogy and the wife’s abetment drove the brilliant boy to the path of an extreme crime. Now, the nemesis was inevitable. He must meekly digest all sorts of caprices, contempt, criticism, derision, disrespect and neglect. The young couple went there not as guests, but as criminals to spend a long period of rigorous imprisonment. There they were reduced to drawer of water and hewer of wood. They had to do all sorts of physical labour, without getting any respect & recognition. The relatives were hideously cruel to them. One day, he was asked to write a sloka (= aphorism, verse, etc.). The significant sloka was full of instructions : One should shake the seat before sitting; one should avoid the path frequented by ladies; one should avoid the place inhabited by criminals; one should restrain the senses and forgive. One intelligent merchant purchased the sloka. It had important guidelines. He was amply benefitted. The merchant had his merchandise in his boats. He went to a distant land where a gang of dacoits pretended to be generous people and invited the merchant to a feast.

The dacoits placed some explosives below the seat meant for the merchant. But the merchant, following the first instruction, shook the seat and the explosive material exploded. So, the instruction saved his life; he immediately left the place and took shelter in the boat. Next, the merchant, in course of his voyage, anchored near a place of matriarchy and magic. It was very difficult for young males to come out of the place. The merchant, Folk Tales of Tripura 454 following the second advice, did not go inland. Next, the merchant and his assistants reached a place of cheats. Following the third advice, the merchant left the place. The merchant had left home about twelve years ago. He was longing for homecoming. The merchant returned home. It was midnight. His wife eagerly, silently opened the door. But seeing a youngster in the bed, the merchant was about to kill him. But remembering the fourth advice, the merchant controlled himself and came to know that the youngster had been his son. So, the sloka saved the life of the dear son. In those days, voyage was highly risky. One had to suffer hunger, cold, hardship, misery and mischief. This merchant also faced trouble; but every time his sharp common sense, his acumen and his reliance on the sloka saved him. The merchant was not a brilliant student, but he was a practical man. His wife was made of a stern stuff. She did never abet her husband. During his absence, she looked after the entire household admirably. The return of the merchant from the voyage in distant lands was an occasion of joy to the family and the neighbours. The experience of the voyage became the

subject of discussion. The merchant was a modest man, with nothing of the opportunist in his nature. He was frank & free to admit the benefit derived from the sloka. After a few days, the merchant visited the house where the young couple had been working like servants for the last twelve years. The merchant admitted the benefit derived from the sloka. The grateful merchant again paid for the sloka. In the meantime, the period of penance came to an end. The young couple, after a lot of sad experiences, turned their steps homeward. 65. A scholar & a boatman Brahmanbaria is the name of a medieval village on the eastern bank of the mighty river Meghna; the river, originating from the hills of Manipur, flows northward Folk Tales of Tripura 455 and then southward and meets the Bay of Bengal near Noakhali. The kings of Tripurapatronised the settlement of many Brahmans in this village; hence it came to be known as Brahmanbarfa. It was the month of Sravana (= July-August). The rainy season was in its climax. One day, one Brahman scholar received a sad news of death of one of his relatives living in a village on the western bank of the river. So, he had to go there, and small boat was the only means of transport & communication in those days. Clad in white clothe, the Brahman set out with an umbrella and a small packet of sacred books and reached the river-ghat. A boatman was waiting there with his boat for passengers; he offered him a seat in the boat. The Brahman sat comfortably and asked the name of the boatman. The boatman replied : My name is Sumanta.

The Brahman remarked : Very good, a good name indeed! Do you know its history? Sumanta answered : Guruji! 1 do not know. The scholar said : You do not know the meaning & history of your name! Then, you have spoiled the four annas (= the first quarter; about 25 years) of your life. Long, long ago, Sumanta was the charioteer of Ram and Lakshman. Sumanta asked : Guruwji! What is inside your packet? The scholar replied : It contains some sacred books. Do you know what is written in these books? The boatman replied : I am illiterate; I do not know. The scholar commented : Then, you have frivolously frittered away eight annas (= the second quarter, about 50 years) of your life. What a waste of your time! A change came over Sumanta’s face. He said : Guruji! boating is my hereditary vocation. We are doing it generation after generation. If husking pedal goes to heaven even, it husks. Our family priest advised thus : Trust on god, but keep your powder dry. So, we annually worship the water goddess, Ganga Devi; and carry on this hazardous job. Folk Tales of Tripura 456 Sumanta’s pole of bamboo (=Laki) was beating the water. The boat was moving usually. The waves were marching against the boat; the boat was rushing. A fish leaped out of the water and plunged back into it. The scholar looked above & around. It stirred emotion in his mind. He stood up and stretched his arm toward the horizon. In north-east India rain often falls heavily; the rainfall of a month (July) is usually more than the rainfall of central India for one year. Nevertheless, suddenly,

the hope of the scholar was dumped by a violent gust of wind. A mighty thunder broke the conversation. Then came a squall of lightning, rain, tempest, storm. The waves of the water were splashing the boat violently. The boat was swinging. The terrible wind was shrieking past the ears of the scholar. In such a raging river neither man nor boat could hope to survive. The scholar’s bundle of books did not seem to be of any help; he stared at Sumanta with helplessness. He had read a number of books, but a mere reading of those books did not help him at the critical moment. Quite frightened, he was murmuring & weeping. But Sumanta was not the man to abandon hope and to surrender. He had faced several critical moments. He asked the scholar : Guruji! do you know swimming? If you can get out of the boat, do while there is time. The scholar replied : I do not know swimming. Sumanta remarked : Then, you are going to spoil the sixteen annas (four quarters) of your life. Sumanta was an astute boatman. He had a long rope to anchor & fasten the boat. He asked the scholar to hold an end of the rope very carefully. The other end of the rope was in the hand of Sumanta. Soon the boat got capsized. Sumanta swiftly jumped and began swimming very fast. The drowning scholar caught the rope. Sumanta struggled very hard and rescued the scholar. The scholar appreciated the robust common sense Folk Tales of Tripura 457 of Sumanta and blessed him heartily. Sumanta wittily added: I am not the fool you think I am. The scholar

walked away slowly towards his destination. 66. Ramkanta Babu & his dog Having tempestuously destroyed the university of Nalanda in 1201 A.D., and devastated the university of _ Vikramsilain 1203 A.D., Ikhtiyar Uddin Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khilji treacherously usurped the throne of Bengal in c. 1204 from Raja Lakshman Sen & unleashed the reign of terror. | Raja Lakshman Sen fled and took refuge at Vikrampur of Dacca in eastern Bengal. Streams of Hindus flowed eastward down all the roads leading in that direction. Anga & Vanga & Kalinga relapsed into barbarism; the decadent & demoralised natives had sunk into the depths of ignorance, chaos & confusion. Subsequently, when the fiendish hordes had extended their supremacy up to eastern Bengal, many fugitives concealed themselves in the jungles and crossed the mighty river Meghna to take shelter in the plains of Tripura. One such fugitive was the ancestor of Ramkanta Babu. Ramkanta Babu’s ancestor was active & energetic. The ancestor’s name was Gangaram. Gangaram was god- fearing peasant; he got settled at Vikrampur; he had his wife, and one daughter and one son. The daughter’s name was Yamuna; she was a charming girl. The son’s name was Kanuram. The alien hordes one day cruelly killed Gangaram & his wife, and kidnapped Yamuna; she became a fanatic renegade. Kanuram, being horrified, fled eastward. Kanuram became orphan. The orphan boy, being tired & hungry, took shelter in the shade of a big banyan tree. Being afraid of the alien tyranny, some families, at that time, turned their steps eastward with the intention of settling in the kingdom of Tripura. Kanuram came to Tripura with such a family and remained with the family for a few years.

The Meghna River was the natural borderline Folk Tales of Tripura 458 — ——~ between eastern Bengal and Tripura. The Meghna Valley was at that time very thinly populated. There were marshes, streams, patches of jungles and wild animals, birds, snakes, mosquitoes, fishes & crabs. In the early & medieval periods, individual men scarcely dared to face those hazards. Kanuram was now a young man; his body was strong enough to undergo hardship. With the blessing and permission of his guardian, he set up his own hearth & home. In the wilderness, there was scope for reclamation and extension of one’s farm. Kanuram took full advantage of the free gift of nature. The kings of Tripura were interested in the land revenue only. The affectionate guardian arranged the marriage of his daughter with Kanuram. Kanuram used to work with knife and hoe, and his wife used to carry away the earth in bamboo- baskets on her head in order to level the uneven land and to raise baulk & ridge. The young couple worked energetically with ambition & hope. The couple were careful to attend to every detail of the domestic issues. Within a few years, Kanuram became a rich landlord. Kanuram had a happy family with his wife and son and landed property. His son’s name was Ramgopal. The year Ramgopal had been born, Kanuram started the worship of Durga Devi. At the time of his death, Kanuram bequeathed to . his son a large estate, ponds, domestic animals & birds, and the tradition of the worship of Durga Devi. Ramgopal maintained the tradition faithfully. He did not add anything new to the estate. He struggled to maintain the tradition. He was wise to consolidate the

large estate; he did not take the risk of expansion. He too had a happy family with his devoted wife and son; the son was named Ramkanta. At the time of his death, Ramgopal bequeathed to his son the large estate and the tradition of the worship of Durga Devi. Ramkanta Babu had a watch dog. The dog was Folk Tales of Tripura 459 healthy & courageous, running round with curly tail held erect and barking in a terrifying manner at the slightest hint of burglary. In the evening, during the rainy season in particular, the wild jackals used to slink & sneak about the fields & farms for fish, crab & domestic birds, and at times used to yell one after another. The yelling of the jackals would be challenged by the responsibe barking of the village dogs. Ramkanta Babu was moderate in eating & in personal expenditure; but he was liberal in the distribution of bounty to his relatives, neighbours and domestics. His conversation was sprightly. The villagers were happy with his behaviour; they used to wait eagerly for the arrival of the month of the worship of Durga Devi. It was a festival of the village. The villagers used to do all menial work gladly & spontaneously. For three days (seventh, eighth & ninth tithi in the evening a group of young men used to dance, clashing symbols, beating drums and brass metals and holding burning charcoal in an earthen pot. The men, women and children used to Swarm in front of the temple. There was a visible atmosphere of goodwill. Prashad and food were important parts of the festival. Particularly on the eighth tithi the villagers themselves would take rice, pulses, vegetables

& spices from the store of Ramkanta Babu and cook and eat together at noon. Ramkanta Babu’s dog was neither a pet dog nor a guide dog. The dog belonged to the category of guard dog & watchdog. The dog’s natural tendency was to guard & protect the owner’s property, & to sound the alarm at the approach of strangers. The dog would face a strange dog or any other beast stiffly with tail held erect and with a threatening growling. So, for about five days, Ramkanta Babu had to take a precautionary measure: he would tie the dog to a pole at a safe distance with.a tether. The dog would snap & snarl. To pacify the dog, Ramkanta Babu used to caress the dog from time to time. Folk Tales of Tripura 460 The dog was very much devoted to him. The new arrival into the family of Ramkanta Babu was named Ramdulal. The parents and the relatives and the neighbours were quite happy at the birth of the baby. It was impressed upon Ramdulal from his early childhood that he was to have the opportunity of inheriting a large estate. This privilege was always held before him as a great luck. Consequently he had no struggle, no sacrifice, no suffering in his life; he was grown up amidst plenty & pleasures. He was an easygoing and good-natured young man. A quiet, easy life in his native village was his natural element. In bringing up the child, the parents did not accustom Ramdulal to domestic jobs! Upon the death of Ramkanta Babu, the mantle fell on the young shoulders of Ramdulal. The devoted dog was terribly shocked by the death of Ramkanta Babu.

The dog stopped taking food immediately after the death of Ramkanta Babu. The dog died thus. Ramdulal now took up the work of management. He too wielded influence over his neighbours; he too maintained the tradition of the worship of Durga Devi. But in the absence of the watchdog, he hired a dog from a neighbour and tied the hired dog to a pole with a tether for five days. To him tethering the dog was a part of the festival. Ignorant of the logic, he followed it blindly. He failed to grasp what lay behind the act of tethering; he failed to get at the wisdom of precaution; such a poor quality of reasoning was advantageous to the mischief mongers! 67. Kill the cat in the first night of marriage There was a rich peasant; he was adventurous, ambitious & a bit arrogant. His wife was beautiful, but a bit indulgent. The family had lands, farms, fields, ponds, cattle & servants. The couple had two twin daughters only. The daughters were brought up in luxury. They used to indulge in rich diet and costly dress. Time rolled on. The daughters attained the age of puberty. They were healthy, wealthy and haughty. Folk Tales of Tripura 461 Naturally the parents were thinking about the marriage of their daughters. As they had no son, they expected the prospective grooms to settle in the bride’s house. The daughters added one more condition: the grooms must be ready to tolerate a good number of flaps of slipper on their heads daily. There were youths eager to marry the healthy and beautiful girls. The prospect of inheriting the large property was alluring to them. They were ready to be

gharjamai (= son-in-law in parent-in-law’s house). But the humiliating condition of flapping daily by the bride was a serious & disappointing one. There were ghataks (=match- makers) in almost every village. The rich peasant assured the local match-maker a good gift for his service. The match-maker, after his best efforts, convinced two poor youths. The two poor youths argued to themselves: pain is forgotten where gain follows. We are suffering from Starvation; there we shall get all comforts and rich diet. So, what is the harm ? One day, the match-maker along with the two poor youths came to the house of the peasant. The peasant enquired about their whereabouts and reiterated the conditions clearly and directly. The two poor youths agreed to abide by the conditions. The peasant had already made adequate arrangement for the residence of the would-be couples in two separate houses, quite distant from one another. On an auspicious day the two marriage ceremonies were simultaneously solemnised. Immediately after the completion of the rituals, the couples were sent to their respective houses. The submission of the young husbands to their wives was complete; they could not go out. The marriage had made them members of a community in which they were treated like aliens. After a few months, the two brothers met on the way. One brother was found miserable with baldness on his head. The other brother was found cheerful with Folk Tales of Tripura 462 dark hair and healthy body. The baldheaded brother wanted to know the mystery of his brother’s cheerfulness. The cheerful brother said : In the very night of marriage, arrangement was made at the floor of the house for offering the first food & clothe to me ; at that time one

hungry pet cat slipped round me. The cat was mewing with an intention to sneak fish from my dish. I instantly & forcefully struck the cat’s head. The cat fell unconscious and died. Deeply terrified, the new bride never dared to flap. The foppish & drab bride changed her tune and said : I am the half of yourself. Knowing the secret of the cheerful brother’s happiness, the sorrowful brother returned home with a determination to imitate the brother. The sullen young man became serious. In the evening he sat at the floor of the dining-room to take his meal. As usual, one pet cat slipped round him. Instantly he whammed the pet. The cat died. His wife was there. She at once sprang to her feet and wrathfully grimaced. She disparagingly and angrily said : You, poor fellow ! have you forgotten the condition of marriage? What prompted you to kill my pet cat? Henceforth, I will teach a good lesson with one hundred strokes daily. In an agony of repentance & fear, the tactless brother left the dining-room without taking food and threw himself on the bed. But the bold bride took her full meal. She came with a slipper and taught him a good lesson with one hundred strokes. Since that night, she beat him black & blue. She was a rigorous taskmistress! a formidable force! The imprudent brother killed the cat too late. It was too late indeed! So, he was destined to suffer and perish in the quagmire. The younger brother was naturally anxious about the health of the elder brother. After a few years the younger brother managed to meet the feeble-minded elder brother and found him almost

completely shattered and commented : Dada, you F -ve Folk Tales of Tripura 463 rere irrecoverably lost the first chance in the first night of marriage. As time went on, the elder brother’s position grew more and more difficult & distressful. The surrender of liberty for luxury is ruinous. 68. He bites the hand that feeds him Rambali was born in a peasant family. He was likely to have a sense of a little of buoyant feeling, because of his moderate income from two sources : landed property, and service under the Tripura Raj. Rambali was by profession a Muhun, by conviction an idealist honest man and by temperament tactless egoist. He was neither tall nor short. He was a man of some capacity. Anybody who had gone to him for help got it. One day a young man named Rajkumar came from a distant village. His identity was obscure. His parentage was unknown. He approached Rambali for help. Rambali smiled at him and directed him to sit on a bench. He talked to him and asked him to come again after two days. The young man retired to the house of his distant . relative. . It was a fateful evening. Rambali & his younger brother sat for the Supper. The meal was served. Meanwhile, Rambali said : A young boy sought our help; | like to donate a few acres of land; what is your opinion? The younger brother looked thoughtful first and afterward said : The young boy seems to be active but wicked; we should think twice in this respect. Rambali blurted out to the brother - You are narrow-minded ‘and selfish. Rambali suddenly stood up, threw away the dish

of food, spurned his wooden seat and left the kitchen room without eating food. The kick split the wooden seat into two parts. The rice & curry lay strewn. That night other members of the family were not in a position to take their food. Rambali blustered; the brother murmured & the ladies whispered. All went to bed. The next day Rambali verbally donated about five acres of land to the voung boy. And the following day Folk Tales of Tripura 464 Rambali took him to the eastern hills; introduced him with the village chief of the hills people and requested the chief to sell all cotton to Rajkumar for his business. The young boy soon earned a lot from the business. He built his hut; purchased a pair of bullocks and started cultivation. Within a year or two he purchased fertile lands and married. But the young man turned out very mischievous at first imperceptibly, but as the years rolled on, more daringly. He took part in plots & intrigues against his benefactor. The abominable atmosphere of conspiracy that Rajkumar introduced brought in sycophancy & cliquishness. Rajkumar said to himself : I must secure alliance with this clan. The younger brother of Rambali had a daughter; the intriguer arranged the marriage of the daughter with one of his own kinsman. As the years rolled on, the intriguer became the father of a son and a daughter. The plotter arranged the marriage of his daughter with a sycophant belonging to the clan of Rambali. Thus the plotter tightened his own hands, and strengthened his grip against the idealist donor. Behind his eagerness to pursue the cotton business vigorously, to purchase additional lands quickly, to buy a pair of

healthy bullocks visibly, to build a comfortable house distinctly & to marry early lay his impatience to spoil the reputation of Rambali, to emulate & outshine Rambali. Earlier, Rambali had established a Pathsala- (= a village school) on his own plot of land at the eastern shore of his frontal tank of water. It became very popular. To disgrace Rambali, the intriguer made plots and got the school shifted at a place near the house of his son- in-law. Rambali next proceeded to establish another school in hill Tripura. To check the recurrence of raids from the eastern hills, the British government took an effective step by way of demarcating the boundary line in 1854. ‘olk Tales of Tripura 465 Now, Rambali established his second school in hill Tripura, about two miles eastward from his house. Rambali had three daughters. And one of the daughters, Basanti, became widow. She lost her husband and sons; they died of cholera; creeping into a palanquin, she had gone to her father-in-law’s house with hope. Basanti came back on foot to her father’s house with despair. Possessed of inordinate greed, the intriguer had an eye on the property of Rambali who had no male successor up till now. The absence of a male heir cast a dark shadow over the mind of Rambali. During the dewy . season, Rambali made his last & successful attempt for a son. Rambali & his wife started on the adventurous journey, which after terrible hardship led them to the famous temple of Kali Devi in Calcutta. They bowed down and lay prostrate in humble reverence & prayer. They continued in that position for three days & nights; on

the third day the priest offered them two red flowers (= Jaba) and blessed them. His wife swallowed the flowers. They came back home. In course of time two sons were born : Sures & Mahes. The news of birth of the two sons was shocking to the intriguers. It frustrated their plot of grabing the property of Rambali. For a time Rambali saw happy days. But tragedy was in the air. He was extremely worried about the future of his daughter & sons. The problem of their security used to worry him day & night. So seriously did his mental health suffer from the plots & intrigues that Rambali, fearing that his children would be suborned to death, himself became a victim of heart disease. Worse was to follow speedily. In October he performed the traditional worship of Durga Devi. The next day he cut dry bamboo & wood and said : If I suddenly die, you will be in great trouble.’ He realised that his sun was setting fast. On the third day he died. Rambali, who had not injured anybody during the course of his life of 62 years, passed away Silently. Folk Tales of Tripura 466 Now, the responsibility of performing the cremation, observing the mourning, accomplishing the funeral rites, looking after the young brothers and managing the estates fell upon the young shoulders of Basanti. She arranged a meeting of the village elders & priests. They decided to accomplish the rite solemnly & simply, and to entertain the kinsmen & near relatives only. Day after day went by. On the 13th day the rite & feast were arranged. It was now noon. Streams of people, in

hundreds & thousands, were found coming. The bereaved family did not invite them. Still the people were coming & coming. It was beyond the imagination & arrangement of the family! On being politely asked, they reported that Rajkumar had invited them on behalf of the bereaved family. Rajkumar was not at all authorised to invite. It was utterly beyond the capacity of the bereaved family to entertain them. But following the prevailing social custom, arrangement was made; as many as sixty two chullah were made and the invitees were humbly requested to prepare their food. Only one family of the kinsmen came forward and offered additional quantity of rice, vegetables & pulses to meet the emergency. It was the family of Bhagavatiprasad. What was more shocking was that while the Sraddha ceremony had been going on, Rajkumar appeared upon the scene and directed Basanti to bring out stashed money. Basanti said : There is no hidden treasure. Rambali’s monthly salary was of one figure only. Rajkumar became furious; he came with hoe, spud & chopper; he crushed & pulled down the fence of bamboo & timber-work of the hut, and started digging the floor with spud & hoe. It was a fearful spectacle, a panic! Disorder in the house : floor dug, earthenware smashed, bedding thrown down, wooden seats overset; fence wrecked, utensils scattered about, roof twitched, etc. spoke of the terrible audacity of Rajkumar, and utter helplessness of the bereaved family and lack of solidarity Folk Tales of Tripura 467 a epee ce of the clan. The spectators were stunned at the devastation. “Hearing this, the world keeps mum, like picture dumb.” During the heinous operation, Rajkumar’s battle-cry was : ‘Basanti! unearth money’, ‘Basanti!

unearth money’. He used to repeat the battle-shout with every strike, with every swoop, with every kick. Rajkumar found no money, as there had been no hidden treasure. Rajkumar strutted out of the house. Tears rolled down through the wrinkled face of Rambali’s widow. The members of Rajkumar’s family chuckled! While Rajkumar had epitomized perfidy and ingratitude, his son Kaliprasanna was the perfect example of conspiracy & cruelty. Kaliprasanna had it to say : Barber and washerman should be beaten once a year for getting better service. It was his conviction & practice. The father and the son made considerable inroads into the clan and the village of Rambali. They elicited loyalty. They resorted to the use of terror and a secret service. The shrewd son went further, and made family- relation with another family of the village. That family had one widow. The widow had no child. Kahprasanna gave her occasional gifts and addressed her as his adopted daughter. His intention was to utilise the widow as his secret agent against the family of Rambali. The widow’s name was Subodhbala. Being persuaded by Kaliprasanna, Subodhbala under the pretension of good-will visit, made a few attempts to drop pellet of poison into the drinking water pot of Rambali’s family. She made similar attempt against Bhagavatiprasad, because Bhagavatiprasad had given rice & pulses in October. Her attempts failed because of the cautiousness of the two families. After that, Subodhabala’s conscience pricked : ‘What would happen to me after my death? What am I doing? This question worried her; she secretly admitted the guilt and disclosed the news of the plot to the families concerned and warned them. Folk Tales of Tripura 468

Jealous of the family of Rambali, the plotter went about very cunningly to accomplish his evil design. Kaliprasanna attempted to bribe a sorcerer to kill Basanti, Sures & Mahes through black magic. The local sorcerers disagreed. Then he went to the eastern hills, & bribed a powerful sorcerer. The sorcerer directed him to collect hair, nail, piece of clothe of the target. Kaliprasanna compelled the local washerman & barber to collect those objects. The barber secretly kept the target group informed. It portended something dangerous. Basanti immediately took preventive steps : she secretly invited a local sorcerer, and the sorcerer made talismans for all the members of the family. Poaching & illegal timber cutting were very common crimes committed by Kaliprasanna. He would some time let his cattle loose at night in the fields of Rambali to devour the young plants. He would secretly throw broken pieces of glass, filth, garbage, litter, wastage, iron, etc. into the fields of Rambali. The cultivation of those lands was highly risky because of that nuisance. The land revenue due to the donated lands had to be paid by Rambali & his children; the lands were only verbally donated; so officially Rambali & his children were responsible to the government for the payment of land revenue. The spontaneous celebration of games & sports on the occasion of Chaitra Sankranti (= middle of April) used to arouse great enthusiasm in the village. The games would be played by boys & young men, while a motley crowd used to enjoy and gossip. On such an occasion, Sures & Mahes participated in one side. Kaliprasanna was in the opposite side; he plotted to swindle and strangulate Sures & Mahes to death. One intelligent

neighbour, apprehending the evil motive & impending murder, indicated indirectly to Sures &Mahes; Sures & Mahes immediately withdrew, retired and fled. Henceforth Basanti never allowed her brothers to participate in such games. Folk Tales of Tripura 469 The death of Basanti was a great loss to the family. For about four decades she shouldered the risks & responsibility of her father’s family. The savage hatred & jealousy of Rajkumar’s family against the family of Rambali turned into a menace to the village. Basanti had to bear the brunt of the brutality. Terror paralysed the village life. Everybody used to dread that refugee family. The notorious refugee became the defacto ruler of that village. Kaliprasanna raised a high & strong embankment across a shallow gorge, obstructing the natural outlet of water, with the evil motive of submerging the crops of Sures & Mahes in the gorge. Mahes was out of the Station; the royal administration did not sanction leave; his wife Pritilata arranged a meeting of the village elders and lodged the complaint. They listened to her complaint, shook their heads, chewed betel leaf, emitted tobacco smoke, whined, mumbled, murmured and left. With her usual strength of mind, Pritilata later derisively pointed out the precedents of their cowardly behaviour. After a few months, banks of clouds appeared & heralded lightning, thunderstorms and heavy shower. The gorge looked like a sea. At last, the accumulated water gushed out suddenly and broke the embankment violently & loudly. Kaliprasanna had one distant relative in the capital of Tripura and he was in the royal service. Being provoked by Kaliprasanna, that very relative destroyed the service records of Mahes and inflicted a heavy damage. Kaliprasanna’s wife was a fraud; she made a number

of attempts to cheat the family. She, one day, approached Pritilata & said in a twangy tone : I like to go to my relative’s house, but I have no gold ornaments; kindly give your gold ornaments for a week only; I shall return those ornaments after coming back home. Pritilata quickly understood the evil motive & refused to lend her ornaments. Kaliprasanna’s son was another swindler: he too attempted to deceive. Folk Tales of Tripura 470 The villagers became divided into three groups; one very small group supported Rambali’s family; one group incited Rajkumar’s family; a large group remained neutral, timid spectators. Misjudgement and misplacement of charity lay at the root of sufferings of Rambali’s family! Some myths & legends of Tripura-land Several ancient settlements in Tripura had their local myths and legends. Some of these myths and legends became famous, and found place in the royal chronicle of Tripura. Tripura remains an ancient source of mythology. However, many myths and legends have become obscure; some of them have passed into oblivion. An account of a few myths & legends is noted here. 1. Sati’s right leg fell in Tripura Here we have a very ancient myth, known all over Hindusthan. Brahma had several sons; Daksha was one of them. Daksha had several sons and daughters; Sati was one of them. Sati was blossomed into a charming girl; Sati was given to Siva. But the relation ended in tragedy. | The bohemian life of Siva was disgusting to Daksha. Siva had some malevolent demons and spirits and snakes as his associates; Siva had burning ghats and dark places as his favourite abodes; Siva had hemp and tobacco and wine as his favourite drinks. Siva was arrogant and

unpredictable. Once Prajapati arranged a sacrifice ( Yajna). Siva and many others were present. When Daksha had entered the place, Siva did not stand up to show respect to Daksha. Daksha silently decided to take vengeance on Siva. Accordingly, after some time Daksha arranged a big sacrifice and invited many high dignitaries; but he did not invite Sati and Siva. Upon hearing the good news of the magnificent sacrifice, Sati decided to go there uninvited; Siva tried to dissuade her. But the restless daughter went to the careless father’s house. Daksha Folk Tales of Tripura 471 did not talk to her, and did not even look at her. Sati felt neglected and insulted. Daksha’s derogatory remarks about Siva added insult to the injury. Even the invited guests also ridiculed and grimaced and bestowed a contemptuous look on Sati. Sati felt a violent commotion and pain inside. Unable to check her anger and emotion, Sati rushed and jumped into a fire to commit self- immolation. Apprehending the dire consequences of Siva’s violent reaction, the invited guests fled away helter-skelter. In the pandemonium the ceremony was utterly disturbed. Siva came to know of the tragedy. He became very furious. His retinue destroyed everything in the house of Daksha. Not only that, Siva himself came down to the spot of sacrifice and took the dead body of Sati on his shoulders. Siva roamed about in the world and started crying “Sati, Sati”. Siva and his retainers started to create havoc in the world. The hermits and the sages became very afraid. The ordinary people and even the animals shivered. Siva carried her deadbody over on his shoulders not without difficulty to himself and to others.

At long last, the gods sought the aid and advice of Vishnu. Vishnu sent his Sudarsan chakra to cut the corpse into pieces. Thus various parts of the corpse fell at different places. Altogether fiftyone pieces fell at fiftyone places. In this way every spot became a famous Pithasthan. The right leg of Sati fell in Tripura on the bank of the river Gomati. That very place had become a very popular centre of pilgrimage; it was once the capital of Tripura. The place is now known as Udaypur. It is located about 50 miles to the south of Agartala. The kings of Tripura adorned it with tanks and temples. 2. The killing of Tripurasur An ancient locality in the Gomati Valley had another remarkable myth. It runs as follows: Brahma’s son was Marichi; Marichi’s son was Kasyapa. Daksha’s son-in-law was Kasyapa. Aditi and Folk Tales of Tripura 472 Diti were Daksha’s daughters; Aditi and Diti were Kasyapa’s wives. Aditi was mother of some Devas; Diti was mother of some demons. The relation between the two groups of children was not at all satisfactory. In course of time they turned into hostile forces. The devas under the leadership of Indra, and the Ashuras under the leadership of Tarakashura and Hiranyakasipu, etc. fought on a number of occasions. The churning of the ocean of milk was a famous occasion. The nectar, emerged from the ocean, made the devas energetic; the ashuras were left enervative. The ashuras did severe penance and received a boon from Brahma. The ashuras appraoched Maya to build for them three cities. Maya built Tripura. The ashuras renewed their atrocities against the devas. The aggrieved devas approached Siva. Siva made

elaborate preparations to teach the ashuras a lesson. The devas approached Viswakarma to construct a chariot and other weapons for Siva. The devas supplied all necessary provisions. Siva and his associates settled on the bank of the river Gomati. Thus equipped, Siva stayed with full preparation. At last, a terrible battle ensued. The leader of the ashuras, Tripurashura, was killed on the spot. Along with the leader, thousands of ashuras were murdered. The bones of the demons were left scattered here and there. . The hills and valleys of Tripura were strewn with ashurer haddi (= demons’ bones). A temple was erected on the spot. The spot became a centre of pilgrimage. The kings of Tripura took care to protect and preserve the spot with temples and walls and tanks. The spot, where Sati’s right leg fell, lies only a few miles to the south of this spot of Tripurashura- vadha. 3. The god’s tragic visit to Tripura Unakoti Parvat is the name of a hill range in the north-east corner of Tripura. In other words, it lies to Folk Tales of Tripura 473 the south-west of Assam. A treasure of incalculable value _ lay there in this very Unakoti Parvat. Here we have a very old myth. The myth runs as follows: Once a group of gods held a discussion. The conversation turned on religion. Are all the people pious enough to perform the rites and rituals? Some people may not have faith or time to observe ceremonies! So a team of gods-decided to personally verify the matter. The adventure was got ready. The gods descended at the foot hills of the Himalayas. They had to pass time here in incognito. Here they were, as if, wandering

travellers and pilgrims. ; They were duly ‘received by some sages. They halted and rested there for a few days. The sages offered hospitality and then directed them in their onward journey. In the course of the long journey, numerous deities and their retainers came to join, from sheer love of adventure. Walking and walking, and crossing many mountain peaks and rivers and valleys, and encountering many wild animals, the deities at long last came to the north- east corner of Tripura. It was a beautiful hill, surrounded by tropical forests. Even only a thousand years ago, the circumstances of Tripura were significantly different from those with which we are familiar in the twentyfirst century. The gross and materialistic behaviour of the people disappointed the gods; out of despair, some of the gods bemoaned. But what should be the rational solution? The famous shrines like Gaya, Kasi, Mathura and Vrindaban were very distantly situated! As a sort of solution to the problem, the gods decided to build up another shrine in Tripura. They selected the hill for the construction of the proposed shrine. One crore gods were expected to assemble on the eighth day of the bright fortnight of Chaitra (April-May) at the site of the new shrine. The supreme God cautioned them to complete the work within one night and to leave Folk Tales of Tripura 474 the shrine before dawn. In a team-spirit they finished the work; but one god was found missing. Hence the assemblage was one short of a crore; that is, unakoti. All the gods were waiting for the missing god to arrive. Besides, they were extremely tired. However, they were supposed to leave before the first caw of a crow. But

alas! As fate would have it, a crow cried out, and all the gods were immediately transformed into images of stone. Thus, the adventure ended on an air of urgency and tragedy. Henceforth, the hill came to be known as Unakoti Parvat, and it became a very old shrine to attract pilgrims. Pilgrims visit it once a year on the occasion of Astami- snan mela in the month of Chaitra (April-May). An obscure legend even connects it with Kapil Muni : Kapil Muni also had practised tapashya in this shrine. The sacred hill has two names: Unakoti Parvat, and Raghunandan Parvat; situated atop the hill, the shrine had picturesque beauty; but the disastrous earthquake of 12 June 1897 utterly ravaged the shrine. 4. Treasure in a pond Hrishyamukh is the name of a prosperous locality in the south-western corner of Tripura. It consists of a cluster of villages. Most of the residents are of the Bengali Hindu castes. Hrishyamukh lies to the western foothill of the Tulshi Parvat, and to the east of the district of Noakhali. Noakhali was within the kingdom of Tripura. To the western side of Hrishyamukh, there was a rural hamlet. Within that hamlet there was a very ancient pond of considerable size. With its lonely surroundings, big size, high embankments, formidable depth of water, sacrificial wooden post at the centre of the water, and thickly wooded shores, the pond was a geographic nightmare for a solitary traveller. From a tall, thorny date-tree would hang a few nests of the little weaver-birds. From the branches of a tall tree many bats would remain from morning to evening in a hanging Folk Tales of Tripura 475 ©

position with heads cast downward. In the evening many foxes would skulk and scream loudly. According to popular belief, a treasure of incalculable value lay there in the pond. Here we have a little-known myth. The myth runs as follows:- Once upon a time a poor and pious family had an auspicious occasion of worship of a deity. The poor family could not make adequate arrangements. Naturally, the husband and wife were in great tension. At the eleventh hour, the goddess appeared to the wife in the form of an old woman, and sought a handful of rice. The wife gladly offered. The old woman observed the look of tension on her face and wanted to know the cause of her despair. The wife explained. The old woman then said: My daughter! you clean the ghat of the pond with broom, water, cowdung; and offer flowers, tulshi leaf & lamp there and solicit the number of plates, glass, bowl, jar, etc. from the deity of the pond; and after the completion of the ceremony, clean those utensils and return honestly. The old woman suddenly vanished; and the wife informed her husband about the advice. It was worth a try. The next day they followed the advice and mysteriously found many utensils of gold. It was a great relief to the family. After the ceremony, they took care to return all the utensils. The invited guests were astonished to see the utensils and plates. Upon an inquiry, they came to know the mystery. Henceforth, it became a relief to the residents of the locality; they too duly worshipped the deity and in return used to get those utensils and to return accordingly.

After many years of happy alliance between the deity and the local devotees, a sad experience happened. One family duly sought utensils and got those utensils. But the greedy housewife stashed one utensil inside a heap of cowdung. The rest of the utensils were returned. Alas! the utensils remained at the ghat for three days and three nights. Rumour spread. The goddess appeared to Folk Talés of Tripura 476 the housewife in dream and directed her to return the utensil the very next day. Afraid of the dire consequences, she returned it and confessed her guilt. Henceforth, the deity stopped the practice of lending the precious utensils. Not only that, a great flood overflooded the locality and the pond. The next day the middle portion of the western bank of the pond was found broken. The big cage of utensils left the pond and went to the Bay of Bengal through the passage. S. The spot where one horse was shot dead by a prince Ghora-mara chhara is the name of a stream in the western part of Tripura. Flowing from the north-eastern hillocks & valley, the stream meets the river Haora near a locally well-known village named Ranir-bazar. The stream was named after a sad incident. The legend is quite clear and consistent. It runs as follows:- Attacks by the enemy aliens kept on rushing the princes and the people of Tripura for centuries. The ruling dynasty had to shift its capital several times. The penultimate shifting was in 1760 A.D. by Maharaj Krishna Manikya (1748-1783). The last two capitals were known by the same name, Agartala, or at best old Agartala & new Agartala. In 1838 A.D. a primary begining was made

lor new Agartala; The princes and the people lived on in old Agartala. The town of old Agartala stood in the east, while the town of new Agartala stood in the west; the distance between the two towns was of a few miles. The tract between the two towns consisted of valleys, paddy fields, river and streams and hamlets. Maharaj Birchandra Manikya (1862-1896) had several sons and daughters; Radhakisor (1856-1909) and Samarendrakisor (1862-1935) were famous princes of Maharaj Birchandra Manikya. Radhakisor and Samarendrakisor were step-brothers. Later, Radhakisor became the next king (1896-1909). Maharaj Radhakisor Manikyva was habitually ,charitable, high-minded, moderate and temperate. Folk Tales of Tripura 477 i — Right from his boyhood, Samarendrakisor was given indulgence by his parents (= Maharaj Birchandra Manikya and Rani Bhanumati Devi). He used to move here and there recklessly. His character was full of contradictions, of good and bad qualities. He wrote excellent books; but selfishness was his ruling passion. He used even black magic against his elder brother, Radhakisor. He plotted to trouble and endanger Radhakisor. He had a terrible streak of cruelty and violence in him. One day in the morning Samarendrakisor set forth upon his way from old Agartala to new Agartala. The plain land on both sides of the road was rich with crops. The prince rode on his horse. The young prince was strong and stout, bright and beautiful. He was moving faster than a walk, but not so fast as gallop. The dusty road would remain a little busy and crowded with carts, cows, peasants, merchants and the royal servants. But the prince with his horse was a masher. His dazzling dress was his mark of distinction. The people and the peasants

used to leave space for the prince. They would shout in his honour. After covering a distance, the prince trotted his horse to a narrow stream. The stream was narrow and shallow. The horse was hesitant to cross the stream by a gallop. The horse baulked. The prince expected the horse to cross the stream through a long jump. The prince whipped the horse. But the horse remained hesitant. The prince could not control his anger; he dismounted and unsheathed his pistol and promptly shot the horse. The horse lay dying whining with pain and eyes popping. The peasants rushed to the spot, but they had to press their palms across their mouths. They ' stared. The prince strutted back to old Agartala. Folk Tales of Tripura 478 Appendices 1.
