This collection of folk-tales has two major divisions; one group of tales is related to the culture of the greater Tripuri communities; another group of tales is related to the culture of the Bengali people. A folk-tale is called Kereng Kathma by the Tripuri communities. A folk-tale is called Rupkatha or Galpa by the Bengali people. The Tripuri communities have preserved much of

their ancient culture and possess a great store of folk- lore. Tripura State Tribal Cultural Research Institute has done a commendable service in the collection and compilation and publication of several folk-tales of the Tripuri communities. The Education department of the Government of Tripura also has done a praiseworthy work in the collection and publication of some folk-tales of the Tripuri communities. High hills, dense forests, springs, rivers, wild animals and birds, a subsistence economy, simple technology, compact village life, bachelors’ dormitory, polytheism, magic, witchcraft and sorcery, etc. once used to provide an ideal background for the survival of many myths and tales. In the Tripuri folk-tales there are stories about animals, plants, family life, love & romance, humour, Folk Tales of Tripura 479 jealousy, cruelty, wickedness, foolishness, unusual heroism, magic, chain of events and formula, Cinderella, etc. The stories about the cunningness of fox are almost absent in the Tripuri folk-tales. Significantly another group of tales about the capacity of Muslim Pirs and Fakirs are absent in the Tripuri folk-tales. Another aspect about the Tripuri folk-tales is that Chand Sadagar type of character is conspicuously absent. Not only that, no Tripuri folk-tale begins with the common formula of many Bengali tales : “There was a poor Brahman”. But, there are many stories of metamorphosis and some stories of heroism. A myth regarding the nearness of heaven and earth is to be found in Tripura also. The Tripuri folk-tales have a certain categories of characters. Such as (a) deities, demons®ghosts, fairies; (b) wild & domestic animals, birds, snakes, insects; (c) gatherers, hunters, shifting cultivators, priests, chiefs, kings and adventurers; (d) even local flora. Some of the Tripuri folk-tales are very buoyant; these

stories give the impression that behind them there are reserves of power, the monarchy. Tripuri gods are thought, of marrying and having children and forming relations - with mortals; this picturesque Tripuri anthropomorphism has partly coloured the Tripuri myths & folk-tales. In this respect, Greek imagination and Tripuri imagination are identical. As with the tales of all countries, so with the Tripuri folk-tales, the primary aim is to give enjoyment to the hearers, particularly to the children to whose compelling demand ‘lease tell us a story’ many elders often submit. Besides, folk-tales constitute one of the instruments of social control. How jealousy, cruelty, greediness and selfshness are invariably punished by some mysterious ways is shown through folk-tales; how love and affection, service and sacrifice, courage and wit are rewarded is also exemplified. Next, to come to the Bengali folk-tales, a few words Folk Tales of Tripura 480 have to be added. The Bengali folk-tales also have the primary aim of entertainment, and have the lessons of punishing evil deeds, and rewarding noble deeds. Here it may be relevant to refer to the country tales of Britain; John Wain edited Selected Stories of Thomas Hardy (1840- 1928), and Macmillan, London, published those stories in 1966. In the introduction, John Wain wrote: “The traditional country tale often deals with high-born people, whose lives were a natural focus of interest to the villagers.” It is well-known that the Bengali society belongs to the traditional four-fold caste structure. And usually, life of the Brahmans was the natural focus of respect and interest. So, the common formula of most of the Bengali folk-tales is to begin with the phrase ‘There was a poor Brahman.’ Besides, the stories of Chand

Sadagar, of trickster Teton (=Tetna, Tedon), of fox, of birds and animals, are common in the Bengali folk-tales. The popular formula tale of the crow has its close parallel in the Assamees also. The Cinderella type of tales are also common in the Bengali tales. It is very significant to point out that an air of helplessness, of surrender and submission, of an appeal for divine redress, is conspicuous in some of the Bengali folk-tales. Bengali gods are thought of as marrying and having children and forming relations with mortals; this picturesque Bengali anthropomorphism has largely coloured the Bengali myths and folk-tales. Bengali anthropomorphism has its parallel in Tripuri ahitnropamorp nism and in Greek anthropomorphism. The archaic word Motif is originally a French term. S 260.1 Human sacrifice The custom of human sacrifice, commonly known as Nara-bali, was once a fact, and not a fiction. It is neither a myth nor a legend; it is history. It is part of the history of medieval Tripura. So it deserves an explanation. Head-hunting was the archaic form of human sacrifice. Head-hunting has been found sporadically all over the globe. So far as the north-eastern part of Bharat is concerned, the ancient greater Assam was well-known for head-hunting. Most of the hill tribes, such as Garo, Khasia, Naga and Kuki, formerly were head-hunters. Head-hunting here was associated with marriage and |

with the victim’s obligation as a servant in the next world....The young girls were instigators of head-hunting and used to refuse to marry young boys who had not yet hunted human heads; (Ref. Encyclopaedia Britannica, Vol. 11, pp. 201-202). In ancient Tripura there was a cruel king named Tripur. His capital punishment at the hand of Siva was a relief to the people. The queen begged for a son. The posthumous prince Trilochan was a pious king. Trilochan was destined to introduce the worship of 14 gods. In Tripura, so far as the custom of human sacrifice is concerned, the kernel of the story is like this: fourteen deities, once having been in a precarious situation, and having misused and betrayed the dedicated service of Rani Hiravati, the queen of Raja Trilochan, and in return for her hospitable reception of them, blessed the queen. Out of this kernel, the Tripuri dynasty wisely developed a war cult. The peril of attacks and battles was thrust upon Tripura since 1240 A.D. The gods and kings, as if, went together to protect the land and the people from the cruel hands of the foreign invaders. The worship of 14 gods (= Chaudda Devata) was made Folk Tales of Tripura 485 institutionary; and a similar arrangement was made for Tripureswari Kali Mata. While all Tripura have been continuing for centuries to worship Chaudda Devata and references to Chaudda Devata are numerous as those of Tripureswari Kali Mata in the chronicles of Tripura, the most famous shrines of Chaudda Devata and Tripureswari Kali Mata in Tripura proper are in the Gomati Valley. It must be pointed out that following the damage of the temples of Udaypur in the Gomati Valley by the invaders,

the royal family in 1760 shifted the seat of Chaudda Devata northward to the Haora Valley at old Agartala. The names of the Chaudda Devata are: Hara, Uma, Hari, Ma, Bani, Kumar, Ganapa, Bidhi, Kha, Abdi, Ganga, Sikhi, Kama & Himadri. The temple of Chaudda Devata continues to enjoy the patronage of the royal dynasty of Tripura. The Chaudda Devata temple has an elaborate order of priests and attendants; the order is as follows: Chantal Chief Priest Khapang Toinai Vice Chief Naran Deputy to the Chief Priest Badifang Storekeeper and cashier Yakchu One who washes the animals to be sacrificed Galim One who decapitates the animals Binandia Watchman Purohit One who reads out the Chandi Talua One who prepares the naivedya Mali Sweeper Padrai Militaryman of the gods Oakma Builder of the temporary shed Katia One who prepares the meat Laichikak One who hoists the flag Sutradhar Throne cleaner Banik Image checker Acharya Image checker The worship of the deities in the temple is a daily affair. Being a Sakta temple, animal sacrifice is a part of Folk Tales of Tripura 486 worship. One male goat is sacrificed every day; meat and rice, etc. are offered to the deities at noon. The age-old practice of unrestricted sacrifice of he-goat, buffalo, sheep, tortoise, pigeon, swan, egg and even human being was limited for the first time by Maharaj Dhanya Manikya (c. 1490-1515 A.D.). There were secret agents and spies to find out spotless boys for the sacrifice. The agents were known as: Maichhili. The victim would be allowed to indulge in all kinds of amusements, food, games, dress. To avert the searching eyes of the spies, parents used to bore a hole in the ear lobes of their

boys. Maharaj Dhanya Manikya strictly prohibited the practice of sacrificing the innocent boys. With a strong disregard for local belief, the king made the proclamation; it aroused mixed emotion. Maharaj Govinda Manikya (1660-1661; 1667-1672) went a step further and restricted the number of sacrifice of animals also. The worship of the deities reaches its climax during the week- long festival held in the month of Ashdd (June-July). The annual festival is called Khadrchi Puja; thousands of pilgrims attend; hundreds of he-goats, and pigeons and eggs are offered. E.A.Gait comments that the Chutiyas used to offer human sacrifices to Kesai Khanti; Gait adds: Humans were also formerly offered by the Tipras, Kacharis, Koches, Jaintias and other Assam tribes. (A History of Assam; P. 42). A subtle process of assemblage of various cults and their gradual attenuation continued in Tripura for a long period of time. Several factors contributed to the attenuation of the practice of human sacrifice and animal sacrifice; these are: statesmanship of a few kings, acculturation, Bhakti movement, British administration’s reformative spirit. | At the end of this particular enquiry, .a brief remark may be added on a few analogous myths and rites occuring elsewhere. It has to be pointed out that this primary survey did not find any unique motif in the folk- Folk Tales of Tripura 487 lore of Tripura. Like the ancient elders of other countries, the ancient elders of Tripura spent a lot of ingenuity at the why of some peculiar features of some flora and fauna, and of some distinct natural phenomena. They spent their imagination in making a punishment fit for a crime, and in making a reward fit for a good deed.

In Greek mythology a monster named Eurynomos with grinning feeth had a liking to devour the flesh of the dead, leaving only their bones; (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.31). It is not surprising that an almost identical folk-tale occurs in Bengali myth also. In Tripuri mythology the name of a benevolent god (=Garia) occurs very prominently. Garia is highly respected as a divine culture-hero. He has prescribed a philosophy of life based on a synthesis of Jnan, Karma and Bhakti. In Greek mythology, Prometheus is equally honoured as a divine culture-hero. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.54). Both the gods are concerned in the welfare of the human beings. In Tripuri mythology, the name of a kindhearted goddess (=Larima) occurs in connection with the funeral rites. She cooks food in the distant hills and offers food to the deceased; her food makes the deceased people forget their former existence and family-life. It is believed that a big timber (= Bufang Kebeng) is set cross-wise to separate the world of the dead from the world of the living. In Greek mythology, a body of water separates the two world, and Lethe’s magical drink makes the dead forget his former existence. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, PP. 88-89). ~ |; VaUr In Tripuri mythology the benevolent goddess Khuluma is the patroness of cotton cultivation, ie | spinning and weaving. Similarly, in Greek mythology the goddess Athena is the patroness of spinning & weaving. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.112). In Tripuri mythology and in Bengali mythology some Folk Tales of Tripura 488 deities are believed to appear to a disciple in the form of an old man or an old woman; the deities appear either

in dream or in disguise. In Greek mythology also similar belief is to be found.(A Handbook of Greek Mythology, PL Pi; The Hindu mythology of Bharat describes at length the battle of the Devas and the Ashuras. The Greek mythology too contains a similar tale.(A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.117). In Bengali mythology the cowherds worship a god named Baghai to keep the dreaded tigers and wolves away from the cattle. In Greek mythology Apollo is a god worshipped by shepherds for the protection of sheep.(A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.136). In Hindu mythology of Bharat the name of Biswakarma occurs prominently as a divine architect & smith carpenter. In Greek mythology Hephaistos is worshipped as a divine smith.(A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.165-166). In Tripuri mythology the names of two malevolent deities (=Buracha and Haichukma) occur distinctly. Buracha is the husband; while Haichukma is the wife. They are hill-gods. They cause panic and disease, and conceal domestic animals & birds. In Greek mythology, the name of a similar type of god is Pan. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.P.167-168). Coming to Greek mythology, mention may be made of Nymphs; Nymph means ‘young marriageable brides’. They are spirits. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.P.172- 173). Similar belief is to be found among the Tripuris and the Bengalees. In Greek mythology, the gods are human in form and human in character. They do much as men do, live in houses in heaven, eat food, marry and give birth to children and on occasion quarrel and become jealous and punish.(A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.176).I n Tripuri mythology also the character of the gods is Folk Tales of Tripura 489 identical. In Bengali mythology also the character of

the gods has been depicted similarly. The jealousy of step-mother against the step- children is a common theme in Tripuri folk-lore, in Bengali folk-lore and in Greek folk-lore. In Greek mythology, the second wife of Athamas was named Ino; -Ino hated and plotted against her step-children. (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.196). In Bengali folk-lore there was a landlord who had received a similar gift of understanding the dialects of birds and beasts. In Greek mythology, one boxer named Euthymos, while roaming here & there, came to an affected village and drubbed the ghost effectively, (A Handbook of Greek Mythology, P.279). In the Mahabharat the legend of Bhim punishing the demon Bak-Rakshash is well-known; Bhim offered to save the affected villagers, but set no condition; the Pandavas took no advantage out of the situation. A reference to Sir James George Frazer’s (1854- 1941) famous book The Golden Bough may be an aid to focus on some significant practices of Tripura. In certain ancient and medieval kingdoms of Africa the socially approved cruel practice of regicide was prevalent among some warlike people. Infirmity or old age or an end of a fixed term of a king, or some public calamities like drought, famine, epidemic or defeat in battle provided the occasion of the custom of putting kings to death, (The Golden Bough, PP.264-283). In some kingdoms of south-east Asia a mild and humane version of the

practice of regicide has been noted by Frazer. In Cambodia the king annually abdicated for three days in Folk Tales of Tripura 490 PO the month of February. In Siam a temporary king is appointed for three days in the month of April, (The Golden | Bough, PP.283-285). In Tripura the famous festival of Kharchi Puja is celebrated during the rainy season in | Ashad (June-July). This festival is followed by a respite of 15 days. After the interval, another famous festival called Ker Puja is celebrated. The priests of the Chaudda Devata temple officiate here in the Ker Puja also. The Ker Puja provides a significant occasion to nominally punish the king for his acts of omission and commission. As a token of punishment the chief priest (= Chantat Maharaj imposes a fine of one rupee. The king instantly pays the fine. The king is not asked to abdicate the throne. This is a very mild and soft and humane form of taking the king into account for his negligence of duties. It may be added that in the hills of Tripura each Tripuri hamlet has a council of elders. The village headman is known as Kami-fang or Chaudhuri. There is no fixed tenure of office; but an assessment 1s usually made every year during the month of Chaitra (April-May). Here also drought, famine, epidemic, inter-village or intra-village quarrels, etc, provide occasion to ask the headman to step down gently. It is alleged that the benevolent god Garia is displeased with the inept handling of the affairs of the village. In The Golden Bough (PP. 180-188), Frazer graphically described the belief about the absence and recall of the soul. The soul of a sleeper is supposed to wander away

from his body and to visit the places, to see the persons and to perform the acts of which he dreams. If the soul is detained, distracted or destroyed, the concerning person must die. Such belief exists among the tribes of Africa, among the Red Indians, among the Karens of Burma and many other people of south-east Asia. Similarly, the Tripun communities also believe that a sleeper’s soul wanders away in the shape of a grasshopper; so they do not hurt a grasshopper, and they do not wake a sleeper. Folk Tales of Tnpura 491 In modern Greece, when the foundation of a new building is to be laid, it is the custom to kill a cock, or a ram or a lamb, and to let its blood flow on the foundation- stone; (The Golden Bough, P. 191). In Tripura similar practice was in vogue among the Tripuri people. When the foundation of a new bridge was being laid, the Bengali contrators used to sacrifice a he-goat. In Odisha there was a belief: ‘The sky was very near the earth’. One day an old woman, at the time of sweeping her court, hit the sky with her broom, and the sky went up; (Elwin: Tribal Myths of Orrisa, P. 29). Elwin recorded almost identical belief among some communities of the north-east frontier of India; (Elwin: Myths of the North- East Frontier of India, PP. 23-24). The same belief is to be found in Tripura, particularly among the Tripuri communities. An interesting feature

The Teton types of tales are also abundant in Tripura. J. Borooah’s book Folk-tales of Assam (PP. 20-26) contains an interesting story ‘The Jungle crow and the Wren’. It has its parallel among the Bengali people of Tripura. My mother Snehalata (1912-1992) narrated it to us. My cousin brother Hemanta’s (c.1929-2003) pleasant narration of Teton tales was a delightful occasion to us. These tales centre round a character called Tetna or Teton or Tenton. In the Bengali tales the triciksters possess no values, they are thugs, they are deceivers, but they are not debauchees. The Bengali tales and the Assam plains tales are almost identical so far as the character of tricksters is concerned. But the North American Indian tales depict a trickster in a different Folk Tales of Tripura 492 way; here the trickster is a creator & destroyer, giver & negator, a benefactor and a buffoon. (Elwin : Myths of the North-East Frontier of India, pp. 137-138). The Arunachal Pradesh tales correspond to the North-American type. It is significant to refer to the story of Bhombaldas. This ancient story, in its simplest outline, runs as follows: Two friends once in a journey found themselves deep in the woods. Night fell. They found a lonely house there. They could not guess that it was the residence of ghosts. The ghosts were then roaming outside at night. The two friends halted inside the house during the absence of the ghosts. Before dawn, the ghosts returned, but failed to go inside. The two friends frightened them away.

Now, in Grimm’s Fairy Tales there is a similar story : the weak & despised animals. frightened away the robbers and lived happily in the snug house in the woods. In south-east Asia and in Japan also there is a similar story : an egg, a scorpion, a needle, a piece of feces and a rice mortar entered the house of an old woman during her absence, and on returning, the old woman met a series of pre-planned accidents and died there. Among the Riang community of Tripura, there is a similar story : The hen and the wild cat. Among the Indians of the northwest coast of North America the story of Raven’s war on the South wind is of the same type. Now, according to A. Arne such stories stand in interdependent relationship in their origins, and their origins may be traced to Bharat. (Hoebel : Man in the Primitive World; pp. 474-475). 2. A note on the quality of life : Folk-lore serves different purposes to different groups of people: enjoyment to the children, romance to the young people, moral lesson to the elders, and reflection on the quality of life to the students of social anthropology. A student of social anthropology should subordinate the narration to the reflection on the character and quality Folk Tales of Tripura 493 of life. From the survivals in myths, folk-tales, proverbs, games, popular cults, beliefs, and also from legend and history we can form an idea about the quality of life- patterns which form the hinterland to the folk-lore. In other words, folk-lore may be analysed in terms of the conditions of the ancient & medieval time. Analysis may _be carried forward beyond the boundary of written words.

During the medieval period a major part of Bharat was under the despotic rules of several groups of hordes from the Middle East. The basic components of civilised life such as rule of law, constitution, independent judiciary, legislature, public hospitals and secular academy were absent. The foreign hordes, having destroyed the ancient Indian academies, introduced their own religious academies. The local Brahmans sporadically & precariously maintained the traditional system of education through the Tol & Chatuspati . The two systems of education lived in separate worlds. Between the alien autocrats and the local natives there was an invisible wall. There was no economic dynamism, no social mobility, no political democracy, no stabilising force. The local human energies remained suppressed. There was not an iota of moderation and reasonableness in public administration. The maniacal despots would not take effective steps in case of natural calamities; but many of them would let loose the forces of men- made calamities. There was no secular programme of national educational goals. A nation under such dangerous despots was an awful scene. Few dared think of complete independence from the grip of the despotic alien rule, though there were slow and mild undercurrents of nationalism. In view of the engulfing reign of terror, exploitation & enslavement, the weariness of the local natives to maintain their own religion preoccupied the minds of most of them. The natives underwent the harrowing experience for several centuries. There was chaos & confusion, disorder & Folk Tales of Tripura 494 destruction all around in the life of the natives. The natives plunged into ill-health, illiteracy, poverty, superstition and timidity. It utterly depraved them. The quality of life was naive, poor, primitive, shoddy, short

and tradition-bound. The intellectual life was paralysed. Political tryanny, economic exploitation, social enslavement & religious persecution racked Bharat & afflicted the natives. Such a sordid life forced their minds towards imaginative conceptualisation for innovating the worship of new gods. The alien hordes and their leaders and their lords lived in a splendour that many natives could not even imagine. By force & fraud, they moved from rags to riches. They squeezed the sugarcane & left the dry rind. The foreign hordes kept on rushing even the native kingdoms of the north-eastern corner of Bharat. Tripura felt the onslaught for centuries. The armies of Tripura poured out their blood like water in the battle-fields at the Meghna Valley. The evil influence of the medieval alien rule radiated all over Hindusthan and over greater Bharat. So, one sided idealization of medieval life simply because it has passed away, is unhistorical. For redress, the natives used to appeal to gods, and resorted to rites & rituals and invented many imaginary ritual-tales. Under such contrasting situation, the qualitative difference between the Tripuri folk-tales and the Bengali folk-tales has to be understood. The Tripuri folk-tales are animated by a spirit of royal majesty, knightly chivalry, pageantry of the medieval battles and vigorousness of independent peasant life of the hills. Some of the Tripuri tales have dramatic cadence. The formula type of folk-tales afford a fairly interesting insight into the action of the hills people with regard to the punishment of some crimes. These tales represent a chain of actions, as well as a chain of crimes. In these tales, when the ultimate offender had been brought to justice, the chief was obliged to make an inquiry into

Folk Tales of Tripura 495 the cause & effect, and to examine several offenders one after another, and to punish the original criminal only. That certainty of punishment did a lot in the maintenance of law and order there. In future, any alteration in criminal administration in the direction of making punishment of the original criminal uncertain and political, may result in an increase in crime rate and in degeneracy of social life. By contrast, the Bengali folk-tales are undermined by a sense of feebleness, helplessness, spinelessness & fatalism. To read the Bengali folk-tales is to apprehend to what a distressful generation the Bengalees belonged during the medieval period. The rational faculty of the common people sunk very low. So, they depended on the plausible stimulus of supernatural blessings. For about a century the distress bitterly rasped their nerves. A relief, a renaissance, a self-confidence started coming to them with the Victorian reformative spirit of the British administration in India and with migration to independent India after 1947. Now a belief in the efficacy of modern science, education and healthcare is reducing their dependence on folk-deities, and loosening the grip of some old rites & rituals. The Vedic sages invoked : Let noble thoughts come to us from all sides. But unfortunately, many ignoble thoughts have forced their entry here. Those ignoble thoughts have affected the minds of millions of natives. It has manifested itself in a deeply twisted logic devoid of rationality. A misleading, tremendous impact on the native minds remains manipulative. Millions of natives do not even care to know how far and how deep their society has sunk. Even at a sane attempt at arousing conscientious perception towards national problems,

many natives get annoyed & displeased. The rottenness is deep-rooted. Rebarbarisation plot also is afoot. If it does not arouse their consciousness, the natives deserve the fate. Millions of natives, when left to themselves, Folk Tales of Tnpura 496 neither know nor care to know, who massacred whom. And several pseudo-secularists have cunningly distorted the history to whitewash the crimes of the hordes. Many natives purposely & criminally supress conscience. 3. A note on ethnography of Tripura As a branch of anthropology, ethnology makes a comparative study of races distributed over a wide range of area. As a branch of anthropology, ethnography makes an intensive study of a particular race or a particular group of people. What follows is an ethnographic study of the Tripuri people, and that too about their administrative aspect only. Socio-economic and political organisation comes into being whenever communities are segmented on some basis. The socio-economic and political organisation may be outlined here, using a few general societal types, such as family, band, lineage, clan, tribe, chiefdom and kingdom. Family is the cradle of civilization : affection, cooperation, procurement of food, shelter and clothing are its primary duties. The next stage is band : in band level all the members are related; kinship is a basic institution; family ties remain in tact. Next group is lineage : a lineage is a group of families descended from a common ancestor about six or seven generations earlier. Next group is clan : a clan is a larger group of families in which the common ancestor dates back more than seven generations; clan members are not permitted to intermarry. A clan is usually served by a headman. He is the focal point of a clan because of his personality,

moderation & knowledge. Next group is tribe : a tribe consists of some clans; tribe members are not premitted to marry outside the tribe. A tribe may have part-time priests, messengers, executives. The village council is fully developed at this stage. Next group is chiefdom : in chiefdom some families are more wealthy, prestigious and powerful than others. This society is not egalitarian. A chiefdom possesses part-time executives, priests, Folk Tales of Tripura 497 Se a er er ee ee messengers, and other council- members. The chief mediates between the conflicting parties, and organises rites & rituals and ceremonies. Next stage is kingdom : kingdom possesses a central government and many full-time employees & servants: consolidation of some chiefdoms into a large unit of political organisation produces a kingdom. Kingdom monopolises the right to use force and inflict capital punishment and to levy taxes. Obviously, this society is not egalitarian. Kingship is usually hereditary. Heterogeneity may be another feature of kingdom; it may include families, bands, lineages, clans, tribes & chiefdoms. This basic anthropological perspective of archaic cultural complexity in general may provide a framework of reference to indicate the level of cultural complexity attained by some of the Tripuri communities. Most of the Tripuri communities consist of certain common levels of cutural complexity such as family, band, lineage, clan & tribe; difference arises beyond these primary levels. The Dev Barman community (5,43,848 in 200 1) represent a very mature and sophisticated level of cultural complexity. They attained the high level of kingdom. Beginning in the distant past as a small band without any stratification, the Tripuri community expanded its support-base, developed kingship, built a kingdom, consolidated military system, worked out a few

levels of internal differentiation, reached a point of visible strata during the medieval period and recently (= after 1947) entered a modern situation where the rigidity of the traditional strata is getting relaxed. The Riang community (1,65,103 in 2001) represent a mature level of cultural complexity. They attained the level of chiefdom. Almost every Riang village had a council, consisting of Kach-kdo (= Chaudhuri), Yakcu (=Minister), Akcdi (=Priest), Khandal (=Peon) and Kangreng (Messenger). The Riang community had an administrative Folk Tales of Tripura 498 body at the top level. The following is the list of the names of the officials: 1. Kami Kachkao Chief 2. Chapia Khan Chief Minister 3. Chapia Minister 4. Huklai Chaudhurn Zonal chief 5. Chheng Krak Chief of army 6. Akcai Priest 7. Vaidya Physician 8. Yak Sunga Swordsman 9. Dalai Executor of corporal punishment 10. Dar-Kalim Assistant Priest 11. Bhandan Store-keeper 12. Khang Kalem Collector of contributions 13. Hazari Secretary to the Minister 14. De-Hazan Secretary to the Minister 15. Karma Assistant Swordsman 16. Dharia Helper to the Chief Priest 17. Daoa Messenger 18. Khandal Bodyguard to the Chief 19. Duguria Drum beater 20. Muria Flute Player 21. Su-nat Flute Player 22. Musa-nai Dance Master 23. Rica-nat Musician 24. Bau-nai Organiser of feasts 25. Som-nat Cook The Riang people were once a powerful people. They fought many battles on behalf of the kings of Tripura. The Jamatia community (74,949 in 2001) represent a mature level of cultural complexity. They attained the level of chiefdom. Almost every Jamatia village had a village council. The Jamatia people were once a powerful people; they fought many battles on behalf of the kings of Tripura; they provided the standing army to the kings

of Tripura. The highest authority among the Jamatia Folk Tales of Tripura 499 community was called Hada Akrd. The post was not hereditary. The qualities of head & heart were the primary considerations. The instrument of his administration was a council. The Chakma community (64, 293 in 2001) represent a mature level of cultural complexity. They attained the level of chiefdom. Almost every Chakma village had a village council. The Chakma people were once a powerful people; their main concentration was in Rangamati of the Hill Tract of Chittagong. The highest authority among the Chakma community was called Raja. The instrument of his administration was a council, consisting of such officials as Dewan (= Minister), Talukdadr (= District Administrator), Khisa (Administrator of a Mouza), Karbari (= village chief), etc. The devastating affect of partition has shattered their chiefdom. The Magh community (30,385 in 2001) represent a mature level of cultural complexity. They attained the level of chiefdom. The Magh people were once a powerful people in the Hill Tract of Chittagong and in Arakan of lower Burma. In 1662 AD. the Magh Raja offered hospitality to the fugitive king Govinda Manikya of Tripura. The instrument of the Magh Raja’s administration was a council of elders. The foreign attacks and invasions devastated their chiefdom in the CHT. To sum up this note, rural Tripura was largely looked after for centuries by village councils; each council was headed by a Chaudhuri. They had no salary, no legal training; no office; but they had intelligence, intimate knowledge, integrity & solvency. They execised administrative, economic, socio-religious & local judicial functions efficiently & economically. Almost similarly in rural England, the British king Edward I (1272-1307) selected several local gentlemen,

designated them Conservator of Peace, & entrusted on them the honorary duty of maintaining peace in the countryside. Edward III (1327-1377) changed the Folk Tales of Tripura 500 designation to Justice of Peace. For an analogy, we may refer to the social strata of three communities of South America : the Olmec, the Maya & the Aztec; they attained a high level of cultural complexity. 4. A note on folk-tale From time immemorial people have been telling myths, legends, folk-tales, allegories, riddles, proverbs, jokes & folk:songs to one another. These are oral literature. To the childish importunity for telling a story many elders have been submitting spontaneously. The habit of telling stories and of listening to those stories is a sort of craze, eternal and universal. Some of the ancient folk-tales were recorded long ago. Ancient Indian examples of recorded folk-tales are the Pancha-tantra, the Hitopodesa, the Vetal Pancha-vimsati, the Katha sarit sagar, and the Jataka. Ancient Greek example of recorded folk-tales is the Aesop’s Fables. Ancient European example of recorded folk-tales is the Beowulf. Ancient Arabian example of recorded folk-tales is the Thousand and one nights. In Germany the two brothers, Jacob Ludwig Karl Grimm (1785-1863) and Wilhelm Grimm (1786-1859) seriously & systematically studied folk-lore. In 1839 Dr. James Cowles Prichard’s (1786-1848) cogent paper on The extinction of Native Races effectively stimulated the imagination of the British Association at Birmingham and led to the preparation of a famous questionnaire in 1843, and the foundation of The Ethnological Society in 1843. In Britain in 1846 W. J. Thoms introduced the word ‘folk-lore’ in English usage. Then again in Britain a group of folklorists formally founded a folk-lore society in 1878 in London.

The word ‘folk-lore’ is a broad, generic term; it includes myths, legends, folk-tales, allegories, proverbs, riddles, jokes, ballads,folk-songs, etc. ; Myths: Myths are cosmological, supernatural, etiological, & archaic in nature. Traditional explanations regarding Folk Tales of Tripura 501 the origin of earth, earthquake, heaven, planets, animals, flora & fauna fall within the category of myth. Legends: Legends are semi-historical in nature. Traditional account about king, queen, prince, princess, hero, war-lord fall within the category of legends. Any fragment of real history preserved for a long time in legends may be called saga. Folk-tales: Folk-tales are problematic in nature. Traditional narrations about crisis, calamity, jealousy, horror of incest, unusual marriage, battles, crimes come within folk-tale. Allegories: Allegories are symbolic in nature. Stories, poems and pictures with a hidden meaning and an indirect suggestion are called allegories. A description of one thing under the image of another is the technique in allegory. Proverbs: Proverbs are pedantic in nature. Proverbs express maximum thoughts with minimum words. Proverbs cover a wide range of subjects which appeal to the imagination of mature age. Riddles: Riddles are psychic in nature. Puzzling & deceptive questions may be called riddles. Riddles stimulate thoughts. Jokes: Jokes are humorous in nature. Humour, jest, sportive remarks are known as jokes. Ballads: Ballads are poematic in nature. Simple, short, romantic and sentimental poems are usually known as ballads. Folk-songs: Folk-songs are musical in nature. Traditional, rural, unsophisticated, simple songs of unknown authorship belong to the category of folk-song. The characteristic features of folk-tales are: Timeless setting: Folk-tales are works of art, not chronicles of facts. Folk-tales generally begin with such expressions as ‘long ago’, ‘once upon a time’, ‘in old days’, ‘formerly’, etc. Folk-tales are, says R. H. Crapo, stories

Folk Tales of Tripura 502 placed in a timeless setting. Vague location: Folk-tales have no definite place of occurrence. The locus standi of folk-tales is uncertain. Folk-tales usually hegin with such expressions as ‘in a forest’, ‘in a village’, ‘in a hamlet’, ‘in a city’, etc. Folk- tales are, says R. H. Crapo, stories of vague location. Anonymous authorship: It is very difficult to ascertain the authorship of folk-tales. In some remote past and in some remote place, an intelligent person might have started a nucleus of a story; subsequently matters gathered around the central mass. Theme: Folk-tales quite naturally have a wide range of topics. Accordoing to George Wright (1954) aggression is an important theme of folk-tale. Clyde Kluckahn (1965) identified five major themes: catastrophe, castration, incest, monster-slaying & sibling rivalry. The list may not be complete. In any way, anxiety-related matters figure prominently in the themes of folk-tales. A popular theme is the rescue of a beautiful princess stolen away & stashed elsewhere. Another familiar theme is the Cinderela-type of tragic episode. Diffusion: Tales were widely disseminated from community to community, hamlet to hamlet. The wide diffusion of some fables & fairy tales may be attributed to migration & movement of people, common talk & hearsay, pilgrimage, trade & transport, war & expedition. Many European folk-tales may be traced to Indian sources. H. G. Rawlinson clearly explained this fact in his scholarly article: India in European literature & thought. Stage setting: Folk-tales are not murky, vague, disjointed, notional ideas. To make a story attractive & vivid, the stage is peopled with actor & actress; and some issues are set before them. Often in an allegory, flora or fauna are the main characters. Substitution of animals

and birds for human beings is immaterial. Size & Structure: Folk-tales widely vary in size & structure. The size varies from a few paragraphs to Folk Tales of Tripura 503 several pages. And the structure too varies from simple to complex types. Co-operative interconnections, says R. V. Cassill, is an important feature of a good fiction. Folk- tales too possess this quality. Purpose: The immediate purpose of the narration of folk- tales is entertainment. Folk-tales are told to entertain the children, to release a tension, to lighten the tediousness of a long journey or of a hard work & to impart a moral lesson. There is thus a clear point of view, a centre of interest. Animism: The latin word anima means life, soul; a belief that even air, cyclone, earth, great rivers & lakes, stone, hill, planets, rain, rainbow, flora & fauna, etc. have life & soul, is called animism. So all these natural objects & flora & fauna and human beings were supposed to be able to talk to each other. Animism is an essential part & motif of folk-lore. Animistic belief finds no difference in the kind of existence of a man, a dog, a tree or a stone. In an animistic belief, an animal can carry on business like human beings do; and a lion can preside over their chamber of commerce. Primitive philosophy: The archaic questions & answers regarding certain startling natural phenomena heralded the dawn of crude, primitive philosophy of a bewildering variety. Background: Folk-tales were not produced in a vaccum. Folk-tales were shaped & coloured by flora & fauna, topography & weather, administrative patterns & life- patterns of a people. Folk-tales embody the thoughts &

feelings, worries & anxieties of a people. The freshness and simplicity of the preliterate people are reflected in folk-tales. All primitive minds were not illogical, and all modern minds are not rational. Point of focus: The preliterate people held in high esteem the members of their royal family, and their village Folk Tales of Tripura 504 ———————— headmen, & landlords, their priests and the Brahmans. Their life-patterns were the common focus of interest to the villagers. This is why in many ancient Indian folk- tales the main actors were the Brahmans. Europe also had similar trend. The traditional country-tale, comments John Wain, often deals with high-born people, whose lives were a natural foucs of interest to the villagers. To conclude, the eloquence of a story-teller and the vividness of a story, verisimilitude of an episode are no criteria of scientific truth. Folk-tales are scientifically false, but psycho-socially true. Do the folk-tales remain archaic in their tone and intonation throughout the centuries? Do they reflect the . changing aptitude of the people? In point of time, certain explanatory tales regarding natural phenomena like thunder, lightning, rainbow, hailstorm, earthquake, eclipse, sunrise, sunset, moon, Stars, milkyways; origins of plants, animals, beasts, birds, human beings, etc., told by the ancient elders in response to the questions of the ancient children, seem to be the oldest of all tales. Modern social sciences call them myth and animism. In other words, a belief in the existence of any god or demon or any supernatural personality behind the natural phenomena is called animism. To substantiate, according to the ancient Indian mythology, Devraj Indra causes thunder, lightning, etc. Later came the allegorical tales, and the animistic tales. Here the heroes and the heroines are mostly

animals and birds. It is the indirect way of instruction or defamation. The Hitopodesa, and the Aesopic tales belong to the category of allegorical tales. Much later came the sophisticated stories and witty tales of modern manufacture. Leo Tolstoy (1828-1910), Guy de Maupassant (1850-1893), and Tagore (1861-1941) and many others contributed to this category of sophisticated tales. Cassill comments that co-operative interconnections of parts and logical sequence of events Folk Tales of Tripura 505 are the main features of the modern stories. Do the folk-tales serve any purpose? What do the myths and folktales stand for? This question has evoked a variety of answers. Interpretations have been offered from various points of yiew. These interpretations may be called theories of folk-lore. What follows is an attempt at a brief introduction of those theories : _ The allegorical theory : Tales are allegories to conceal some deep meaning, to hide some wisdom; to prevent truths or confidential knowledge passing into the hands of impious persons. Francis Bacon’s (1561- 1626), De Sapientia veterum was likey to be an attempt at indicating deep meanings underlying ancient myths. The symbolic theory: The ancient priests set forth certain truths, principles and formulas through symbols. It is difficult to decode the symbols. So, the symbols were misunderstood subsequently. The natural phenomenon theory : It is supposed that the gods control the forces of nature. The mechanism of sun and moon, earthquake and cyclone explains the formidable force of the natural phenomena. The theological theory : In the. Srimad Bhagavatam there are several didatic stories. The Jataka contains a number of tales about the previous life of the Buddha (563-483). The Bible is supposed by some people to be an

ancient source of myths. The hero theory: The hero worship is a common human tendency. The names of certain mythical figures or personalities were invented to add dignity to ancestry after attaining power; an ordinary person invents a long geneology claiming higher and better origin. The rationalistic theory: All myths are perversions of real history. Most of mythical stories are the result of delusion, hallucination and misunderstanding. The story of a monster half-horse and half-man is an example of perversion. In India the story of a prince riding on a Pakshiraj Ghora may be another example. Folk Tales of Tripura 506 The Philological theory : Mythology springs from imaginative treatment of physical forces. Primitive man was preliterate and imaginative. He expressed his awe through myths. In course of time, the original meaning of words was corrupted into something else. The anthropological theory : The origins of myths can be traced back among primitive men. The archaic primitive form was subsequently developed into literary form. 5. A note on rational interpretation of myth Myths may mesmerise the minds of millions of people. Myths and legends may be different in different countries and in different groups of people. Myths may not be taken as historical evidence. In myth an animal half-horse and half-bird may exist; a prince may come riding on that animal to rescue a princess. A woman may be turned into a stone. To remove a veil from a myth is the task of research. A few examples of this sort of mysterious myth may be briefly noted here. Myths disillusionise a researcher. 1. In ancient Bharat Rishi Gautam and his wife Ahalya were living in an asram in a sylvan environment. One

day Gautam went to a river to bathe. During his absence, Indra came and molested Ahalya. On returning home, Gautam cursed both; Ahalya was turned into a stone. After several centuries, during the Treta Yoga, Rama touched the stone by his foot, and immediately Ahalya stood up in all her beauty and youth. This mythical story is to be found in the Valmiki Ramayana and in the Katha-Sarit-Sagara. To this mythical legend, a rational interpretation can be added thus : During the absence of Gautam, a gang of local debauchees lasciviously raped Ahalya. The notorious libertines quickly decamped. Ahalya was left helpless. On reaching home, Gautam saw the utter helplessness of Ahalya; she became dejected, depressed, dispirited, heavyhearted & sad. Her life became forlorn and wretched. Rama treated her with compassion and Folk Tales of Tripura 507 understanding. Rama salvaged her to her dignity. Rama was the contemporary saviour. On the contrary, the mood of the hermitage of Rishi Atri & Anusuya at Chitrakut was quite cordial, hospitable, welcoming and sociable. 2. Another example : the myth of Unakoti Hills of Tripura Long, long ago a team of gods journeyed for several days; they halted at several asrams in the guise of pilgrims. At last they reached a pleasant hilly place in Tripura. The hungry gods halted there. They were to awake and leave the place before dawn. But the exhausted gods fell asleep. The sun rose in time. So the gods were turned into stones. This is another example of sheer incredible myth. One rational interpretation of this simple myth may be like this : The rising Tripuri dynasty had its capital in and around Kailasha-har at the foothills of the Unakoti Hills. The

Tripuri dynasty had a mission & vision for nation-building activities. For making a holy shrine, the Tripuri’ dynasty engaged some sculptors and provided all necessary support for the preparation of rock-cut images of Hindu gods. According to another scholar, it is a contribution of the local Saivites. According to Dr. S.R. Das (1916-1996), it is a work of 8th century A.D. 3. H.J Rose has furnished a similar myth from Greek mythology. Thessaly was, long ago, much plagued by herds of wild cattle. The king declared to give rewards for a remedy. A group of courageous archers, riding on horseback, rapidly shot down many of the beasts. The archers came from a very distant place and accomplished the job at night and retired without ado. From this episode arose a myth : the saviours were a mixture of man and horse; (Rose : A Handbook of Greek Mythology; pp. 4-5) 6.
